## Add and Manage Risk Categories
 Risk categories are broader categories of risk as opposed to a specific piece of critical data or a critical process. You can identify and include as part of your risk assessment the risk categories that are critical to your study outcome; for example, technology or complexity.
 Adding critical data to the risk assessment helps you focus and monitor the most important data to ensure:
- Protocol compliance, patient safety, data quality, and data integrity. 
- Product or treatment efficacy. 
 You can:
- Add risk categories to the risk assessment. 
- Add, view, edit, and delete questions associated with a risk category. 
- Score a risk category's level of risk to the study. 
- Assign a risk score weight to a risk category. 
- Add and manage the risks associated with risk categories. 
- View the total sum of all risk category risk scores to get a general sense of the study's level of risk. 
- View the risk categories included in the risk assessment. 
- View the risks associated with risk categories. 
- Delete risk categories. 
- View and export Categorization Audit Reports. 
## Add Risk Categories to the Risk Assessment
 Risk categories are broader categories of risk as opposed to a specific piece of critical data or a critical process. You can identify and include as part of your risk assessment the risk categories that are critical to your study outcome; for example, technology or complexity.
 You can add risk categories by: 
- Creating new risk categories at the study level. 
- Using a preexisting study-level critical data template. 
 Note:  Risk categories are permanently inherited from the parent critical data or critical processes. Updating the risk category on the parent critical data or critical processes does not update existing associated risks. To change the risk category for a critical data or critical process, create a new critical data or critical process with the updated risk category and link your risks accordingly. 
 When adding risk categories, you can add questions for the study team to consider when evaluating the risk category's risks.
 Adding critical data to the risk assessment helps you focus and monitor the most important data to ensure:
- Protocol compliance, patient safety, data quality, and data integrity.

## Score a Risk Category's Level of Risk to the Study
 You can score a risk category's level of risk to the study. RBQM calculates the risk score for each risk category based on the following risk factors: Impact, Detectability , Probability. To learn more, see Risk Scores . 
 RBQM tallies the collective sum of each risk category's risk score to determine the Total Risk Categorization Score. To learn more, see View the Total Risk Categorization Score . 
- Access RBQM , and then click Risk Assessment > Categorization  in the left-hand menu.
 The Categorization page appears. 
- Optional . To filter the Categorization table to show only risk categories assigned to a specific category, click the View by menu, and then select a category. 
- In the row of the risk category you want to update, click a number in one or more of the following columns:
- Probability – Select a value on a 3-point risk score scale: 
- On a 3-point risk score scale:  High probability = 3, Medium probability = 2, Low probability = 1. 
- On a 5-point risk score scale:  High probability = 5, Medium probability = 3, Low probability = 1. 
- Impact – Select a value on a 3-point risk score scale:  
- On a 3-point risk score scale:  High impact = 3, Medium impact = 2, Low impact = 1. 
- On a 5-point risk score scale:  High impact = 5, Medium impact = 3, Low impact = 1. 
- Detectability – Select a value on a 3-point risk score scale: 
- On a 3-point risk score scale:  Difficult to Detect = 3, Medium to Detect = 2, Easy to Detect = 1.
- On a 5-point risk score scale:  Difficult to Detect = 5, Medium to Detect = 3, Easy to Detect = 1.
- If necessary, assign a risk score weight to a risk category . 
 The Risk Category Score column updates to reflect the risk category's risk score. RBQM calculates the Risk Category Score by multiplying the Category Probability, Category Impact, Category Detectability, and Risk Category Weight. 
 Risk Category Score = (Probability x Impact x Detectability) x Risk Category Weight 
 The maximum risk category score is 27. Color coding indicates the severity of the risk where values 0.1-3.0 appear in green (minimal risk), 3.1-9.0 appear in yellow (moderate risk), and 9.1-27.0 appear in red (high risk). To learn more, see Risk Scores . 
## Assign a Risk Score Weight to a Risk Category
 You can assign a risk weight to risk categories to rank the importance of the risk category. 1.0 is the default weight. Values range from 0.1 (lowest) to 1.0 (highest). Do not enter 0. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Risk Assessment > Categorization  in the left-hand menu.
 The Categorization page appears. 
- Optional . To filter the Categorization table to show only risk categories assigned to a specific category, click the View by menu, and then select a category. 
- In the Risk Category Weight column, click the number in the row corresponding to the risk category you want to update. 
- Click the Up or Down arrow to adjust the risk category weight.
 Note : 1.0 is the default weight. Values range from 0.1 (lowest) to 1.0 (highest). Do not enter 0. 
- Click anywhere outside of the Risk Category Weight cell.
The risk category's Risk Category Weight value and Risk Category Score update.

## View the Total Risk Categorization Score
 The Total Risk Categorization Score shows at the top of the Risk Assessment > Risk Categorization page.  
 Total Risk Categorization Score = The combined total risk category score of all risk categories included in the Risk Assessment 
 For example: 
- 10 risk categories with the following risk category scores: 10 + 12 + 8 + 10 + 6 + 4 + 15 + 15 +10 + 10. 
- The sum of the risk scores for all categories equals 100. 
 The Total Risk Categorization Score uses a color-coded meter to indicate the study's level of risk based on the risk categories. Green indicates minimal risk; yellow indicates moderate risk; red indicates high risk. The color associated with the score is calculated by dividing the Total Risk Categorization Score by the number of risk categories x 27. RBQM then converts the result to a percentage. In the example above, the percentage that determines color calculates as 100/(10 x 27) = 0.37 or 37%.  
 RBQM shows the color of the Total Risk Categorization Score as Yellow based on the percentage: 
- 0-32% (Green)  
- 33%-66% (Yellow) 
- 67%-100% (Red) 
 For example: 
 The Total Risk Categorization Score can give you an overall sense of the study's level of risk. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Risk Assessment > Categorization  in the left-hand menu.
 The Categorization page appears. The Total Risk Categorization score shows at the top right-hand corner of the page.

 Column Descriptions

- Review Status – A color-coded pill icon shows the review status for each risk associated with the critical data:
- Red – Overdue. The Current Date > Target Review Date, indicating the Risk Review is overdue. 
- Yellow – Due Soon. The Current Date is between Last Review Date and Target Review Date, indicating the Risk Review is due soon.

The risk score is calculated by multiplying each risk factor's score together (Probability x Impact x Detectability). The maximum risk score is 27.

- A risk score of 4-9 appears with a yellow color-coded block and indicates. 
- A risk score of 10-27 appears with a red color-coded black and indicates a high risk. 
## View and Export Categorization Audit Reports
 Audit Reports allow you to  track actions made on the risk categorization of your study . This provides a single, traceable record of updates for audit readiness. For example, you can 
- Identify specific changes that were made (like adding risks to a risk category, deleting risk categories from the risk assessment). 
- Track the study personnel who made updates. 
- Identify when the updates were made. 
 Note :   You require permissions to view the audit trail. To learn more, see   RBQM Building Blocks and Permissions . 
- Access RBQM , and then click   Risk Assessment > Categorization   in the left-hand menu. The Categorization page shows. 
- Click the Clock     icon next to the page header. A new browser tab opens to the Audit Viewer > Categorization Audit Report page. 
- Optional: You can click Show Filters  above the upper-right corner of the table to filter the reports by  Start Date  and  End Date . 
 Tip :   In Audit Viewer, you can click   Export   and then  Excel ,   CSV , or   PDF   to download the report locally and view offline or sort data by column headings.   Report exports include the entire history, regardless of the filters applied in the Audit Viewer window. 
 Important:  Categorization Audit Report records actions made on the risk categorization of your study after 30-July-2026. Any actions  made on the risk categorization prior  to this date is excluded from the audit report.
 Note:   Any changes to risks on Categorization page will be recorded in Risk Inventory Audit Report. To learn more, see Generate Risk Inventory Audit Report .

===== PAGE: add_and_manage_risk_mitigations.html | Add and Manage Risk Mitigations =====
## Add and Manage Risk Mitigations
 As part of a study's risk assessment, study teams generally set a risk score threshold. For risks whose scores exceed the threshold, study teams can closely monitor and review, take action on, and create risk mitigation strategies to control, reduce, or eliminate the study risks. You can: 
- Add risk mitigations to risks in and specify the functional plan—such as a data review plan, safety monitoring plan—in which to document the mitigations. 
- View the risk mitigations associated with a risk. 
- Edit a risk's set of mitigations. 
- Delete mitigations. 
## Add Risk Mitigations
 You can add risk mitigations to risks in and specify the functional plan—such as a data review plan, safety monitoring plan—in which to document the mitigations. Risk mitigations help you control, reduce, and eliminate study risks. 
 You can access the risks to which you want to add risk mitigations in two ways:
- When viewing a holistic view of the risks in your study's risk inventory. 
- When viewing the risks associated with specific critical data, critical processes, or risk categories in the risk assessment. 
- If necessary, do either of the following:
 Access the Risk Inventory. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Risk Assessment > Risks in the left-hand menu. 
The Risk Inventory page appears. 
 Access the critical data, critical processes, or categorization in the Risk Assessment. 
- Access RBQM , and then in the RBQM left-hand menu , do any of the following: 
- To add risks to critical data, click the Critical Data tab.
 The Critical Data page appears. 
- To add risks to critical processes, click the Critical Processes tab.
The Critical Processes page appears.
- To add risks to risk categories, click the Categorization tab.
The Categorization page appears. 
- Do either of the following:
- If on the Risk Inventory page : In the Risks tab > Risks table > Risk ID column, click the Risk ID for the risk to which you want to add a risk mitigation. 
- If on the Critical Data page, Critical Processes page, or Categorization page, do one of the following :
- To add mitigations to a new risk : In the Add Risk column, click the blue Plus icon, , in the row of the corresponding critical data, critical process, or risk category to which you want to add a risk mitigation .
 Note : Before you can add a KRI to a new risk, you must first enter a Risk Name , Date Entered , and Review Frequency on the risk's Details tab. To learn more, see  Add Risks to the Risk Assessment .
- To add mitigations to an existing risk :  In the Name column, click the Down Arrow , , to the left of the critical data, critical process, or risk category whose risks you want to view, and then in the Risk ID column, click the risk ID to which you want to add a risk mitigation . 
- In the Risk Review or Add Risk subpage, click the  Details tab. 
- In the Mitigation and Actions section, click + Add Mitigation . If one or more mitigations already exist, click the black Plus icon, , next to Mitigation . 
- In the Mitigations and Plans panel, enter or select the following:
- Title –  Enter a title for the mitigation. 
- Description   – Optional . Enter up to 255 characters describing the mitigation mechanism to follow. For example, "The s ite must contact patients at least 48 hours before the site visit to remind them of the upcoming site visit and to follow up on pending Adverse Events (AEs)." 
- Functional Plans Affected – Select one or more from the list of functional plans.
 Note : If you build Plan Documents and add risk assessment tables as components to your plan, the risk assessment tables include the Functional Plan Affected column field for each mitigation added to risks. You can filter tables in plan documents to show only mitigations that apply to the plan. 
- Click Save . 
- Optional . Repeat steps 2-6 for each additional risk mitigation you want to add. 
- Click Save .

===== PAGE: add_and_manage_risks.html | Add and Manage Risks =====
## Add and Manage Risks
 You can identify and add to the risk assessment the study risks associated with critical data, critical processes, and risk categories. By adding risks to the risk assessment, you can track and monitor risks and, if necessary, take risk mitigating actions to eliminate risks or minimize the risks' impact on the study.
 In addition, you can:
- View and edit an individual risk's details. 
- Document risk review actions taken. 
- Mark risks as reviewed. 
- Close risks. 
- Delete risks. 
- Add and manage QTLs associated with risks. 
- Add and manage KRIs associated with risks. 
- Add and manage risk mitigations. 
## Add Risks to the Risk Assessment
 You can identify and add to the risk assessment the study risks associated with critical data, critical processes, and risk categories. When logging risks, you can:
- Identify high-level details about the risk such as rationale for tracking, current risk status, or recommended actions to address or manage the risk. 
- Set the frequency in which your team must review the risk. 
- Score each risk in your study by assessing the probability, impact, and detectability of the risk; also known as the risk score . 
 By adding risks to the risk assessment, you can track and monitor risks and, if necessary, take risk mitigating actions to eliminate risks or minimize the risks' impact on the study.
 Tip : After adding a risk, you can optionally a ssociate QTLs and KRIs to the risk or add risk mitigations . 
- Access RBQM , and then in the RBQM left-hand menu , do any of the following: 
- To add risks to critical data, click the Critical Data tab.
 The Critical Data page appears. 
- To add risks to critical processes, click the Critical Processes tab.
The Critical Processes page appears.
- To add risks to risk categories, click the Categorization tab.
The Categorization page appears.
- In the Add Risk column, click the blue Plus icon, , in the row of the corresponding critical data, critical process, or risk category to which you want to associate a new risk. 
- On the Add Risk subpage >  Details tab > Details section, select or enter the following:
 Field Descriptions 
- Label (Required) – Enter up to 255 characters for the name of the risk. 
- Status  – Select the risk status: 
- Closed – The risk is no longer tracked as part of your study's ongoing risk assessment. For example, the risk is irrelevant to the study to due to protocol changes or the risk is acceptable to your study. Risks marked as closed do not appear in the Risk Inventory and do not get tallied in the study's total risk score.  
- Open – The risk is currently included as part of your study's ongoing risk assessment. The risk shows in the Risk Inventory and gets tallied in the study's total risk score. 
- Transfer – The risk has been transferred to another party or organization to manage and is no longer a part of your risk assessment. The risk shows in the Risk Inventory, but does not get tallied toward the study's total risk score. 
- Watch – The risk is open, but considered a lower priority in your risk assessment and likely requiring a lower review frequency. The risk shows in the Risk Inventory and gets tallied in the study's total risk score. 
- Response  – Select the risk response: 
- Accept – The risk is below your study's risk threshold and considered an acceptable risk in your study. No action must be taken on the risk. The Risk Inventory does not track risks marked as accepted. In general, it is best practice to close risks that you accept. 
- Eliminate – The risk no longer requires inclusion in the study's risk assessment. You can close or delete the risk for your study. 
- Mitigate – The risk requires mitigating actions to lower the risk's severity. 
- Monitor – The risk requires monitoring and review but no mitigating actions. 
- Transfer – The risk should be transferred to another party or organization to manage and no longer be a part of your risk assessment. 
- Description – Enter up to 3000 characters to provide further details about this risk and rationale for documenting and tracking the risk. 
- Owner – Enter or select the name of the person responsible for tracking the risk.  
- Source – The source of the risk. For example, from the Case Report Form (CRF) or third-party source documents. 
- Include in Report – Select Yes to include the risk in the risk plan report. Otherwise, select No to exclude. For example, you can exclude company operational risks documented in the risk assessment that are not directly related to the actual study. 
- Category – The Category selection automatically takes on the same category as the parent critical data, critical process, or risk category that risk is associated with. If necessary, s elect a different category. In general, the Category selection should match that of the category selected for the risk's associated critical data, critical process, or risk category. 
- Date Entered (Required) – Enter the date the risk is entered into the risk record in DD/MMM/YYYY format. You can also use the date picker calendar to select the date. 
- Date Closed –   You cannot manually edit this field. Instead, the date is automatically set to the Current Date when the Risk Status value changes to Closed. The Closed Date appears on the Add Risk and Risk Review pages. When the Risk Status is Closed or Transferred, the Target Review Date is set to Not Applicable.
 Note : When a risk is closed or transferred, you can no longer edit fields on the Risk Review page except for Risk Status. If you reopen the risk by changing the Risk Status, you can edit the fields again.
- Optional . In the Score section, select the following risk factor scores to generate the risk's overall risk score :
- Probability – Select a value on a 3-point risk score scale:  High impact = 3, Medium impact = 2, Low impact = 1. On a 5-point risk score scale:  High probability = 5, Medium probability = 3, Low probability = 1. 
- Impact – Select a value on a 3-point risk score scale:  High impact = 3, Medium impact = 2, Low impact = 1. On a 5-point risk score scale:  High impact = 5, Medium impact = 3, Low impact = 1. 
- Detectability – Select a value on a 3-point risk score scale:  High impact = 3, Medium impact = 2, Low impact = 1. On a 5-point risk score scale:  Difficult to Detect = 5, Medium to Detect = 3, Easy to Detect = 1.
 Note : RBQM automatically multiplies the Probability, Impact, and Detectability risk factor scores to generate the risk score. On a 3-point risk score scale, the maximum risk score is 27. Color coding indicates the severity of risk where values 1-3 appear in green (minimal risk), 4-9 appear in yellow (moderate risk), and 10-27 appear in red (high risk). On a 5-point risk score scale, the maximum risk score is 125. Color coding indicates the severity of risk where values 1-5 appear in green (minimal risk), 6-25 appear in yellow (moderate risk), and 26-125 appear in red (high risk). To learn more, see Risk Scores . 
- In the Mitigations and Actions section, select or enter the following:
 Field Descriptions 
- Mitigation – Click the Add Mitigation button to add mitigations to the risk. To learn more, see  Add and Manage Risk Mitigations . 
- Action Required     – Selecting Yes indicates that there was an action taken on the risk as part of the latest risk review. Selecting No indicates no actions were taken in the latest review. 
- Review Frequency (Required) – Select Weekly , Every Other Week , Monthly , or Quarterly . RBQM uses the Review Frequency to calculate when the target review date is approaching.  
 Note : For new risks, the Review Frequency affects the Target Review Date as follows:
- Weekly – The Target Review Date is 7 days after the risk is entered. For example, if the risk is entered on February 1, then the Target Review Date is February 8. 
- Every Other Week – The Target Review Date is 14 days after the risk is entered. 
- Monthly – The Target Review Date is 30 days after the risk is entered. 
 Note : 30 days are added to the Entered date. For example, an Entered date of February 1 (in a nonleap year) shows a Target Review Date of March 2, that is, 30 days after the Entered date.
- Quarterly – The Target Review Date is 90 days after the risk is entered. 
 For existing risks, the Target Review Date is based on the Review Frequency and the Last Risk Review Date.
- Action Taken – Click the Add Action button to add and document one or more actions for reviewing the risk. For example, if you drafted a report, added a KRI to the risk, changed risk review milestone dates, or completed a risk review. When adding actions, select or enter the following:
- Action Taken Date (Required) – Enter the date of the first risk review action in DD/MMM/YYYY format. 
- Action Completed Date (Required) – Enter the date the risk review action is completed in DD/MMM/YYYY format. 
- Action Taken (Optional) – Enter up to 3000 characters documenting actions taken related to tracking the risk. 
 Tip : You must only select or enter a Label , Date Entered , and Review Frequency to save the risk.
- Click  Save .
You can now monitor and manage the risk from the Risk Inventory. 
 Note: If you save a risk with one or more expected fields empty, a notification message appears and the risk saves, but is marked as incomplete. In complete risks on the Risk Inventory page appear with a   , warning icon. If you hover your cursor over the icon, an   Incomplete   flag appears.

- Mitigation – Click the Add Mitigation button to add mitigations to the risk. To learn more, see  Add and Manage Risk Mitigations . 
- Action Required     – Selecting Yes indicates that there was an action taken on the risk as part of the latest risk review. Selecting No indicates no actions were taken in the latest review. 
- Review Frequency (Required) – Select Weekly , Every Other Week , Monthly , or Quarterly . RBQM uses the Review Frequency to calculate when the target review date is approaching.  
 Note : For new risks, the Review Frequency affects the Target Review Date as follows:
- Weekly – The Target Review Date is 7 days after the risk is entered. For example, if the risk is entered on February 1, then the Target Review Date is February 8. 
- Every Other Week – The Target Review Date is 14 days after the risk is entered. 
- Monthly – The Target Review Date is 30 days after the risk is entered. 
 Note : 30 days are added to the Entered date. For example, an Entered date of February 1 (in a nonleap year) shows a Target Review Date of March 2, that is, 30 days after the Entered date.
- Quarterly – The Target Review Date is 90 days after the risk is entered. 
 For existing risks, the Target Review Date is based on the Review Frequency and the Last Risk Review Date.
- Action Taken – Click the Add Action button to add and document one or more actions for reviewing the risk. For example, if you drafted a report, added a KRI to the risk, changed risk review milestone dates, or completed a risk review. When adding actions, select or enter the following:
- Action Taken Date (Required) – Enter the date of the first risk review action in DD/MMM/YYYY format. 
- Action Completed Date (Required) – Enter the date the risk review action is completed in DD/MMM/YYYY format. 
- Action Taken (Optional) – Enter up to 3000 characters documenting actions taken related to tracking the risk. 
 Tip : You must only select or enter a Label , Date Entered , and Review Frequency to save the risk.
- Click  Save .
 Note:  If you save a risk with one or more expected fields empty, a notification message appears and the risk saves, but is marked as incomplete. In complete risks on the Risk Inventory page appear with a   , warning icon. If you hover your cursor over the icon, an   Incomplete   flag appears. 
## Document Risk Review Actions Taken
 When reviewing risks, you can document one or more actions that you performed as part of your risk review. For example, if you drafted a report, added a KRI to the risk, changed risk review milestone dates, or completed a risk review. Documenting the risk review actions taken helps:
- Track the review actions you have performed on the risk throughout the study. 
- Communicate to team members risk review actions that you and others have performed. 
- Provides auditable traceability.

## Mark Risks as Reviewed
 As part of the risk monitoring plan, study teams typically agree on and establish a frequency for how often and consistently to review risk performance and update risk details as necessary. After reviewing a risk in RBQM, you can formally mark the risk as reviewed. Marking risks as reviewed updates the Risk Inventory and Risk Review window to:
- Set the risk's status to 'Reviewed'. 
- Post the timestamp of the risk's last review performed. 
- Post the name of the user who performed the last review of the risk. 
 Marking risks as reviewed helps communicate to you and others on your team which risk reviews are up to date and on time and which risks require review. This helps ensure that your team follows the established risk monitoring plan.
 You can access the risks you want to mark as reviewed in two ways:
- When viewing a holistic view of the risks in your study's risk inventory. 
- When viewing the risks associated with specific critical data, critical processes, or risk categories in the risk assessment.

## Add and Manage QTLs Associated to Risks
 QTLs are study-level metrics that indicate if a study parameter's reported data has breached a preidentified data quality  threshold or upper limit . You can: 
- Link QTLs to risks to evaluate and monitor whether the risk level is improving based on how you are managing or mitigating the risks. 
- View and edit the details of QTLs associated with risks 
- Unlink QTLs from risks. 
 To learn more, see  Add and Manage QTLs Associated with Risks . 
## Add and Manage KRIs Associated to Risks
 Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) are predefined study metrics that enable you for the duration of the study to systematically:  
- Identify and track known or anticipated risks to data quality. 
- Evaluate country and site performance in a study. 
- Ensure study conduct operates as planned. 
 You can:
- Link KRIs to risks to evaluate and monitor whether the risk level is improving based on how you are managing or mitigating the risks. 
- View and edit the details of KRIs associated with risks 
- Unlink KRIs from risks. 
 To learn more about KRIs, see  Add and Manage KRIs Associated with Risks .
## Add and Manage Risk Mitigations
 Risk mitigations  help control, reduce, or eliminate risks to the study outcome. You can: 
- Add risk mitigations to risks. 
- View the risk mitigations associated with a risk. 
- Edit a risk's set of mitigations. 
- Delete mitigations. 
 To learn more, see  Add and Manage Risk Mitigations .

## Add and Store Custom KRI Configurations as Reusable Templates
 You can add and store custom numeric KRI or custom percentage KRI  configurations as templates to study-level template groups. Adding and using specific custom KRIs as templates: 
- Enables you and your team to quickly and easily reapply common custom KRIs as needed across study configurations. 
- Promotes faster study start time. 
- Ensures consistency and accuracy in custom KRI details across studies. 
 To learn more about templates, see Data Surveillance Template Library .
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > KRIs in the left-hand menu.
- In the Configuration and Reporting card, click KRI Configuration . 
- On the KRI Risk Indicators page > KRI Configurations tab, click any custom numeric or percentage KRI in the Name column.
 Note : You can only export existing custom KRIs as a template. When creating custom KRIs, you must first save the KRI, and then open the KRI from the table on the KRI Risk Indicators page > KRI Configurations tab.
- At the bottom of the Custom Numeric KRI or Custom Percentage KRI window, click Export as Template . 
- Select the Template Group within your organization's global template library where you would like to store the custom KRI template.
 The list of template group names   shows in parentheses the client division name that the template group belongs to. 
 Tip : For more information about template groups, see  View, Add, and Manage Template Groups .
- Enter a Template Name . 
- Click Export .
A confirmation message appears at the top of the page. You can now find the custom KRI template in your organization's global template library stored in the selected template group. You can also now import and use the KRI configuration template when creating custom KRIs in other studies within the same  client division (CD) .

- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > KRIs in the left-hand menu.

The Add to SRI column now shows for that KRI, indicating that the KRI will not be included in RBQM's site risk calculation in upcoming data refreshes.
 Note : You cannot remove system KRIs from RBQM's site risk calculation.

===== PAGE: ai_data_reconciliation_knowledge_graph.html | AI Reconciliation Knowledge Graph =====
## AI Reconciliation Knowledge Graph
 The AI Reconciliation algorithm works on a proprietary knowledge graph. The knowledge graph contains information about conditions, treatments (medications and procedures), and the relationships between them. The condition-treatment relationships are built based on best-in-industry biomedical drug databases, for example,  ChEMBL , drug-indication database ,  and condition-treatment relationships specified by medical experts in clinical trial data. The algorithm identifies data discrepancy findings and calculates a confidence score that reflects the degree of certainty in the identified discrepancies. See image 1 for details on the algorithm, and image 2 for details on the confidence score calculation. 
 The Knowledge Graph uses the following coding dictionary versions to provide results: 
- MEDRA: 28.0-English 
- WHODrug: Global-B3-202503-English-Drugs  (March 2025), Global-B3-English-Atcs.

===== PAGE: ai_reconciliation.html | AI Reconciliation =====
## AI Reconciliation
 While conducting a study, study managers must ensure the accuracy of data that sites enter. Bad or missed data reconciliation could mean a delay in submission or even impact study approval. Manually reconciling data is: 
- Time-consuming and tedious due to manual data review. 
- Prone to errors as individuals without clinical experience usually do the reconciliation.   
 AI Reconciliation is a Data Surveillance capability that runs AI-based algorithms on study data to automatically reconcile data and report missing and duplicate information in place of manual data reconciliation. 
## What Is AI Reconciliation?
 AI Reconciliation is a Data Surveillance  capability that runs proprietary AI-based algorithms on study data to: 
- Identify patient records with anomalies, duplicate, or missing information. 
- Find relations between conditions, treatments, or ongoing medical history using medical databases. 
- Output the identified records in a readable and shareable report format. 
 AI Reconciliation lists the identified records in the following reports:
- Conditions Without Treatments 
- Worsening Conditions 
- Overlapping Conditions 
- Overlapping non-Worsening Conditions and Ongoing Medical History 
- Invalid CTCAE Grade 
- Missing Lab for CTCAE Grade 
- Overlapping Treatments 
- Treatments Without Conditions or Ongoing Medical History 
 AI Reconciliation Report Type 
 AI Reconciliation Report 
 Description 
 | Conditions 
 | Conditions without Treatments  
 | Shows a list of patients with adverse events (Conditions) that do not have any associated concomitant medications (Treatments) recorded on the day or after the condition started, and before the condition ended. 
 | Worsening Conditions 
 | Shows a list of patients with conditions that appear worsening, but 
- do not have any associated ongoing medical history (MH) or non-worsening related condition record.
OR 
- have a non-worsening related condition record report after the worsening condition start date 
 | Overlapping Conditions 
 | Shows a list of patients with two or more of the same conditions whose start and end data overlap. 
 | Overlapping non-worsening Conditions and ongoing MH 
 | Shows a list of patients with non-worsening conditions whose start and end date overlap with ongoing medical history (MH) start date. 
 | 
 | Invalid CTCAE Grade 
 | Shows a list of patients whose adverse events grades are not allowable as per CTCAE criteria v 5.0 , or have grades present, but not required, or with required grades not present. 
 | 
 | Missing Lab for CTCAE Grade 
 | Shows a list of patients whose adverse events (AE) grades depend on laboratory values, but with no appropriate laboratory date collected between the AE Start Date and AE End Date. 
 | Treatments 
 | Treatments without Conditions or ongoing MH 
 | Shows a list of patients with treatments (concomitant medications or concomitant procedures) that do not have any associated
- Conditions recorded that started before, or on the day the treatment started.
OR 
- Ongoing medical history (MH). 
 | Overlapping Treatments 
 | Shows a list of patients with two or more of the same treatments whose start and end data overlap.
## What Is the Purpose of AI Reconciliation?
 The purpose of AI Reconciliation is to apply AI-based algorithms to your study data to automatically reconcile data and report missing and duplicate information instead of manual reconciliation. 
## What are the Benefits of AI Reconciliation?
 AI Reconciliation:
- Ensures accurate data reconciliation. 
- Saves time compared to manual reconciliation. 
- Produces easily readable and shareable reports and report findings. 
- Helps study teams overcome resource deficiencies. 
## Who Uses AI Reconciliation?
 The most common AI Reconciliation users are:
- Data Managers 
- Clinical Operations users 
## How Does AI Reconciliation Work?
 AI Reconciliation aims to reconcile AEs, reactogenicity, concomitant medication, concomitant procedure, and medical history data coming from Medidata Rave. Once your study is in Data Surveillance, you can map the data sets and variables that Data Surveillance consumes for AI Reconciliation to run its analysis on to generate reports and identify discrepant data findings . 
 Then, AI Reconciliation runs its proprietary AI-based algorithms on the mapped study data and identifies and displays records that require reconciliation in the following reports: 
- Conditions Without Treatments 
- Worsening Conditions 
- Overlapping Conditions 
- Overlapping non-Worsening Conditions and Ongoing Medical History 
- Invalid CTCAE Grade 
- Missing Lab for CTCAE Grade 
- Overlapping Treatments 
- Treatments Without Conditions or Ongoing Medical History 
 To learn more, see  About AI Reconciliation Reports .
 In AI Reconciliation, you can:
- View the list of report findings and associated finding details. 
- Investigate the patient profile of the patient associated with the record. 
- View or link other treatments, conditions, or ongoing medical history as being related to a finding. 
 Note : You can link treatments, conditions, or ongoing medical history only for the following reports:
- Conditions without Treatments 
- Worsening Conditions 
- Treatments without Conditions or ongoing MH 
- View and submit Rave queries on report findings. 
- Manually agree or disagree with findings . 
- Manually mark findings as reviewed or unreviewed 
 Note : You can refresh data in AI Reconciliation up to two times a day based on Rave refresh schedules. For more information, see   Clinical Data Studio Data Pipeline .
## How Does AI Reconciliation's Algorithm Recognize Data That Requires Reconciliation?
The AI Reconciliation algorithm uses business rules to surface potential discrepancies in patient data. In the Conditions without Treatments and Treatments without Conditions reports, the algorithm leverages a Knowledge Graph (KG) that contains information such as condition- treatment relationships, which enables Data Managers and Clinical Operations users to identify and decide if data discrepancy exists in reconciled data. In the Knowledge Graph, relationships are built based on biomedical drug databases and enriched with WHODrug/MedDRA to enable integration with clinical data.
 Note : AI Reconciliation Reports rely on preferred terms to identify discrepancies. Preferred terms come from Medidata Coder which uses coding dictionaries to code verbatim terms, or an external coder which uses MEDRA or WHODrug data dictionaries. For more information on selecting study data source, see  Map Event Analysis Data . 
## How does the AI Reconciliation's Algorithm Assign Confidence Scores to Findings?
 Confidence refers to the AI Reconciliation algorithm calculated degree of certainty that a record is indeed a finding. In other words, that a data anomaly such as the absence of a necessary treatment for a given condition, exists in the listing. 
 For all listings, confidence level is based on predefined rules detailed in Review AI Reconciliation Reports Findings .

## AI Reconciliation FAQs
## What algorithms drive AI Reconciliation Reports?
 AI Reconciliation reports are driven by a set of algorithms that identify discrepancies by reconciling records within forms and across forms. For more information, see About AI Reconciliation Reports . 
## What data is used for AI Reconciliation Reports?
 AI Reconciliation reconciles data across Adverse Events, Medical History, Concomitant Treatment, Concomitant Procedure forms, and Labs. For more information, see  About AI Reconciliation Reports . 
## How and when does AI Reconciliation get updated based on cumulative and incremental user feedback?
 We continuously make efforts to improve the quality and output of AI Reconciliation algorithms. As the algorithms rely on multiple components for performance, we continue to improve the algorithms to deliver the most accurate results and enhance product functionality. To improve the accuracy of the Conditions without Treatment, Treatment without Conditions, and on-going Medical History reports,  we update the knowledge graphs to include additional treatments and conditions when the underlying biomedical databases get updated. These pre-scheduled updates are made annually. We also monitor the algorithm's performance and user feedback. In the unlikely scenario that the model performance deviates beyond a prespecified threshold, we can retrain the model with new labels.
 The AI Reconciliation algorithm updates in two ways: 
- Instant updates 
- Periodic updates 
 For more information, see  About AI Reconciliation Reports . 
## How accurate is the AI Reconciliation algorithm before study level fine tuning?
 The accuracy of the AI Reconciliation algorithm applied to a study, is measured in two ways. These metrics establish the performance of the algorithm and ensure the quality of findings.
- True Positive False Negative Percentage 
The AI Reconciliation algorithm has a true positive rate of identifying findings with 90% accuracy, and a false negative rate of 5% on test data. The true positive indicates the percentage of times the algorithm identifies a finding correctly. The false negative indicates the percentage of times the algorithm does not display a condition or treatment as being a finding. 
- Confidence Level 
The AI Reconciliation algorithm also assigns a confidence score that quantifies the certainty of a finding being an anomaly. This enables data managers to evaluate the reliability of findings, prioritize investigative efforts, and make informed decisions. A subject matter expert validates the the most prevalent, high confidence condition and treatment findings and non-findings, making up to 80% of total occurrences. These metrics establish the performance of our proprietary AI Reconciliation algorithm and ensure the quality of our findings.

===== PAGE: anomalous_data_detection_methodology.html | Anomalous Data Detection Methodology =====
## Anomalous Data Detection Methodology
## Clustering Variables
 The variables are clustered by computing the distance between each pair, based on an appropriate metric, and assigning variables to the same cluster when the distance between them is small. Different types of variables require different distance metrics. For example, you must define the distance between two numeric variables differently from the distance between two categorical variables for a general treatment of the clustering of variables.   
 The distances between pairs of variables are defined in matrix form. Hierarchical clustering is performed on the variable distance matrix to cluster the variables. The cluster tree is then cut at an appropriate height to define the variable groups (clusters). 
## Univariate Anomaly Detection
 Univariate Anomaly Detection identifies unusual (erroneous) values based on automated examination of each variable, including derived variables considered in on their own. It uses the distribution of values observed for a given variable. It identifies values that are very high or low (numeric variables), or rare (binary / categorical variables) in relation to other patients. Univariate Anomaly Detection is performed for each variable in the study. 
- For continuous numeric variables, a robust Box-Cox transformation is used, followed by robust estimation of the mean and standard deviation and scoring of values based on Z scores. 
- For categorical and binary variables, the empirical distribution is used and values are scored based on deviance residuals. 
- For discrete numeric variables, the best discrete distribution is identified, the parameters are robustly fitted, and the values are scored by a deviance-style residual. 
## Bivariate Anomaly Detection
 Bivariate Anomaly Detection identifies unusual (erroneous) values based on automated examination of pairs of variables, including derived variables. It uses the joint distribution of values observed for a given pair of variables. It identifies values for a variable that represent an unusual conditional on the observed value of the paired variable. This enables anomaly detection even when a data value is not unusual on its own. Bivariate Anomaly Detection proceeds by fitting a relationship between the pair of variables and then scoring deviations from that fitted relationship. 
## Flagging Unusual Values
 If a pair of data values for a single patient has a score greater than a specified value (the default value is 2.95), that pair is flagged. Each of the data values in the pair is flagged because either of the two values or their co-occurrence can be the source of the anomaly. 
 A data value can be flagged multiple times, if the variable appears in many rules. However, to avoid double counting of an anomalous value, a given data value is counted only once as being a flagged value, no matter how many times is flagged.

===== PAGE: at-risk_parameter_detection_methodology.html | At-risk Parameter Detection Methodology =====
## At-risk Parameter Detection Methodology
 At study startup, your project team should preidentify study-level parameters that are critical to quality and define the QTLs that you want to monitor for risk. Your team can then build the custom QTLs you want to track in your study in RBQM Configuration. When building custom QTLs, you define:
- Parameter  – The t itle for the study variable that you want to assess at the study level. 
- Definition  – Details that explain what the parameter is meant to monitor and how it is measured.
- Expectation % – The QTL's expected mean value as a percentage based on historical data.
 Note : Your project team should establish the QTL's expected value during the study startup and before data collection begins. This helps avoid potential bias influenced by preexisting knowledge and assumptions from historical data from previous studies, literature, and other avenues.
- Final Population (# of patients) – Total number of patients expected to enroll in the study.
- Trigger Point – The minimum required number of patients that meet the QTL's conditions for RBQM to analyze and output the QTL's results in the QTL Dashboard.
- Numerator Query – Configurable mathematical expressions using operators and conditions on study data-derived variables to define how RBQM calculates and analyzes the QTLs you want to track in your study. 
- Denominator Query – Configurable mathematical expressions using operators and conditions on specific data population subsets to define how RBQM calculates and analyzes the QTLs you want to track in your study. 
 You can then activate QTLs to trigger RBQM to calculate the QTL percentage values and analyze QTL performance.
 The logic expression used to build the numerator query and denominator query ultimately calculates the parameter's QTL percentage value by: 
- Threshold – Two standard deviations above the QTL's predefined, expected value. RBQM considers parameters whose QTL values exceed the threshold as at risk. This indicates potential underlying systemic issues, which may compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues. 
- Upper Limit – Three standard deviations above the QTL's predefined, expected value. RBQM considers parameters whose QTL values exceed the upper limit as high risk. This indicates potential underlying systemic issues, which may compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues. 
 Note: How RBQM Auto-calculates the Threshold and Upper Limit
 A common and effective method for computing the confidence interval (CI) of a given distribution is the approximation of the normal distribution from the Central Limit Theorem, given the sample size, n, is large enough (n>50). However, when n is small (n<50), using pure normal approximation in terms of computing CI can lead to noticeable approximation error. To better tackle this potential problem, the Wilson score interval method is used to compute the CI in the QTL algorithm. The Wilson method provides more accurate intervals, particularly for small sample sizes. As the sample size increases (n>100), the Wilson method’s approximation approaches that of the normal distribution, ensuring accurate CIs across varying sample sizes. 
 Furthermore, RBQM's statistical analysis also flags and identifies when a QTL is a: 
- QTL Excursion – A parameter's current observed QTL percentage value that:
- Exceeds the upper limit, and 
- Is impossible to move the QTL value back within a healthy range of the QTL's expected value no matter the actions taken by the project team. 
 QTL excursions indicate that the study quality is compromised to the point that the study may need to be shut down or restarted. 
 The QTL excursion prediction methodology uses the “best-case-scenario” method, which assumes that future observed QTL percentage values will be the “best case scenarios” for the study. For example, if an observed QTL percentage value at a given time point significantly exceeds three standard deviations above the expected value, then the “best-case-scenario” method:
- Computes the remaining number of patients still to enroll in the study (based on the final population provided in the QTL configuration), and 
- Determines that if no additional patients prematurely discontinue the study, then RBQM would still consider the parameter's QTL value as an excursion. 
 Lastly, for each activated QTL, the QTL Dashboard graphically renders:
- Each predefined study parameter's QTL percentage value. 
- RBQM's statistical analysis and approximation of the QTL threshold and upper limit. 
- RBQM's statistical analysis of whether the parameter's QTL value is within a healthy range of the expected QTL value or whether it exceeds the threshold value or upper limit value. 
 You can observe and track RBQM's analyses on the QTL Dashboard from three different perspectives:
- Live View – Meters that show each study parameter's currently observed QTL value and QTL performance based on RBQM's most recent study data analysis. The Live View depicts the QTL performance relative to the expectation, threshold, and upper limit.  
- Patients View – Funnel plots that show each study parameter's currently observed QTL performance relative to the expectation, threshold, and upper limit based on the number of patients enrolled in the study. However, in particular, the Patient View shows the QTL's projected threshold and upper limit values based number of enrolled patients using RBQM's statistical analysis. 
- Time View – Line graphs that show each study parameter's observed QTL value recorded over time on each date that RBQM performed a study data analysis. The Time View depicts the QTL's historical performance relative to the expectation, threshold, and upper limit.

===== PAGE: audit_trail_review.html | Audit Trail Review =====
## Audit Trail Review
 Audit trails are secure, computer-generated, time-stamped electronic records allowing for the reconstruction of the course of events relating to the creation, modification, or deletion of electronic GxP records. They capture the following: 
- Who   accessed or interacted with the data 
- What   action was performed such as addition, deletion, modification, or query 
- When   the change occurred 
- Why   the data was altered if available. 
 By analyzing audit trail data from clinical data, study teams may:
- Identify and monitor improper data capture changes, unusual data entry patterns. 
- Detect unauthorized access to data. 
- Assess risks with data integration and more. 
 In Clinical Data Studio, Audit Trail Review is a capability in RBQM that enables study teams to explore complex audit data sets using Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs). Data managers, central monitors, and other team members use audit trail as a data source, and Audit Trail Review (ATR) as another tool in their RBQM toolbox to identify signals of risk as recommended by industry  papers and ICHE6 (R3) guidelines.  
  For specific chat prompt use cases and examples, see Chat Prompt Use Cases .
## What Is Audit Trail Review?
 An audit trail review involves examining the history of transactions captured in an audit trail to ensure compliance with regulations, detect any discrepancies, and verify the integrity of data. Efficient audit trail review is essential in maintaining data security, ensuring accuracy in financial reporting, and supporting forensic investigations in cases of fraud or unauthorized access. 
 Audit Trail Review (ATR) allows efficient, self-service audit trail reviews. ATR leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to parse user questions related to study-specific audit trails. The system uses relevant study information passed through internal Medidata APIs to generate subsets of the audit trail for end users to analyze. The process follows privacy guidelines and validation standards to ensure there is no data leakage to any third-party system.   
 For more information, see Medidata's Audit Trail Review webinar . 
## What Is The Purpose of Clinical Data Studio's Audit Trail Review?
 Audit Trail Review (ATR) provides an intuitive interface that makes audit data exploration simple and accessible. Users can extract actionable insights from vast and complex Medidata Rave audit trail datasets using ATR., and make smarter study data decisions.  
 Audit Trail Review: 
- Seamlessly filters massive Rave data sets, where you can type a question into the interactive ChatGPT like  interface to iterface field to generate a manageable, meaningful data set from your audit trail data. 
- Enables you to save chats, export data or publish datasets for further use within Clinical Data Studio. 
- Enables you to configure published audit data sets, that can be used in KRIs and listings, and in the future self-serve visuals and anomaly detection. 
## Who Uses Audit Trail Review?
 Clinical study data managers and study team members use Audit Trail Review to ensure operational study data integrity.
## How Does Clinical Data Studio's ATR Work?
 Audit Trail Review (ATR) pulls in a subset of operational metadata from Rave to show edits, updates, and deletions made to data endpoints. ATR uses Large Language earning Models (LLMs) to explore complex study data and retrieves audit data sets that match queries you build in the form of questions. You type questions into a chat interface powered by Generative AI to formulate queries. The chat prompt reiterates the main point or the gist of your query. Once you confirm this, ATR executes the query against audit tables operational Rave data to generate meaningful audit data sets that facilitate data quality checks. You can further download or publish audit data sets for use in your study as part of listings or KRIs (Numeric or Percentage). 
 Important : In a study, a udit review activities must not be investigative on all data at all times. It must rather be driven by study risk where audit data can help monitoring for potential issues. Audit review must be intentional and targeted. 
## What Type of Data Can Audit Trail Review Retrieve?
 Using audit trail review, you can get information on audits at the datapoint level for the following audit subcategories: 
- Query data 
- Inactivated data 
- Created data 
- Modified data 
 In addition, you can also: 
- Filter audit data by patient, site, country, user, and audit time. 
- Get datapoints that were modified a large number of times. 
- Get datapoints modified with or without a query. 
 Important : Vague or ambiguous questions may lead to the chat interface providing variable responses. We recommend formulating questions as clearly as possible. For more information see Create Audit Trail Reviews .
## What Are the Benefits of Audit Trail Review?
 Audit Trail Review helps you to monitor and enhance your study risks to operational data integrity, ensuring:
- Protocol compliance, patient safety, data quality, and data integrity. 
- Product or treatment efficacy.

===== PAGE: audit_trail_review_ai_and_llm_model_working_methodology.html | Audit Trail Review AI and LLM Model Working Methodology =====
## Audit Trail Review AI and LLM Model Working Methodology
 Audit Trail Review (ATR) uses the  Claude LLM , pre-trained, fine-tuned internally to provide information relevant to study data. Medidata uses the following Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Large Learning Model (LLM) practices to ensure data quality and security.
## How We Ensure Periodic Tuning Of AI Models
 The ATR model adheres to Medidata's Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for Artificial Intelligence (AI). The SOP outlines practices for evaluation, iteration, and release. The process ensures continuous improvement and adaptation to evolving requirements. Key points we follow from the SOP include:
- Programmatic validation – Programmatically parse and validate the output of the language model to ensure it meets strict requirements, such as adherence to study metadata, and reduces LLM hallucination risks. 
- Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) – Use RAG to ensure that the model stays aligned with the evolving study metadata. 
- Few-shot prompting and in-context learning – Use the LLM's in-context learning capability using few-shot prompting, which serves as examples of the desired behavior. While this does not directly affect the model's tuning, it ensures generating accurate outputs across diverse user queries. 
- Feedback incorporation – Review feedback, including cases where the model's performance deviated from expectation. Use the feedback to guide updates along with stakeholder and client feedback. 
- Model versioning – Maintain the most up-to-date foundation model to ensure the AI system is pre-trained on the most recent data available. 
## Our Approach to the Explainability of AI-Generated Outcomes
 Medidata prioritizes the explainability of AI-generated outcomes through a combination of design principles and interactive features. These include: 
- Natural language explanations – Audit Trail Review (ATR) provides clear, easy-to-understand descriptions of outputs in natural language. These explanations are customized for non-technical audiences, and ensure transparency about how the AI model generates answers. 
- Mapping user input to metadata – The ATR model uses study-specific metadata to map information you provide to relevant operations within the model, and provides valid and study-specific results.  
- User confirmation workflow – ATR requires interactive user confirmation in natural language. This ensures alignment with the user’s intent. and makes the model’s reasoning transparent. 
## Our Approach to Machine Learning (ML) Operations 
 Medidata's approach to ML operations focuses on ensuring that the end-to-end machine learning lifecycle is reproducible, transparent, and efficient. Key elements include: 
- Version control – Maintain all components of the machine learning pipeline, including code, data sets, and models, in version control systems. Version control ensures traceability and the ability to track or roll back changes, as necessary, and reproduce results. 
- Benchmark data sets – Execute validation against a benchmark data set to ensure any changes to the ML model are measured against pre-established standards. 
- Automated pipeline execution – Automate the ML model pipeline to streamline the training, evaluation, and deployment process. Automation promotes efficiency, and limits the risk of human error. 
- Multidimensional validation process – The validation workflow incorporates a combination of automated and manual review that provides an additional layer of scrutiny and addresses complex edge cases.  
## Machine Learning (ML) Technique Used for Interactive User Feedback
 You can interact with the ATR model using a Yes or No feedback mechanism that confirms that the LLM and AI models interpret what users request.  A user's response establishes a decision point in the workflow that ensures the ML model proceeds with data processing only after explicit user approval. The feedback is not automatically used for model retraining in a formal supervised learning approach. However, it contributes to performance evaluations, and can be used to inform periodic manual updates to improve the ML model's performance over time. 
## ATR Study Level Data Flow
 The image shows how study data in Audit Trail Review flows into a M edidata-owned instance of Bedrock API that ensures no data leakage occurs to third-party applications. 
## How We Maintain Data Privacy
 Audit Trail Review (ATR) maintains data privacy programmatically and by design to ensure appropriate safeguards. The following components list the mechanisms used to ensure data privacy and protection. 
- The large language model (LLM) operates within a private, secure environment that is owned and managed by Medidata. This prevents exposure of proprietary data to third-party vendors. 
- The AI model does not have direct access to the audit trail database, with only validated SQL queries executed within ATR. Each query is automatically restricted by trial-specific parameters, ensuring that only data relevant to the selected trial can be securely accessed and returned. 
- The AI model is only exposed to study metadata (which includes information about forms, fields, sites, and countries) and the underlying audit trail database schema. By limiting exposure to the available data, the framework ensures that raw patient data is never exposed to the AI model, providing additional privacy protection. 
- User queries are processed in isolation and secured by user and trial-specific credentials ensuring that no additional data or metadata from one query influences the outcome of another. 
- The AI system message is tailored to prevent data leakage. The AI model generates output based solely on the user's input and with constraints to a specific trial. Red teaming validates the ability of the model to accurately identify and reject user queries that pose any risk of data leakage across users. 
- User-supplied parameters for SQL query generation are extracted and independently validated to ensure content compliance and safe execution.

## Clean Patient Tracker
 The Clean Patient Tracker is a summary dashboard that visualizes, lists, and prioritizes outstanding data cleaning tasks for enrolled patients across Data Surveillance. It streamlines the vetting and review process by highlighting exactly where action is needed. 
## What Is the Purpose of Clean Patient Tracker?
 Clean Patient Tracker allows you to track in one centralized location the progress of patient data cleaning and prioritize activities based on the outstanding tasks. 
## Who Uses Clean Patient Tracker?
 Study teams including data managers, project managers and clinical operations teams. 
## How Does Clean Patient Tracker Work?
 To use the tracker effectively, it is important to understand how Data Surveillance categorizes patient status based on outstanding work. 
## In Progress Patients 
 An In Progress patient is any patient whose data is associated with one or more outstanding data cleaning tasks. A patient remains in this status as long as any of the following require attention:
- Listing Reviews: Records that have been flagged but not yet vetted. 
- AI Reconciliation: Report records requiring manual review or confirmation. 
- Missing CRFs: Missing case report forms (missing pages) that require reconciliation within the study. 
- Vendor Queries: Pending or unaddressed vendor queries associated with the patient. 
- Open Queries: Any existing queries in the study awaiting a response. 
 Clean Patient Tracker automatically pulls in the following study data: 
- The number of open queries from Medidata Rave. 
- The number of open vendor queries. 
 You can also select to show the following: 
- The number of unreviewed approved listing records for up to 25 listings that you select to track in Listings 
- The number of unreviewed records in reports from AI Reconciliation. 
- The Rave form status you want to track. 
 Note : You must first configure the missing pages source, from statuses, and the AI Reconciliation reports you want to track. For more information, see  Clean Patient Tracker Configuration . 
 Tip : For the most up-to-date counts, first refresh individual listings on the Listings page and refresh the AI Reconciliation reports , and then recalculate   in Clean Patient Tracker . 
## Clean Patients 
 A clean patient is a patient whose data is not associated with any outstanding data cleaning tasks. 
## What Are the Benefits of Clean Patient Tracker?
 Clean Patient Tracker:
- Consolidates in one centralized location the metrics regarding outstanding data cleaning tasks  
- Increases study team-level coordination and prioritization of outstanding data cleaning tasks. 
- Promotes faster insights into data cleaning progress

===== PAGE: condition_without_treatments_algorithm_methodology.html | Condition Without Treatments Algorithm Methodology =====
## Condition Without Treatments Algorithm Methodology
 The AI Reconciliation algorithm for the Conditions Without Treatments report assumes that patients take a treatment in response to a condition, when the condition expects a treatment. The algorithm is trained to identify a condition expecting a treatment where no treatment exists. For example, for a headache (condition) the expected treatment can be an aspirin (medication). So if a listing shows a headache, and no aspirin is added as treatment on the AE form, the listing is marked as a finding. Further, the treatment for a condition must treat the condition, and the treatment start date must lie in the same time frame of the condition start and end dates.

===== PAGE: configure_ai_reconciliation_reports.html | Configure AI Reconciliation Reports =====
## Configure AI Reconciliation Reports
 Configuring Data Surveillance to auto-populate the essential AI Reconciliation reports in Clean Patient Tracker: 
- Enables your organization to incorporate AI Reconciliation reports data into Data Surveillance for tracking and analysis. 
- Ensures Clean Patient Tracker analyses the most recently available AI Reconciliation reports to produce the most accurate data analysis. 
- Ensures data analysis quality by reducing data entry error. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Configuration > Clean Patient Tracker in the left-hand menu.
 The Clean Patient Tracker Configuration page appears. 
- In the AI Reconciliation section, select from the following:
- To configure Conditions without Treatments: click Conditions without Treatments .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Conditions without Treatments column is set to obtain data from your data source.  
- To configure Invalid CTCAE Grade: click Invalid CTCAE Grade .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Invalid CTCAE Grade column is set to obtain data from your data source.   
- To configure Missing Lab for CTCAE Grade: click Missing Lab for CTCAE Grade .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Missing Lab for CTCAE Grade column is set to obtain data from your data source.  
- To configure Overlapping Conditions: click  Overlapping Conditions .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Overlapping Conditions column is set to obtain data from your data source.  
- To configure Overlapping non-worsening Conditions and ongoing MH: click Overlapping non-worsening Conditions and ongoing MH .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Overlapping non-worsening Conditions and ongoing MH column is set to obtain data from your data source. 
- To configure Overlapping Treatments: click Overlapping Treatments .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Overlapping Treatments column is set to be sourced from your data source.  
- To configure Treatments without Conditions or ongoing MH: click Treatments without Conditions or ongoing MH .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Treatments without Conditions or ongoing MH column is now set to obtain data from your data source.  
- To configure Worsening Conditions: click Worsening Conditions .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Worsening Conditions column is set to obtain data from your data source.  
- Click Apply. 
- Click  Save .
The selected columns appear in Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table.
 Tip : After mapping AI Reconciliation reports we recommend triggering Clean Patient Tracker to recount the number of outstanding patient data cleaning tasks to ensure Clean Patient Tracker reports the correct metrics.

===== PAGE: configure_kri_risk_category_weight_for_site_risk_calculation.html | Configure KRI Risk Category Weight for Site Risk Calculation =====
## Configure KRI Risk Category Weight for Site Risk Calculation
 The KRI Dashboard visually signifies sites that RBQM assesses as being medium or high risk to your study's performance. KRI Configuration enables you to configure t he weightage (low, medium, or high) that a particular KRI risk category carries when RBQM calculates a site's overall level of risk. C ustomizing the risk category  weight that RBQM applies when assessing site risk more precisely determines at-risk sites based on your study goals and protocol.   
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > KRIs in the left-hand menu.
- On the Key Risk Indicators page, click the Risk Category Weight tab. 
- For each risk category, select one of the following weights:
- Low – KRIs belonging to a risk category with low weightage have a reduced impact on RBQM's assessment of a site's performance risk level. Select Low for KRI risk categories that you feel should have less influence on determining a site's performance. 
- Medium – KRIs belonging to a risk category with medium weightage have a standard impact on RBQM's assessment of a site's performance risk level. Select Medium for KRI risk categories that you feel should have a moderate influence on determining a site's performance. 
- High – KRIs belonging to a risk category with high weightage have an increased impact on RBQM's assessment of a site's performance risk level. Select High for KRI risk categories that you feel should have a heavy influence on determining a site's performance.
 Note: You cannot enable Add for SRI for a KRI on the Key Risk Indicator page if the KRI's risk category has no assigned weight. 
- Click Save .

===== PAGE: configure_manual_or_automatic_missing_page_count_entry_from_external_datasets.html | Configure Manual or Automatic Missing Page Count Entry =====
## Configure Manual or Automatic Missing Page Count Entry
 Configuring Data Surveillance to autopopulate missing page counts in Clean Patient Tracker: 
- Enables your organization to seamlessly incorporate your missing page report data into Data Surveillance for tracking and analysis. 
- Ensures Clean Patient Tracker analyses the most recent available missing page counts to produce the most accurate data analysis. 
- Reduces the time and effort to track missing page counts. 
- Ensures data analysis quality by reducing data entry error.   
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Configuration > Clean Patient Tracker in the left-hand menu.
 The Clean Patient Tracker Configuration page appears. 
- In the Missing Pages Source section, do either of the following:
- To configure manual page count entry: click Manual , and then click Save .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Missing Pages column is now set for manual entry. There are no further required steps. 
- To autopopulate missing page counts directly from Medidata Rave, click Rave .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Missing Pages column is now set to be sourced from Rave. There are no further required steps.
 Notes:
- If you configure Data Surveillance to autopopulate missing page counts from Rave, then you cannot manually edit entries in the Missing Pages column. 
- Missing pages from Rave are based on missing pages expected to date, and excludes folders for future visits based on the window dates. That is, Missing Pages Count = Expected to Date - Touched. 
- Expected to Date is the count of all forms for the patient, and is based on the end window related to the instance date.
- If the end window is defined on a folder, and if the date is less than or equal to the current date and time, then it is counted. Otherwise, it is not counted.
- If the end window is yesterday's or today's date, the associated forms are counted. 
- If end window is tomorrow, the associated forms are not counted. 
- If no end window is defined, all forms are counted. 
- Touched (Entered) is the count of forms for the patient that have submitted data. 
- Calculation Rule: Missing pages from Rave are calculated based on the forms that exist for a patient. For example, if an edit check adds a form to a patient as a result of a value entered (male patient, hence no pregnancy form), that form is not included in future calculations of the missing pages count. So in this example, the count for missing pages for male patients does not include the form. For more information on Expected to Date and Entered, see Rave Page Status Report. 
- To autopopulate missing page counts from an externally ingested dataset: click External .
If you selected External, continue on to Step 3.
 Note : If you configure Data Surveillance to autopopulate missing page counts from an external dataset, then you cannot manually edit entries in the Missing Pages column. 
- In  Dataset , select the externally ingested dataset from which you want to derive and autopopulate missing page counts.
 Note : The dataset must be ingested using  Data Connect's Imports capability or Ingestor to be made available for use in Data Surveillance.
- Do either of the following:
- In Missing Page Count , select the specific column from the selected dataset from which you want to derive and autopopulate missing page counts. 
- In Expected Page Count and Entered Page Count , select the specific column from the selected dataset containing the expected page count and then the column containing the entered page count.
Data Surveillance calculates the difference between the expected and entered page count and autopopulates those numbers in Clean Patient Tracker. 
- Click Save.
 Tip : After mapping missing page count report datasets, we recommend triggering Clean Patient Tracker to recount the number of outstanding patient data cleaning tasks to ensure Clean Patient Tracker reports the correct metrics. 
 Important : If the missing pages mapping changes from manual to external, or external to manual, then the data in the Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Missing Pages column is overwritten to match the newly selected source. The missing page count in Clean Patient Tracker is extracted from the missing pages report available in Rave.

===== PAGE: configure_modules.html | Add, Edit, And Delete Signal Configurations =====
## Add, Edit, And Delete Signal Configurations
 For any study environment , you can define and add custom signal configurations for modules. These configurations target specific facets of your study data that you want to monitor for potential risk.
- A  signal is a potential issue identified through data analysis.
- An issue is a confirmed finding that is the result of a signal validated through monitor review, site discussion, or site visit.  
  The signals you configure based on a specific threshold, produce automated signal reports on each module you include. 
## View and Access Custom Signals Configurations 
 You can view existing configurations for each module. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals Configuration page appears. 
- Select any module from the left-hand Settings menu.
The corresponding configurations page appears to the right, listing all existing configurations for the module. 
## Enable or Disable Signal Configuration
 Data managers can monitor all or some of the following modules for potential risks. However you may not want to monitor all modules at a given time, for example, if the study has no requirements to monitor a specific type of data. You can enable or disable a module while configuring signals. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals Configuration page appears. 
- For each module in the left-hand Settings menu, toggle on or off the button.
Automated signals appear only if you enable a module (toggle on), and then add configuration details. 
 Note : if you toggle off a module with previously saved configurations, they remain saved. Signals from a deactivated module do not appear in the automated signals report when you refresh data. They appear once the module is enabled (toggled on).

===== PAGE: configure_rave_form_statuses.html | Configure Medidata Rave Form Statuses =====
## Configure Medidata Rave Form Statuses
 To track the Medidata Rave form statuses for each patient in the  Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table, you can also configure whether you want to show forms that are: 
- Incomplete, or 
A page is Incomplete if at least one visible field:
- Has no changes, or 
- Is a lab field is with a missing a required analyte range,  or is missing a required clinical significance, or has a clinical significance but is either out of the alert range, missing a clinical significance comment, or missing required lab units. 
- RequiresReview, or
 A page is in RequiresReview status if it has at least one visible field:
- and i s touched or has change count > 0 
- and   has at least one unreviewed review group 
- and i s active, or “Allow Review/Verify on Inactive Data” is enabled 
- RequiresFreeze, or
 A page is in RequiresFreeze status is active: 
- 
- And has at least one visible and active field 
- And the field is not frozen not entry locked. 
- RequiresLock, or
 A page is in RequiresLock status if  i t is active: 
- 
- And has at least one visible and active field 
- And the field is not data locked 
- RequiresSignature, or
 A page is in RequiresSignature status if it is active: 
- 
- Has at least one visible and active field 
- The page/form requires a signature 
- The signature is missing or outdated 
- No field on the page breaks the signature 
- NonConformant, or
 A page is NonConformant if: 
- 
- It is active 
- Has at least one visible and active field 
- The field has non-conformant data 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Configuration > Clean Patient Tracker in the left-hand menu.
 The Clean Patient Tracker Configuration page appears. 
- In the Form Status section, select from the following:
- To configure incomplete forms: click Incomplete .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Incomplete column is set to obtain data from Rave.  
- To configure incomplete forms: click Requires Review .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Requires Review column is set to obtain data from Rave.  
- To configure incomplete forms: click Requires Lock .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Requires Lock column is set to obtain data from Rave.  
- To configure incomplete forms: click  Requires Freeze .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Requires Freeze column is set to obtain data from Rave.  
- To configure incomplete forms: click Requires Signature .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Requires Signature column is set to obtain data from Rave. 
- To configure incomplete forms: click Non conformant .
The Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Non conformant column is now set to be sourced from Rave.  
- Click Apply. 
- Click  Save .
The selected columns appear in Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table.
 Tip : After mapping missing page count report datasets, we recommend triggering Clean Patient Tracker to recount the number of outstanding patient data cleaning tasks to ensure Clean Patient Tracker reports the correct metrics.  
 Important : If the missing pages mapping changes from manual to external, or external to manual, then the data in the Clean Patient Tracker > Patients table > Missing Pages column is overwritten to match the newly selected source. The missing page count in Clean Patient Tracker is extracted from the missing pages report available in Rave.
