===== PAGE: configure_the_expected_risk_review_fields.html | Configure the Expected Risk Review Fields =====
## Configure the Expected Risk Review Fields
 You can configure Risk Assessment and Risk Inventory to s ignify the specific risk details and risk actions that your study team is expected to enter and document when adding or updating risks in the risk assessment. Marking risk assessment fields as expected helps ensure your study team addresses and fulfills all risk documentation requirements as dictated by the protocol. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > Risks in the left-hand menu.
The Risk Assessment Configuration pages shows. 
- In the Risk Expected Fields > Risk Details section, select any of the following field names to signify as being fields that expect entries when adding or updating risks in the risk assessment :
- Score – When logging risks, you can s core each risk in your study by assessing and assigning on a 3- or 5-point scale the Probability, Impact, and Detectability of the risk; also known as the risk score . Risk Assessment automatically multiplies the Probability, Impact, and Detectability risk factor scores to generate the overall risk score.  
- Response – The risk response:
- Accept 
- Eliminate   
- Mitigate 
- Monitor 
- Transfer 
- Owner – T he role of the person responsible for tracking the risk. 
- Category 
- Status – The risk status:
- Closed 
- Open 
- Transfer 
- Watch 
- Description – Extra details about this risk and rationale for documenting and tracking the risk. 
- Source – The source of the risk. For example, from the Case Report Form (CRF) or third-party source documents. 
- Include in the risk plan report – Select Yes or No to include or exclude the risk in the risk plan report. For example, you can exclude company operational risks documented in the risk assessment that are not directly related to the actual study. 
- In the Risk Expected Fields > Risk Actions   section, select any of the following field names to signify as being fields that expect entries when adding or updating risks in the risk assessment :
- Action Required – Document one or more actions for reviewing the risk. For example, if you drafted a report, added a KRI to the risk, changed risk review milestone dates, or completed a risk review. 
- Action Taken – The date of the first risk review action. 
- Closed Date – The date the risk review action is completed. 
- Click Save Changes .

===== PAGE: copy_designs_to_different_studies.html | Copy Designs To Different Studies =====
## Copy Designs To Different Studies
 Studies within the same therapeutic area usually follow the same standards and are similar. Hence copying designs between studies allows data managers to build new master designs by copying existing designs between studies and removing or replacing missing data set variables. You can copy both published and draft designs. If you copy designs or elements between studies, the original study or element might have patient data that does not match exactly with the destination study. 
 Note : Design copies retain all derived variables and flags (percentage KRIs). You must delete the derived variables and flags from the new design destination, save the design, and then once again add the derived variables and flags to the new design. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Patient Profiles in the left-hand menu.
The Patient Profile Designs page shows. 
- Click the Published Designs tab or the Draft Designs tab, and then find the design you want to duplicate. 
- Click   within the row of corresponding design. 
- Click Copy to another Study . 
- In the Copy dialog, select the following:
- Client Division – Shows all client divisions that you have access to. Select the client division containing the target study you want to copy to. 
- Study Group – Shows all study groups you have access to within the selected client division. Select the study group containing the target study you want to copy to. 
- Study – Shows all studies you have access to within the selected study group. Select the study you want to copy to. 
- Study Environment – Shows all study environments you have access to within the select study. Select the study environment that you want to copy to. 
- Click  Copy .
 Note :  A copied design with missing variables shows a yellow warning banner at the top of the Designs page. Yellow markers also appear next to elements with missing data within the copied design.
You cannot copy or set a design with missing variables as a master for Detect.

- Client

===== PAGE: create__edit__and_delete_visualizations.html | Create, Edit, and Delete Custom Graphs =====
## Create, Edit, and Delete Custom Graphs
 You can create Custom Graphs to chart the relationship between any combination of datasets on a single visual using real-time study data on demand. 
 Custom Graphs enables you to flexibly plot any study data you want to visualize, catering to your specific needs or area of interest.  
 You can view the data in the optimal graphical rendering—whether in a bar graph, stacked bar graph, line graph, multiline graph, donut graph, or segmented donut graph. 
 You can also edit and delete Custom Graphs. In addition to standard data sets, you can also use queries and audit data sets to build Custom Graphs. 
## Create and Edit Custom Graphs
 You can create Custom Graphs to chart the relationship between any combination of datasets on a single visual using real-time study data on demand. 
 Custom Graphs enables you to flexibly plot any study data you want to visualize, catering to your specific needs or area of interest. For example: 
- Medical monitors can view the number of adverse events per site.
- Site monitors can track patient enrollment rate.   
- Data managers can view missed visits or data entry delays. 
- CRAs can view, track, and compare patients records for pulse against blood pressure.  
- Study managers can see the number of nonrandomized patients in the study or track the number of study dropouts per month. 
 You can also view the data in the optimal graphical rendering—whether in a bar graph, stacked bar graph, line graph, multiline graph, donut graph, or segmented donut graph. 
 Graphically visualizing study data relationships enables you to more effectively: 
- Gain a clearer understanding or perspective of the study data. 
- Identify study trends and patterns. 
- Track study performance. 
- Build and share reports or present on study data metrics using clear, visually appealing graphical renderings. 
 You can also edit Custom Graphs. For example, you can fix an error or a typo in the custom graph's configuration. Or you can quickly edit an existing visualization without fully create a new visualization to:
- Generate an alternative view of the study data. 
- Change the data you want to visualize. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Custom Graphs in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Custom Graphs page, do one of the following:
- To import a custom graph template, click Create Custom Graphs > I mport Template , then select a Template group and a template from the list. Then click Use Selected Template . 
- To create a custom graph, click Create Custom Graphs . 
- To edit a custom graph , click the  More icon in the corresponding row of the custom graph you want to edit, and then click Edit . 
- If you import a custom graph template, then you can edit fields in the Chart Configuration and Display Settings sections if needed. Then, go to step 12. 
- If you follow the steps to create or edit a custom graph, then in Chart Type , select one of the following chart types:
- – Bar chart. Bar charts typically visualize and compare variable data points based on value, count, or frequency.  For example, a bar chart might plot the number of adverse events recorded per site in a study.
 Tip : We recommend using bar charts to graph variables on the x-axis with more than five data points.
- – Line chart. Line charts typically visualize and track variable data point trends on a timeline or frequency. For example, a line chart might visualize the monthly percent or count of randomized patients recorded in the study over the course of two years. 
- – Donut chart. Donut charts visualize the total count of values within a single variable. For example, the count of patients in the study with hypertension. 
- – Scatter plot. Scatter plots display the relationship between two numeric, continuous dependent variables. For example, scatter plots show t he shift from baseline to post baseline using maximum or minimum values, and detect unexpected outcomes like identify high panic concentrations, or show discrepancies between actual and nominal time. 
- Click the Y-Axis menu, and select a data set and variable.
 Note : For scatter plots, you must select numeric variables on the y-axis; otherwise, the custom graph does not render. 
- Select a y-axis aggregation.
 Note : If you select the Count aggregation, the custom graph plots the total number of all individual log lines in the dataset, not the total number of unique records by record type.
 Note : For scatter plots, you must select numeric variables on the x-axis;  otherwise, the custom graph does not render. 
 Important : For line charts, you must select an aggregation for a   text variable on the y-axis;   otherwise, the custom graph does not render. 
 Tip : For donut charts, we recommend selecting the Percentage aggregation for optimal visualization and readability.
- Optional. Click Add Median line .
 Note : A median line appears across the custom graphs chart.
- Click the X-Axis menu and select a data set and variable.
 Note : You cannot configure an x-axis in donut charts.
 Note : For scatter plots, you must select numeric variables on the x-axis;  otherwise, the custom graph does not render. 
 Tip : For line graphs, we recommend that you use date variables on the x-axis to create a timeline or visualize trends.
- Optional. Select an x-axis aggregation.
 Tip : For line charts, we recommend not selecting an aggregation on the x-axis unless you are plotting date or time variables on the x-axis. If  you do not select an aggregation   for a date variable on the x-axis,   then the line chart plots the data for every single day in the database. 
 Important : If you add an aggregation to any nondate variables in the x-axis, then you must add a dataset and variable in the Color Series . Otherwise, the custom graph cannot render.
- Optional . To further breakdown the study data being visualized to show and compare segmented data subcategories for deeper insights and analysis: Click the Color Series menu, and select a data set and variable. Selecting a color series modifies the charts into the following chart types:
- Stacked Bar Chart – Segments the variable represented in each bar by subcategory and visualizes the variable's relative distribution of data by subcategory. For example, a stacked bar chart might show the total number of adverse events reported per site and further breakdown the adverse events by type and number of each specific adverse event reported.
 Note : If you plot a stacked bar chart with more than 50 data points, the chart fits to scale all bars in the page view, and you cannot distinguish the colored bar segments.
- Multiline Chart – Plots multiple lines on a single visual to simultaneously view and compare trends across multiple data subcategories. Each line represents a subcategory. For example, a line chart might show the weekly number of patients that get randomized in a study over the course of two years. But a multiline chart might further visualize the number of the weekly number of patients that get randomized in a study over the course of two years by race. In which case, the chart would show multiple lines representing each race recorded in the study data.
 Tip : We recommend limiting multiline charts to show a maximum of five lines to ensure optimal chart readability. Otherwise, we recommend plotting the data in a bar graph.
- Segmented Donut Chart – Segments the variable represented in the donut chart by subcategory and visualizes the variable's relative distribution of data by subcategory. You can aggregate segmented donut charts by count or percentage. For example, a segmented donut chart might show the percentage distribution of the patient population with hypertension by gender.
 Note : The color palette shows the default colors that the visualization uses to represent the subcategories in the charts. The color palette is read-only. 
- Optional . To chart a specific data subset from the y- and x-axis variable selections: Click the Chart Filters menu, do the following: 
- Enter or select a data set.

- Y-axis Title – Enter a short, concise title describing what the y-axis represents.

- Click Refresh Data to generate or regenerate the visualization.
The visualization appears in the Preview section.  Click a chart type below to learn how to interpret and interact with the chart. 
 Bar Chart 
- Bar charts typically visualize and compare variable data points based on value, count, or frequency. 
- Each bar represents a variable data point within a data set. 
- You can hover your cursor on any bar to view the data point's x- and y-axis value. 
 Stacked Bar Chart 
- Stacked bar charts segment the variable represented in each bar by subcategory and visualize the variable's relative distribution of data by subcategory. 
- Each bar represents a variable data point within a data set. 
- Each bar can be stacked—or segmented— to show one or more data categories within the variable data point. 
- You can hover your cursor on a bar segment to highlight that data category in all bars and to view the data category value, x-axis value, and y-axis value. 
- The legend shows all subcategories within the primary variable being visualized. 
- You can hover your cursor on a subcategory label in the legend to highlight all segments representing that subcategory. 
- You can click a subcategory label to remove all segments representing that subcategory from the chart. Reclick to view the subcategory's segments again. 
 Line Chart 
- Line charts typically visualize and track variable data point trends on a timeline or frequency. 
- You can hover your cursor on any data point in line charts to view the data point's x- and y-axis. 
 Multiline Chart 
- Multiline charts plot for multiple lines on a single visual to simultaneously view and compare trends across multiple data subcategories within a variable. 
- Each line represents a subcategory. 
- You can hover your cursor on a data point in specific line to view that value's x- and y-axis value. 
- The legend shows all subcategories within the primary variable being visualized. 
- You can hover on a subcategory label in the legend to highlight that subcategory's line in the chart. 
- You can click a subcategory label in the legend to remove that subcategory's line from the chart. Reclick to view the subcategory's line again. 
 Scatter plots 
- Scatter plot showing systolic and diastolic blood pressure, both numeric, continuous variables in a dataset. 
- You can hover your cursor on a data point in specific plot point to view that value's x- and y-axis value. 
- The legend on the x-axis shows the primary variable (male, female, uncharacterized). 
 Donut Chart 
- Donut charts visualize the total count of values within a single variable.   
- D onut charts show values   up to   two decimal points. 
 Note : D onut charts may not chart all patients in a data set if there are missing or incomplete patient records. Therefore, f or donut charts using the Percentage aggregation, the value shown inside the donut may not add up to 100%. 
 Segmented Donut Chart 
- Segmented donut charts split the variable represented in the donut chart by subcategory and visualize the variable's relative distribution of data by subcategory. 
- You can hover your cursor on a segment in the donut chart to view that subcategory's value. 
- The legend shows all subcategories within the primary variable being visualized. 
- You can hover on a subcategory label in the legend to highlight that subcategory's segment in the chart. 
- You can click a subcategory label in the legend to remove that subcategory's segment from the chart. Reclick to view the subcategory's segment again. 
 Note : Segmented d onut charts may not chart all patients in a data set if there are missing or incomplete patient records. Therefore, f or segmented donut charts using the Percentage aggregation, the value shown inside the donut may not add up to 100%. 
 Tip : If the visualization you want to view experiences slow performance, we recommend that you refresh the page, use more chart filters, and then regenerate the preview. 
- Click Save in the lower-left corner of the page.
 Note : Saved Custom Graphs update daily using real-time data based on the latest study data snapshot processed by Data Surveillance. 
## Create Data Aggregation Custom Graphs Across Multiple Datasets
 You can create Custom Graphs that aggregate study data across multiple datasets. For example, you can visualize:
- Adverse events by visit over time 
- Dosing reactions by dosing date 
- Tumor sum MM by visit cycle 
- Device response by visit week 
- Access Data Connect , and then click Transformations in the left-hand menu. 
- Click Add Project , and enter the following settings: 
- Project Name – Enter a project name. 
- Project Type – Select Derived datasets . 
- Click Add project .
The Transformations table updates to include the new project at the top of the list. 
- Click the new project name in the Transformations table, and then click View / Modify . 
- In the Data Source panel: click the Rave EDC menu, click the visit dataset ; for example, AE, and then drag and drop a dataset form into the Target section. 
- In the Data Source panel > Rave EDC menu, click the target event dataset ; for example, SV, and then drag and drop a dataset form into the Target section. 
- In the Target section, click the More icon on the event dataset, and then click Join .
The Join Datasets page appears. 
- In the Dataset Details section, enter a New Dataset Name . 
- Click the Right Join menu, and then select Inner Join .
 Note : Ensure the event dataset is on the left of the inner join and the visits data set is on the right. For example:
- Click the Match Conditions panel, and then select the appropriate fields to match rows of data across datasets—usually patient_id at a minimum. 
- Click the Select Fields panel, and then select all fields that you want to include in the datasets. 
- Click Apply Join . 
- After the Join Datasets page reloads, click X in the upper-right corner of the page. 
- In the Transformations page > Target section, click the More icon on the new dataset, and then click Replicate or Filter .
The Replicate or Filter Datasets page appears. 
- Enter a New Dataset Name . 
- Click the Conditional Filter toggle to activate.
The activated toggle has a blue background with the slider on the right side, . 
- Click the Filter Conditions panel, and then configure the filter condition using the selection operators, variables, functions , and values to construct your filter rule. 
- Click the Select Fields panel, and then select all fields you want to include in the datasets. 
- Click Apply Replicate or Filter . 
- After the Replicate or Filter Datasets page reloads, click X in the upper-right corner of the page. 
- In the Transformations page > Target section, click the More icon on the new dataset, and then click Group .
The Group Datasets - Min, Max, Avg, Sum page appears.
- Enter a New Dataset Name . 
- In New Keys , add new keys.
 Tip : New keys are the data points under which the grouping will occur.
- Click the Select Fields panel, select the fields that you want to perform an aggregation on, and then select the variable type that you want to categorize each field. For example, Count. 
- Click Apply Group.  and click the X on the top once the page has finished processing. 
- After the Group Datasets - Min, Max, Avg, Sumpage reloads, click X in the upper-right corner of the page.
The new dataset is now available for use in Data Surveillance and RBQM. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Custom Graphs in the left-hand menu. 
- Click Create Custom Graph . 
- In the Chart Type section, click the Line Chart icon. 
- Click the   Y-Axis   menu, and select the transformed dataset and event aggregated count variable. 
- Click the   X-Axis   menu, and select the visit variable. 
- Optional. Select an x-axis aggregation.
 Tip : For line charts, we recommend not selecting an aggregation on the x-axis unless you are plotting date or time variables on the x-axis. If  you do not select an aggregation   for a date variable on the x-axis,   then the line chart plots the data for every single day in the database. 
 Important : If you add an aggregation to any nondate variables in the x-axis, then you must add a dataset and variable in the Color Series . Otherwise, the custom graph  cannot render.
- Optional . To further breakdown the study data being visualized to show and compare segmented data subcategories for deeper insights and analysis: Click the Color Series menu, and select a data set and variable. Selecting a color series modifies a line chart into a:
- Multiline Chart – Plots multiple lines on a single visual to simultaneously view and compare trends across multiple data subcategories. Each line represents a subcategory. For example, a line chart might show the weekly number of patients that get randomized in a study over the course of two years. But a multiline chart might further visualize the number of the weekly number of patients that get randomized in a study over the course of two years by race. In which case, the chart would show multiple lines representing each race recorded in the study data.
 Tip : We recommend limiting multiline charts to show a maximum of five lines to ensure optimal chart readability. Otherwise, we recommend plotting the data in a bar graph.
- Optional . To chart a specific data subset from the y- and x-axis variable selections: Click the Chart Filters menu, do the following: 
- Enter or select a data set. 
- Enter or select a variable. 
- Select a comparator, such as= or !=, and then select or enter a comparator value.

## Create Tabular Custom Graphs
 Tabular Custom Graphs enable you to segment populations of interest and identify patient groups for further investigation. Investigating counts or percentages of required parameters in study data enables data managers to:
- Understand treatment efficacy by comparing outcomes and treatments. 
- Evaluate compliance looking at rates of completion and adherence to medication. 
- Explore differential subgroup responses based on demographic or baseline characteristics. 
- Examine how well groups meet primary and secondary endpoints. 
- Analyze AE trends relative to outcomes, treatments, or other effect states 
 Note : You must have at least one Tabular Visual type collection in Data Connect to create tabular Custom Graphs in Data Surveillance.
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Custom Graphs in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Custom Graphs page, click  Create Custom Graph . 
- In Chart Type, select .
The left-hand pane updates to show Tabular Datasets.
 Note : Chart filters, Color series fields become disabled if you select tabular charts. 
- In Rows , drag and drop one dataset from the left-hand Tabular Datasets pane.
 Note : You can select only one tabular dataset at a time. 
- In  Columns , select one or many variables from the tabular dataset you added into Rows.
 Note : Y ou can have multiple columns for each row for a tabular custom graph . 
- In Display Settings , enter or select the following: 
- Title  – Enter a short, concise title describing what the chart represents. 
- Description – Enter details describing what the chart represents. For example, text describing the summarization for the tabular chart. 
- Click Refresh Data to generate or regenerate the custom graph.
The custom graph appears in the Preview section. 
- Click Save in the lower-left corner of the page. 
## Edit Tabular Custom Graphs
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Custom Graphs in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Custom Graphs page, do one of the following to edit a tabular custom graph :
- Click a tabular custom graph  on the Custom Graphs page, then click Edit from the top right corner.
- Click the More icon, , in the corresponding row of the custom graph you want to edit, and then click Edit .
 Important Note : 
- If you edit a tabular custom graph where the tabular dataset variables are no longer available from Data Connect , a "A new tabular report configuration is available. " message appears. Click View Configuration under the message and follow steps to  create a tabular visualization . 
- If you had selected a specific dataset variable in the row or column field while creating a tabular custom graph, and it now appears disabled, a " Variable is no longer available. " message appears. 
This indicates that the variable is no longer available in Data Connect . If you then select a new dataset and configure the tabular custom graph with new rows and columns, and then click Preview, a " The data configuration has changed. Refreshing will reload the chart with the latest settings."  message appears. 
- Update the fields you want to edit. 
- Click Refresh Data to generate or regenerate the custom graph.
The custom graph appears in the Preview section.  
- Click Save . 
## Save Custom Graphs As Template
 You can save Custom Graphs as a template and reuse them across study environments.
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Custom Graphs in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Custom Graphs page, click the More icon in the corresponding row of the custom graph you want to save as a template. 
- Click Save as Template .

 You can delete Custom Graphs. For example, to manage and organize the list of Custom Graphs in your study or to remove obsolete Custom Graphs. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Custom Graphs in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Custom Graphs page, click the More icon in the corresponding row of the custom graph  you want to delete. 
- Click Delete . 
## Download Custom Graphs
 You can download Custom Graphs as PDF files for easy circulation and review with study team personnel. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Custom Graphs in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Custom Graphs page, click the chart you want to download.  
- Click Download from the top right corner of the page. 
- Click Confirm .
The PDF version of the bar, line and donut charts downloads to your browser.
 Note : For all Custom Graphs, you can download the file as both a PDF and a CSV file.

## Create, View, Delete, and Submit Vendor Query Sets
 While reviewing data listing records, you can raise queries on data ingested from Medidata Rave. Similarly, you  can create Vendor Queries to report and track queries or problems with external vendor data; for example, lab reports with missing patient data. You can assign Vendor Queries as part of vendor issue sets to approved vendors for further action, like a response addressing the data issue. 
 Vendor Queries enables:
- Seamless communication of discrepancies and inconsistencies with vendors. 
- Faster reconciliation of Rave and external vendor data. 
 Tip : Play the video below to watch how to create and submit vendor queries.
 &amp;lt;p&amp;gt;&amp;lt;br/&amp;gt;&amp;lt;/p&amp;gt;  
## Customize Column Configurations
 You can customize column configurations directly using the   More icon, above the Listing table when previewing a draft or approved listing. 
 Note: 
- If you specify column configuration while creating a draft listing, the listing retains the configuration when it is approved. 
- You can reconfigure columns of an approved listing, but these changes are temporary and only visible to you. If you refresh or reload the page, the columns revert back to the original configuration. 
- If you move an approved listing back to draft listing without modifying the expression, the column configuration remains unchanged. 
- If you edit the expression in an approved listing, newly added columns are automatically enabled for column configuration, and the existing columns retain their original configuration. 
- If you use the Copy Listings or Import Listing feature, you lose column configuration of the original listing. 
 Fix Column Configurations 
 To better customise the results, you can hide, unhide, fix a table's columns to appear to the left or right. For example, you can hide columns of no interest.
- If necessary, view an approved listing's results . 
- Click ,  More icon, above the Listing table. 
- Click Columns Configuration .
A slide out panel appears. 
- Drag and drop fields under Columns to either Left Fixed Columns or Right Fixed Columns . The fields you place under each appear as such in the listings table. For example, you fix Patient, Site or Country to the left.
 Note : We recommend:
- Fixing only Patient, Site and Country columns as left columns. 
- Only fixing columns that you can see on your screen as per your screen resolution. 
- Including some columns that are neither fixed as left or right fixed columns, so that horizontal scrolling remains. 
 Do not fix all columns in the listings table. That is, fix some columns to the left, and the remaining to the right. This may cause the screen to freeze (UI Gridlock), where the fixed elements from the left and right sides have essentially met in the middle, leaving no room for the scrollable data to actually render.   
## View Vendor Query Sets
 While reconciling data, you can group patient listings with external data issues into vendor query sets. You can then submit the vendor query sets for further clarification to vendors on the Vendor Queries page . Viewing the submitted Vendor Queries in Data Surveillance shows all the patient records included in the vendor query set at once. You can view only submitted vendor query sets. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Vendor Queries in the left-hand menu.
The Vendor Queries page shows the following:
 Summarization Cards 
- All  – All vendor query sets in the study. 
- Draft – Query sets not yet submitted to the vendor. 
- Submitted  – Vendor query sets submitted to vendors. 
- In Progress  – Query sets that the vendor is currently reviewing. 
- Completed  – Query sets that have all queries fulfilled. 
 Column Descriptions 
- Query Set Name – Vendor query set name.  
- Vendor – The approved vendor group to whom the query set is assigned. 
- Status – Indicates the vendor query set status: submitted, in progress, draft or completed. 
- Sent – Date you submitted the vendor query to the vendor 
- Due – Date the vendor query set is due for a response. 
- Completed – Date the vendor query completed. 
- Completion Comments – Comments entered when the query is completed. 
- Count – Number of vendor queries in the vendor query set. 
- If necessary, click the column headers to sort the Vendor Query Sets table. 
- Click the , the More icon, and then the View Query Set option.The Queries page lists the vendor queries in the vendor query set, along with the vendor group name, submitted date, due date, and the completed date, if applicable.
- 
 Column Descriptions 
- Patient – Patient ID for the record. 
- Site – Site number associated with the record. 
- Country – Country in which the site resides. 
- Listing – Approved data listing name. 
- Vendor Query – Type of vendor query you submitted. One of the following:
- Missing 
- Mismatch 
- Extra Vendor Record 
- Query Description – The system provided issue description or one that you entered corresponding to the vendor query type. 
- EDC Data – Data set variables from Rave. 
- Vendor Data – Data set variables from the vendor. 
## Download Vendor Query Sets
  You can download vendor queries and access the file offline outside of Data Surveillance. You can mark patient records included in the vendor query sets as reviewed on the Listings page once the vendor takes action. For example, the vendor provides clarification to your queries or supplies the missing records. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Vendor Queries  in the left-hand menu.
- Click one of the following options:
 Summarization Cards 
- All  – All vendor query sets in the study. 
- Draft – Query sets not yet submitted to the vendor. 
- Submitted  – Vendor query sets submitted to vendors. 
- In Progress  – Query sets that the vendor is currently reviewing. 
- Completed – Query sets that have all queries fulfilled. 
 Column Descriptions 
- Query Set Name – Vendor query set name.  
- Vendor – The approved vendor group to whom the query set is assigned. 
- Status – Indicates the vendor query set status: submitted, in progress, draft or completed. 
- Sent – Date you submitted the vendor query to the vendor 
- Due – Date the vendor query set is due for a response. 
- Completed – Date the vendor query completed. 
- Completion Comments – Comments entered when the query is completed. 
- Count – Number of vendor queries in the vendor query set. 
- If necessary, click the column headers to sort the Vendor Query Sets table. 
- Click the Query Set Name hyperlink. 
- The Queries page lists all the queries in the vendor query set. 
- Click , the More icon on the right in the vendor query set name banner. 
- Click  Download query set.
 The vendor query set downloads in CSV format to your browser. You can access the downloaded file and view the list vendor queries included in the vendor query set offline.
 Note : You can download vendor query sets with any status multiple times. However, the Submitted date corresponds to the date you first downloaded the file for submission, or the date you submitted the query to the vendor.
## Delete Draft Vendor Query Set
 You can delete draft vendor query sets. For example, if the patient record pertains to a patient no longer participating in the study, or if the data issue is no longer an aberration, you can delete the query set with the issue before it is submitted.
 Note : You cannot delete submitted Vendor Queries.
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Vendor Queries in the left-hand menu.
- Click Draft from the following options: 
- All  – All vendor query sets in the study. 
- Draft – Query sets not yet submitted to the vendor. 
- Submitted  – Vendor query sets submitted to vendors. 
- In Progress  – Query sets that the vendor is currently reviewing. 
- Completed – Query sets that have all queries fulfilled. 
- For any vendor query set, click the  More icon . 
- Click Delete Query Set . 
## Submit Vendor Query Sets
 While reviewing an approved listing's results on the Listings page, you can create vendor queries to group patient records with vendor data issues into vendor query sets. While creating, you must assign the vendor queries to approved vendors. Data Surveillance permits only one unsubmitted vendor query set per vendor to ensure vendors receive only one notification at a time about outstanding action on data issues. Submitting vendor queries opens a two way communication channel between vendors and data managers, and leads to obtaining accurate and complete study data. 
 There are two ways in which you can submit vendor queries to vendors for action: 
- Send vendor queries as a file in an email.
 With this method, you must manually track any vendor response you receive on the queries, and enter them back into Data Surveillance. 
- Submit Vendor Queries directly to vendors within Data Surveillance. 
With direct vendor query submission, you can track progress, responses, and the query status in real time, all within Data Surveillance. 
## Send Vendor Queries in an Email
 You can add vendor queries for external data issues in patient records on the Listing page. On the Vendor Queries page, you can then submit the vendor query set  you raised for patient records. You can then download the submitted vendor query set and send it to the vendor by email for further action.  
 Once the vendor responds to the issues, for example, sends the missing records, or information about mismatched records, or no further vendor action is required, you can mark the patient records as reviewed on the Listings page. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Vendor Queries in the left-hand menu. 
- Click Draft from the following options: 
- All  – All vendor query sets in the study. 
- Draft – Query sets not yet submitted to the vendor. 
- Submitted  – Vendor query sets submitted to vendors. 
- In Progress  – Query sets that the vendor is currently reviewing. 
- Completed – Query sets that have all queries fulfilled. 
- If necessary, click the column headers to sort the Vendor Query Sets table. 
- Click the Query Set Name hyperlink.
 The Queries page appears. By default, all vendor queries appear preselected. You can deselect records you do not want to submit as part of the vendor query set. You can also edit queries in the vendor query set. 
- Click  Edit Details , then update the following as required.
- Query Set Name – Query set to which the vendor query belongs. 
- Due Date – Due date by when you must submit the vendor query. 
- Vendor Group – Vendor group name for whom you raised the vendor query. 
- Click , the More  icon, above the Queries table. 
- Select Download query set. 
- The Status column for the vendor query set now reads Submitted. 
The Vendor Queries file downloads in CSV format to your browser. You can share the file with the vendor for further action.
Once the vendor responds, you can mark the data listing records as reviewed . 
## Send Vendor Queries Directly to Vendors
 You can submit vendor queries directly to vendor on the Vendor Queries page. When vendors respond, comment, or close the query, the status of the submitted query updates instantly so you can track vendor queries and plan data reconciliation accordingly.
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Vendor Queries  in the left-hand menu.
The Vendor Query Sets page shows. 
- Click Draft from the following options: 
- All 
- Draft 
- Submitted 
- In Progress 
- Completed 
- If necessary, click the column headers to sort the Vendor Query Sets table. 
- Click the Query Set Name hyperlink.
 The Queries page appears. By default, all vendor queries appear preselected. You can deselect records you do not want to submit as part of the vendor query set. You can also edit queries in the vendor query set. 
-  Click Edit Details , then update the following as required.
- Query Set Name – Query set to which the vendor query belongs. 
- Due Date – Due date by when you must submit the vendor query 
- Vendor Group – Vendor group name for whom you raised the vendor query.
 Note : You can submit a vendor query if all the three fields are non-empty.
- Click Save . 
- Click Submit to vendor .
The vendor query now appears under the Submitted card, with the sent date and the due date updated. The vendor receives an email notification about vendor queries assigned. Once the vendor responds, or comments on the query, the Status column updates from Submitted to Progress. The Summary cards at the top of the Vendor Queries page also show vendor queries with the In Progress status. 
 Once the vendor closes a query set, the vendor query is marked complete, and the Status column updates to Completed. For more information on how vendors respond to queries assigned, see Respond To Queries As A Vendor .

===== PAGE: create_and_view_stacked_datasets.html | Create and View Stacked Datasets =====
## Create and View Stacked Datasets
 Study data can sometimes contain datasets that share numerous common variables. For example: 
- Medidata Rave may include variations of the same type of eCRF, or 
- Study data may come from multiple sources such as a Rave vitals dataset and an external vitals dataset, or 
- Screening data and study collection data may have similar data points. 
 You can merge datasets with common variables into one dataset called a stacked dataset. Stacked datasets include all variables from all the source datasets, even variables without any common matches across the source datasets. You can use stacked datasets across the Data Surveillance and RBQM capabilities just like you use any other dataset. For example, to build data listings , visualizations , patient profile design elements , or derived variables . Or you can use stacked datasets to configure data mappings , custom QTLs , or custom KRIs . 
 In instances where multiple datasets have numerous shared variables, merging the datasets into one stacked dataset: 
- Simplifies the organization of your study data. 
- Streamlines your ability to access, review, and work with study data throughout Data Surveillance and RBQM. 
- Optimizes the reports, statistical analysis, and visual outputs that Data Surveillance and RBQM produce on your study data. 
 Note : You require the   View Detect CSM Configuration building block to access the Stacked Datasets page. You require the   Manage Detect CSM Configuration building block to create stacked datasets. 
## Access and View Stacked Datasets
 You can view the list of stacked datasets in your study along with associated details for each dataset. You can also view:
- All variables that comprise a specific stacked dataset. 
- The common variables across all source datasets that comprise a stacked dataset. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Stacked Data Sets in the left-hand menu.
The Stacked Datasets page appears. The table lists all stacked datasets in your study.
 Column Descriptions 
- Name – The unique dataset name. 
- OID – The dataset's unique object identifier. 
- Source Datasets – The original datasets that were merged to form the stacked dataset. 
- Created On – The stacked dataset creation date. 
- Created By – The user who created the stacked dataset. 
- In the Name column, click any stacked dataset name.
The Stacked Dataset window appears and shows the following information:
 Field Descriptions 
- Full Match – The number of variables that exist in and are common across datasets being previewed.
- Partial – The number of variables that exist in and are common across at least two datasets but not all datasets being previewed. 
- No Match – The number of variables that only exist in one dataset and are not common across any other dataset being previewed. 
- Variables – The list of unique variable OIDs existing across all datasets being previewed. 
- Stack – Specifies whether the variable OID is a full match, partial match, or has no common matches across any other data sets being previewed.
- Full – The variable OID exists in and is common across datasets being previewed.
- Partial – The variable OID exists in and is common across at least two datasets but not all datasets being previewed. 
- No Match – The variable OID only exists in one dataset and is not common across any other datasets being previewed. 
- Source Datasets – The list of prospective datasets that would be merged to create the stacked dataset. A black check mark indicates that the variable exists within the dataset. 
## Create Stacked Datasets
 You can merge datasets with common variables into one dataset called a stacked dataset. Stacked datasets include all variables from all the source datasets, even variables without any common matches across the source datasets. 
 You can use stacked datasets across the Data Surveillance and RBQM capabilities just like you use any other dataset. For example, to build data listings , visualizations , patient profile design elements , or derived variables . Or you can use stacked datasets to configure data mappings , custom QTLs , or custom KRIs . 
 Stacked datasets: 
- Simplify the organization of your study data. 
- Streamline your ability to access, review, and work with study data throughout Data Surveillance and RBQM. 
- Optimize the reports, statistical analysis, and visual outputs that Data Surveillance and RBQM produce on your study data. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Configuration > Stacked Data Sets in the left-hand menu.
The Stacked Datasets page appears.
- Click New Dataset . 
- In Dataset Name , enter a unique name for the stacked datasets. 
- In Dataset OID , enter a unique stacked dataset OID. The OID is the dataset object identifier, which helps identify and track the dataset. 
- In the Select Source Dataset section, select the check box for each dataset you want to merge into the stacked dataset.
 Note : You can merge up to 10 source datasets to create a stacked dataset.
- Click Preview .
The Stacked Dataset Preview window appears and shows the following:
 Field Descriptions 
- Full Match – The number of variables that exist in and are common across datasets being previewed.
- Partial – The number of variables that exist in and are common across at least two datasets but not all datasets being previewed. 
- No Match – The number of variables that only exist in one dataset and are not common across any other dataset being previewed. 
- Variables – The list of unique variable OIDs existing across all datasets being previewed. 
- Stack – Specifies whether the variable OID is a full match, partial match, or has no common matches across any other data sets being previewed.
- Full – The variable OID exists in and is common across datasets being previewed.
 Note : There must be at least one variable OID that is a full match across datasets to save and create a stacked dataset.
- Partial – The variable OID exists in and is common across at least two datasets but not all datasets being previewed. 
- No Match – The variable OID only exists in one dataset and is not common across any other datasets being previewed. 
- Source Datasets – The list of prospective datasets that would be merged to create the stacked dataset. A black check mark indicates that the variable exists within the dataset. 
 Tip : Previewing stacked datasets helps you assess the common variables across a set of datasets to determine if merging the datasets into one stacked dataset is an appropriate decision.
- Click Close . 
- Confirm your source dataset selections, and then click Save .
 Note : There must be at least one variable OID that exists in and is common across all selected source datasets to create a stacked dataset.

===== PAGE: create_audit_trail_reviews.html | Create Audit Trail Reviews =====
## Create Audit Trail Reviews
 During a study, teams perform audits on operational study data using audit trails. Audit reviews reveal incorrect data processing, help prevent inaccurate data reporting, and identify the need for additional training of personnel. You can use RBQM to create audit trail reviews, which include operational data that shows the events relating to creation, modification, or deletion of study data. 
 You can build audit data sets by engaging with a chat interface powered by Generative AI and Large Learning Models (LLMs), that parses complex study data to capture non-clinical records that match the question you ask. For example, you can ask a question about audit data between two dates for the Joint Counts data set. The records in the audit data set are not patient records, but operational data that match your question in the Joint Counts data set, that your study team wants to review. 
 By creating and using audit data sets, you can: 
- Extract insights to make better data decisions. 
- Ensure protocol compliance, patient safety, data quality, and data integrity. 
 Note : You must have the Manage Audit Trail Review building block added to your Cloud Administration role to create audit data sets. For more information, see RBQM Building Blocks and Permissions . 
## Create Audit Data Sets
- Access RBQM , and then click Audit Trail Review in the left-hand menu.
The Audit Trail Review page shows a new audit session by default.
- Optional. Click Audit Review from the upper-right corner of the page. 
- In the New Audit Review section, type a question in the prompt field. The AI-enabled chat assistant is named Dot. The prompt shows a default message: Ask Dot about data that you need for auditing purposes....  You can ask questions like:
- What are the critical data points that have changed this year? 
- What data points were modified after the database was locked on 12/12/2024? 
- Give me audits where data in vitals form was modified more than 10 times. 
- Show me queries created against vital signs form. 
- The chat interface summarizes, and provides a confirmation of your question. For example, if you asked a question like Show me critical data that was data collected or entered after midnight 12/12/2019 EST,  the confirmation message may read as  You are asking for audits on critical fields that were created on or after December 13, 2019. Is that correct?
 Note : You can ask questions in English only. Filtering by time is not currently supported. 
-   Do one of the following: 
- Click No , if the question confirmation does not match what you asked. Retype or edit the question as per the audit trail data you want to view. 
 OR Click  Yes, if the question confirmation matches what you asked.
The chat interface shows a message, "Great, let me generate the dataset for you.". 
- Repeat steps 3, 4, and 5 until the chat interface shows a question confirmation you asked.
The Data Preview section shows the generated audit data set.
 Note : 
- The AI assistant Dot, can make mistakes, and we recommend you check the output shown in the Data Preview section before you proceed. 
- The Audit time that you see in the Data Preview section is in UTC.  
- Optional. Click the More icon  in the upper-right corner of the chat interface section, then click View SQL. The section shows the underlying SQL code used to retrieve audit data from Medidata Rave. You can use this information to validate the results shown in the Data Preview section. 
 Note : Each question you enter is processed individually as ATR does not store the conversation history in the current chat session. However, you can save prompts, and access them through Saved Chats. 
## Audit Trail Data Limitations
 Currently Audit Trail Review (ATR) has the following limitations:
- ATR times out if the Large Language Model (LLM) that processes your query takes more than five minutes to retrieve audit data. 
- ATR does not support:
- Results at any level other than data points. For example, a question like  Give me all sites in the data,  does not produce a result. 
- Filtering on data point values. 
- Question prompts asking for all audits in the study . 
## Audit Subcategories
 ATR retrieves data for questions you ask based on the following Rave sub-categories:
- 
- Regarding data creation 
- EnteredNonConformant 
- Entered 
- EnteredEmpty 
- EnteredWithMissingCode 
- EnteredInForeignLocale 
- Regarding inactivated data 
- InactivatedWithReasonCode 
- Inactivated. For example, " Give me audits for critical data which was inactivated". 
- Regarding data modified or entered
- Activated 
- Entered 
- EnteredByDdeAutoReconcile 
- EnteredEmpty 
- EnteredEmptyWithChangeCode 
- EnteredForeignLocale 
- EnteredForeignLocaleWithChangeCode 
- EnteredNonConformant 
- EnteredWithChangeCode 
- EnteredWithMissingCode 
- Regarding queries
- QueryOpen 
- QueryAnswer 
- QueryAnswerByChange 
- QueryClose 
- QueryCancel 
 For more information, see Audit Subcategories .
## Recommended Chat Practices
 We recommend the following while entering questions in the chat option:
- Be specific : If you know the form, variable, site, or patient name, add that to your chat question.  
- We recommend using the term form instead of data set in your questions, for example, "show audits for Adverse Events form".  
- Dates : Specify complete dates. For example, instead of "List audits for Tuesday", say " List audits for Tuesday, 7th Jan 2024". You can also use relative dates, like "show audits for the AE form for the last 10 days". 
- Responses Shown:  The AI assistant Dot returns responses that best align with questions you ask allowable operations within ATR, or the LLM's processing of the input, or conditions you provide based on patterns learned through training. 
- User Specific Audits:  While searching for audits by a specific user, type the initial for the user's first name, then add a space, and then the last name. For example, J Smith. Do not add extra spaces between the first and last names.  
- Within the same chat session, if responses are incorrect, add more specific information to guide responses. If responses are correct, save the chat so you can rerun the chat prompt or edit it in future.

===== PAGE: create_derived_variable__with_difference_in_dates_calculation.html | Create Derived Variable with Difference in Dates Calculation =====
## Create Derived Variable with Difference in Dates Calculation
 You can calculate the number of days between two date-based data set variables into a single derived variable . For example, AE Start Date - Randomization Date display the number of days between when the AE started and when the subject was randomized. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Derived Variables in the left-hand menu. 
- Click  Create Derived Variable . 
- Identify and drag a data set  from the Data Sets list into the Configure Variable section. For example, Adverse Events. 
- Enter the derived variable’s identification information. 
- Name – Object identifier (OID) of derived variable. For example, AE Start Date/End Date. Must be unique. 
- Label  – Name for derived variable to appear in other applications. This can be the same as the Name field, or a more specific descriptor. For example, Adverse Event Duration. 
- Select Difference In Dates   from the  Derived Variable Type   menu. 
- Drag date variables into the respective Variable 1 and Variable 2 fields.
- Optional . Click Preview to display the preview panel.
With the preview panel, you can review the derived variable and adjust the variable's parameters before saving.
- Click  Save .
 In Data Surveillance and RBQM, the list of available datasets and variables that you can view and select from include derived variables at the bottom of the list. In Data Surveillance, the list of available datasets and variables appends derived variable names with the blue DERIVED icon.

===== PAGE: create_derived_variable_from_expression.html | Create Derived Variable from Expression =====
## Create Derived Variable from Expression
 You can build a derived variable by using the expression builder to apply mathematical and logical operations on data set variables.  For example, use derived variables to show particular values such as “If Visit Name = Day 1, then show “Randomization”, Else = "Null "" or"If SYSBP > 60, then show LOW, else HIGH”. These expressions can use multiple conditions and can be rather complex. You can also build a logical expression with conditional logic. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Derived Variables in the left-hand menu. 
- Click  Create Derived Variable . 
- Identify and drag a data set  from the Data Sets list into the Configure Variable section. For example, Adverse Events. 
- Enter the derived variable’s identification information. 
- Name – Object identifier (OID) of derived variable. For example, "AESER+AESER_TXT". Must be unique. 
- Label  – Name for derived variable to appear in other applications. This can be the same as the Name field, or a more specific descriptor. For example, "AE Serious, Full". 
- Select Expression Builder from the Derived Variable Type menu. 
- (Optional) Form the conditional expression: 
- Navigate to the Operator tab, and drag If Then Else into the expression builder. 
- Drag data set variables into the respective If , Then , and Else fields. 
- Complete the expression: 
- Navigate to the  Data Set s  tab, and drag data set variables into the expression builder fields.
 Note : If data set variables include unknowns, the data set replaces them with interpolated (enriched) fields like _INT, or _DTC. For example, the source date is missing the day, the enriched _INT field interpolates the 1st day of the month, and _DTC fields drop the unknown value. If the source field uses dictionary terms, the enriched _TXT field shows the coded terms.
- Navigate to the Operator  tab, and drag various operators and values i nto the expression builder fields.
 Note : If you leave the expression incomplete, the following warning message appears: " Complete the expression by specifying at least one variable, one operator, and one variable or value to compare". 
- Optional . Click  Preview  to display the preview panel.
With the preview panel, you can review the derived variable and adjust the variable's parameters before saving.
- Click  Save .
 In Data Surveillance and RBQM, the list of available datasets and variables that you can view and select from include derived variables at the bottom of the list. In Data Surveillance, the list of available datasets and variables appends derived variable names with the blue DERIVED icon.

 | Checks if the compared value contains a substring from a selected data set variable values.

If the source field uses dictionary terms, the enriched _TXT field shows the coded terms. Enriched fields are used to provide more detail about the about source fields, or to add derived information that is not directly present in the original source.

===== PAGE: create_signals.html | Create and Edit Signals =====
## Create and Edit Signals
 Signal creation is a critical function in the clinical data review cycle that enables proactively identifying and  managing potential data issues, ensuring comprehensive oversight and timely interventions. Creating signals based on data analysis for modules configured in your study enables you assess discordant observations from KRIs, QTLs, Patient Profiles, Statistical Monitoring etc. You can then further take action on such observations by creating and assigning issues, thereby significantly streamlining site and study oversight. You can create automated and manual signals in the signals report. 
## Automatically Generate Signals
 You can automatically generate signals in the signals report based on modules you configure in RBQM > Configuration > Signals . Automated signals generate based on a combination of two factors: one, the modules configured, and two, the thresholds set for specific modules. The data you see in a signal is from every configured module, based on the source module's last successful data update.  
- Access RBQM , and then click RBQM > Configuration > Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals Configuration page appears. 
- Add Custom Configurations . 
Automated signals generate based on custom configurations. The signals table includes the following columns:
 Signal Columns 
- Signal ID   – Unique signal number per study environment associated with the auto-generated or user defined signal. 
- Site – The site associated with the signal.
For QTLs, the site reads as "All Sites". 
- Country  – The country where the site is situated. For QTLs, the field reads as "All Study Countries".
- Patient  – One or many patients who meet the signal threshold at the site. The field shows up to 10 patients, with the remaining concatenated with a "+" icon. You can hover to view all patients. 
- Analysis – One module from Patient Profiles, KRIs, QTLs, Under and over Reporting, Rounding, Propagation, or Potential Duplicate Patients. 
- Name – The variable for the module on which the signal is generated. Some example are  KRI Name, AE Entry Delay, Missing Visit Percentage, Manual Query Rate,Non-System Query Delay, Percent Out of Window Visit, Number of SAEs per Patient-Month, Number of AEs per Patient-Month etc. 
- Observation – An automated observation based on the text used in signal threshold. Updated observation values appear in the signal report only if the value is at or above the set threshold. Sample description text for a KRI AE Entry Delay of 17 days when you set a threshold as "high" - The AE Entry Delay of 973 exceeds the threshold of 17 .
 Note : If the observation value falls below the module's configured threshold, it does not get updated when you refresh Signals data. The last value at which the threshold was met shows as the observation.
 Observations and Patient Information for Modules 
 Patient information and observations do not appear for all modules as in some cases, signal data appears at the site level, not at the patient level. The following table shows further details.

Sample Description text - The site is an outlier considering the time it takes to report AEs (considering AE Visit Date and First Entry Date). - Due Date – The due date for the signal. 
- Status – A signal has the following statuses: 
- New – A newly created signal not yet assigned to an assignee or acted upon. 
- Open – A signal assigned to an assignee. 
- Resolved – A signal marked as resolved. 
- Watched – A signal that may require intervention or action, but currently is being watched. No action is made on a watched signal, it is not assigned to an assignee. 
- Dismissed – A signal that is dismissed. For example, if the observation may not be a potential issue for the time period in review. 
- Closed – A signal closed as it is no longer of interest. 
- Reopened – A signal reopened after it was closed. 
- Assignee – The name of the person assigned to the signal for further action. If no assignee exists, click the , Add assignee option to assign the signal to an assignee. 
- Category – Select from a list of existing categories or create a new category. 
- Opened By – The person who opened the signal. 
- Opened Date – The date the signal was opened. 
- Closed By – The person who marked the signal as closed. 
- Closed Date – Date the signal was closed. 
- Issues – A yes or no value that indicates if a signal is an issue. 
- Issue Type – A signal can have a protocol deviation or a non-protocol deviation issue type.  
- Issue Target – An issue associated with a signal can be external or internal. 
 Note : F or a new study, the first time you click RBQM > Signals, the Signals page appears empty until signals get generate. Click the Refresh button at the top right corner of the page to get the latest auto-generated signals. To get the most updated signals, you must refresh the Signals data daily. Auto-generated signals appear based on the latest data snapshot for each configured module available at 6:00 am (EST). If you make any   custom signal configurations   after 6:00 am (EST), the changes are not visible on the Signals page until the next day.

===== PAGE: data_anomaly_detection.html | Data Anomaly Detection =====
## Data Anomaly Detection
 Data Anomaly Detection provides a graphical representation of RBQM's analysis for a single variable or pair of variables in your study data. You can use Data Anomaly Detection to determine  outliers , anomalies, risks, and trends in your study data, and further investigate or report your data findings as necessary. 
## What Is Data Anomaly Detection?
 Statistical Monitoring's Data Anomaly Detection capability provides a graphical representation of RBQM's analysis for a single variable or a pair of variables in your study data. Data Anomaly Detection renders as frequency distribution plots , box-and-whisker plots , or scatter plots . To learn more, see Data Anomaly Detection Plot Visualization Types . 
 Data Anomaly Detection is conducted across all data types (date, numeric, and text) and within all data contexts (visit-based, event-based, and single-record per patient). 
## What Is the Purpose of Data Anomaly Detection?
 You can use Data Anomaly Detection to determine your study data's  outliers , anomalies, unusual data associations, risks, trends, and missing data at the data point-, patient-, site-, and country-level. 
 Depending on the type of data finding, you can: 
- Create queries in Medidata Rave.
- Create issues. 
- Generate or update risks in the Risk Assessment.
## What Are the Benefits of Using Data Anomaly Detection?
 Determining the outliers, anomalies, risks, and trends in your study data puts you and your life sciences team in an optimal position to:
- Understand your study's operational performance at the site and country level, and
- Take mitigating actions on your study, such as:
- Cleaning data,
- Opening issues,
- Opening queries ,
- Issuing corrective actions, and
- Coordinating additional training.
## Who Uses Data Anomaly Detection?
 Different clinical research team members use Data Anomaly Detection for various unique purposes. For example, data managers might investigate data point- or patient-level inconsistencies. Central monitors might investigate site- or country-level data issues. Or medical monitors might investigate signals regarding patient safety.
## How Do I Read Anomalous Plots?
 Depending on the variable or variables you select to view, Statistical Monitoring applies several unique Data Anomaly Detection Plot Visualization Types . 
 Click a data analysis type below to learn how to interpret the anomalous plot based on which type of data analysis RBQM applies to the variable.
 Text Analysis Plot 
- The Y-axis shows the error or discrepancy score .
- The X-axis shows each unique text value as entered by the patients in the eCRF for the selected variable. By default, the text values appear from highest error score to the lowest error score.
- The number of times that the text value occurs within the variable shows on the plot in a blue rectangle, orange hexagon, or red pentagon. For example, . 
- Each color-coded shape is defined below:
- Blue Rectangle   – The text value's error score is less than 2.95. This means that the text value has a statistically normal number of occurrences within the variable. 
- Orange Hexagon   – The text value's error score is between 2.95 and 4.95. This means that the text value has a higher- or lower-than-normal number of occurrences within the variable. Thus, RBQM considers the data type an outlier. 
- Red Pentagon   – The text value's error score exceeds 4.95. This means that the text value has a significantly higher- or lower-than-normal number of occurrences within the variable. Thus, RBQM considers the data type an extreme outlier. 
- You can hover your cursor on a blue square, orange hexagon, or red pentagon to view the text value name and its error score.
- You can click a blue square, orange hexagon, or red pentagon to view additional information about that data point in a separate panel to the right of the plot.

- Data Point Score – A numeric score generated by Statistical Monitoring's high-dimensional data anomaly detection algorithms , which measures the discrepancy of an individual data point relative to the overall study data. Data point scores help you uncover outliers, anomalies, risks, and trends in your study data, which may require follow-up action. An error score of less than 2.95 indicates statistically normal data; between 2.95 and 4.95 indicates outlier data; exceeding 4.95 indicates extreme outlier data.

## How Does Statistical Monitoring Analyze the Data in Data Anomaly Detection?
 Statistical Monitoring automatically runs analytics on new or updated standardized and preprocessed study data from the Medidata Data Fabric to generate data analysis and visualization outputs. To learn more about how Statistical Monitoring receives and analyzes study data, see Clinical Data Studio's Data Pipeline . 
 On the Data Anomaly Detection page, depending on the variable or variables you select to view, Statistical Monitoring uses five different types of data analysis :
- Text Analysis 
- Numeric Analysis 
- Text Versus Text Analysis 
- Numeric Versus Numeric Analysis 
- Numeric Versus Text Analysis 
 Each type of data analysis renders using one of three specific data visualizations: 
- Frequency Distribution Plot 
- Box-and-whisker Plot 
- Scatter Plot 
 Statistical Monitoring's analytics uses a unique data anomaly detection methodology  that: 
- Identifies all the outlier  study data values, 
- Calculates a discrepancy score  for each outlier data value based on how unusual that data value is, and 
- Flags the data values on the data anomaly detection plot as normal, outlier, or extreme outlier. To learn more, see Investigate Data Using Data Anomaly Detection Plots . 
 The single- and multi-value analysis (in addition to other algorithms) roll up to aggregate levels: Patient, Site, Country, Variable, Domain, and Risk Category.
 Statistical Monitoring's comprehensive, multidimensional data analysis and visualization allows you to effectively identify study areas requiring attention that might otherwise go unnoticed. Thus, Statistical Monitoring lends to clean data and efficiently run studies that are readily available for submission at the study's completion.

## Data Anomaly Detection Plot Analysis Types
 When you select variables to view in the Data Anomaly Detection plot visualization, Statistical Monitoring applies one of five different types of data analyses depending on the variable  or variables you are viewing. 
 Each data analysis type renders using one of three specific data visualizations: frequency distribution plot , box-and-whisker plot , or scatter plot . Each data analysis type also has a unique plot sorting and filtering options .
 Note : You can find c ommon examples for each data analysis type below. However, actual outputs vary from study to study based on the variable relationships that Statistical Monitoring's data analysis identifies. 
## Text Analysis
 Statistical Monitoring analyzes the frequency and distribution of the unique text values existing within an individual variable in the study data. For example, text analysis might visualize and compare the frequency of each unique, patient-entered text value for 'reason for discontinuation' for a given study variable. RBQM conducts text analysis across visit-based, event-based, and single-record per patient data contexts. The analysis produces a frequency distribution plot visualization. For example: 
 Tip : Click image to enlarge.
## Numeric Analysis
 Statistical Monitoring analyzes the distribution of all numeric and date values existing within a single variable in the study data. For example, numeric analysis might visualize the raw distribution of the numeric values patients entered for ALT values for a given study variable. RBQM conducts numeric analysis across visit-based, event-based, and single-record per patient data contexts. The analysis produces a box-and-whisker plot visualization. For example: 
 Tip : Click image to enlarge.
## Text Versus Text Analysis
 Statistical Monitoring analyzes the combined frequency and distribution of the unique text values existing within two paired variables in the study data. For example, text versus text analysis might visualize and compare how many times patients entered a paired combination of text values for the severity of adverse events across those two variables. RBQM conducts text versus text analysis across visit-based, event-based, and single-record per patient data contexts. The analysis produces a frequency distribution plot visualization. For example: 
 Tip : Click image to enlarge.
## Numeric Versus Numeric Analysis
 Statistical Monitoring analyzes the combined distribution of all numeric and date values existing within two paired variables in the study data. For example, numeric versus numeric analysis might visualize the raw distribution of the numeric values that patients entered for systolic versus diastolic blood pressure across those two variables. RBQM conducts numeric versus numeric analysis across visit-based, event-based, and single-record per patient data contexts. The analysis produces a  scatter plot visualization. For example:
 Tip : Click image to enlarge.
## Numeric Versus Text Analysis
 Statistical Monitoring analyzes the distribution of all numeric and date values existing in the study data against all existing text values across two paired variables. For example, numeric versus text analysis might compare the distribution of height among female patients against the height of among male patients. RBQM conducts numeric versus text analysis across visit-based, event-based, and single-record per patient data contexts. The analysis produces multiple side by side  box-and-whisker plot visualizations. For example:
 Tip : Click image to enlarge.

===== PAGE: data_discrepancy_finding_identification_methodology.html | AI Reconciliation Report Data Discrepancy Identification Methodology =====
## AI Reconciliation Report Data Discrepancy Identification Methodology
 In AI Reconciliation, a condition is an adverse event that occurs after patients enroll in a study. A treatment is the medication or procedure patients take in response to a condition in the same study. This article focuses on how the AI Reconciliation algorithm works for the Treatment Without Conditions and the Conditions without Treatments and Ongoing MH reports. 
 Patients take treatments in response to a condition when a condition  expects a treatment. The AI Reconciliation algorithm identifies conditions that expect treatments, and do not have corresponding treatments. A condition and treatment are a pair if the treatment treats the condition, and the start date of the treatment lies within the timeframe of the condition starting and ending. A treatment treats a condition if the indication for the treatment matches the condition, or if the algorithm can deduce that the treatment treats the condition using the medication-indication table.
 Components used to calculate Confidence in the Conditions Without Treatments and Treatments without Conditions or Ongoing MH reports are as follows:
 Conditions Without Treatments

 Condition Without Treatments Algorithm Methodology 
 Treatments Without Conditions and Ongoing MH 
- 
 Treatments Without Conditions and Ongoing MH Algorithm Methodology

===== PAGE: data_oversight.html | Task Oversight =====
## Task Oversight
 While conducting studies, Lead Clinical Data Managers (LCDMs) and Clinical Data Team Leads (CDTLs) may use multiple systems to gather critical operational data needed to manage their studies effectively. This leads to: 
- Lack of complete visibility   – It is time-consuming to get a complete, a complete view of Clinical Data Studio (CDS) operational activities, and user work compliance without manually consolidating data from various sources. 
- Increased risk and inefficiency   –The necessity to switch between capabilities to check on statuses and risk, introduces unnecessary friction, increasing the time spent on oversight, and potentially delays identifying critical issues. 
- Delayed decision-making   –   Without centralized metrics, lead data managers struggle to quickly answer fundamental questions about work progress, delaying timely interventions and increasing operational risk for the sponsor. 
 To overcome this Clinical Data Studio includes a Task Oversight dashboard.
 The Task Oversight dashboard serves as a singular place to understand key operational activities like setup, data import, refresh, and data review as documented in Data Connect and Data Surveillance.  
## What Is Task Oversight?
 Task Oversight is a Data Surveillance capability that shows study metrics and key performance indicators (KPIs) from Patient Profiles, Vendor Queries, Listings, AI Reconciliation, and Data Connect.
## What Is the Purpose of Task Oversight? 
 Task Oversight allows you to track and monitor in one centralized dashboard the progress of patient data in your study that requires vetting and review. The key performance indicators for each module gives insight into the health of study data and allows you to plan interventions or follow up. 
## How Does Task Oversight Work?
 Task Oversight reads data from the following modules based on their latest refresh data snapshot.
- Patient Profiles. 
- AI Reconciliation. 
- Listings. 
- Custom Graphs. 
- Vendor Queries, and 
- Data Connect. 
 Updates made to records, such as marking listings as reviewed or unreviewed, or similar actions in any of the modules, reflects in the metrics shown on the Task Oversight dashboard instantly. 
## What Are the Benefits of Task Oversight?
   Task Oversight provides: 
- Complete operational transparency –   Lead Clinical Data Managers (LCDMs) and Clinical Data Team Leads (CDTLs) can access   critical operational metrics and user work compliance from a single page. 
- Flexibility to select key operational metrics – You can select metrics of interest to display on the Task Oversight dashboard, such as:
- Metrics covering  reviewed  patient profiles, and last refresh date. 
- Visibility into listings created, last refresh date, and records reviewed/not reviewed per listing. 
- Tracking unreviewed AI Reconciliation data per report. 
- Tracking   reviewed  vendor queries per query set. 
- Reduced friction and risk – By centralizing information, Task Oversight avoids the need to switch between multiple applications, bringing critical information directly into one page.  
## How Do I Access Task Oversight?
 Access Task Oversight .

===== PAGE: data_sets.html | Data Sets =====
## Data Sets
 Data Surveillance's Data Sets capability ingests your team's study data from:  
- Medidata Rave, or any other electronic data source like Veeva EDC. 
- Third-party vendor data—for example, protocol deviations, lab data, or any data not uploaded through Rave—which gets uploaded through Data Connect's Imports capability  or through Ingestor . 
 Note : New studies will import external, third-party data using Imports. However, legacy studies that have previously ingested data through Ingestor can continue to import data through Ingestor.
 You can then use the Data Sets capability to view your study's data sets to:
- Holistically explore and investigate your entire set of study data, and 
- Investigate patients' case report forms in Rave or Veeva EDC. 
 This initial exploratory study data analysis can help determine if you should create any data listings to monitor data that may be of high risk to the study.
 Note: In Data Surveillance and RBQM, s tudy data automatically refreshes four times daily at approximately 9:00am (EST), 3:00pm (EST), 9:00pm (EST) and 3:00am (EST), and the data presented within the user interface is current as of 11:00 pm (EST) the previous day, 5:00 am (EST) the same day, 11:00 am (EST) the same day, 5:00 pm (EST) the same day, respectively. Each study data refresh produces a data snapshot. Updated data from Rave, and  activated datasets from Data Connect are available in 6 to 12 hours within Data Surveillance and RBQM. For more information, see  Clinical Data Studio Data Pipeline .
