- Optional . Filter the data set table to help find the information you need. 
- Optional . Use the page navigation below the data set table to sort through the list of records. 
- Optional . Click a hyperlinked Patient ID to view that patient's case report forms in Rave. 
## Filter Data Set Tables
 To help scan data set tables to find specific records , you can filter the table to show:
- All data set records. This is the default view. 
- Only data records for specific tables columns. For example, you can show or hide records for specific variables in the data sets table. 
- Only data records with specific values in specific table columns. For example, you can show only records associated with specific patient IDs in the table. 
- Do any of the following:
- To show only data records for specific table columns: click   , the More icon, and then click Columns Configuration , at the top-right corner of the data set table, select or clear the columns you want to show or hide, respectively, and then click Apply . 
- To show only data records with specific values in specific table columns: click the Filter button, , at the top-right corner of the data set table, click More filters , select a column name, click the column filter (for example, ), select all data values you want to view in the table, click Select , and then click Apply Changes . 
## Fix Column Configurations
 To better customise the results, you can hide, unhide, fix a table's columns to appear to the left or right. For example, you can hide columns of no interest.
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Datasets in the left-hand menu.
The Datasets page shows. 
- Click any dataset. 
- Click ,  More icon, above the dataset table. 
- Click Columns Configuration .
A slide out panel appears. 
- Drag and drop fields under Columns to either Left Fixed Columns or Right Fixed Columns . The fields you place under each appear as such in the listings table. For example, you fix Patient, Site or Country to the left.
 Note : We recommend:
- Fixing only Patient, Site and Country columns as left columns. 
- Only fixing columns that you can see on your screen as per your screen resolution. 
- Including some columns that are neither fixed as left or right fixed columns, so that horizontal scrolling remains. 
 We do not recommend:
- Fixing all columns, that is, fixing some columns to the left, and the remaining to the right. This may cause the screen to freeze (UI Gridlock), where the fixed elements from the left and right sides essentially meet in the middle, leaving no room for the scrollable data to actually render.

===== PAGE: data_surveillance_configuration.html | Data Surveillance Configuration =====
## Data Surveillance Configuration
 Data Surveillance Configuration is a Data Surveillance capability that allows you to: 
- Map the specific study data that you want Data Surveillance and RBQM to report on and visualize. 
- Create and manage: 
- Vendors to which you want to communicate vendor data issues. 
- Derived variables. 
- Stacked datasets. 
- Review reports. 
## What Is Data Surveillance Configuration?
 Data Surveillance Configuration is a Data Surveillance capability that enables you to perform all data mapping and various study configuration tasks in one central location. 
## What Is the Purpose of Data Surveillance Configuration?
 Data Surveillance Configuration provides a single, centralized location for: 
- Mapping the data that Data Surveillance and RBQM consume to produce the reports, statistical analysis, and visual output for: 
- Data Anomaly Detection Plots 
- Event incidence plots 
- Under-over reporting events 
- Potential duplicate patients 
- Rounding and propagation of vital sign records. 
- AI Data Reconciliation reports 
- RECIST 1.1 Dashboard 
- Creating and managing:
- Vendors to which you want to communicate vendor data issues. 
- Derived variables that you want to add for inclusion in your study's list of datasets. 
- Stacked datasets, which enable you to merge datasets with common variables into one dataset. 
- Review reports, which allow you to capture activity logs and findings across data review and reconciliation cycles conducted within Data Surveillance and RBQM. 
 To learn more, see: 
- Data Mapping 
- Vendor Configuration 
- Derived Variables 
- Stacked Datasets 
- Review Reports 
## Who Uses Data Surveillance Configuration?
 Risk managers, data managers, and any personnel involved with study risk management use Data Surveillance Configuration. 
## What Are the Benefits of Data Surveillance Configuration?
 Data Surveillance Configuration: 
- Allows you to quickly configure in a simple, centralized workspace the specific study data that you want Data Surveillance and RBQM to analyze. 
- Helps your organization target and review unique and specific facets of your study that you want to monitor for risk. 
## How Does Data Surveillance Configuration Work?
 Study teams must first properly set up studies in Medidata Rave , and then sites must enter study data directly in Rave or upload third-party data through Ingestor . To learn more, see Medidata Detect's Data Pipeline . Medidata's platform data workflow enriches and transforms all tagged study data , at which point, Data Surveillance pulls in the study's data sets and variables into your study environment. You can use Data Surveillance Configuration to: 
- Map the data that Data Surveillance and RBQM  consume to produce the statistical analysis and visual renderings for:
- Statistical Monitoring analyses 
- Data anomaly detection and trends 
- Event incidence and under-over reporting events 
- Potential duplicate patients 
- Rounding and propagation of vital sign records 
- AI Data Reconciliation reports 
- RECIST 1.1 dashboard reports 
- Create, activate, and deactivate vendors to which you want to communicate vendor data issues. 
- Create and update derived variables . 
- Create stacked datasets and view the list of stacked datasets in your study. 
- Add, Edit, And Delete Review Reports. 
 You can refresh the AI Data Reconciliation, RECIST 1.1 dashboard, and listings in the Data Listings capability to render their respective reports and data analyses based on the most recently ingested study data. You can schedule data refreshes to occur and on a preset frequency or manually trigger data refreshes ad-hoc. W ith each data refresh, Medidata's microservice algorithms consume and analyze the configured study data mappings and all activated KRIs and QTLs, and then Data Surveillance and RBQM report and visualize the statistical analyses in: 
- 
- Data Anomaly Detection 
- Trends 
- Event Incidence 
- Under-Over Reporting Events 
- Weekend and Holiday Visits 
- Potential Duplicate Patients 
- Rounding and Propagation 
- AI Reconciliation 
- Custom Graphs 
- RECIST 1.1 
- KRI Dashboard 
- QTL Dashboard 
- Risk Assessment 
- Risk Inventory 
 Note : In Data Surveillance and RBQM, s tudy data automatically refreshes four times daily at approximately 9:00am (EST), 3:00pm (EST), 9:00pm (EST) and 3:00am (EST), and the data presented within the user interface is current as of 11:00 pm (EST) the previous day, 5:00 am (EST) the same day, 11:00 am (EST) the same day, 5:00 pm (EST) the same day, respectively. Each study data refresh produces a data snapshot. Updated data from Rave, and   activated datasets from Data Connect   are available in 6 to 12 hours within Data Surveillance and RBQM.  For more information, see   Clinical Data Studio Data Pipeline .

===== PAGE: data_surveillance_template_library.html | Data Surveillance Template Library =====
## Data Surveillance Template Library
 You can use templates in Data Surveillance and RBQM to save and store commonly used data listing , custom graph,  QTL , custom numeric KRI, or custom percentage KRI configurations for reuse within a study.
## What Are Templates?
 Templates are listing, custom graph, QTL,  custom numeric KRI , or custom percentage KRI  configurations that you can save and store in your organization's global template library. 
## What Is the Purpose of Templates?
 You can store and reuse common listing, custom graph , QTL, and KRI configurations that your organization is likely to include in multiple study configurations.
## Who Uses Templates?
 Members of your organization who build studies can save and store listing, custom graph , QTL, and custom KRI configurations as templates in your organization's template library.
 Members of your organization who review data; for example, study managers or data managers, can import and reuse listing and KRI configuration templates in studies.
## What Are the Benefits of Templates?
 Adding and using specific listings,  custom graphs, QTLs, and custom KRIs as templates:
- Enables you and your team to quickly and easily reapply common data listings, custom graph s,  QTLs, and custom KRIs as needed across study configurations. 
- Promotes faster study start time. 
- Ensures consistency and accuracy in listing, custom graph , QTL, and custom KRI details across studies. 
## How Do Templates Work?
 In Listings , Custom Graphs ,  QTL Configuration , and KRI Configuration , you can save listing, custom graph , QTL, or custom KRI configurations, respectively, as templates. When you save templates, you export and store the templates in a template group.
 Template groups generally comprise a collection of templates that you might logically bundle together and use when building studies. For example, you could have a template group that consists of one or more listings, or a combination of listings, QTLs, and KRIs. Templates in the template group may pertain to studies based on therapeutic area, phase, or therapy . 
 Template groups live at the study  level . You can access and reuse templates for any study across studies . Your organization has its own client division-level global template library in Data Surveillance and RBQM . You can create template groups in the template library. The template library also stores and lists the collection of your organization's templates groups and associated templates. 
## How Do I Create, Manage, and Use Templates?
 See:
- View, Add, and Manage Template Groups 
- Add Listings as Templates to Template Groups 
- Add Custom Graphs Templates to Template Groups 
## Permission Requirements
 Template access requires the following permissions:
- Manage Detect Templates 
- View Detect Templates 
 To learn more about permissions, see  RBQM Building Blocks and Permissions .

===== PAGE: derived_variables.html | Derived Variables =====
## Derived Variables
 Derived variables are custom configured data set variables. You can use derived variables across the Data Surveillance and RBQM capabilities just like you use any other variable. For example, to build data listings , visualizations , or patient profile design elements . Or you can use derived variables to configure data mappings , custom QTLs , or custom KRIs .
## What Are Derived Variables?
 Derived variables are custom  data set variables  formed by various data set calculations such as text concatenation and text substrings. 
## What Is the Purpose of Derived Variables?
 With derived variables, you can  perform the following actions: 
- Create Derived Variable from Expression   – Use the Expression builder to a pply mathematical and logical operations to   data set variables . For example,use derived variables to show particular values such as “If Visit Name = Day 1, then show “Randomization”, Else = "Null "" or"If SYSBP > 60, then show LOW, else HIGH”. These expressions can use multiple conditions and can be rather complex. 
- Create Derived Variable to Show Data Refresh Date   – Use Data Refresh Date to s how the day  that the data refresh occurs in Derived Variables. Today’s date is typically used as a reference derivation for subsequent derivations. This date field is dynamic, meaning the value for “Today’s Date” will constantly update with each data refresh. 
- Create Derived Variable with Difference in Dates Calculation   – Use Differences in date derivations to calculate the number of days between two dates. For example, AE Start Date - Randomization Date display the number of days between when the AE started and when the subject was randomized. 
- Create Derived Variable with Concatenated Text –  Use Concatenate derived variables to link text variables. For example, if a field in Medidata Rave exists for “Visit” and another field for “Timepoint”, you can link the values in these two text fields together to create a new derived field.   
- Create Derived Variable with Text Substring – Use Substring derivations to derive a subset of alphanumeric or numeric characters from a given text field. For example, if a field value for a visit is “Visit 1 Day 29”, but if you only want to display “Day 29”, you can substring out “Visit 1” using a substring derivation.    
- Merge Variables to Data Sets   – Use Merge derivations to bring variables from one dataset into another, that is, to m erge a  data set variable   from one data set into a target data set. These derivations vary depending on which types of datasets you use to perform the merge (multiple record per patient datasets vs. single record per patient datasets). When merging from MRPP to MRPP, a “linking” variable must be present in the dataset to ensure the merge functions as designed. 
- Check all that Apply – U se Check all that apply derivations when Rave data is structured such that multiple options can apply to a single field. For example, multiple races can be selected in the demographics form. By using this derived variable type, you can automatically concatenate Boolean data set variables to create a text variable.  
- Conditional Concatenate   - Use Concatenate derivations to concatenate mathematical and logical expressions. For example, you can bring together values in two fields, namely "Visit" and " Timepoint" in Rave, to create a new derived field. 
 You can also update derived variables' names and labels.
 Important : Your  customer-defined platform role   must include the following permissions to create and update derived variables:
- View Derived Variables 
- Manage Derived Variables 
## Who Uses Derived Variables?
 Clinical study managers, clinical research associates, site monitors, central monitors, safety monitors, medical monitors, data managers, biostaticians, programmers, and clinical reviewers.
## How Does Derived Variables Work?
 The Derived Variables capability in Data Surveillance and RBQM enables you to create derived variables. You can then:
- View and investigate the derived variables as part of your overall study data review process. 
- Use derived variables to : 
- Build data listings . 
- Create visualizations . 
- Add elements to patient profile designs . 
- Configure within Data Mapping the datasets and variables that Data Surveillance and RBQM use to consume and produce the reports, statistical analysis, and visual output for: 
- Data anomaly detection and trends . 
- Potential duplication patients . 
- Rounding and propagating vital sign records . 
- RECIST 1.1 dashboard plots . 
- Define and add custom QTLs and custom KRIs that target specific facets of your study data that you want to monitor for risk. 
 In addition, you can: 
- View the derived variables in your study data along with configuration details for each derived variable. 
- Edit Derived Variables . 
- Copy Derived Variables 
- Merge Variables into Data Sets 
 Note : In Data Surveillance, the list of available datasets and variables that you can view and select from appends derived variable names with the blue DERIVED icon. 
## What Are the Benefits of Derived Variables?
 With derived variables, you can  perform the following actions: 
- Create Derived Variable from Expression – A pply mathematical and logical operations to data set variables. 
- Create Derived Variable to Show Data Refresh Date – S how the day  that the data refresh occurs in Derived Variables. 
- Create Derived Variable with Difference in Dates Calculation – C alculate the number of days between two dates. 
- Create Derived Variable with Concatenated Text – Link text variables. 
- Create Derived Variable with Text Substring – Derive a subset of text. 
- Merge Variables to Data Sets – Merge a  data set variable   from one data set into a target data set. 
- Check all that Apply - Concatenate Boolean data set variables to create a text variable. 
- Conditional Concatenate - Concatenate mathematical and logical expressions.  
 You can also update derived variables' names and labels.

- Create Derived Variable with Text Substring – Use Substring derivations to derive a subset of alphanumeric or numeric characters from a given text field. For example, if a field value for a visit is “Visit 1 Day 29”, but if you only want to display “Day 29”, you can substring out “Visit 1” using a substring derivation.    
- Merge Variables to Data Sets   – Use Merge derivations to bring variables from one dataset into another, that is, to m erge a  data set variable   from one data set into a target data set. These derivations vary depending on which types of datasets you use to perform the merge (multiple record per patient datasets vs. single record per patient datasets). When merging from MRPP to MRPP, a “linking” variable must be present in the dataset to ensure the merge functions as designed. 
- Check all that Apply – U se Check all that apply derivations when Rave data is structured such that multiple options can apply to a single field. For example, multiple races can be selected in the demographics form. By using this derived variable type, you can automatically concatenate Boolean data set variables to create a text variable.  
- Conditional Concatenate   - Use Concatenate derivations to concatenate mathematical and logical expressions. For example, you can bring together values in two fields, namely "Visit" and " Timepoint" in Rave, to create a new derived field. 
 You can also update derived variables' names and labels.
 Important : Your  customer-defined platform role   must include the following permissions to create and update derived variables:
- View Derived Variables 
- Manage Derived Variables 
## Who Uses Derived Variables?
 Clinical study managers, clinical research associates, site monitors, central monitors, safety monitors, medical monitors, data managers, biostaticians, programmers, and clinical reviewers.
## How Does Derived Variables Work?
 The Derived Variables capability in Data Surveillance and RBQM enables you to create derived variables. You can then:
- View and investigate the derived variables as part of your overall study data review process. 
- Use derived variables to : 
- Build data listings . 
- Create visualizations . 
- Add elements to patient profile designs . 
- Configure within Data Mapping the datasets and variables that Data Surveillance and RBQM use to consume and produce the reports, statistical analysis, and visual output for: 
- Data anomaly detection and trends . 
- Potential duplication patients . 
- Rounding and propagating vital sign records . 
- RECIST 1.1 dashboard plots . 
- Define and add custom QTLs and custom KRIs that target specific facets of your study data that you want to monitor for risk. 
 In addition, you can: 
- View the derived variables in your study data along with configuration details for each derived variable. 
- Edit Derived Variables . 
- Copy Derived Variables 
- Merge Variables into Data Sets 
 Note : In Data Surveillance, the list of available datasets and variables that you can view and select from appends derived variable names with the blue DERIVED icon. 
## What Are the Benefits of Derived Variables?
 With derived variables, you can  perform the following actions: 
- Create Derived Variable from Expression – A pply mathematical and logical operations to data set variables. 
- Create Derived Variable to Show Data Refresh Date – S how the day  that the data refresh occurs in Derived Variables. 
- Create Derived Variable with Difference in Dates Calculation – C alculate the number of days between two dates. 
- Create Derived Variable with Concatenated Text – Link text variables. 
- Create Derived Variable with Text Substring – Derive a subset of text. 
- Merge Variables to Data Sets – Merge a  data set variable   from one data set into a target data set. 
- Check all that Apply - Concatenate Boolean data set variables to create a text variable. 
- Conditional Concatenate - Concatenate mathematical and logical expressions.  
 You can also update derived variables' names and labels.

## Design Patient Profiles
 The workflow progress bar below illustrates the recommended patient profile design workflow from creation to completion.
 The goal of Patient Profiles is to build patient profile designs. You build the patient profile design infrastructure using containers of information known as elements. Elements consist of headers , flags ,  tables , and timelines . And then you populate your elements with data in the form of variables, which derive from multiple preloaded study environment-specific data sets.
 At this point, you can create your design  and begin adding elements .
 When adding elements, and based on the element type you are working with, you can:
- define element details; 
- adjust the placement of variables, rows, and columns within elements; 
- configure variable data points to show in the color of your choosing; 
- and much more. 
 After adding elements to your profile design, you can:
- arrange where the elements appear in the design layout ; and 
- apply color-coding to entire element sections. 
 Meanwhile, throughout the course of the patient profile design process, you can:
- view patient profiles   with study data to help you evaluate how the profile design is taking shape in real time. 
 When satisfied with your design and layout, you can:
- review and generate reports based on the profile design. 
 You can also perform various design management tasks such as:
- Reassign Master Designs 
- Duplicate Designs Within Studies 
- Delete Designs 
- Rename Designs 
 Note : In Data Surveillance, s tudy data automatically refreshes twice daily at approximately 9:00am (EST) and 9:00pm (EST), and the data presented within the user interface is current as of 11:00 pm (EST) the previous day, and 11:00 am (EST) the same day, respectively. You can refresh Patient Profiles twice daily based on these refresh schedules. For more information, see Clinical Data Studio Data Pipeline.

## Map Data Set Analysis Data
 You can configure within Data Surveillance Configuration the data sets and variables that RBQM uses to consume and produce the statistical analysis and visual output for data anomaly detection plots. 
 Tips :   
-   You do not need to build a patient profile to view the data anomaly detection analysis on your study data in Statistical Monitoring. You can quickly configure in a simple, centralized workspace in Data Mapping the specific study data that you want RBQM to analyze. 
-  You can also create derived variables using Data Connect for cross domain analysis.  
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu.
The Data Mapping page appears with the Dataset Configuration tab selected by default. 
- Locate the visit data set in the Data Sets list, and then click and drop the visit data set in Visit Dataset Selection .
 Important : You must include your visit data set in the data set configuration to ensure RBQM thoroughly and accurately reports against the timeline of events.
- After configuring your visit data set, scroll back to the Data Sets list, and find and click a data set containing variables that you want to configure RBQM to consume and analyze.
 Tip : The selected data set name shows above the Record Per Patient field. Click the image below to enlarge.
- In Record Per Patient , select Single Record (SRPP) or Multiple Record (MRPP) .
The currently selected data set expands in the Data Sets list and shows the selectable list of variables contained within the data set.
 Note :  You must select the record per patient first before you can select the variables you want to configure for analysis.
- In Record Per Patient , select one of the following:
- Single Record (SRPP) – A patient record that is only collected once per patient within the data set; for example, demographics, randomization, or end of study. 
- Multiple Record (MRPP) – A patient record that is collected multiple times per patient within the data set; for example, weight, blood pressure, or pulse. 
- Select the variables within the data set that you want to configure RBQM to consume and analyze.  indicates that the variable is selected for consumption and analysis in RBQM data anomaly detection plot analysis.
 Tip : Select only critical data that you want RBQM to consume and analyze. This ensures that RBQM produces the cleanest, most effective statistical analysis and visual output on the data most pertinent to your study.
 Important : If you want to identify anomalies in other fields, you cannot configure more than: 
- 200 fields across all forms for large studies 
- 1200 fields across all forms for small studies 
- Optional . Select Pivot Data to pivot a transposed study data set that you want RBQM to analyze.
Selecting Pivot Data reveals three more optional fields: Procedure Name, Procedure Value, and Category.
 Note : You most likely should not need to pivot data ingested from Medidata Rave.
- As necessary, click and drop the data sets you want to use for:
- Procedure Name   –   Optional .   The name of the test done that collected the records in the data set.   Procedure Name only appears when you turn on the Pivot Data button. 
- Procedure Value   –   Optional . The values collected in the procedure name's fields. Procedure Value only appears when you turn on the Pivot Data button. 
- Category   –   Optional .   A subset of the records collected in the data set. Category only appears when you turn on the Pivot button. 
- Repeat steps 5-9 for each data set containing variables that you want to configure RBQM to consume and analyze.
 Tip : Data Surveillance signifies data sets that have at least one variable included in the data set configuration with a green marker next to the data set name in the Data Sets list. For example: . Data sets that have no variables included in the error plot configuration have a blue marker: 
 Important : Do not map more than 3000 variables cumulatively across all datasets; otherwise, Data Anomaly Detection cannot visualize the analysis.
- Click Save .
The next data refresh in Statistical Monitoring will run the data anomaly detection plot analysis on the data sets and variables currently saved and configured in the data set configuration.

===== PAGE: dm_-map_event_analysis_data.html | Map Event Analysis Data =====
## Map Event Analysis Data
 You can map the data sets and variables that Data Surveillance and RBQM consume to analyze conditions, treatments, and medical history events for event incidence, under-or-over reporting of events, and AI data reconciliation reports. You can map data both from Medidata Rave or externally coded studies. 
 Event analysis configuration:
- Simplifies data mapping by requiring only the key variables for Data Surveillance and RBQM to perform its study data analysis.  
- Optimizes data mapping by consolidating the configuration and mapping tasks in one centralized location. 
- Allows you to capture data for multiple domains like Adverse Events, Reactogenicity, Concomitant Medication, and Concomitant Procedures.
- Ensures Data Surveillance and RBQM analyze the correct terms and saves hours of configuration time. 
 Important : Within the event analysis configuration, you must always: 
- Select the exact field from Rave and ensure the field mapping does not include a suffix; for example, _TXT or _DTC. 
- Pick the raw or verbatim terms for conditions, treatments, and medical history terms. This enables Data Surveillance and RBQM to provide the most accurate event incidence, under-over reporting events, and Reconciliation analysis.  
- Event Incidence, AI Reconciliation and Under Over Reporting do not support data entry as a check box option in Rave for Ongoing MH.
## Set Data Source
 Data Surveillance and RBQM use the study you configure as the data source in the Event Analysis tab for analysis and reporting. Data managers can set up either fully ingested Rave studies or externally coded studies.
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu.
 The Data Mapping page appears. 
- Click the Event Analysis tab. 
- Click Set Data Source . 
- The Set Data Source window shows a ' Selecting a different data source will remove all current mappings. Would you like to proceed?' message. Select one of the following:
- Rave , if your study is fully ingested into Rave. 
- External , if you are using a study with a combination of Rave and externally coded data from WHODRUG or MEDRA dictionaries. That is, if you are using derived datasets generated and activated in Data Connect, your study data uses an external code as data source. 
- Click Confirm .
 Note : You can configure only one data source at a time. For new studies, no default data source selection exists. For existing studies, based on the data source you select, all existing event analysis mappings for conditions, treatments and medical history are removed. You must reconfigure the data mappings.
 Before selecting an external data source, you must first import that external data using Data Connect's Imports capability  or through Ingestor . For more information, see Clinical Data Studio's Data Pipeline . You cannot perform data reconciliation activities or submit queries for derived datasets in AI Reconciliation  if you do not map to the correct study data source.

===== PAGE: dm_-map_potential_duplicate_patient_data.html | Map Potential Duplicate Patient Data =====
## Map Potential Duplicate Patient Data
 Duplicate patients are patients who enroll in clinical trials for financial gain or for extra dosages of medication. Duplicate patients threaten both participant safety and the integrity of research findings. Statistical Monitoring uncovers potential duplicate patients by analyzing six demographics: date of birth, gender, height, weight, race, ethnicity. In addition, Statistical Monitoring analyzes the physical distance within 100 miles of site location of each patient to find patients that look very similar. 
 With Data Mapping, you can map the six demographic parameters: date of birth, gender, height, weight, race, and ethnicity to the corresponding reference variables from data sets in your study environment and save the configuration, which Medidata's data science microservice algorithms consume. Based on the analytics, Statistical Monitoring automatically generates the configuration data analysis and renders the visualization output as a global heat and site level map. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu.
 The Data Mapping page appears. 
- Click the Potential Duplicate Patients tab. 
- For each of the following reference demographic, select a variable to map from any data set in your study. For example, you can map the Date of Birth demographic to DOB from the Chemistry (CHEM) data set.
- Date Of Birth   
- Weight  
- Height  
- Gender 
- Race
 Note : If Race data values are collected by selecting a check box for each race in Medidata Rave, then we suggest creating a Check All That Apply derivation using the Derived Variables capability. Doing so ensures that RBQM pulls in all possible race values as mappable variables as part of the Duplicate Patient Configuration. To learn more, see Create Derived Variable with Check All That Apply .
- Ethnicity
 Note : You can select mapped variables, including derived variables, from different data sets to map to the reference demographic.
 Tip : The Data Set and Mapped Variable menus include duplicate field options. Be sure to select the exact field from Rave and ensure the field mapping does not include a suffix (_TXT, _DTC, for example). If one of the six fields required to be mapped do not exist in Rave, you can use a proxy and the algorithm will still work; however, it will be less accurate.
- Click Update .

 You can configure the vital sign data sets and collection date variables that RBQM consumes to analyze and visually render the sites that may be rounding and propagating vital sign records.

===== PAGE: download_kri_configuration_reports.html | Download KRI Configuration Reports =====
## Download KRI Configuration Reports
 You can download key risk indicator (KRI) configuration reports, which contain pertinent configuration information about the KRIs in your study environment. The reports provide configuration details in a clear, easy-to-read, and exchangeable format.
 Note : System KRIs are not available in KRI Configuration Report download files.
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > KRIs in the left-hand menu.
- On the Key Risk Indicators page, click Report .
The Detect Configuration Manager - Config Report - KRIs XLS file downloads to your machine. 
- Open the file.
 Column Descriptions 
- Risk Category – A broad, categorized area of risk within which individual key risk indicators are identified, tracked, and mitigated. Risk categories and data sets have a parent-child relationship. 
- Risk Category Weightage – Indicates whether the KRI's risk category is configured as Low, Medium, or High Risk. 
- Indicator Type  – Specifies whether the KRI is a numeric KRI or percentage KRI . 
- Indicator Name  – The unique label that identifies the KRI. 
- Description  – Details about what the KRI is, what it is meant to calculate and track, or any other helpful information. 
- Status – Indicates whether the KRI is active or inactive. Active KRIs get their data filtered, calculated, and shown in the KRI Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory.  Inactive KRIs do not get calculated or shown in the KRI Dashboard, Risk Assessment, or Risk Inventory. System KRIs are active by default. 
- Add to SRI – Indicates whether or not the KRI is configured as being factored in to RBQM's site risk analysis. 
- Calculation Type  – The type of calculation that the custom KRI uses to perform on the selected variable. Custom KRIs can use one of the following standard calculation types:
- Count  – Calculates the average record count in the selected data set. The Count calculation is only available at the data set level. 
- 
- Count Values  – Calculates the average count of records in the study that meet a specified criteria based on the selected variable. Valid only for data of a 1 or 0. 
- Mean  – Calculates the mean value of a numeric data field based on the selected variable at the site. 
- Rate  – Calculates the average record count in the selected data set over time. The Rate calculation is only available at the data set level. 
- Rate Values – Calculates the average percentage in a site of non-missing, non-zero values for a given variable. Use cases include the fraction of Adverse Events which are Serious, where Serious was 1 for an SAE, and 0 for a non-SAE event, or the fraction of a lab parameter out of normal range. 
- Standard Deviation  – Calculates the amount of dispersion or variance in a set of observed values based on the selected variable. 
- Percentage  – A user-defined binary expression that assesses if subjects meet specified conditions or criteria within a targeted risk area.
 Note : The percentage calculation type only applies to custom percentage KRIs.
- Dataset – The  data set  that the custom KRI uses to perform the KRI calculation on. 
- Variable – The  variable  that the custom KRI uses to perform the KRI calculation on. 
- Threshold Type –  Indicates whether the KRI's threshold is user-defined or system-defined. 
- Moderate Risk Threshold –  The configured value for the KRI's lowest risk limit. 
- High Risk Threshold – The configured value for the KRI highest risk limit. 
- Numerator Expression – The identified logic configured for the KRI's numerator used to query for matching subjects. The numerator expression targets the entire data set population. 
- Denominator Expression – The identified logic configured for the KRI's denominator used to query for matching subjects. The denominator expression targets a specific dataset population subset. 
- Created On – The KRI's original creation date. 
- Updated By – The last person to update the KRI configuration. 
- Updated On – The date when the KRI configuration was most recently updated. 
- Modification Note – The reason for changing KRI configuration. 
- Deactivated At – The date when the KRI was last deactivated.

## Download QTL Configuration Reports
 You can download quality tolerance limits (QTL)  configuration reports, which contain pertinent configuration information about the QTLs in your study environment. The reports provide configuration details in a clear, easy-to-read, and exchangeable format.

The Detect Configuration Manager - Config Report - QTLs XLS file downloads to your machine

 Column Descriptions 
- Parameter  – A study variable that is assessed at the study level. 
- Definition  – A dditional details that explain what the parameter is meant to monitor and how it is measured. 
- Status  – Indicates whether the QTL is currently active or inactive. Active QTLs are set so that their data gets filtered, calculated, and shown in the QTL Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory . Inactive QTLs do not get calculated or shown in the QTL Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory. 
- Expectation  – T he QTL's expected median value based on historical data. 
- Trigger Point – The minimum required number of patients that meet the QTL's conditions for RBQM to analyze and output the QTL's results in RBQM. 
- Final Population – Total number of patients expected to enroll in the study. 
- Numerator Expression – Details the numerator query's full condition set configured for the QTL. 
- Denominator Expression – Details the denominator query's full condition set configured for the QTL.

- Deactivated By – The person who deactivated the QTL.

## Download the Listings Table
 You can download the Listing Manager page > Listings table locally as a CSV file. Downloading the Listings table enables you to:

- 
 If necessary, access the Manage Listing page.

The Data Listings page shows.

 The Listings table downloads as a CSV file to your browser. The Listings Manager CSV file contains the following details:
- Name – The listing's object identifier (OID). 
- Expression – The data listing's user-defined conditional expression, which Data Surveillance runs against your study data to capture the patient records within a specified variable that match the expression's defined specifications. In general, expressions are built to identify and report high-risk data points that your study team can review and investigate as necessary.

- Created – The listing's creation date is formatted as: DD MON YYYY 
- Updated by – The user who most recently updated the listing. 
- Last Updated – The data listing's creation date or when the last saved edit occurred. The date is formatted as: DD MON YYYY

- Status – Shows either Draft or Approved. The status indicates whether the listing is in approved or draft status. 
- Activated – Shows either Yes or No. Yes indicates that the listing currently shows in its Approved Listings table or Draft Listings table. No indicates that the listing is currently hidden from the Approved Listings table or Draft Listings table.

===== PAGE: dv_-_create_derived_variable_from_expression.html | Create Derived Variable from Expression =====
## Create Derived Variable from Expression
 You can build a derived variable by using the expression builder to apply mathematical and logical operations on data set variables.  For example, use derived variables to show particular values such as “If Visit Name = Day 1, then show “Randomization”, Else = "Null "" or"If SYSBP > 60, then show LOW, else HIGH”. These expressions can use multiple conditions and can be rather complex. You can also build a logical expression with conditional logic. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Derived Variables in the left-hand menu. 
- Click  Create Derived Variable . 
- Identify and drag a data set  from the Data Sets list into the Configure Variable section. For example, Adverse Events. 
- Enter the derived variable’s identification information. 
- Name – Object identifier (OID) of derived variable. For example, "AESER+AESER_TXT". Must be unique. 
- Label  – Name for derived variable to appear in other applications. This can be the same as the Name field, or a more specific descriptor. For example, "AE Serious, Full". 
- Select Expression Builder from the Derived Variable Type menu. 
- (Optional) Form the conditional expression: 
- Navigate to the Operator tab, and drag If Then Else into the expression builder. 
- Drag data set variables into the respective If , Then , and Else fields. 
- Complete the expression: 
- Navigate to the  Data Set s  tab, and drag data set variables into the expression builder fields.
 Note : If data set variables include unknowns, the data set replaces them with interpolated (enriched) fields like _INT, or _DTC. For example, the source date is missing the day, the enriched _INT field interpolates the 1st day of the month, and _DTC fields drop the unknown value. If the source field uses dictionary terms, the enriched _TXT field shows the coded terms.
- Navigate to the Operator  tab, and drag various operators and values i nto the expression builder fields.
 Note : If you leave the expression incomplete, the following warning message appears: " Complete the expression by specifying at least one variable, one operator, and one variable or value to compare". 
- Optional . Click  Preview  to display the preview panel.
With the preview panel, you can review the derived variable and adjust the variable's parameters before saving.
- Click  Save .
 In Data Surveillance and RBQM, the list of available datasets and variables that you can view and select from include derived variables at the bottom of the list. In Data Surveillance, the list of available datasets and variables appends derived variable names with the blue DERIVED icon.

===== PAGE: dv_-_create_derived_variable_to_show_data_refresh_date.html | Create Derived Variable to Show Data Refresh Date =====
## Create Derived Variable to Show Data Refresh Date
 You can create a derived variable to show the day when the data refresh occurs in Derived Variables .  Today’s date is typically used as a reference derivation for subsequent derivations. This date field is dynamic, meaning the value for “Today’s Date” will constantly update with each data refresh. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Derived Variables in the left-hand menu. 
- Click  Create Derived Variable . 
- Identify and drag a data set f rom the Data Sets list into the Configure Variable section. For example, Adverse Events.
 Note : If data set variables include unknowns, the data set replaces them with interpolated (enriched) fields like _INT, or _DTC. For example, if the source date is missing the day, the enriched _INT field interpolates the 1st day of the month, and _DTC fields drop the unknown value. If the source field uses dictionary terms, the enriched _TXT field shows the coded terms. Source fields refer to the original source of a data point, while enriched fields add extra information or context to the source data. Enriched fields are used to provide more detail about the about source fields, or to add derived information that is not directly present in the original source. 
- Enter the derived variable’s identification information. 
- Name – Object identifier (OID) of derived variable. For example, Today. Must be unique. 
- Label  –  N ame for derived variable to appear in other applications. This can be the same as the Name field, or a more specific descriptor. For example, Today. 
- Select Today   from the Derived Variable Type   menu.

- Click  Save .
 In Data Surveillance and RBQM, the list of available datasets and variables that you can view and select from include derived variables at the bottom of the list. In Data Surveillance, the list of available datasets and variables appends derived variable names with the blue DERIVED icon.

===== PAGE: dv_-_create_derived_variable_with_check_all_that_apply.html | Create Derived Variable with Check All That Apply =====
## Create Derived Variable with Check All That Apply
 You can combine multiple Boolean data set variables into a single derived variable. 
 U 
 se Check all that apply derivations when Medidata Rave data is structured such that multiple options can apply to a single field. For example, multiple races can be selected in the demographics form. By using this derived variable type, you can automatically concatenate Boolean data set variables to create a text variable.

## Create Derived Variable with Text Substring
 You can truncate text-based data set variables into a subset of text. Use Substring derivations to derive a subset of alphanumeric or numeric characters from a given text field. For example, if a field value for a visit is “Visit 1 Day 29”, but if you only want to display “Day 29”, you can substring out “Visit 1” using a substring derivation. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Derived Variables in the left-hand menu. 
- Click  Create Derived Variable . 
- Select a data set from the Data Sets list and drag into the Configure Variable section. For example, Adverse Events.
 Note : If data set variables include unknowns, the data set replaces them with interpolated (enriched) fields like _INT, or _DTC. For example, if the source date is missing the day, the enriched _INT field interpolates the 1st day of the month, and _DTC fields drop the unknown value. If the source field uses dictionary terms, the enriched _TXT field shows the coded terms. Source fields refer to the original source of a data point, while enriched fields add extra information or context to the source data.   Enriched fields are used to provide more detail about the about source fields, or to add derived information not directly present within the original source.  
If derived datasets from Data Connect include raw dates, and were activated in Data Connect prior to March 2025, you must add raw dates, republish, and activate the datasets in Data Connect for use in Data Surveillance. For more details, see Add Partial Dates for Published Derived Datasets . 
- Enter the derived variable's  identification information.

- Select Substring from the Derived Variable Type menu. 
- Drag a text variable into the  Variable field. 
- Complete the Substring wizard:
- Character start – Enter the first character of the derived variable data. Character start defaults to one and must be one or greater. 
- Character count – Enter the length of the derived variable data. Character count defaults to one and must be one or greater.
 Note :  If the substring parameters exceed the parameters of the original text, then empty spaces appear in substring. For example, if the o riginal text is "Intermittent", c haracter start is 6, c haracter count is 10, then t he result is "mittent" with three trailing spaces.

 You can merge a data set variable containing multiple records over multiple visits with another data set containing multiple records over multiple visits. For example, merging an Adverse Events data set variable to the Chemistry data set. 
 Important: 
- You must add a subset value and preference, even if you merge SRPP to SRPP, or SRPP to MRPP. 
- For a subset value, add the study ID.

- Click   Create Derived Variable .

 Note:   If data set variables include unknowns, the data set replaces them with interpolated (enriched) fields like _INT, or_ DTC . For example, if the source date is missing the day, the enriched _INT field interpolates the 1st day of the month, and _DTC fields drop the unknown value. If the source field uses dictionary terms, the enriched _TXT field shows the coded terms. 
- Enter the derived variable’s identification information: 
- Name – Object identifier (OID) of derived variable. For example, Adverse Events – CHEMDT. Must be unique.

 Note : Always confirm that you have selected the correct merge type for the dataset. Otherwise, Data Surveillance and RBQM will fail to refresh and output its statistical analysis on future data snapshots.

- Complete the merge wizard: 
- Source Merge Variable – Drag the data set variable that you want to merge into the target data set. 
- Target Merge Variable – Drag the data set variable that you want the source merge variable to merge with.
The source merge variable aligns with each record of the multiple-record target variable.
 Note : The Source Merge Variable and Target Merge Variable name must be the same.
- Subset Variable – If applicable, d rag a data set variable from the selected source merge variable's data set that you want to merge a value from. The subset variable serves as a reference variable to narrow down the multiple-record source data set variable into a single record to merge into the target data set.
 Note : The Subset Variable must be different from the Source Merge Variable and Target Merge Variable. Otherwise, Clinical Data Studio's data workflow may not work correctly.
- Subset Value –   If applicable, select a value from the list to merge into the target data set. The subset value is a value from the selected subset variable. The subset value completes the process to narrow down the multiple-record source data set to single record.
 Note : Derived Variables populates the subset value field based on the selected subset variable. In some cases, the subset values may not contain values. In those cases, you may disregard the field.
- Preference –   Optional . If applicable, based on the selected subset variable and subset value, select which source data set variable value to merge into the target data set. For date or numeric values, select to merge the maximum or minimum value from the source data set variable. For text values, the first reported value is automatically merged. 
- Click  Save .

===== PAGE: event_incidence.html | Event Incidence =====
## Event Incidence
 The Event Incidence Plot shows the reported events and the incidence rate in which those events occurred within a domain at the site and study level. You can use the Event Incidence Plot to determine sites whose reporting of events may require further investigation or corrective action as well as whether a drug should be discontinued. 
## What Is the Event Incidence Plot?
 The Event Incidence Plot is a scatter plot that shows the reporting incidence of reported concomitant medications and adverse events at the site and study level.
## What Is the Purpose of the Event Incidence Plot?
 You can use the Event Incidence Plot to:
- Analyze which sites have incidence rates for a given event that are considered statistically different. RBQM considers these sites as outliers  or extreme outliers when compared to overall incidence rates across all sites.
 Note : RBQM identifies o utliers as sites that have higher or lower incidence rates than the study level or sites with no events. RBQM's algorithms account for the number of patients at a site when determining if the site is an outlier. 
- Confirm that reported adverse events are in line with protocol expectations (that is, identify prevalence of unexpected events for sites, countries, or overall). 
- Identify potential correlation between events (such as, if many patients at a site experience upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) and increased heart rates). 
- Identify patients at outlier sites that have unusual reporting patterns and review data using direct link to patient profiles (such as, identify events with overlapping start/stop dates, report symptoms rather than diagnosis).  
- Quickly identify "unable to code" terms or sites with high incidences of "unable to code" terms.  
## Who Uses the Event Incidence Plot?
 The following types of users, among many others, use the Event Incidence Plot:
- Central Monitors – Determine if sites are correctly tracking events. For example, if sites are over or underreporting events. 
- Data Managers – Ensure sites are tracking the right information or entering information correctly. 
- Medical Monitors – Evaluate how often events occur at sites to determine drug safety and efficacy. 
## What Are the Benefits of Using the Event Incidence Plot?
 By analyzing event terms in your study, you can:
- Identify whether sites are tracking events correctly. For example, whether a site is overreporting or underreporting adverse events . 
- Confirm that adverse events are in line with expectations according to the study’s safety plan. 
- View event trending patterns. For example, if many patients at a site experience headache. 
- Centralized Statistical Monitoring (CSM) correlation between events. For example, if many patients at a site experience URTI and increased heart rate. 
- Identify sites that have significantly higher or lower incidence rates for individual events compared to overall study event incidence rates. 
 Based on your findings, you can determine appropriate corresponding actions such as:
- Investigating sites to ensure sites properly follow protocols and procedures. 
- Discontinuing the drug. 
## How Do I Use and Interpret the Event Incidence Plot?
 See  Investigate Data Using the Event Incidence Plot .
## How Do I Refresh Event Incidence to Output the Latest Study Data Analysis?
 See  Schedule or Trigger When Statistical Monitoring Refreshes and Outputs the Latest Study Data Analysis .
## How Do I Review Individual Patient Profiles?
 See  View Individual Patient Profiles from the Event Incidence Plot Page .
## How Do I Log and Track Issues?
 You can manually raise signals for Event Incidence Plots, and raise issues for the signals. See log issues that require further investigation or mitigation on the   Signals page .  
## How Do I View the Event Incidence Plot Audit Report?
 The Event Incidence Plot Audit Report no longer exists as there are no auditable actions in Event Incidence .

===== PAGE: event_outlier_detection_methodology.html | Event Outlier Detection Methodology =====
## Event Outlier Detection Methodology
 Statistical Monitoring identifies sites with outlying reported event data by calculating the p -value for each event term reported at the site level. Statistical Monitoring also calculates the p -value for sites where the event was not reported. 
- p -value – A Statistical Monitoring calculation that measures the probability of a site experiencing a given event's incidence rate compared to that event's overall incidence rate across all other sites in the study. 
- Extreme Outlier Site – Sites with a p -value  less than 0.01 for a given event's incidence rate. The probability of the site having its current incidence rate for an event is extremely low considering the event's incidence rate across all other sites. This indicates that there may be issues with how this event has been reported at the site, which may require further investigation. 
- Outlier Site – Sites with a p -value  between 0.01 and 0.05 for a given event's incidence rate. The probability of the site having its current incidence rate for an event is very low considering the event's incidence rate across all other sites. This indicates that there may be issues with how this event has been reported at the site, which may require further investigation. 
- Normal Site – Sites with a p -value  greater than 0.05 for a given event's incidence rate. The probability of the site having its current incidence rate for an event is statistically normal considering the event's incidence rate across all other sites. 
 Important :  RBQM does not factor events that occur only once in the study into the event incidence analysis.

The listing results download to your browser as a .xlsx file. 
- Open and save the file.
The report name is formatted by default as <listing name>_<snapshot date in weekday, dd Mmm yyyy hh_mm_ss>. For example, "Listing Name Wed, 05 Apr 2023 03_13_05".
 Field and Column Descriptions 
- Updated By – The last user to refresh the data listing. 
- Last Updated – The timestamp of the data listing's last successful data refresh. 
- Patient ID – The ID of the patient whose data matched the criteria specified in the listings conditional expression. 
- Site – The site that the patient belongs to. 
- Country – The three-letter abbreviation for country in which the site resides. 
- Rave Query Status – Specifies whether the Rave query is currently open, processed, or closed. 
- Variable – Each column header to the right of the Rave Query Status column header represents a variable that the data listing's expression is configured to run against. Variable columns list the variable's data point entries captured by the data listing's conditional expression.

===== PAGE: flag__track__and_audit_reviewed_study_data.html | Flag, Track, and Audit Reviewed Study Data =====
## Flag, Track, and Audit Reviewed Study Data
 You can mark outlier data points  on Data Anomaly Detection plots as reviewed. Marking outlier data points as reviewed helps you and other team members identify which data has or has not been reviewed. This optimizes your overall team performance by preventing repeat work and helping your team recognize and focus on the data that still requires review. 
## Flag Reviewed Study Data
 After you review individual outlier data points on Data Anomaly Detection plots, you can mark those data points as reviewed. Marking outlier data points as reviewed helps you and other team members identify which data has or has not been reviewed.
 Important : Only users with Review CSM permissions can mark study data as reviewed.
- If necessary,  access the Data Anomaly Detection page . 
- Select the Domain Set . 
- Select the Variable .
The list of plots associated with the selected variable show in the Plot table below.
- Plot Name – The variable or variables that RBQM has analyzed. 
- # Outliers  – The total number of the variable's data points that are considered outliers. 
- Click a plot name.
 The selected plot shows in the plot visualization along with summary information below. 
- Scroll down the Data Anomaly Detection page to the Summary section. 
- Click the View By filter and select Data: Top 100 Outliers . 
- Find the data point you want to mark as reviewed in the Summary table.
 Tip: Filter and Sort the Summary Table to Help Find the Data You Need
- To filter the Summary table to show only data from a specific patient, click the Patient filter, and select a patient ID. 
- By default, the Summary table is sorted by Discrepancy Score .  Click any column header to sort the table by that column. The sorted header shows in blue font.  indicates that the column is sorted in descending numeric order (highest value at the top, lowest at the bottom).  Click a column header twice  to sort in ascending numeric order (lowest value at the top, highest at the bottom). 
- Click  in the Actions column for the corresponding data point. 
- Click Mark as Reviewed .
 Important : The Mark as Reviewed option is only active for users with Review CSM permissions. Otherwise, this option is grayed-out and inactive.
 The data point's Status column updates to show , which indicates the data point as reviewed. The review status change also gets recorded in the data point's review audit history. To learn more about the review audit history, see Track and Audit Reviewed Study Data .

===== PAGE: generate_and_download_qtl_reports.html | Generate and Download QTL Reports =====
## Generate and Download QTL Reports
 You can generate reports to view the historical performance of one or more parameters whose QTLs you are tracking in your study. QTL reports provide a larger, clearer view of the QTL graph and more comprehensive details than what the QTL Dashboard provides. You can also download QTL reports to store locally to better view and share reports without the need to log in to RBQM. 
- Access RBQM , and then click QTLs in the left-hand menu.
 The QTL Dashboard page shows. 
- Click Generate Report .
The Generate QTL Report window appears.
 Column Descriptions 
- QTL Name – The descriptive title for the parameter whose QTL values you are tracking. 
- Observed Today – The parameter's QTL value as of RBQM's most recent data analysis on your study data. 
- Expectation – The expected patient population percentage to not meet the study parameter's criteria. 
- Upper Limit – T he maximum patient population percentage to not meet the study parameter's criteria before the QTL is considered high risk. 
- Select the check box next to each QTL that you want to include in the report. 
 Tip : Select the check box in the QTL Name column header to select all QTLs. 
- Click Report Preview in the lower right-hand corner of the Generate QTL Report module.
The Report Preview generates the QTL's Time View line graph, which shows QTL performance relative to expectation over time. A Summary table supplements the graph underneath. 
- The following details explain how to read and interpret the QTL Report: 
- The name and description of the parameter appears at the top of each QTL line graph. 
- The x-axis represents the dates in which RBQM performed a data analysis. 
- The y-axis represents the observed QTL percentage value. 
- The solid green line represents the expected patient population percentage to not meet the study parameter's criteria. QTL percentages that RBQM assesses as in range of the expectation are considered healthy and do not require any action. 
- The dotted yellow line represents t he minimum patient population percentage that cannot meet the study parameter's criteria before RBQM considers the parameter to be at risk. P arameters whose QTL values exceed the threshold indicate potential underlying systemic issues, which may compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues. 
- The dotted red line represents the minimum patient population percentage that cannot meet the study parameter's criteria before RBQM considers the parameter to be high risk. P arameters whose QTL values exceed the upper limit indicate potential underlying systemic issues, which may compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues. 
- A solid blue line represents the observed QTL values that are within an acceptable range at each timepoint when RBQM performed a data analysis. 
- A solid red line represents observed QTL values that are considered an excursion  at each timepoint when RBQM performed a data analysis. 
- The actual observed QTL value data point is represented by:
- (blue) – The observed QTL value is within the acceptable range below the threshold. 
- (red) – The observed QTL value has exceeded threshold. P arameters whose QTL values exceed the threshold indicate potential underlying systemic issues, which may compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues. 
- (red) – The observed QTL value is an excursion . RBQM flags and identifies QTL excursions when : 
- The percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's specified criteria has exceeded the upper limit, and 
- Is impossible to move the QTL value back within a healthy range of the QTL's expected value no matter the actions taken by the project team.
 Important : QTL excursions indicate that the study quality is compromised to the point that the study may need to be shut down or restarted.
- You can hover your cursor on any data point to view:
- Date – The dates in which RBQM performed a data analysis on your study data and recorded the parameter's QTL value. 
- # of Patients – The number of patients enrolled in the study. 
- Observed – The parameter's QTL value as observed on the specific date when RBQM performed a data analysis on your study data. 
- Expectation – The predefined, expected patient population percentage to not meet the study parameter's criteria. 
- Threshold – The minimum percentage of the patient population that cannot meet the study parameter's criteria before RBQM considers the parameter to be at risk. 
- Upper Limit – The minimum percentage of the patient population that cannot meet the study parameter's criteria before RBQM considers the parameter to be high risk. 
- The Summary table includes the following columns: 
- Date – The date in which RBQM performed a data analysis on your study data and recorded the parameter's QTL value. 
- Observed – The parameter's QTL value as observed on the specific date when RBQM performed a data analysis on your study data. 
- Expectation – The expected patient population percentage to not meet the study parameter's criteria. 
- Threshold – The maximum tolerable patient population percentage that cannot meet the study parameter's criteria. 
- Upper Limit – T he maximum patient population percentage to not meet the study parameter's criteria before the QTL is considered high risk. 
- Status – States the QTL's status on the date that the RBQM study analysis ran. Statuses can be: 
- In Range (green) – The percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's specified criteria is considered within a healthy range of the expectation. Generally, in range QTLs require no action 
- Out of Range (yellow) – The percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's specified criteria have exceeded the tolerance threshold . RBQM considers parameters whose QTL values exceed the threshold as at risk. This indicates potential underlying systemic issues, which may compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues. 
- Above Upper Limit (red) – The percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's specified criteria has exceeded the tolerance upper limit. RBQM considers parameters whose QTL values exceed the upper limit as high risk. This indicates potential underlying systemic issues, which may compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues 
- QTL Excursion! (red) – RBQM flags and identifies QTL excursions when : 
- The percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's specified criteria has exceeded the tolerance upper limit, and 
- It is impossible to move the QTL value back within a healthy range of the QTL's expected value no matter the actions taken by the project team.
 Important : QTL excursions indicate that the study quality is compromised to the point that the study may need to be shut down or restarted.
- Click Download to save the report locally on your machine.

 You can create a summary report listing the Quality Tolerance Limits (QTLs) associated with risks to your study. This information is useful when creating or updating Clinical Study Reports (CSRs) for your clinical trial. The latest version number generated for the QTL Summary Report appears at the top of the Reports page. 
 Note : Your role must include the Generate Reports building block to access and work with the QTL Summary Report.

- Click the QTL Summary Report tab. 
- Use the latest data that is available from the study-level risk assessment to update the QTL Summary details. You can edit these fields:  
- Sponsor - Enter one to 255 characters to identify the sponsor of the study. 
- Protocol Version Number - Enter one to 50 characters to identify the version number of the protocol used by the study. 
- QTL Summary Report Version - Enter one to 50 characters to identify the version number of the QTL Summary Report. 
- Click the check box next to participants assigned to read or review the report. If a participant is missing from the list, click Add to add the participant name . 
- Optional . Select Yes in the Review Required column to also assign the participant as a reviewer. 
 Note : The QTL Summary Details save automatically. When finished updating the details, click Generate QTL Summary Report .

 Click to add a new participant. Or you can update an existing participant record by clicking the participant name in the list.  
- Edit these  fields:
- Title  (optional) - Dr., Mr., Mrs., Ms., or Prof.  
- First Name - Enter up to 255 characters for the first name of the participant. 
- Last Name  - Enter up to 255 characters for the last name of the participant. 
- Participant's Role - Enter up to 255 characters for the role of the participant in the study.  
- Company Name - Enter up to 255 characters for the name of the company the participant works for. 
- Review Required - Select Yes or No . 
- Click Done  or  Add Another  to autosave the new participant information. Click Update to autosave changes to an existing record.  
 Note : When you add a participant, that name appears in all participant lists for all Risk Management reports. Similarly, removing a participant deletes the name from all participant lists in Risk Management.

===== PAGE: history.html | History =====
## History
 On the History page, you can:
- Schedule when and how often Statistical Monitoring renders and reflects a specific study's latest study data analysis. 
- Manually trigger Statistical Monitoring to render and reflect a specific study's latest study data analysis. 
- Stop or suspend scheduled data refreshes. 
- View a list of previous data snapshots and the time stamp for when Statistical Monitoring generated each snapshot. 
- Select a previous data snapshot to enter History View mode to see how the data looked throughout Statistical Monitoring when that snapshot occurred. 
## Set Data Refresh Schedule
 Users with the proper permissions can schedule when and how often Statistical Monitoring renders and reflects a specific study's latest study data analysis. Therefore, you can control when Statistical Monitoring renders your latest batch of study data to accommodate  your organization's data review schedule and pace. 
 Important : Only authorized users can view the Schedule page and set the data refresh schedule. Also, Statistical Monitoring data refreshes occur independently and separately from data refreshes that occur in other RBQM capabilities such as QTL Dashboard and KRI Dashboard. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Statistical Monitoring > History in the left-hand menu.
The History page shows. 
- Select the following:
- Snapshot Schedule  – Select the frequency in which you want Statistical Monitoring to trigger the data refresh. 
- Start  – Select the time of the month that you want the data refresh to trigger. The Start menu only appears if you select a Monthly , Bi-Monthly , or  Quarterly frequency. 
- Day  – Select the weekday within the specified weekly, monthly, or quarterly cadence that you want the data refresh to trigger. The Day menu does not appear if you select First Day of the Month or Last Day of the Month from the Start menu.
 Tip: Display This Week's Latest Study Data
 To show the current week's latest data, select the Weekly frequency, and then select the weekday that is two days ahead of the current day. For example, if today is Tuesday and you want to view the latest data for this week, select the Weekly frequency, and then select Thursday .
- Click Save .
 Statistical Monitoring will automatically  refresh to show visual renderings of the latest study data analysis as scheduled.
 Tip: Last Updated Timestamp
 The upper- right corner of all Statistical Monitoring pages shows the date and time when the most recent data snapshot generation process started . t does not represent the date and time when the data in Statistical Monitoring was last refreshed. For example, . 
 Therefore, the Last Updated timestamp may be earlier than the time at which the refreshed data becomes available in Statistical Monitoring.
## Refresh Data Now
 Important : Only users with the proper permissions can:
- View the Refresh Analytics Now button on the Schedule page. 
- Trigger Statistical Monitoring to render visualizations from the most recent study data analysis. 
 Users with the proper permissions can manually trigger Statistical Monitoring to render and reflect a specific study's latest study data analysis. Therefore, you can control when Statistical Monitoring renders your latest batch of study data to accommodate  your organization's data review schedule and pace.
 The upper- right corner of the Schedule page shows the timestamp of the currently rendered study data's most recent completed run through Statistical Monitoring's analytics.  For example,  . 
 Important : C SM data refreshes occur independently and separately from data refreshes that occur in other RBQM capabilities such as QTL Dashboard and KRI Dashboard. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Statistical Monitoring > History in the left-hand menu.
The History page shows. 
- Click Refresh on the upper-right hand corner of the page.
Statistical Monitoring refreshes to show visual renderings of the most recent study data analysis. The Last Updated field updates to show the time stamp of the currently rendered study data's most recent completed run through Statistical Monitoring's analytics. 
## Stop or Suspend Scheduled Data Refreshes
 You can discontinue or suspend scheduled data refreshes from occurring for closed studies or studies undergoing database lock or data clean up. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Statistical Monitoring > History in the left-hand menu.
The History page shows. 
- In Snapshot Schedule , select  None . 
- Click Save . 
## View Historical Data Snapshots
 Statistical Monitoring provides a list of historical data snapshots . You can select a data snapshot to enter History View mode to see how the data looked throughout Statistical Monitoring at the time when the snapshot occurred. By viewing historical data snapshots, you can efficiently audit studies and reconcile the data and actions made between snapshots.
- Access RBQM , and then click Statistical Monitoring > History in the left-hand menu.
 The History page lists all prior data snapshots from most recent at the top to oldest at the bottom. 
- Click the row of the snapshot you want to view.
Statistical Monitoring automatically navigates you to the Overview page in History View. While in History View, a blue banner shows at the top of all Statistical Monitoring pages. The banner indicates the date when the historical snapshot's data refresh occurred. For example:
 In addition, the upper- right corner of all Statistical Monitoring pages shows the time stamp of when the historical snapshot in view occurred.  For example,  
- Click Exit History View in the blue banner to revert to the latest data snapshot. 
 Notes About History View
- History View mode shows the actions that occurred in the immediate data snapshot following the snapshot date you selected to view. For example, say you selected to view a data snapshot with a date of 17 Oct 2020 and the following data snapshot took place on 22 Oct 2020. In such case, History View mode shows the data in Statistical Monitoring as of 17 Oct 2020, but shows the actions made in Statistical Monitoring up until 22 Oct 2020. 
- While in History View mode:
- Data is read-only. 
- The Error Plots page > Summary section > Actions column does not appear. 
- The Event Incidence Plot page > Summary section > Actions column does not appear. 
- You cannot deep link into Issue Management. 
- You cannot update track review data. 
- Track reviews and issues created are those that occurred against the selected historical snapshot or previous snapshots. That is, the created dates may be after the snapshot date, but before the following snapshot. 
- On the Issues slide-out panel, the Assignee column and Status column do not appear. 
- On the Issues slide-out panel, the Is Closed column appears.
 Note : If the issue was resolved after the date of the snapshot in view, then Is Close has a value of No. If the resolved date occurred before the date of the snapshot in view, then Is Close has a value of Yes.
## View Snapshot Schedule Audit Reports
 You can generate audit reports to view the  history of snapshot schedules created in your study environment. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Statistical Monitoring > History in the left-hand menu.
The History page shows. 
- Click   next to the Snapshot Schedule field.
