===== PAGE: investigate_data_using_the_under-over_reporting_events_plot.html | Investigate Data Using the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot =====
## Investigate Data Using the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot
 You can use the Under-Over Reporting Events plot to identify potentially noncompliant sites and countries whose adverse event, concomitant medication, and medical history reporting patterns significantly differ from the study norm. 
 Note: Last Updated Timestamp
 The Last Updated timestamp reflects the date and time when the most recent data snapshot generation process started. It does not represent the date and time when the data on the Under-Over Reporting Events plot was last refreshed. Therefore, the Last Updated timestamp may be earlier than the time at which the refreshed data becomes available on the Under-Over Reporting Events plot.
## Access and View the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot
 You can view funnel plots depicting the site- and country-level reported rate of: 
- Adverse events over time in months. 
- Concomitant medications compared to the combined number of reported adverse events and ongoing medical history events. 
- Medical history events compared to total number of enrolled patients. 
 You can also simultaneously view and compare the Adverse Events, Concomitant Medication, and Medical History funnel plots.
- Access RBQM , and then click Statistical Monitoring > Under-Over Reporting in the left-hand menu.
The Under-Over Reporting Events page shows. 
- Do any of the following:
- Click Adverse Events to view the Under-Over Reporting Adverse Events Plot. Adverse Events is the default selection. 
- Click Concomitant Medication to view the Under-Over Reporting Concomitant Medication Plot. 
- Click Medical History to view the Under-Over Reporting Medical History Plot 
- Click View Side by Side to view the Adverse Events, Concomitant Medication, and Medical History plots simultaneously side by side. 
- Optional : Each plot displays site-level data by default. Click the   View By   menu to toggle between site-level and country-level view. 
## Filter the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot to View Site- or Country-level Data
- Do either of the following: 
- To view the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot data by site: click the View by filter above the Under-Over Reporting Events plot visualization, and then select Site . Site is the default selection. 
- To view the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot data by country: click the View by filter above the Under-Over Reporting Events plot visualization, and then select Country . 
## Zoom In on Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Data
 You can zoom in on a specific section of the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot. Zooming in helps you get a closer, more granular view of specific data points on the plot. 
- Click, hold, and drag your cursor to draw a box on a specific section of the plot that you want to zoom in on. 
- If necessary, click   Reset Zoom   at the upper right of the visualization to return to the default zoom level. 
## Interpret the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot
 Your proficiency in reading and understanding the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot greatly affects your ability to determine outliers, anomalies, risks, and trends in your study's reported event data. This determination helps ensure you take efficient, well-informed follow-up actions in how you further investigate or report your study data findings.
 Click a plot type below to learn how to read and interpret the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot based on analysis type.
 Adverse Events 
 You can use the Under-Over Reporting Adverse Events plot to identify sites and countries that have significantly different patterns of adverse event (AE) reporting compared to the study norm. Identifying, monitoring, and appropriately addressing sites and countries that may be under or overreporting adverse event data ensures:
- 
- Patient safety oversight. 
- Drug labels include appropriate safety information, including potential drug-to-drug interactions. 
 The following details explain how to read and interpret the Adverse Events plot .
- The Y-axis vertically charts the average number of reported adverse events at a site or country over time in months. 
- The X-axis horizontally charts the site or country's duration in the study in months. 
- Each blue dot, , represents a site or country data point. 
- The data point size increases based on the number of patients enrolled at the site or country. 
- You can hover your cursor on a data point to view:
- Country name 
- Site – The site ID. Only appears when viewing the plot by site. 
- AE Rate – The average number of reported adverse events at a site or country over time in months. Calculated as: N umber of AEs / Exposure Time in Months
 Note : Exposure time is the study days across all patients.
- Exposure in Months – The sum of months on the study across all enrolled patients. 
- # of Patients – Number of patients enrolled at the site or country. 
- You can click a data point to view that site or country's details in the Under-Over Reporting Adverse Events Plot Summary Table. To learn more, see Use and Interpret the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Summary Table . 
- RBQM normalizes the AE rate reported at each site or country across the overall study data and uses funnel lines to visually output the:
- Upper 99% Limit – An AE rate that is at the 99% confidence interval above the study's average AE rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported AE rate lies above the upper 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers. Extreme outliers may warrant prompt investigation to  understand the type of events that are overreported; for example, signs and symptoms versus diagnosis . The Upper 99% Limit is represented by the uppermost solid, blue line in the funnel plot : 
- Upper 95% Limit – An AE rate that is at the 95% confidence interval  above the study's average AE rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported AE rate lies above the upper 95% limit to be potential outliers. Outliers may warrant investigation to understand the type of events that are overreported; for example, signs and symptoms versus diagnosis . The Upper 95% Limit is r epresented by the uppermost dotted, gray line in the funnel plot: 
- Mean – The average reported AE rate across all sites or countries in the study. The mean is represented by the solid, yellow, middle line in the funnel plot: 
- Lower 95% Limit – An AE rate that is at the 95% confidence interval  below the study's average AE rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported AE rate lies below the lower 95% limit to be potential outliers. Outliers may warrant investigation to understand type of events that are underreported; for example, mild events . The Lower 95% Limit is r epresented by the lowermost dotted, gray line in the funnel plot: 
- Lower 99% Limit – An AE rate that is at the 99% confidence interval below the study's average AE rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported AE rate lies below the lower 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers. Extreme outliers may warrant prompt investigation  to understand the type of events that are underreported; for example, mild events . The Lower 99% Limit is r epresented by the lowermost solid, blue line in the funnel plot: 
 Concomitant Medication 
 You can use the Under-Over Reporting Concomitant Medication plot to identify sites and countries that have significantly different patterns of concomitant medication reporting compared to the study norm. Identifying, monitoring, and appropriately addressing sites and countries that may be under or overreporting concomitant medication data can help address: 
- Unreported adverse events and medical history events. 
- Variability in over-the-counter medication reporting. 
 The following details explain how to read and interpret the Concomitant Medication plot .
- The Y-axis vertically charts the average number of reported concomitant medications per combined number of reported adverse events and ongoing medical history events at a site or country. 
- The X-axis horizontally charts the total combined number of reported adverse events and ongoing medical history events at the site or country. 
- Each blue dot, , represents a site or country data point. 
- The data point size increases based on the number of patients enrolled at the site or country. 
- You can hover your cursor on a data point to view:
- Country name 
- Site – The site ID. Only appears when viewing the plot by site. 
- CM Rate – The average number of reported concomitant medications per combined number of reported adverse events and ongoing medical history events at the site or country. Calculated as:  Number of CMs / (Number of AEs + Number of Ongoing MH)
 Note : Depending on aggregation—whether per site or per country—the CM rate is further divided by either number of sites or countries. 
- AE + Ongoing MH – The total combined number of reported adverse events and ongoing medical history events at the site or country. 
- # of Patients – Number of patients enrolled at the site or country. 
- You can click a data point to view that site or country's details in the Summary Table. To learn more, see 
- Use and Interpret the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Summary Table. 
- RBQM normalizes the AE rate reported at each site or country across the overall study data and uses funnel lines to visually output the:
- Upper 99% Limit – A CM rate that is at the 99% confidence interval above the study's average CM rate when a site or country reports a given combined total number of adverse events and ongoing medical history events. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported CM rate lies above the upper 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers, which my warrant prompt investigation. The Upper 99% Limit is represented by the uppermost solid, blue line in the  funnel plot : 
- Upper 95% Limit – A CM rate that is at the 95% confidence interval  above the study's average CM rate when a site or country reports a given combined total number of adverse events and ongoing medical history events. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported AE rate lies above the upper 95% limit to be potential outliers, which my warrant investigation. The Upper 95% Limit is r epresented by the uppermost dotted, gray line in the funnel plot: 
- Mean – The average reported AE rate across all sites or countries in the study. The mean is represented by the solid, yellow, middle line in the funnel plot: 
- Lower 95% Limit – A CM rate that is at the 95% confidence interval below the study's average CM rate when a site or country reports a given combined total number of adverse events and ongoing medical history events.  RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported CM rate lies below the lower 95% limit to be potential outliers, which my warrant investigation. The Lower 95% Limit is r epresented by the lowermost dotted, gray line in the funnel plot: 
- Lower 99% Limit – A CM rate that is at the 99% confidence interval below the study's average CM rate when a site or country reports a given combined total number of adverse events and ongoing medical history events.  RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported CM rate lies below the lower 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers, which my warrant prompt investigation. The Lower 99% Limit is r epresented by the lowermost solid, blue line in the funnel plot: 
 Medical History 
 You can use the Under-Over Reporting Medical History plot to identify sites and countries that have significantly different patterns of medical history reporting compared to the study norm. Identifying, monitoring, and appropriately addressing sites and countries that may be under or overreporting medical history event data ensures: 
- Patient eligibility is properly assessed. 
- There are no unreported exclusionary medical history conditions. 
- Adverse events are indeed newly emerged events as opposed to the potential worsening of previously unreported medical history events. 
 The following details explain how to read and interpret the Medical History plot .
- The Y-axis vertically charts the average number of reported medical history events per enrolled patient at a site or country. 
- The X-axis horizontally charts the number of enrolled patients at a site or country. 
- Each blue dot, , represents a site or country data point. 
- The data point size increases based on the number of patients enrolled at the site or country. 
- You can hover your cursor on a data point to view:
- Country name 
- Site – The site ID. Only appears when viewing the plot by site. 
- MH Rate – The average number of reported medical history events per enrolled patient at the site or country. Calculated as: N umber of MH / Total Patients
 Note : Depending on aggregation—whether per site or per country—the MH rate is further divided by either number of sites or countries. 
- # of Patients – Number of patients enrolled at the site or country. 
- You can click a data point to view that site or country's details in the Under-Over Reporting Adverse Events Plot Summary Table. To learn more, see Use and Interpret the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Summary Table . 
- RBQM normalizes the AE rate reported at each site or country across the overall study data and uses funnel lines to visually output the:
- Upper 99% Limit – An MH rate that is at the 99% confidence interval above the study's average MH rate based on the number of enrolled patients at the site or country level. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported MH rate lies above the upper 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers, which my warrant prompt investigation. The Upper 99% Limit is represented by the uppermost solid, blue line in the  funnel plot : 
- Upper 95% Limit – An MH rate that is at the 95% confidence interval  above the study's average MH rate based on the number of enrolled patients at the site or country level. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported MH rate lies above the upper 95% limit to be potential outliers, which my warrant investigation. The Upper 95% Limit is r epresented by the uppermost dotted, gray line in the funnel plot: 
- Mean – The average reported MH rate across all sites or countries in the study. The mean is represented by the solid, yellow, middle line in the funnel plot: 
- Lower 95% Limit – An MH rate that is at the 95% confidence interval  below the study's average MH rate based on the number of enrolled patients at the site or country. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported MH rate lies below the lower 95% limit to be potential outliers, which my warrant investigation. The Lower 95% Limit is r epresented by the lowermost dotted, gray line in the funnel plot: 
- Lower 99% Limit – An MH rate that is at the 99% confidence interval below the study's average MH rate based on the number of enrolled patients at the site or country. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported MH rate lies below the lower 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers, which my warrant prompt investigation. The Lower 99% Limit is r epresented by the lowermost solid, blue line in the funnel plot: 
 View Side by Side 
 You can simultaneously view and compare the Adverse Events, Concomitant Medication, and Medical History funnel plots . Adverse events, concomitant medication, and medical history funnel plots tend to correlate with each other. Viewing all three side by side helps you identify anomalous event data that may warrant investigation. 
 Tip : We recommend clicking an individual site or country's data point in the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot to highlight that specific site or country of interest on the plot. Then, click View Side by Side . This gives you the optimal perspective to compare and investigate individual sites or countries with anomalous reporting patterns across adverse events, concomitant medication, and medical history. For example, if a site significantly overreported adverse events but underreported concomitant medications.

## Use and Interpret the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Summary Table
 The Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Summary table lists all sites and countries with reported adverse events in the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot visualization. The Summary table also summarizes key adverse event reporting-related metrics for each site and country. 
- Do either of the following: 
- To view the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Summary Table by site: click the View by filter above the Under-Over Reporting Events plot visualization, and then select Site . 
- To view the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Summary Table by country: click the View by filter above the Under-Over Reporting Events plot visualization, and then select Country . 
- Scroll down to the summary table below the Under-Over Reporting Events plot visualization. 
- Depending on the whether you view the Adverse Events plot, Concomitant Medications plot, or Medical History plot, the Summary table has the following columns:
 Adverse Events Plot Summary Table Column Descriptions 
- Site  – The site the patient belongs to. Only appears when viewing the plot by site. 
- Country – The country in which the site is located. 
- # of Sites – The total number of sites in the country. Only appears when viewing the plot by country. 
- # Patients – The number of patients enrolled at the site or country. 
- # of AEs – The total number of reported AEs at the site or country. 
- Exposure (Months) – The site's or country's duration in the study in months. 
- Reporting – Indicates whether AEs are being overreported, underreported, or reported at a statistically normal rate when compared across all other sites or countries in the study.  
- Normal – The site or country's reported AE rate is considered statistically normal. 
- Over – The site or country's reported AE rate is at least at the 95% confidence interval above the study-reported mean. Therefore, RBQM considers the site or country to be a potential outlier that may be overreporting adverse events, which may warrant investigation. 
- Under – The site or country's reported AE rate is at least at the 95% confidence interval below the study-reported mean. Therefore, RBQM considers the site or country to be a potential outlier that may be underreporting adverse events, which may warrant investigation. 
- Significance Rate – A RBQM calculation that measures the probability of a site or country experiencing its reported adverse event rate compared to the overall adverse event rate reported rate across all sites or countries in the study. 
- Extreme Outlier – Sites or countries with a significance rate less than 0.01 for its reported adverse event rate. The probability of the site or country having its current adverse event rate is extremely low considering the adverse event rate across all sites or countries. This indicates that there may be issues with how adverse events have been reported at the site or country, which may require further investigation. 
- Outlier – Sites or countries with a significance rate between 0.01 and 0.05 for its reported adverse event rate. The probability of the site or country having its current adverse rate event is very low considering the adverse event rate across all sites and countries. This indicates that there may be issues with how adverse events have been reported at the site or country, which may require further investigation. 
- Normal – Sites or countries with a significance rate greater than 0.05 for its reported adverse event reported rate. The probability of the site or country having its current adverse event rate is statistically normal considering the adverse event rate across all other sites and countries. 
- Actions – Click and then View by Country to view the summary table by country. Only appears when viewing the plot by site.

- # Patients – The number of patients enrolled at the site or country. 
- # of CM – The total number of reported concomitant medications at the site or country. 
- # of AEs – The total number of reported adverse events at the site or country.

===== PAGE: investigate_data_using_trends_plots.html | Investigate Data Using Trends Plots =====
## Investigate Data Using Trends Plots
 Trend plots graphically show a single variable's data at each site side by side using a box-and-whisker plots or stacked bar chart. You can use trend plots to pinpoint sites with abnormal or incorrect data that may warrant investigation. 
## Sort, Filter, Highlight, and Zoom In on Trends Plot Data
 The trends plot visualization provides a unique set of plot sorting, filtering, highlighting, and zoom options based on which whether you are viewing data analysis for a text or numeric variable. You can use the sorting, filtering, highlight, and zoom options to:
- View and interpret your study data from multiple view points, and 
- Find and drill down on specific data. 
 Click a data analysis type below to learn to sort, filter, highlight, and zoom in on trends plot data based on the data analysis RBQM renders in the trends plot visualization.
 Text Variable Analysis 
 Sort the Plot Data 
 You can sort the data in the Text Analysis plot visualization using the following options:
- Alphabetical Text  – Displays site IDs on the x-axis from left to right in alphanumeric ascending order; for example, from 1 on the left to 100 on the right. This is the default plot setting. 
- High - Low – Sorts the x-axis based on site IDs with the most number of text variable occurrences on the left to least number of occurrences on the right. 
- Low - High – Sorts the x-axis based on site IDs with the least number of text variable occurrences on the left to most number of occurrences on the right. 
 Tip : Click Reset Plot to reset to the default Alphabetical filter view.
 Filter the Plot to Display Specific Country- or Site-related Data Points 
 You can filter the plot to show only data points that correspond with a specific country or site. 
- Navigate to the Summary section below the plot visualization.
 Note : By default, the plot shows all data points associated with the selected variable
- Do any of the following:
 Filter the trends plot to display specific country-related data points 
- Click the View By filter, select Country , and then either select a country from the Country  filter or click a specific country's row in the table. 
 Filter the trends plot to display specific site-related data points 
- Click the View By filter, select Site , and then either select a site from the Site filter or click a specific site's row in the table. 
 Based on your filter selection, the trends plot visualization highlights the specified country- or site-related data points and dims all other data points. 
 Highlight Specific Text Entries in the Plot 
 You can configure the plot to highlight specific text entries that occurred at each site. 
- Click Highlight. 
- Do either of the following:
- Click All to highlight all data points. All is the default selection. 
- Click a specific text entry to highlight on that entry at each site in the bar chart. 
 Tip : Click Reset Plot to reset to the default All highlight.
 Numeric Variable Analysis 
 Filter the Plot to Display Data Based on Range and Outliers 
 You can filter the Numeric Analysis plot visualization using the following options:
- Outer Values – Filters the plot so that only data points that are outside of the interquartile range show. For example, if a plot contains a high volume of data points, then you can use the Outer Values filter to show only data that is outside of the interquartile range to help you focus more on the data you need. 
- Outliers – Filters the plot to show only outlier data points. Selecting this option helps you better identify anomalies in your study data that may require further investigating or reporting. 
- Box Plot – Filters the plot to show the plot's lower whisker value, 25th percentile value, median value, 75th percentile value, and upper whisker value. Using the Box Plot filter helps you better see the variables' distribution of data. 
 Tip : Click Reset to reset to the default filter view. The default visualization shows all data points as well as the box plot and whiskers.
 Sort the Plot Data 
 You can sort the data in the Numeric Analysis plot visualization by Alphabetical order, Mean, Median, or spread (Q3-Q1).
- From the Sort by filter, select one of the following options:
- Alphabetical  – Sorts site IDs on the X-axis in ascending alphanumeric order (A on the left; Z on the right). 
- Mean  – Sorts the X-axis based on box plot from lowest mean on the left to highest mean on the right. 
- Median  – Sorts the X-axis based on box plot from lowest median on the left to highest median on the right. 
- Spread (Q3-Q1)  – Sorts the X-axis based on box plot from smallest middle 50th percentile on the left to largest middle 50th percentile on the right. 
 Tip : Click Reset Plot  to reset to the default filter view. The default visualization shows all data points as well as the box plot and whiskers.
 Filter the Plot to Display Specific Country-, Site-, or Patient-related Data Points 
 By default, the trends plot shows all data points associated with the selected variable. But you can also drill down further and filter the plot to show only data points that correspond to a specific country or site. 
- Navigate to the Summary section below the plot visualization.
 Note : By default, the plot shows all data points associated with the selected variable.
- Do any of the following:
 Filter the trends plot to display specific country-related data points 
- Click the View By filter, select Country , and then either select a country from the Country  filter or click a specific country's row in the table. 
 Filter the trends plot to display specific site-related data points 
- Click the View By filter, select Site , and then either select a site from the Site filter or click a specific site's row in the table. 
 Based on your filter selection, the trends plot visualization highlights the specified country- or site-related data points and dims all other data points. 
 Zoom In on Data Points on a Specific Section of the Plot 
 You can zoom in on a specific section of the Numeric Analysis Plot. For plots that have a high volume of data points, zooming in helps you get a closer, more granular view of specific data points on the plot. 
- Click, hold, and drag your cursor to draw a box on a specific section of the plot that you want to zoom in on. 
- If necessary, click Reset Zoom at the upper right of the visualization to return to the default zoom level. 
## Interpret Trends Plots
 Your proficiency in reading and understanding trends plots greatly affects your ability to determine trends in your study data. This determination helps ensure you take efficient, well-informed follow-up actions in how you further investigate or report your study data findings.
 Click a data analysis type  below to learn how to interpret the trends plot based on whether you are viewing the data analysis for a text or numeric variable.
 Text Variable Analysis 
 Tip : Click image to enlarge.
- Text variable analysis renders using a stacked bar chart. 
- The Y-axis shows the variable's total number of text value occurrences recorded at each site. 
- The X-axis shows the site IDs where the text value entries occurred. By default, the site ID numbers list from left to right in ascending alphanumeric order. For example, 1 on the left; 100 on the right. 
- Reported text values at each site are represented by a color-coded stacked bar. Each specific text value is segmented and denoted in a unique color in the stacked bar. 
- You can hover your cursor on each individual site's bar to view:
- Each unique text value reported at the site. 
- The number of times each unique text value was reported at the site. 
- How each unique text value is color-coded and represented on the stacked bar.
 Numeric Variable Analysis 
 Tip : Click image to enlarge.
- Numeric variable analysis renders using a box-and-whisker plot. 
- Each patient data point on the box plots is represented by a blue square, orange circle, or red diamond:
- Blue Square  – The patient data point's  discrepancy score is less than 2.95. This means that the patient data point has a statistically normal numeric value within the variable. 
- Orange Circle    – The patient data point's discrepancy score is between 2.95 and 4.95. This means that the patient data point has a higher- or lower-than-normal numeric value within the variable. Thus, RBQM considers the numeric value an outlier. 
- Red Diamond   – The patient data point's discrepancy score exceeds 4.95. This means that the patient data point has a significantly higher- or lower-than-normal numeric value within the variable. Thus, RBQM considers the numeric value an extreme outlier. 
- You can hover your cursor on any blue square, orange circle, or red diamond to view the following data point-specific information:
- Patient  – The patient ID for the patient represented in the data point.  
- Value  – The raw value entered in the eCRF for the patient with regards to the variable. 
- Site  – The site the patient belongs to. 
- Country  – The country in which the site is located. 
- Disc Score  –  A numeric score generated by Statistical Monitoring's high-dimensional data anomaly detection algorithms , which measures the discrepancy of an individual data point relative to the overall study data. Discrepancy scores help you uncover outliers, anomalies, risks, and trends in your study data, which may require follow-up action. An error score of less than 2.95 indicates statistically normal data; between 2.95 and 4.95 indicates outlier data; exceeding 4.95 indicates extreme outlier data. 
- By default, the variable's data points show on an overlay of a box-and-whisker plot. All data points that lie within the green box, , are within the interquartile range range for all data points within the variable. 
- If you choose the Box Plot filter option, the visualization removes all data points from the box-and-whisker plot. Doing so helps you better view the variable's distribution of data in terms of (from top to bottom) the variable's upper whisker value , 75th percentile value, median, 25th percentile value, and lower whisker value . T he green box,  , also shows the interquartile range . For example:
- Box Plot Threshold   – Provides a clear visual indicator for where the upper whisker value, 75th percentile value, median, 25th percentile value, and lower whisker value lie within the box plot.

===== PAGE: investigate_protocol_deviations_using_the_protocol_integrity_report.html | Investigate Protocol Deviations Using the Protocol Integrity Report =====
## Investigate Protocol Deviations Using the Protocol Integrity Report
 In the Protocol Integrity Report (PIR), you can process protocol deviations (PD) autopopulated from Medidata Rave queries and other sources. 
## Review Protocol Deviations
 You can review automatically populated or manually entered protocol deviations (PD). 
- On the In-Progress tab, click Review for the PD to open the Proposed Deviation page.
- Update the Details and Comments tabs, and click Submit review , Confirm deviation , or Approve deviation.
 Tip :  Use Case 
 You are an Approver, such as the Chief Medical Officer or a biostatistics staff member. You receive an assignment notification to evaluate a PD's scientific integrity. You can resolve the PD in one of two ways:
- Click Approve to change the status to Approved. 
- Click  Dismiss and provide a mandatory reason (for example, non-PD or duplicate). 
## Add Protocol Devitations
 You can manage automatically populated protocol deviations (PD) from Rave and Data Surveillance Listings, or add deviations directly to the Protocol Integrity Report (PIR) manually or from a clinical trial management system (CTMS). 
 You can directly create manual PD records by selecting existing study values for Site, Patient, and Visit when entering data.
- Click Add proposed deviation . 
- Select  Manual and click Next . 
- Enter the deviation details and click Add . 
## Review Potential Deviations
 You can select queries that qualify as protocol deviations. Submitting these queries moves them to the Proposed Deviations queue. 
 Note : Closed or Answered Rave queries appear as potential deviations. You can review the answer text to confirm whether a protocol deviation occurred. Dismiss queries that are not protocol deviations to exclude them from the PIR process. Accept confirmed deviations to change their status to Proposed. The query text must start with PD , Protocol Deviation , Potential PD , PDSD , or Potential Protocol Deviation to categorize it as a potential deviation. 
- Click the right arrow on the Add Proposed Deviation button and select Review potential deviations . 
- Select one or more queries and click Submit . 
## Dismiss Deviation
 You can dismiss approved protocol deviations (PD). Dismissing deviations moves the records to the static Dismissed Deviations panel. 
- On the Approved tab, click the More icon for the PD and select Dismiss deviation . 
- Enter the details and click Dismiss deviation . 
## Add Comment to Deviation
 You can comment on approved protocol deviations (PD).
- On the Approved tab, click the More icon for the PD on the Approved Deviations or Dismissed Deviations list.
- Select Comment and click +Add comment .
- Enter the details and click the check icon to save the comment. 
## Review PDAP Changes in PIR
 Protocol Deviation Assessment Plan (PDAP) updates—for example, following a protocol amendment—save the new version and automatically update associated Protocol Integrity Report (PIR) records.
 PIR records highlight to indicate an update from the PDAP. You can acknowledge these updates to clear the change flag.
 Note : PDAP updates do not flag deviations previously assigned the Dismissed status.

===== PAGE: investigate_site_visits_on_non-business_days.html | Investigate Site Visits On Non-Business Days =====
## Investigate Site Visits On Non-Business Days
 Patients enrolled in a study receive specific medications according to the research plan. To determine the drug's safety and efficacy, the patient visits the investigator's or doctor's office at a scheduled cadence. This is known as a scheduled visit. Scheduled visits do not occur on non-business days of the week such as weekends or holidays. Visits recorded as taking place on weekends or holidays can indicate potential fraud, misconduct, or even simple data entry errors by sites. 
 Statistical Monitoring breaks down at the study or selected country level how many scheduled patient visits occurred on each weekday throughout the study. You can view scheduled patient visits to help you investigate whether falsified or erroneous patient records exist in your study data and monitor sites of interest. 
 Note: Last Updated Timestamp
 The Last Updated timestamp reflects the date and time when the most recent data snapshot generation process started. It does not represent the date and time when the data in Weekend and Holiday Visits was last refreshed. Therefore, the Last Updated timestamp may be earlier than the time at which the refreshed data becomes available in Weekend and Holiday Visits.
- Access RBQM , and then click Statistical Monitoring > Weekend and Holiday in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Weekend and Holiday Visits page > Visit Days tab, do either of the following: 
- To view the visit data for study visits, click Countries , and then select All .
The weekday cards update to show the number of visits taken place on each weekend for the entire study.
- To view the visit data for a specific country, click Countries , and then select the country you need from the list.
The weekday cards update to show the number of visits taken place on each weekend for the selected country.
- Click the weekday card pertaining to the day of the week whose patient visit data you want to review. 
 The list of scheduled patient visits and visit details recorded on the selected day appear. Visit details include: 
- Site – The site where the visit occurred. 
- Country – The country where the visit occurred. 
- Patient – The patient ID of the patient who attended the visit. 
- Visit Name – The type of visit; for example, an unscheduled visit. 
- Visit Date – The date that the visit occurred. 
- Optional . To help streamline your data investigation, you can filter the patient visit listing by Site , Country , Visit Name , or Visit Date , and then click Apply .
 Filtering Tips
- When viewing a listing of patient visits that occurred on a weekday (as opposed to on a weekend), you can filter the listing by Country and Visit Date to help you identify visits that occurred during a country's holiday. For example, filtering by Canada and United Kingdom, 26 Dec 2022, which happened to be Boxing Day in those countries. Or another example is filtering for United States, 27 Nov 2014, which happened to be Thanksgiving in that country. Patient visits should not occur on these holidays. 
- Central monitors can filter the patient visit listing by Country to focus their review on areas they are most interested in. 
- Site monitors can filter the patient visit listing by Site to focus their review on sites they are monitoring. 
- You can filter by Visit Name and exclude Unscheduled visits from the patient visit listing. Unscheduled visits can occur anytime because they may be for emergency visits. But scheduled visits should only occur during normal working days. Filtering to remove unscheduled visits narrows the lists so you can only focus on scheduled visits.

- Configure the specific KRIs you want RBQM to factor in when calculating each site's performance risk level .

 Based on your observations made from the KRI Dashboard, you can determine: 
- The issues or risks that require further investigate or mitigation.  
- The best approach or mitigating actions to take on the issues or risks. For example, writing an issue against the custom KRI and capturing the custom KRI on a risk inventory.
- The effect the mitigating actions have made on the issues or risks over time. 
 KRI  data also gets filtered, calculated, and rendered in Risk Assessment and Risk Inventory. Data sets and variables you use to build KRI configurations appear with a Medidata Rave, external or derived label next to the name.  Similarly, data sets and variables with critical data points to the study appear with a blue flag

- Download KRI Configuration Reports . 
- Generate KRI Configuration Audit Reports . 
 Important : KRIs do not support datetime operations.

===== PAGE: kri_dashboard.html | KRI Dashboard =====
## KRI Dashboard
 Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) are standard and protocol specific study metrics that enable you to consistently:  
- Identify and/or track known or anticipated risks to data quality. 
- Evaluate country and site performance in a study. 
- Monitor site compliance with data collection. 
 KRIs are predefined metrics that you determine at the outset of a study, KRIs are calculated at site and country level with overall study metric.  
 The KRI Dashboard lists the KRIs that your study monitors and their respective KRI values at each site or country.  
 RBQM includes the following system KRIs are available on most Medidata Rave studies : 
- AE Entry Delay 
- Manual Query Rate 
- Non-System Query Delay 
- Number of AEs per Patient-Month 
- Number of SAEs per Patient-Month 
- Percent Out of Window Visit 
- Percent Missing Visit 
- System Query Rate 
- System Query Delay 
- Visit Entry Delay 
- Modification rate 
 You can also define and track custom KRIs  to help monitor protocol specific risks, more often than not related to non-compliance with collection of critical data. We recommend you balance t he number of custom KRIs against what is critical, the availability of other analyses (such as over/under-reporting), and the resulting operational burden.
 For clinical data trending, and reporting over time including site level reporting consider creating companion visualizations. For more information, see  Custom Graphs . 
 For more information on each KRI, see KRI Descriptions and Calculation Methodologies . 
 Important : You do not create or manage custom KRIs on the KRI Dashboard. Buyt you can do so using KRI Configuration .  
 Important : KRIs do not support datetime operations.
## What Is the KRI Dashboard?
 The KRI Dashboard shows the KRI values and trends for all selected KRIs and summarizes their impact on the  Site Risk Score (SRI) . 
## What Is the Purpose of the KRI Dashboard?
 To ensure quality conduct, studies can implement RBQM by identifying, assessing, monitoring, and mitigating the risks that could affect the quality or safety of a study. 
 The KRI Dashboard allows you to: 
- View all KRIs and respective values - system and protocol specific. 
- Determine which KRI values are outliers  based on statistical or predefined thresholds . 
- View historical trends in site- and country-level KRI data. 
- View sites’ performance respective to other sites within each KRI. 
- Rank sites based on the Site Risk Score (SRI) to allow better site prioritization based on the aggregated score across relevant KRIs weighted based on the risk category 
 Based on your observations made from the KRI Dashboard, you can: 
- Automatically set up signal detection that requires further investigation or mitigation. See the Signals page . 
- Determine the best approach or mitigating actions to take on the issues or risks. 
- Assess the effect the mitigating actions have made on the issues or risks over time. 
## Who Uses the KRI Dashboard?
 Anyone who tracks risk can use the KRI Dashboard. For example: 
- Remote or site monitors - Can view comprehensive overview of site compliance with data collection, reporting as per protocol and study determined expectations. 
- Data Managers – Can use a series of system KRIs that provide a good overview of data currency metrics including query rates, query management timeliness, and data reporting delays. 
- Medical Monitors – Might be interested in viewing safety information, for example, non-serious adverse events (AEs), and serious adverse events (SAEs) reporting patterns. 
## How Do I Use and Interpret the KRI Dashboard?
 See  Investigate Data Using the KRI Dashboard . 
## How Do I Refresh the KRI Dashboard to Show the Latest Data?
 See Schedule or Trigger When KRI Dashboard Refreshes and Outputs the Latest Study Data Analysis .

===== PAGE: kri_descriptions_and_calculation_methodologies.html | KRI Descriptions and Calculation Methodologies =====
## KRI Descriptions and Calculation Methodologies
 You can view and track system KRIs and custom KRIs in the KRI Dashboard . 
## System KRIs
 System KRIs are Medidata-defined KRIs that are standard in all studies analyzed by RBQM. Medidata defines the calculations that are performed on specific data sets and variables based on metrics that most studies typically track. Medidata always provides all customers with the system KRIs. System KRIs are uneditable and in an active state by default; however, you can deactivate system KRIs as needed. 
 The following table lists:
- The current system KRIs you can track in the KRI Dashboard . 
- The KRI category to which the KRI belongs . 
- A description for each KRI. 
- How RBQM calculates each KRI's values. 
 Important : For a KRI and its KRI value to be included in the KRI Dashboard, your study requires:
- At least three sites or three countries to match the minimum data requirements listed in the table below. 
- At least two enrolled patients at each site or country. 
 Important : If there are fewer data points at the site and country level, the statistical model that calculates KRIs may produce less accurate outcomes.
 KRI Category 
 KRI Name 
 Description 
 Calculation 
 Minimum Data Requirements and Considerations 
 Applied Filters 
 | Data Collection 
 | AE Entry Delay 
 | Calculated as the average time in study days between the AE Visit Date and First Entry Date for each individual adverse event. AE Entry Delay is reported at the site, country, and study levels. 
 AE Visit Date is defined as the first visit date following the AE Start/onset Date. 
 First Entry Date is defined as an adverse event's record creation date. 
 | For all adverse events at the site and country level: ((First Entry Date) - (AE Visit Date)) ÷ (Number of Adverse Events) 
 The predefined AE Entry Delay risk thresholds are: 
 • <7 days = Green 
 • >7 and <14 days = Yellow 
 • >14 days = Red 
 | RBQM requires: 
 • Two or more records at a site in the Rave AE data set for the site's KRI value to appear in the Key Risk Indicators table. 
 • Two or more records at a country in the AE Event table for the country's KRI values to appear in the KRI Dashboard. 
 • Two or more study-level records in the AE Event table for the study-level KRI value to appear in the KRI Dashboard. 
 | 1. Subjects must be enrolled.  
 2. AE must have a start date.  
 3. Visits must be active, non-deleted, and scheduled.  
 | Data Collection 
 | Missing Visit Percentage 
 | The percentage of all patient visits that are missing at the site, country, and study level. A patient visit is considered missing if the actual visit has not been entered, but the patient has another date or event that indicates the patient's follow-up time has exceeded the visit window. 
 | For all patients at the site, and country, and study level: ((# of missing visits) ÷ (total # of expected visits at the time of calculation)) * 100 
 The predefined Missing Visit Percentage risk thresholds are: 
 • 0-10% = Green 
 • 10-20% = Yellow 
 • >20% = Red 
 | Visit windows must be configured in the Rave Folders tab. RBQM requires at least three visits reported at the site. 
 | 1. Subjects must be enrolled.   
 2. Visits must be active, non-deleted, and scheduled.  
 3.Denominator is restricted to expected visits whose scheduled window has already passed. 
 | Data Collection 
 | Manual Query Rate 
 | The percentage of manual queries out of the total number of data points that exist for that patient. 
 | ((# of user-created queries from the Rave query source file) ÷ (total # of data points reported for each patient at that site/country)) * 100 
 | The Rave query data set must exist. Third-party data ingested outside of Rave does not produce insights or values for this KRI. RBQM requires at least 50 rows in the query data set for each user-created site or country to calculate and appear in KRI Dashboard. Queries do not get filtered based on if the parent data point is deactivated. Deactivated data with answered queries gets counted. 
 | 1. Subject must be enrolled and have datapoints in the study.  
 2. Queries must be visible, active, not hidden, answered, not cancelled, and specifically exclude auto-queries and "sticky" notes. 
 | Data Collection 
 | Non-System Query Delay 
 | The mean time in days for manual queries to be answered. This is calculated as the difference between the date that a query was answered by a user from the date it was opened in Rave. 
 | For All Queries at the site, country, and study level: ((Date a response was provided in the Rave) - (Date the query was opened in Rave)) ÷ (Number of Queries) 
 The predefined Non-System Query Delay risk thresholds are: 
 • <7 days = Green 
 • >7 and <14 days = Yellow 
 • >14 days = Red 
 | The Rave query data set must exist. Non-Rave ingested data does not produce insights or values for this KRI. RBQM requires at least 50 rows in the query data set for each user-created site or country to calculate and appear in KRI Dashboard. Queries do not get filtered based on if the parent data point is deactivated. Deactivated data with answered queries gets counted. 
 | 1. Subject must be enrolled  
 2. Queries must be active, visible, not hidden, not cancelled, and specifically exclude auto-queries and "sticky" notes. 
 | Data Collection 
 | Percent Out of Window Visit 
 | The percentage of all patient visits that occurred out of window at the site, country, or study level. A patient visit is considered out of window if the actual visit date is before the visit window start date or after the visit window end date configured in Rave. 
 | For all patients at the site, and country, and study level: ((Out-of-window visits for all patients) ÷ (Total # of visits that the patient has actually had at the time of calculation for all patients)) * 100 
 The predefined Percent Out of Window Visit risk thresholds are: 
 • 0-10% = Green 
 • 10-20% = Yellow 
 • >20% = Red 
 | Visit windows must be configured in the Rave Folders tab. RBQM needs at least three visits reported for the site. 
 | 1. Subject must be enrolled and have datapoints in the study.  
 2. Visits must be active, scheduled, touched, non-deleted, and have visit date. 
 3. Scheduled Visits with target dates but missing window dates are always considered in window 
 | Safety 
 | Number of SAEs per Patient-Month 
 | The total number of serious adverse events divided by the number of patient months of follow-up at the site. 
 | # of SAEs ÷ ((Max Clinical Date - Day 0) ÷ 30 for all patients) 
 | For the site or country KRI value to calculate in the KRI Dashboard, RBQM requires that two or more records for that site or country exist in the Rave AE data set. 
 | 1. Subject must be enrolled  
 2. The event must be explicitly flagged as serious. 
 | Safety 
 | Number of AEs per Patient-Month 
 | The total number of adverse events at a site divided by the number of patient months of follow-up at the site. 
 | # of AEs ÷ ((Max Clinical Date - Day 0) ÷ 30 for all patients) 
 | For the site or country KRI value to calculate in the KRI Dashboard, RBQM requires that two or more records for that site or country exist in the Rave AE data set. 
 | 1. Subject must be enrolled  
 | Data Collection 
 | System Query Rate 
 | The percentage of system queries out of the total number of data points that exist for that patient. 
 | ((# of system-created queries from Rave Query source file) ÷ (total # of data points reported for each patient at that site or country)) * 100 
 | The Rave query data set must exist. Non-Rave ingested data does not produce insights or values for this KRI. RBQM requires at least 50 rows in the query data set for each user-created site or country to calculate and appear in KRI Dashboard. Queries do not get filtered based on if the parent data point is deactivated. Deactivated data with answered queries gets counted. 
 | 1. Subject must be enrolled and have datapoints in the study.  
 2. Queries must be visible, active, not hidden, not cancelled, and generated by the auto-query system. 
 | Data Collection 
 | System Query Delay 
 | Mean time in days for users to answer system queries. This is calculated as the difference between the date that query was opened Rave from the time that an answer was provided. 
 | For All Queries at the site, country, and study level: ((Date a response was provided in the system) - (Date the query was opened in the system)) ÷ (Number of Queries) 
 The predefined System Query Delay risk thresholds are: 
 • <7 days = Green 
 • >7 and <14 days = Yellow 
 • >14 days = Red 
 | The Rave query data set must exist. Non-Rave ingested data does not produce insights or values for this KRI. RBQM requires at least 50 rows in the query data set for each user-created site or country to calculate and appear in KRI Dashboard. Queries do not get filtered based on if the parent data point is deactivated. Deactivated data with answered queries gets counted. 
 | 1. Subject must be enrolled  
 2. Queries must be active, visible, not hidden, answered, not cancelled, and generated by the auto-query system. 
 | Data Collection 
 | Visit Entry Delay 
 | The mean time in days between when the visit date occurred and the visit data entry date. 
 | For all visits at the site, country, and study level: ((Event performed date; that is, the Actual Date Provided) - (Data entry Start Date; that is, when the date was entered in the system) where patients day 0 is not null, then averaged at each site, country, and for the study as a whole) ÷ (Number of visits) 
 The predefined Visit Entry Delay risk thresholds are: 
 • <7 days = Green 
 • >7 and <14 days = Yellow 
 • >14 days = Red 
 | Day 0 must exist for patients to be included in the site-level analysis. RBQM requires at least two recorded visits at the site per patient. 
 **Important:** Visit entry delay KRI calculates the difference between the first entry date for a visit and visit date. If the visit date is updated to a future date later on, it may result in the difference being a negative value. In such cases, entries are not considered for calculations. 
 | 1. Subject must be enrolled and have datapoints in the study.  
 2. Visits must be active, touched, and non-deleted. Visit date should not be null

## Custom KRIs
 In addition to system KRIs , you can track user-defined custom KRIs in the KRI Dashboard . Custom KRIs help organizations target and track unique and specific endpoints or area of interests for risk analysis. Authorized users in your study environment can create and activate custom KRIs using Medidata's KRI Configuration . With KRI Configuration, you can create numeric KRIs or percentage KRIs . To learn more, see Add and Edit Custom Numeric and Percentage KRIs . 
 Note : Screen Failure (SF) Rate is no longer available as a system KRI, but you can set it up as custom KRI for studies where SF patient's data is collected in Medidata Rave. In Rave, the patient's Rave Patient Status must be tagged with Screen Failure. 
 Important : For a KRI and its KRI value to be included in the KRI Dashboard, your study requires:
- At least three sites or three countries to enable calculating custom KRIs. 
- At least two enrolled patients at each site or country. 
## Custom Numeric KRIs
 A custom numeric KRI is a key risk indicator that analyzes a single user-specified variable or data set and produces a numeric output for the results or observances. Numeric KRI value calculations are based on one of the following variable types: Mean, Count, Rate, Count Values, Rate Values, Standard Deviation. For example, you can calculate the mean of blood pressure values in your study to determine if any sites or countries show signs of risk regarding blood pressure data. 
 For numeric KRIs, you define: 
- A unique name for the custom KRI. 
- The data sets and variables you want to perform calculations on. 
- The type of calculations you want performed on the data sets and variables: 
- Count  –  Calculates the average record count in the selected data set. The Count calculation is only available at the data set level. This calculates count at the patient level for each site and country and then takes average of patient-level counts to arrive at site-, country-, and study-level values. 
- Count Values – Calculates the average count of records in the study that meet a specified criteria based on the selected field. Valid only for fields with a value of 1 or 0. This calculates count at patient-, site-, country-, and study-level values. 
- Mean  – Calculates the mean value of a numeric data field based on the selected variable at the site. This calculates the mean of a variable at the patient/site/country/study level depending on the values users are seeing. 
- Rate  – Calculates the total average record count divided by patient time on study in months in the selected data set over time. The Rate calculation is only available at the data set level. This calculates rate for a dataset at the patient/site/country/study level depending on the values users are seeing. 
- Rate Values – Calculates the average percentage in a site of non-missing, non-zero values for a given variable. Use cases include the fraction of Adverse Events which are Serious, where Serious was 1 for an SAE, and 0 for a non-SAE event, or the fraction of a lab parameter out of normal range. Valid only for fields with a value of a 1 or 0. This calculates count at patient-, site-, country-, and study-level values and multiply by 100.
- Standard Deviation – Calculates variance in a set of observed values based on the selected field. This calculates value for a field at the patient/site/country/study level depending on the values users are seeing. 
## Custom Percentage KRIs
 A custom percentage KRI is key risk indicator based on a user-defined binary expression that assesses whether or not patients meet specified conditions or criteria within a targeted risk area. Percentage KRI value calculations appear as percentages. For example, the percentage of patients who experienced serious adverse events. Or the percentage of patients with a history of hypertension who had thrombocytopenia between study days 5 and 10. 
 For percentage KRIs, you define: 
- A unique name for the custom KRI. 
- The specific risk category that you want the KRI to target its analysis on. 
- A functional expression for a numerator and denominator using date, number, or text variables within a study environment that queries your study database to assess if patients meet certain conditions or criteria. 
- The denominator includes the number of patients meeting the expression's criteria who are enrolled.
- If the denominator is not specified, it is taken as the total number of enrolled patients. 
- The numerator includes the number of patients meeting the expression's criteria who are enrolled and who also meet denominator criteria. 
 Note : Screen Failure (SF) Rate is no longer available as a system KRI, but you can set it up as custom KRI for studies where SF patient's data is collected in Rave. In Rave, the patient's Rave Patient Status must be tagged with Screen Failure. 
 When activated, a custom KRI's data is consumed, analyzed, calculated, and rendered in the KRI Dashboard .

## KRI Descriptions and Calculation Methodologies
 You can view and track system KRIs and custom KRIs in the KRI Dashboard . 
## System KRIs
 System KRIs are Medidata-defined KRIs that are standard in all studies analyzed by RBQM. Medidata defines the calculations that are performed on specific data sets and variables based on metrics that most studies typically track. Medidata always provides all customers with the system KRIs. System KRIs are uneditable and in an active state by default; however, you can deactivate system KRIs as needed. 
 The following table lists:
- The current system KRIs you can track in the KRI Dashboard . 
- The KRI category to which the KRI belongs . 
- A description for each KRI. 
- How RBQM calculates each KRI's values. 
 Important : For a KRI and its KRI value to be included in the KRI Dashboard, your study requires:
- At least three sites or three countries to match the minimum data requirements listed in the table below. 
- At least two enrolled patients at each site or country. 
 Important : If there are fewer data points at the site and country level, the statistical model that calculates KRIs may produce less accurate outcomes.

===== PAGE: kri_risk_level_alert_methodology.html | KRI Risk Level Alert Methodology =====
## KRI Risk Level Alert Methodology
 RBQM indicates a KRI's level of risk on the KRI Dashboard by color-coding its KRI value and appending asterisks to the KRI value. However, the methodology that RBQM uses to determine a KRI's risk level threshold differs for system KRIs and custom KRIs. 
## System KRIs Risk Alert Methodology
 RBQM uses a standard value-based risk level threshold for the following system KRIs: 
- AE Entry Delay 
- Visit Entry Delay 
- Non-System Query Delay 
- System Query Delay 
- Percent Out Of Window Visit 
- Missing Visit Percentage 
 For AE Entry Delay, Visit Entry Delay, Non-System Query Delay, and System Query Delay, if the KRI's value is: 
- Less than 7 , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in green font and no asterisk. Green suggests that there is nothing about the study data at the site or country that would raise alarm about the risk being monitored. The site or country is likely operating and reporting data as expected. 
- Equal to or greater than 7 but less than 14 , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in yellow font and appended with one asterisk. Yellow* indicates that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site or country resulting in its KRI value to be an outlier. The risk being monitored may warrant investigation at the site or country level. 
- Greater than 14 , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in red font and appended with two asterisks. Red** indicates that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site or country resulting in its KRI value to be an extreme outlier. The risk being monitored may warrant investigation at the site or country level. 
 For Percent Out Of Window Visit and Missing Visit Percentage, if the KRI's value is: 
- Equal to or greater than 0% but less than 10% , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in green font and no asterisk. Green suggests that there is nothing about the study data at the site or country that would raise alarm about the risk being monitored. The site or country is likely operating and reporting data as expected. 
- Equal to or greater than 10% but less than 20% , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in yellow font and appended with one asterisk. Yellow* indicates that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site or country resulting in its KRI value to be an outlier. The risk being monitored may warrant investigation at the site or country level. 
- Greater than 20% , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in red font and appended with two asterisks. Red** indicates that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site or country resulting in its KRI value to be an extreme outlier. The risk being monitored may warrant investigation at the site or country level. 
 RBQM uses a statistical model to determine the risk level for the following system KRIs: 
- Number of AEs Per Patient-Month 
- Number of SAEs Per Patient-Month 
- Manual Query Rate 
- System Query Rate 
 To learn about RBQM's statistical model for its risk level alert methodology, see Statistical Model for Risk Alert Methodology . 
## Custom KRIs Risk Alert Methodology
 You can configure custom numeric and percentage KRIs to use: 
- User-defined risk level thresholds as the basis for the KRI's risk level alert methodology, or 
- The system-defined risk level thresholds based on RBQM's statistical model for the KRI's risk level alert methodology. To learn more, see Statistical Model for Risk Alert Methodology . 
 If the KRI's threshold type is User Defined, then you can define the KRI's: 
- Moderate Risk Threshold 
- High Risk Threshold. 
 If the KRI's value is: 
- Above the user-defined high risk threshold , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in red font and appended with two asterisks. Red** indicates that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site or country resulting in its KRI value to be an extreme outlier. The risk being monitored may warrant investigation at the site or country level. 
- Below the user-defined high risk threshold but above the user-defined moderate risk threshold , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in yellow font and appended with one asterisk. Yellow* indicates that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site or country resulting in its KRI value to be an outlier. The risk being monitored may warrant investigation at the site or country level. 
- Above the user-defined moderate risk threshold and there is no defined high risk threshold , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in yellow font and appended with one asterisk. Yellow* indicates that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site or country resulting in its KRI value to be an outlier. The risk being monitored may warrant investigation at the site or country level. 
- Below the user-defined moderate risk threshold , then the KRI Dashboard shows the KRI value in green font and no asterisk. Green suggests that there is nothing about the study data at the site or country that would raise alarm about the risk being monitored. The site or country is likely operating and reporting data as expected. 
## Statistical Model for Risk Alert Methodology
 RBQM includes each site and country in a  statistical model to determine whether the site or country is significantly associated with a given KRI . RBQM calculates the p-value and slope coefficient for all sites and countries for a given KRI. RBQM then ranks the p-value and slope coefficient for all sites and countries for a given KRI by quantile . RBQM ranks sites and countries with lower p-values higher than those with higher p-values. Likewise, RBQM ranks sites and countries with higher slope coefficients higher than those with lower slope coefficients.  
 RBQM determines a site or country KRI's risk level by calculating the combined average of the p-value quantile value and slope coefficient quantile value for each site and country KRI. Based on the average quantile, the KRI Dashboard  color-codes each site and country KRI value to alert you to the KRI risk level:
- Red** indicates that the KRI value at the site or country has an average quantile value of less than 5% or greater than 95% for a given KRI value. This means that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site or country resulting in its KRI value to be an extreme outlier. The risk being monitored may warrant investigation at the site or country level. 
- Yellow* indicates that the KRI value at the site or country has an average quantile value between 5% and 15% or between 85% and 95% for a given KRI value. This means that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site or country resulting in its KRI value to be an outlier. The risk being monitored may warrant investigation at the site or country level. 
- Green indicates that the KRI value at the site or country has an average quantile value between 15% and 85% for a given KRI value. This suggests that there is nothing about the study data at the site or country that would raise alarm about the risk being monitored. The site or country is likely operating and reporting data as expected. 
- Gray indicates that there are fewer than two patients at the site or country, which is not enough data to determine risk level. 
 For example, let us say a site or country KRI has a p-value of 0.0006 and a slope coefficient of 14.3. In this scenario, the p-value is very low and the slope coefficient is very high compared to those of other sites or countries for the same KRI. Thus, the p-value is assigned a quantile of 100% and the slope coefficient is assigned a quantile of 96%. The resulting average quartile value for that site or country will then be (100% + 96%)/2 = 98%. Since the site or country KRI has an average quantile value greater than 95%, then the KRI Dashboard color-codes the KRI value in red.

===== PAGE: listing__kri__and_qtl_template_library.html | Listing, KRI, and QTL Template Library =====
## Listing, KRI, and QTL Template Library
 You can use templates in Data Surveillance and RBQM to save and store commonly used data listing , custom graph,  QTL , custom numeric KRI, or custom percentage KRI configurations for reuse within a study.
## What Are Templates?
 Templates are listing, custom graph, QTL,  custom numeric KRI , or custom percentage KRI  configurations that you can save and store in your organization's global template library. 
## What Is the Purpose of Templates?
 You can store and reuse common listing, custom graph , QTL, and KRI configurations that your organization is likely to include in multiple study configurations.
## Who Uses Templates?
 Members of your organization who build studies can save and store listing, custom graph , QTL, and custom KRI configurations as templates in your organization's template library.
 Members of your organization who review data; for example, study managers or data managers, can import and reuse listing and KRI configuration templates in studies.
## What Are the Benefits of Templates?
 Adding and using specific listings,  custom graphs, QTLs, and custom KRIs as templates:
- Enables you and your team to quickly and easily reapply common data listings, custom graph s,  QTLs, and custom KRIs as needed across study configurations. 
- Promotes faster study start time. 
- Ensures consistency and accuracy in listing, custom graph , QTL, and custom KRI details across studies. 
## How Do Templates Work?
 In Listings , Custom Graphs ,  QTL Configuration , and KRI Configuration , you can save listing, custom graph , QTL, or custom KRI configurations, respectively, as templates. When you save templates, you export and store the templates in a template group.
 Template groups generally comprise a collection of templates that you might logically bundle together and use when building studies. For example, you could have a template group that consists of one or more listings, or a combination of listings, QTLs, and KRIs. Templates in the template group may pertain to studies based on therapeutic area, phase, or therapy . 
 Template groups live at the study  level . You can access and reuse templates for any study across studies . Your organization has its own client division-level global template library in Data Surveillance and RBQM . You can create template groups in the template library. The template library also stores and lists the collection of your organization's templates groups and associated templates. 
## How Do I Create, Manage, and Use Templates?
 See:
- View, Add, and Manage Template Groups 
- Add Listings as Templates to Template Groups 
- Add Custom Graphs Templates to Template Groups 
## Permission Requirements
 Template access requires the following permissions:
- Manage Detect Templates 
- View Detect Templates 
 To learn more about permissions, see  RBQM Building Blocks and Permissions .

===== PAGE: listings.html | Listings =====
## Listings
 Listings are conditional expressions that parse your study data to identify and report patient data records within a specified variable that may indicate a study risk. 
## What Are Listings?
 Listings are manually configured conditional expressions that parse your study data to capture patient records within a specified variable that match the expression's defined conditions . For example, you can configure an expression to capture patient data records for female patients below age 50 who have had a serious adverse event . 
## What Is the Purpose of Listings?
 At study startup, study teams perform a risk assessment and define the high-risk, critical, or complex study data to monitor for data quality and integrity. To aid in data monitoring, you can create data listings to   identify and report patient data records that may indicate a study risk. The data records captured by the data listing's expression, in general, are the high-risk data points that your study team would want to review, investigate, and potentially mitigate. 
## Who Uses Listings?
 Data managers view, create, edit Listings, and review and validate listings results.
 Other study team members—for example, clinical study managers, clinical research associates, site monitors, central monitors, safety monitors, medical monitors, data managers, biostaticians, programmers, clinical reviewers—use listings to review and validate specific study data that pertains to their role and responsibilities.
## What Are the Benefits of Using Listings?
 By creating and using listings, you can: 
- Focus your data investigation on the most meaningful, high-risk study data. 
- Increase the amount of data you can review while saving time and effort. 
- Ensure protocol compliance, subject safety, data quality, and data integrity. 
- Direct more effective study-mitigating actions. 
## What Are Draft Listings and Approved Listings
- Draft Listings – Listings that have not passed preliminary validation and received approval for team-wide study use. You can only:
- Preview up to 100 patient data records in a draft listing's results. 
- View and edit draft listing configurations 
- Approve draft listings . 
- Approved Listings – Listings that have passed preliminary validation and received approval for team-wide study use. You can:
- View and edit approved listing configurations 
- Review and validate an approved listing's results 
- Track Listings for unreviewed records in Clean Patient Tracker . 
- Refresh an approved listing to view the listing's latest results 
- Export an approved listing's results 
- View and export an approved listing's historical data snapshots 
## How Do Listings Work?
 First, you can optionally  view your study's data sets to:
- Holistically explore and investigate your entire set of study data, and 
- Determine if you should create any Listings to monitor data that may be of high risk to the study. 
 Then you can create draft listings by configuring conditional expressions that run against your study data to capture patient records within a specified variable that   match the expression's defined conditions . For example, you can configure an expression to capture patient data records for   female patients below age 50 who have had a serious adverse event . 
 Your study team can then preview draft listings to ensure the listing passes preliminary validation. In which case, you can approve the listing for team-wide use in your study. Once approved, you and your study team can review and validate the data listing's full set of results . As part of the review process, you and your study team can: 
- Add internal review comments directly on individual data records that appear in a data listing's results. 
- View and submit Medidata Rave queries on Rave-enabled Listings' records directly in Data Surveillance. 
- Mark individual data records as reviewed or in progress. 
 You can also track Listings for unreviewed records in Clean Patient Tracker . 
 Note: In Data Surveillance and RBQM, s tudy data automatically refreshes four times daily at approximately 9:00am (EST), 3:00pm (EST), 9:00pm (EST) and 3:00am (EST), and the data presented within the user interface is current as of 11:00 pm (EST) the previous day, 5:00 am (EST) the same day, 11:00 am (EST) the same day, 5:00 pm (EST) the same day, respectively. Each study data refresh produces a data snapshot. Updated data from Rave, and activated datasets from Data Connect  are available in 6 to 12 hours within Data Surveillance and RBQM. 
 Important : Listings support datetime operations.

- Access and View Approved Listings

- Review Approved Listing Results

- Track and Untrack Individual Approved Listings for Clean Patient Tracker Analysis .

- Access your study-level Critical Data Templates Library .

 Note : If you click Stay , the current audit trail review session continues.
- Optional . Click Rerun to rerun the question. 
- Optional. Click Edit to modify the question.
