===== PAGE: map_data_set_analysis_data.html | Map Data Set Analysis Data =====
## Map Data Set Analysis Data
 You can configure within Data Surveillance Configuration the data sets and variables that RBQM uses to consume and produce the statistical analysis and visual output for data anomaly detection plots. 
 Tips :   
-   You do not need to build a patient profile to view the data anomaly detection analysis on your study data in Statistical Monitoring. You can quickly configure in a simple, centralized workspace in Data Mapping the specific study data that you want RBQM to analyze. 
-  You can also create derived variables using Data Connect for cross domain analysis.  
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu.
The Data Mapping page appears with the Dataset Configuration tab selected by default. 
- Locate the visit data set in the Data Sets list, and then click and drop the visit data set in Visit Dataset Selection .
 Important : You must include your visit data set in the data set configuration to ensure RBQM thoroughly and accurately reports against the timeline of events.
- After configuring your visit data set, scroll back to the Data Sets list, and find and click a data set containing variables that you want to configure RBQM to consume and analyze.
 Tip : The selected data set name shows above the Record Per Patient field. Click the image below to enlarge.
- In Record Per Patient , select Single Record (SRPP) or Multiple Record (MRPP) .
The currently selected data set expands in the Data Sets list and shows the selectable list of variables contained within the data set.
 Note :  You must select the record per patient first before you can select the variables you want to configure for analysis.
- In Record Per Patient , select one of the following:
- Single Record (SRPP) – A patient record that is only collected once per patient within the data set; for example, demographics, randomization, or end of study. 
- Multiple Record (MRPP) – A patient record that is collected multiple times per patient within the data set; for example, weight, blood pressure, or pulse. 
- Select the variables within the data set that you want to configure RBQM to consume and analyze.  indicates that the variable is selected for consumption and analysis in RBQM data anomaly detection plot analysis.
 Tip : Select only critical data that you want RBQM to consume and analyze. This ensures that RBQM produces the cleanest, most effective statistical analysis and visual output on the data most pertinent to your study.
 Important : If you want to identify anomalies in other fields, you cannot configure more than: 
- 200 fields across all forms for large studies 
- 1200 fields across all forms for small studies 
- Optional . Select Pivot Data to pivot a transposed study data set that you want RBQM to analyze.
Selecting Pivot Data reveals three more optional fields: Procedure Name, Procedure Value, and Category.
 Note : You most likely should not need to pivot data ingested from Medidata Rave.
- As necessary, click and drop the data sets you want to use for:
- Procedure Name   –   Optional .   The name of the test done that collected the records in the data set.   Procedure Name only appears when you turn on the Pivot Data button. 
- Procedure Value   –   Optional . The values collected in the procedure name's fields. Procedure Value only appears when you turn on the Pivot Data button. 
- Category   –   Optional .   A subset of the records collected in the data set. Category only appears when you turn on the Pivot button. 
- Repeat steps 5-9 for each data set containing variables that you want to configure RBQM to consume and analyze.
 Tip : Data Surveillance signifies data sets that have at least one variable included in the data set configuration with a green marker next to the data set name in the Data Sets list. For example: . Data sets that have no variables included in the error plot configuration have a blue marker: 
 Important : Do not map more than 3000 variables cumulatively across all datasets; otherwise, Data Anomaly Detection cannot visualize the analysis.
- Click Save .
The next data refresh in Statistical Monitoring will run the data anomaly detection plot analysis on the data sets and variables currently saved and configured in the data set configuration.

===== PAGE: map_event_analysis_data.html | Map Event Analysis Data =====
## Map Event Analysis Data
 You can map the data sets and variables that Data Surveillance and RBQM consume to analyze conditions, treatments, and medical history events for event incidence, under-or-over reporting of events, and AI data reconciliation reports. You can map data both from Medidata Rave or externally coded studies. 
 Event analysis configuration:
- Simplifies data mapping by requiring only the key variables for Data Surveillance and RBQM to perform its study data analysis.  
- Optimizes data mapping by consolidating the configuration and mapping tasks in one centralized location. 
- Allows you to capture data for multiple domains like Adverse Events, Reactogenicity, Concomitant Medication, and Concomitant Procedures.
- Ensures Data Surveillance and RBQM analyze the correct terms and saves hours of configuration time. 
 Important : Within the event analysis configuration, you must always: 
- Select the exact field from Rave and ensure the field mapping does not include a suffix; for example, _TXT or _DTC. 
- Pick the raw or verbatim terms for conditions, treatments, and medical history terms. This enables Data Surveillance and RBQM to provide the most accurate event incidence, under-over reporting events, and Reconciliation analysis.  
- Event Incidence, AI Reconciliation and Under Over Reporting do not support data entry as a check box option in Rave for Ongoing MH.
## Set Data Source
 Data Surveillance and RBQM use the study you configure as the data source in the Event Analysis tab for analysis and reporting. Data managers can set up either fully ingested Rave studies or externally coded studies.
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu.
 The Data Mapping page appears. 
- Click the Event Analysis tab. 
- Click Set Data Source . 
- The Set Data Source window shows a ' Selecting a different data source will remove all current mappings. Would you like to proceed?' message. Select one of the following:
- Rave , if your study is fully ingested into Rave. 
- External , if you are using a study with a combination of Rave and externally coded data from WHODRUG or MEDRA dictionaries. That is, if you are using derived datasets generated and activated in Data Connect, your study data uses an external code as data source. 
- Click Confirm .
 Note : You can configure only one data source at a time. For new studies, no default data source selection exists. For existing studies, based on the data source you select, all existing event analysis mappings for conditions, treatments and medical history are removed. You must reconfigure the data mappings.
 Before selecting an external data source, you must first import that external data using Data Connect's Imports capability  or through Ingestor . For more information, see Clinical Data Studio's Data Pipeline . You cannot perform data reconciliation activities or submit queries for derived datasets in AI Reconciliation  if you do not map to the correct study data source.  
## Map Conditions, Treatments, and Medical History for Event Analysis 
 Data Surveillance and RBQM reports on and analyzes the conditions, treatments, and medical history events you map in the Event Analysis tab. Data Managers can choose to include the analysis information in:
- Event Incidence 
- Under-over Reporting 
- Reconciliation reports 
 Based on the data set you select, Data Surveillance and RBQM identify key variables to perform its study data analysis.  
 Important : You must configure all three event types: conditions, treatments, and medical history, otherwise AI Reconciliation reports and Under-over Reporting plots do not work. Event Incidence plots work if you map any one event type. AI Reconciliation reports do not work if you capture medical dictionary coded information on the portrait section of a hybrid form. You must capture all medical dictionary coded information in the logline sections of a hybrid form for results to appear. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu.
 The Data Mapping page appears. 
- Click the Event Analysis tab. 
- Click New Mapping .
 Note : If you select a new study data source, all existing event analysis mappings for conditions, treatments and medical history are removed. You must reconfigure the data mappings.
- Select one of the following, and then enter the corresponding mapping details:
- Condition Mapping – The mapping of the data set and fields, which record conditions such as Adverse Events or Reactogenicity. Based on the condition mapping, Event Incidence, Under-Over Reporting, and AI Data Reconciliation reports identify which data set to check for event analysis.
 Field Descriptions 
- Data Set – Data set you want Data Surveillance and RBQM to use when it runs its event analysis. 
- Term – Reported term for the condition. For example, for the Adverse Event data set, you can select Adverse Event Name. 
- Start Date – Condition start date. 
- Serious Event Y/N – Whether the adverse event (condition) was serious. Y, Yes, T, True, 1, or Serious values are considered as serious. 
- End Date – Condition end date. 
- Treatment ConMed  – Optional. Concomitant medication used for the treatment.  
- Treatment ConProcedure   – Optional. Concomitant procedure used for the treatment.
 Note :  Selecting Treatment ConMed or Treatment ConProcedure helps filter out reconciled adverse or treated events. If you select Treatment ConMed and Treatment ConProcedure fields, you must further select Concomitant Treatment Type as Medication or Procedure under Treatment Mapping. Otherwise a warning message appears if you do not have a procedure or treatment data set mapped in the Treatment Mapping table. The reference is not saved either.

===== PAGE: map_lab_measurements_data.html | Map Lab Measurements Data =====
## Map Lab Measurements Data
 You can configure the adverse events data sets and specific Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v 5.0 grading data variables that AI Data Reconciliation consumes to analyze laboratory measurement records. 
 Note : If you do not set up the lab measurements data configuration, you cannot view the CTCAE report analysis in AI Data Reconciliation. The CTCAE grade in data you ingest from Medidata Rave must be a numeric value. CTCAE reports do not work if the CTCAE grade is in Roman numerals. Data you ingest from Rave must be in Central Lab data format (derived datasets), that is, each row must correspond to a single analyte name. If this is not the case, for example, if the data is in Local Lab format, you must use   transformations in Clinical Data Studio - Data Connect   to pivot lab data (external datasets). 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu.
 The Data Mapping page appears. 
- Click the Lab Measurements tab. 
- Click Add Lab Measurements . 
- Select or enter the following:
- Dataset – The adverse event data set you want the AI Data Reconciliation algorithm to use to run its analysis on to show data in the CTCAE reports. 
- Collection Date – The date on which the laboratory measurements were collected. 
- Sample Type – The type of biological matter collected in the laboratory from patients to conduct tests.This can be either the panel name or the specimen type on the laboratory test form. For example, if panel name is Hematology, the corresponding specimen type is blood.
 Note : If you configure only panel name or only specimen type in the Sample Type field, the AI Data Reconciliation algorithm still identifies lab records associated with the reported term (AE).
- Analyte Name – The data set variable that corresponds to the type of specific substance or chemical being measured in the laboratory test. Analytes are components in a biological sample whose levels are measured to assess the effects of a drug, or to monitor the patient's health. Examples include glucose, hemoglobin, and cholesterol. 
- Analyte Value – Optional. The data set variable value that corresponds to the analyte.  
- Analyte Unit – Optional . The unit the analyte variable value is measured in. 
- Upper Limit – Optional . The highest analyte value permissible. 
- Lower Limit – Optional . The lowest analyte value permissible. 
- Loinc Code – Optional . The analyte code as per the Logical Observation Identifiers Name and Codes database. 
- Click Save.

===== PAGE: map_patient_milestone_data_for_third-party__fully_ingested_studies.html | Map Patient Milestone Data for Third-party, Fully Ingested Studies =====
## Map Patient Milestone Data for Third-party, Fully Ingested Studies
 For studies that consist of third-party study data that is fully ingested and incorporated into Clinical Data Studio outside of Medidata Rave by way of the Data Connect >  Imports capability, y ou must map patient milestone date data points within Data Mapping. This enables Data Surveillance and RBQM to produce reports, statistical analysis, and visualizations on third-party study data that is fully ingested. 
 You can map  the data set, folder, and mapped variable for the following milestone dates: 
- Patient Enrolled Date 
- Patient Informed Consent Date 
- Patient Randomized Date  
- Patient Screening Date
 Important: Patient Enrolled Date or Patient Randomized Date Mapping Required
 For third-party, fully ingested studies, the following capabilities require Patient Enrolled Date or Patient Randomized Date to be mapped :
- KRI Dashboard 
- QTL Dashboard 
- Event Incidence 
- Under-over Reporting 
- Duplicate Patients 
- Rounding and Propagation 
- Duplicate Patients 
- Statistical Monitoring 
- AI Data Reconciliation (specifically the Treatment Without Conditions report) 
- Clean Patient Tracker 
 Clinical Data Studio factors in the mapped  Patient Enrolled Date or Patient Randomized Date —whichever is mapped— as the start date. The start date start date is taken as an indication for enrolled patients  on the study. The capabilities listed above require the defined start date in order to process the study data and properly generate and visualize their analyses. 
 Important: Additional Notes
- The current process of tagging data for Rave studies does not change. Mapping patient milestone data in the Patient Milestones tab > Patient Master Mapping table is not required for Rave studies whose study data is already tagged in Rave. However, the ability to map patient milestone data in Clinical Data Studio now enables Clinical Data Studio's capabilities to process and run analysis on study data from third-party studies that are fully ingested from the Data Connect > Imports capability. 
- If your study does have Rave-tagged data and you do decide to map patient milestone data  Patient Milestones tab > Patient Master Mapping table , then we recommend that your Rave taggings match your patient milestone mappings to ensure data analysis consistency across system KRIs and graphs. 
- The calculation of system KRIs requires tagging study data in Rave. Clinical Data Studio cannot perform system KRI analysis on third-party, fully ingested study data. Patient Milestone Configuration does not enable for the mapping of data points required for system KRI analysis. 
- You cannot map patient milestone data in Clinical Data Studio until after the first time Clinical Data Studio successfully processes the study data.
 Limitations
 For studies that consist of third-party study data that is fully ingested and incorporated into Clinical Data Studio outside of Rave by way of the Data Connect > Imports capability, the following Data Surveillance and RBQM capability modules do not work: 
- System KRIs 
- AI Reconciliation 
- Event Incidence 
- Sorting visualizations by Schedule of Assessment. 
- Bulk submitting queries 
- Linking to Rave 
- Audit Trail Review 
- Weekend and Holiday Visits 
- TSDV 
- EDC Query Report 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu. 
- The Data Mapping page appears. 
- Click the Patient Milestones tab. 
- In the Patient Master Mapping table, select the  Data Set , Folder , and Mapped Variable for the following:
- Patient Enrolled Date – Mapping Patient Enrolled Date data points enables Clinical Data Studio to analyze study data from third-party, fully ingested studies in the following capabilities: 
- KRI Dashboard 
- QTL Dashboard 
- Data Anomaly Detection 
- Event Incidence 
- Under-over Reporting 
- Duplicate Patients 
- Rounding and Propagation 
- Duplicate Patients 
- AI Data Reconciliation (specifically the Treatment Without Conditions report) 
- Clean Patient Tracker 
- Patient Informed Consent Date – Mapping Patient Informed Consent Date data points is not required for any Clinical Data Studio capability to analyze study data from third-party, fully ingested studies.  
- Patient Randomized Date – Mapping Patient Randomized Date data points enables Clinical Data Studio to analyze study data from third-party, fully ingested studies in the following capabilities:
- KRI Dashboard 
- QTL Dashboard 
- Data Anomaly Detection 
- Event Incidence 
- Under-over Reporting 
- Duplicate Patients 
- Rounding and Propagation 
- Duplicate Patients 
- AI Data Reconciliation (specifically the Treatment Without Conditions report) 
- Clean Patient Tracker 
- Patient Screening Date – Mapping Patient Screening Date data points is required to save the patient milestone mappings. However, mapping Patient Screening data points is not required for any Clinical Data Studio capability to analyze study data from third-party, fully ingested studies. 
- Click Update .

===== PAGE: map_potential_duplicate_patient_data.html | Map Potential Duplicate Patient Data =====
## Map Potential Duplicate Patient Data
 Duplicate patients are patients who enroll in clinical trials for financial gain or for extra dosages of medication. Duplicate patients threaten both participant safety and the integrity of research findings. Statistical Monitoring uncovers potential duplicate patients by analyzing six demographics: date of birth, gender, height, weight, race, ethnicity. In addition, Statistical Monitoring analyzes the physical distance within 100 miles of site location of each patient to find patients that look very similar. 
 With Data Mapping, you can map the six demographic parameters: date of birth, gender, height, weight, race, and ethnicity to the corresponding reference variables from data sets in your study environment and save the configuration, which Medidata's data science microservice algorithms consume. Based on the analytics, Statistical Monitoring automatically generates the configuration data analysis and renders the visualization output as a global heat and site level map. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu.
 The Data Mapping page appears. 
- Click the Potential Duplicate Patients tab. 
- For each of the following reference demographic, select a variable to map from any data set in your study. For example, you can map the Date of Birth demographic to DOB from the Chemistry (CHEM) data set.
- Date Of Birth   
- Weight  
- Height  
- Gender 
- Race
 Note : If Race data values are collected by selecting a check box for each race in Medidata Rave, then we suggest creating a Check All That Apply derivation using the Derived Variables capability. Doing so ensures that RBQM pulls in all possible race values as mappable variables as part of the Duplicate Patient Configuration. To learn more, see Create Derived Variable with Check All That Apply .
- Ethnicity
 Note : You can select mapped variables, including derived variables, from different data sets to map to the reference demographic.
 Tip : The Data Set and Mapped Variable menus include duplicate field options. Be sure to select the exact field from Rave and ensure the field mapping does not include a suffix (_TXT, _DTC, for example). If one of the six fields required to be mapped do not exist in Rave, you can use a proxy and the algorithm will still work; however, it will be less accurate.
- Click Update .

===== PAGE: map_recist_1_1_data.html | Map RECIST 1.1 Data =====
## Map RECIST 1.1 Data
 The RECIST 1.1 Dashboard is a visualization and reporting tool that captures treatment response and disease progression metrics for patients in oncology studies based on the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors ( 
 RECIST 1.1 
 ) methodology.  With t 
 he RECIST 1.1 Dashboard you can: 
- Quantify tumor burden and outcome calculations for patients. 
- Summarize the total count of patients, and those in various stages of treatment response at the selected scan visit type and site. 
- Track tumor burden over a period, and identify discrepant records. 
- Assess the accuracy of RECIST 1.1 calculations and safety monitoring. 
 With Oncology Mapping, you can configure the variables from data sets in your study environment which Data Surveillance's microservice algorithms consume. Based on the analytics and configuration, the RECIST 1.1 Dashboard generates configuration data analysis and produces visualization output as waterfall and spaghetti plots. 
 Note : We recommend you map data on the RECIST tab only if you have access to the RECIST 1.1 Dashboard in Data Surveillance.

 The OID and name appear for all saved fields for both data sets (target field) and corresponding fields (source field). 
 Note : If eCRF form names are different, ensure that you enter the correct field OIDs in the mapping. Confirm that you select the correct data sets from your study for the target and source fields. Otherwise, Data Surveillance fails to refresh and show its statistical analysis on the RECIST 1.1 Dashboard.

===== PAGE: map_vital_sign_data_for_rounding_and_propagation_analysis.html | Map Vital Sign Data for Rounding and Propagation Analysis =====
## Map Vital Sign Data for Rounding and Propagation Analysis
 You can configure the vital sign data sets and collection date variables that RBQM consumes to analyze and visually render the sites that may be rounding and propagating vital sign records.
 You can also optionally further specify and configure the procedure name, procedure value, and category that RBQM analyzes.
 Notes
- If you do not set up the rounding and propagation configuration, you cannot view the  rounding and propagation analysis in Statistical Monitoring. 
- Do not map vital sign data for rounding and propagation analysis if your study does not plan to collect vital signs at least three times per patient across all vital signs datas sets. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Data Mapping in the left-hand menu.
 The Data Mapping page appears. 
- Click the Rounding and Propagation tab. 
- Select or enter the following:
- Reference Name   – A custom name to help you identify the data set configured for analysis. RBQM does not include the Reference Name in its analysis. 
- Data Set   – The vital sign data set that you want RBQM to use to run its rounding and propagation analysis on. 
- Collection Date   – The date variable for the date in which the vital sign collection took place that you want RBQM to run its rounding and propagation analysis on. 
- Procedure Name   –   Optional .   The name of the test done that collected the vital sign records.   Procedure Name is only selectable when you turn on the Pivot button. 
- Procedure Value   –   Optional . The values collected in the procedure name's fields. Procedure Value is only selectable when you turn on the Pivot button. 
- Category   –   Optional .   A subset of the vital sign collected, such as respiratory vital signs or body vital signs. Category is only selectable when you turn on the Pivot button. 
- Pivot – Toggle the Pivot button on, , to pivot a transposed study data set that you want RBQM to analyze. Selecting to pivot the data enables RBQM to consume and analyze the Procedure Name, Procedure Value, or Category selections you optionally choose. indicates that the data set is pivoted.
 Note : You most likely should not need to pivot data ingested from Medidata Rave.
- Click Save .

===== PAGE: merge_multiple-record_variable_to_multiple-record_data_set.html | Merge Multiple-Record Variable to Multiple-Record Data Set =====
## Merge Multiple-Record Variable to Multiple-Record Data Set
 You can merge a data set variable containing multiple records over multiple visits with another data set containing multiple records over multiple visits. For example, merging an Adverse Events data set variable to the Chemistry data set. 
 Important: 
- You must add a subset value and preference, even if you merge SRPP to SRPP, or SRPP to MRPP. 
- For a subset value, add the study ID. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Derived Variables in the left-hand menu. 
- Click   Create Derived Variable . 
- Identify and drag a  data set   from the Data Sets list into the Configure Variable section. For example, Adverse Events.
 Note:   If data set variables include unknowns, the data set replaces them with interpolated (enriched) fields like _INT, or_ DTC . For example, if the source date is missing the day, the enriched _INT field interpolates the 1st day of the month, and _DTC fields drop the unknown value. If the source field uses dictionary terms, the enriched _TXT field shows the coded terms. 
- Enter the derived variable’s identification information: 
- Name – Object identifier (OID) of derived variable. For example, Adverse Events – CHEMDT. Must be unique. 
- Label  – Name for derived variable to appear in other applications. This can be the same as the Name field, or a more specific descriptor. For example, Adverse Events – Chemistry Dates. 
- Select Merge  from the Derived Variable Type menu. 
- Select MRPP to MRPP from the Type of Merge list.
 Note : Always confirm that you have selected the correct merge type for the dataset. Otherwise, Data Surveillance and RBQM will fail to refresh and output its statistical analysis on future data snapshots.
- Navigate to a different data set and drag your required variable to merge into the Source Variable field . 
- Complete the merge wizard: 
- Source Merge Variable – Drag the data set variable that you want to merge into the target data set. 
- Target Merge Variable – Drag the data set variable that you want the source merge variable to merge with.
The source merge variable aligns with each record of the multiple-record target variable.
 Note : The Source Merge Variable and Target Merge Variable name must be the same.
- Subset Variable – If applicable, d rag a data set variable from the selected source merge variable's data set that you want to merge a value from. The subset variable serves as a reference variable to narrow down the multiple-record source data set variable into a single record to merge into the target data set.
 Note : The Subset Variable must be different from the Source Merge Variable and Target Merge Variable. Otherwise, Clinical Data Studio's data workflow may not work correctly.
- Subset Value –   If applicable, select a value from the list to merge into the target data set. The subset value is a value from the selected subset variable. The subset value completes the process to narrow down the multiple-record source data set to single record.
 Note : Derived Variables populates the subset value field based on the selected subset variable. In some cases, the subset values may not contain values. In those cases, you may disregard the field.
- Preference –   Optional . If applicable, based on the selected subset variable and subset value, select which source data set variable value to merge into the target data set. For date or numeric values, select to merge the maximum or minimum value from the source data set variable. For text values, the first reported value is automatically merged. 
- Click  Save .
 In Data Surveillance and RBQM, the list of available datasets and variables that you can view and select from include derived variables at the bottom of the list. In Data Surveillance, the list of available datasets and variables appends derived variable names with the blue DERIVED icon.

===== PAGE: merge_variables_to_data_sets.html | Merge Variables to Data Sets =====
## Merge Variables to Data Sets
 You can merge a data set variable from one data set into a target data set. The target data set  lists the merged data set variable as a derived variable within the variable list. Use Merge derivations to bring variables from one dataset into another, that is, to m erge a  data set variable   from one data set into a target data set.   These derivations vary depending on which types of datasets you use to perform the merge (multiple record per patient datasets vs. single record per patient datasets). When merging from MRPP to MRPP, a “linking” variable must be present in the dataset to ensure the merge functions as designed. 
   In Data Surveillance and RBQM, the list of available datasets and variables that you can view and select from include derived variables at the bottom of the list.   Merging options include: 
- Single-Record Variable to Single-Record Data Set  – Merge a data set variable containing singular records over multiple visits with another data set containing singular records over multiple visits. For example, merging a Demographics data set variable to the Eligibility Criteria data set. 
- Single-Record Variable to Multiple-Record Data Set  – Merge a data set variable containing singular records over multiple visits with another data set containing multiple records over multiple visits. For example, merging a Demographics data set variable to the Adverse Events data set. 
- Multiple-Record Variable to Single-Record Data Set  – Merge a data set variable containing multiple records over multiple visits with another data set containing singular records over multiple visits. For example, merging an Adverse Events data set variable to Demographics data set. 
- Multiple-Record Variable to Multiple-Record Data Set  – Merge a data set variable containing multiple records over multiple visits with another data set containing multiple records over multiple visits. For example, merging an Adverse Events data set variable to the Chemistry data set.

===== PAGE: open_queries.html | Open EDC Queries =====
## Open EDC Queries
 You can view in one consolidated location the detailed list of all open and answered queries raised against patient data for enrolled patients in your study. Viewing and evaluating all open and answered patient queries in your study in one place enables you to review and close queries faster. Therefore, you can more quickly and efficiently lock and freeze patient data. The list of queries automatically refreshes every 6 hours. The number of open EDC queries matches the records in the Queries dataset. 
 Note : The Queries list does not show canceled or closed queries. 
 You can also: 
- Drill down to view queried patients' case report forms in Medidata Rave. 
- Download the Open Queries list to a CSV file. 
 Note: In Data Surveillance and RBQM, s tudy data automatically refreshes four times daily at approximately 9:00am (EST), 3:00pm (EST), 9:00pm (EST) and 3:00am (EST), and the data presented within the user interface is current as of 11:00 pm (EST) the previous day, 5:00 am (EST) the same day, 11:00 am (EST) the same day, 5:00 pm (EST) the same day, respectively. Each study data refresh produces a data snapshot. Updated data from Rave, and activated datasets from Data Connect  are available in 6 to 12 hours within Data Surveillance and RBQM. 
## View Open Query Records
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click EDC Queries in the left-hand menu.
The Open EDC Queries page shows and contains the Queries list. The list includes the following information:
- Patient – The patient ID of the queried patient. You can click a hyperlinked Patient ID to view that patient's case report forms in Rave.
 Note : You cannot link to patient case report forms that exist in Rave Classic.
- Site – The site that the patient belongs to. 
- Country – The country in which the patient's site resides. 
- Status – Specifies whether the patient query is currently open or answered.
 Note : The Queries list does not show canceled or closed queries.  
- Folder – The folder containing query for a patient data point. 
- Form – The name of the form that contains the query for a patient data point. 
- Field – The field name of the patient data point that is queried. 
- Open Date – The date on which the query was opened on the patient data point. 
- Open By – The user who opened the query on the patient data point. 
- Query Data – The contents of the queried data point. 
- Query Text – The user-entered query text opened on a data point. 
- Marking Group – A virtual communication group in which individuals who belong to a specific role receive explicit permissions to conduct query-related actions. 
- Response Text – The site's response to the query. 
- Response Date – The date the query was responded to. 
- Responded By – The user who responded to the opened query. 
- Log Line –  T he specific log line in the form that is queried. 
## Download the Open Query Records List
 You can download the Open Queries list to a CSV file. Downloading the Open Queries list enables you to: 
- Easily exchange the list externally with stakeholders to facilitate communication. 
- Locally save and archive the list. 
 Notes
- You cannot download an Open Query Records list containing over 30,000 records. 
- Larger data sets may take longer to download.  
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click EDC Queries in the left-hand menu.
The Open EDC Queries page shows. 
- In the Open Query Records section, click Download .
The Open Query Records list downloads to your browser as a CSV file. You can save the file locally to your machine.

===== PAGE: patient_profiles.html | Patient Profiles =====
## Patient Profiles
 Patient Profiles is a Data Surveillance capability that enables you to build patient profile designs   using tables, flags, graphs, and timelines   to identify safety signals and ensure patient data consistency. 
## What Is Patient Profiles?
 Unable to render {include} The included page could not be found.
## What Is the Purpose of Patient Profiles?
 Patient Profiles allows you to create profile designs, which are highly configurable templates that you use to design detailed reports for study patients. You can generate physical report documentation based on profile designs for various clinical trial roles—such as data managers or site managers—to review and interpret study data or for FDA consumption.
## Who Uses Patient Profiles?
 Life sciences professionals such as programmers, statisticians, medical writers, and clinicians work in Patient Profiles to view, create, and edit profile designs.
## How Does Patient Profiles Work?
 The goal of Patient Profiles is to build patient profile designs. You build the patient profile design infrastructure using containers of information known as elements. Elements consist of headers, tables, and timelines. And then you populate your elements with data in the form of variables, which derive from multiple preloaded study environment-specific data sets.
 When adding elements, and based on the element type you are working with, you can:
- define element details; 
- adjust the placement of variables, rows, and columns within elements; 
- configure variable data points to display in the color of your choosing; 
- and much more. 
 After adding elements to your profile design, you can:
- arrange where the elements are positioned in the design layout; 
- apply color-coding to entire element sections; and  
 Meanwhile, throughout the course of the patient profile design process, you can:
- view patient profiles  with actual study data to help you evaluate how the profile design is taking shape in real time. 
 When satisfied with your design and layout, you can:
- review and generate reports based on the profile design. 
 The workflow progress bar below illustrates the recommended patient profile design workflow from creation to completion.
 Note : In Data Surveillance and RBQM, s tudy data automatically refreshes four times daily at approximately 9:00am (EST), 3:00pm (EST), 9:00pm (EST) and 3:00am (EST), and the data presented within the user interface is current as of 11:00 pm (EST) the previous day, 5:00 am (EST) the same day, 11:00 am (EST) the same day, 5:00 pm (EST) the same day, respectively. Each study data refresh produces a data snapshot. Updated data from Medidata Rave and   activated datasets from Data Connect   are available in 6 to 12 hours within Data Surveillance and RBQM.  For more information, see Clinical Data Studio Data Pipeline.   
## What Are the Benefits of Patient Profiles?
 To give you a truly great working experience, Patient Profiles:
- Uses Medidata's platform data workflow , which feeds in  high quality, up-to-date, and study environment-specific  study variables with which to populate your profile designs. 
- Provides a simple, open, and intuitive design work space featuring: 
- a consistent accordion structure to select data sets and variables across elements. 
- easy-to-use drag-and-drop functionality to add variables. 
- customizable text for table column headers and timeline data point displays. 
- error-reducing save validations to enforce the use of correct variable types and  prevent creation of incomplete or incorrectly configured elements. 
- Allows you to preview profiles with actual study data while still being designed in real time to evaluate how the profile design is taking shape. 
- Creates elegant, comprehensive reports in PDF or Word format for each patient in your study that include colorful graphics and timelines showcasing important events in a patient’s time on the study while highlighting new or interesting data. 
- Makes blind reviews more attractive and consistent by providing instant access to readable data, allowing a rapid and easy exchange of information.

===== PAGE: perform_signal_operations.html | Perform Signal Operations =====
## Perform Signal Operations
 Each signal is an indication of a potential data issue or glitch that can quickly escalate and become unmanageable, or even threaten the data integrity of a clinical study. With Signals, you can take steps to review and validate, assess, and further investigate signals to assign responsible stakeholders corrective or preventive tasks, and track all progress in one place. 
 Signal operations are based on the status associated with a signal. An automated signal that appears for any module has any one of the following signal statues:
- New 
- Opened 
- Dismissed 
- Watched 
- Resolved 
- Reopened 
- Closed 
 The following image shows the signals status:
 Tip: Click the image to enlarge.
## Dismiss Signals
 If a new or watched signal appears in the signal report, but the Central Monitor assesses the signal to be irrelevant, they can dismiss the signal. You must have the Manage Signals building block to dismiss signals. For more information, see Dismissed Signal .
- Access RBQM , and then click  Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals page appears. 
- In the Signals list table, click , the More icon, for the signal you want to view. 
- From the list of options, click Dismiss . 
- In the Dismiss Signal window, enter a reason for dismissal. 
- Click Dismiss .
The signal status updates to Dismissed.
 Note : A signal with status as Dismissed remains dismissed if the observation value meets the threshold after a data refresh. However, if the central monitor decides on further action, and adds an assignee to the signal, the status changes to Open . If the observation drops below the threshold for a dismissed signal, the signal no longer appears in the signal report after a data refresh.
## Watch Signals
 You can watch a new or dismissed signal to monitor any fluctuations in observation values or potential changes, and then act as needed. Certain signals may not require any investigation or action currently, but watching allows central monitors to  consolidate key signals from various analyses that might need intervention in future. You must have the Manage Signals building block to watch signals. For more information, see Signal Acted Upon. 
- Access RBQM , and then click  Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals page appears. 
- In the Signals list table, click , the More icon, for the signal you want to view. 
- From the list of options, click Watch .
The signal status updates to Watched. 
 Note : You can further raise a watched signal as an issue, or dismiss it, if needed.
## Add Assignee
 If you decide that a signal that appears in the signal report requires action, you can assign the signal to an assignee. The assignee can take further actions and update the action status. You must have the Manage Signals building block to assign signals. For more information, see Signal Acted Upon. 
- Access RBQM , and then click  Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals page appears. 
- In the Signals list table, click under the Assignee column in the row for the signal you want to assign. 
- In the Add Assignee window, complete the following details: 
- Assignee Name – Select from the list the person you want to assign the signal.  
- Due Date – Select a due date. 
- Click Add Assignee . 
 Note : The signal status changes from New to Open. You can assign a signal to only one assignee. You can only create an action for a new signal after you add an assignee.
## Link Risks to Signals
 With linking study risks to signals, you can prioritize efforts and ensure effective study oversight.  
- Access RBQM , and then click  Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals page appears. 
- In the Signals list table, click , the More icon, for the signal you want to view. 
- From the list, click Open Signal Details . 
 A slide-out panel shows four tabs: Details, Comments, Actions, Resolution. 
- Click the Details tab. 
- In the Signal Details section, select one or more risks into the Associated Risks list. 
- Click the check mark. 
- Edit the text in the Description field if needed.
The Description field auto populates based on the description for the configured module. 
- Click Close . 
## Add Comments
- Access RBQM , and then click  Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals page appears. 
- In the Signals list table, click , the More icon, for the signal you want to view. 
- From the list, click Open Signal Details . 
 A slide-out panel shows four tabs: Details, Comments, Actions, Resolution. 
- Click the Comments  tab.
All the comments for the signal appear on the page. 
- Click  Create Comment . 
- Type into the field to add your comments. 
- Click  , the OK icon to save your comment.
The new comment appears with your name. 
## Resolve Signals
 You can resolve signals as needed if satisfactory investigation outcomes emerge, even if there are outstanding actions for the signal. Signals you mark as resolved are sent for further review. For more information, see Signal Acted Upon. 
- Access RBQM , and then click  Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals page appears. 
- In the Signals list table, click , the More icon, for the signal you want to view. 
- From the list of options, click Resolve .
OR
From the list of options, click Open Signal Details . Then click the Resolution tab, and click Add Resolution . 
- On the Mark as Resolved page, complete the following:
- Root Cause – Optional . Type the reason you marked the signal as resolved. For example, if the signal was raised as an issue, you can type the root cause. 
- Mitigation – Optional. Type the mitigation for the signal. 
- Description – Type a brief description for the signal. 
 Note : You can mark signals as resolved if they have status as Open or Reopened.
## Close Signals
 If all investigation pertaining to a resolved signal is satisfactory, you can close a signal. You must have the Manage Signals building block to close signals. For more information, see Signal Acted Upon. 
- Access RBQM , and then click  Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals page appears. 
- In the Signals list table, click , the More icon, for the resolved signal you want to close. 
- From the list, click  Open Signal Details . 
- From the Signals slide out panel, click the  Resolution tab. 
- On the Resolution tab, click Update Status . 
- Select Closed .
The signal status updates to Closed . 
## Reopen Signals
 You can reopen a closed signal if you have the Manage Signals building block added to your Cloud Administration access. For more information, see Signal Acted Upon. 
- Access RBQM , and then click  Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals page appears. 
- In the Signals list table, click , the More icon, for the resolved signal you want to close. 
- From the list, click  Open Signal Details . 
- From the Signals slide out panel, click the  Resolution tab. 
- On the Resolution tab, click Reopen Signal . 
- On the Reopen window, type in the Comments field. 
- Click Confirm .
The signal status updates to Reopened .
 Note : You must assign the reopened signal to an assignee for further action.

===== PAGE: plan_documents.html | Plan Documents =====
## Plan Documents
 A Data Quality Plan (DQP) in a study is a comprehensive document that outlines the strategies, procedures, and measures to ensure the accuracy, completeness, reliability, and integrity of the data collected during the trial. The plan is essential for verifying that the data supports robust conclusions and complies with regulatory standards. The Plan Documents capability enables data managers to build integrated data quality plans that may include risk mitigation methods for the study. 
## 
## What Is Plan Documents?
 Plan Documents is a capability where you can build integrated data quality plans, including adding risk mitigations for your study.
## What Is the Purpose of Plan Documents?
 With plan documents, data managers can build data quality plans that scope out the various aspects of running a study, maintaining data integrity, and mitigating risk to study data. Plan Documents act as a tool to review and monitor data throughout a study, and ensure the successful execution of a clinical trial.
## Who Uses Plan Documents?
 Data managers with Manage Data Quality Plans and View Data Quality Plans building blocks use plan documents. 
## How Does Plan Documents Work?
 You can add mitigations and associate functional plans in the Risk Review section in Risk Management to track risks for better study data accuracy. You can then use various components available under the Plan Documents section to build integrated data quality plans which act as a guide for risk mitigation in the study. 
## What are the Benefits of Plan Documents?
 Plan documents are integral to maintaining data integrity. Plan Documents:
- Streamlines operational planning by enabling the quick creation and management of comprehensive plans, allowing for faster execution.
- Transforms risk data into actionable, dynamic plans that actively guide team member actions.
- Provides enhanced transparency into actions and mitigations linked to each plan, ensuring alignment, accountability, and improved compliance across teams. This turns data quality management into a proactive, integrated process.
## How Do I Create Plan Documents?
 See  Access, View, and Create Plan Documents .

===== PAGE: potential_duplicate_patient_detection_methodology.html | Potential Duplicate Patient Detection Methodology =====
## Potential Duplicate Patient Detection Methodology
 To determine potential duplicate patients, RBQM analyzes enrolled patients from a unique study and identifies and filters through patients that show an exact match on the following variables: 
- Date of birth 
- Ethnicity 
- Race 
- Gender 
 Enrolled Patient Qualifications
 RBQM qualifies enrolled patients as patients that have time on study and subject start date recorded. RBQM calculates:
- time on study as: <subject start date> - <latest subject record date>. 
- subject start date as: subject enrollment date or subject randomization date, whichever is available. 
 RBQM then takes those matched patients and assesses the sites in which they are enrolled to check that:
- The two patients are at different sites. 
- The sites are within 100 miles of each other by using latitude and longitude. 
- The sites are within the same country if latitude and longitude are not available. 
 Lastly, RBQM performs a distance match on height and weight. The calculation for the distance match is:   𝑥=2|𝑥1−𝑥2|𝑥1+𝑥2.   If both the height and weight of the two patients have less than or equal to 1% difference, then RBQM flags those patients at the site as potential professional patients.
 Furthermore, the downloadable Duplicate Patients report .csv file includes a Confidence column that states RBQM's level of confidence that a patient is a duplicate. Values are: Low, Medium, and High. To learn more, see  Export the List and Summary Data of Sites with Potential Duplicate Patients .
 To determine confidence level, RBQM takes the maximum value   𝑥   of the distance match—once again, 𝑥=2|𝑥1−𝑥2|𝑥1+𝑥2—which is obtained either from the distance of height or weight, and applies the maximum x value into the following equation:   𝑦=1−100𝑥.
 The category score is assigned a confidence level as follows:
- Low –  y < 1/3 
- Medium –  if 1/3 < y < 2/3 
- High – y > 2/3

===== PAGE: potential_duplicate_patients.html | Potential Duplicate Patients =====
## Potential Duplicate Patients
 You can view on an interactive heatmap the site locations in your study that RBQM identifies as having potential duplicate patients. Identifying and investigating sites with potential duplicate patients helps e nsure data integrity and i mproves the chance of study success. 
## What Are Potential Duplicate Patients?
 Duplicate patients are   patients who enroll in clinical trials for financial gain or for extra dosages of medication. Duplicate patients most often affect types of studies such as pain, dependencies, or studies where monetary compensation and low impact of multiple dosings prompts some patients to enroll multiple times. 
## Why Should I Care About Potential Duplicate Patients?
 Duplicate patients threaten   both participant safety and the integrity of research findings. 
## How Does RBQM Identify Potential Duplicate Patients?
 RBQM uncovers potential duplicate patients in your study data by analyzing six demographics: date of birth, gender, height, weight, race, and ethnicity. In addition, RBQM also analyzes the physical distance within 100 miles of the site location of each patient to find patients that look very similar. Patients with too many similarities can indicate that those patients are indeed the same person. 
 To learn more, see  Potential Duplicate Patient Detection Methodology . 
## What Is the Potential Duplicate Patients Heatmap?
 Statistical Monitoring visually outputs all site locations in your study on an interactive heatmap. But in particular, the heatmap signifies the site locations where RBQM identifies potential duplicate patients. The heatmap has two view types: 
- Global-level View – A full global view of all worldwide site locations in the study. In global view, r ed circles indicate sites with potential duplicate patients. Blue circles indicate sites with no potential duplicate patients. You can m anually zoom in, zoom out, and scroll the map to focus on geographic areas of interest. 
- Site-level View – A zoomed-in view depicting a selected site with duplicate patients and other sites with potential duplicate patients located within a 100 mile radius. In site-level view, other sites with potential duplicate patients are indicated with purple pins.  
## What Is the Purpose of the Potential Duplicate Patients Heatmap?
 The Potential Duplicate Patients heatmap helps you quickly identify and investigate:
- Sites with potential duplicate patients across all site locations in your study. 
- Individual patients who may be duplicate patients. 
## What Are the Benefits of the Potential Duplicate Patients Heatmap?
 Identifying potential duplicate patients in a study puts you and your life sciences team in an optimal position to: 
- Prevent financial loss. 
- Ensure data integrity.  
- Improve the chance of study success. 
- Avoid delayed time to market. 
- Prevent failed clinical trials. 
## Who Uses the Potential Duplicate Patients Heatmap?
 Anyone assigned with ensuring study data integrity; for example, central monitors or site monitors.
## How Do I Uncover Potential Duplicate Patients?
 See Identify Potential Duplicate Patients In Your Study .
## How Do I Refresh Potential Duplicate Patients to Output the Latest Study Data Analysis?
 See  Schedule or Trigger When Statistical Monitoring Refreshes and Outputs the Latest Study Data Analysis .

 You can preview a draft listing's results by viewing up to 100 patient data records captured by the listing's conditional expression. Previewing a draft listing's results enables you to evaluate whether the listing generates in the expected format with normal looking results. 
 If the preview passes validation, then you can approve the listing for team-wide use in your study. Otherwise, you can edit the draft listing if the listing configuration requires updates for approval.
 Note : The draft listing preview is meant for preliminary evaluation. You must first approve a listing before you can  review and validate a Listing's full set of results .

The Listings page shows.

The Draft Listings table shows the following:
 Table Column Descriptions 
- Name – The listing's object identifier (OID). 
- Expression – The Listing's user-defined conditional expression, which Data Surveillance runs against your study data to capture the patient records within a specified variable that match the expression's defined specifications. In general, expressions are built to identify and report high-risk data points that your study team can review and investigate as necessary. 
- Rave Enabled – A check mark indicates that you can directly within Data Surveillance view and submit Rave queries on the patient records captured by the Listing .

- Site – The site that the patient belongs to. 
- Country – The country in which the site resides. 
- Variable – Each column header to the right of the Country column header represents a variable that the listing's expression is configured to run against. The variable column header shows the human-readable variable name at the top and the variable object identifier (OID) at the bottom. And then the column lists the variable's data point entries captured by the listing's conditional expression.

===== PAGE: protocol_integrity_report.html | Protocol Integrity Report =====
## Protocol Integrity Report
 The Protocol Integrity Report (PIR) functions as a centralized dashboard within the Clinical Data Studio RBQM workspace . You capture, track, review, and manage protocol deviations using this report. 
## 
## What Is Protocol Integrity Report?
 The Protocol Integrity Report (PIR) functions as a centralized dashboard within RBQM workspace . You capture, track, review, and manage protocol deviations using this report 
## What Is the Purpose of Protocol Integrity Report?
 PIR centralizes protocol deviations from multiple sources into a single view . The system aligns identified deviations with the Protocol Deviation Assessment Plan (PDAP) . The alignment standardizes reporting and ensures regulatory compliance . PIR replaces manual tracking with automated record ingestion . The application maintains a complete audit trail . The system also detects duplicate records to guarantee data integrity 
## Who Uses Protocol Integrity Report?
 Central Monitors configure the PDAP and monitor deviations . Data Managers review identified deviations to ensure data integrity . Clinical Research Associates manage and review manual protocol deviations . Study Managers use consolidated reports for trial oversight and decision-making . Approvers evaluate final scientific integrity and approve deviations . 
## How Does Protocol Integrity Report Work?
 PIR organizes protocol deviations into the In progress and Approved tabs . The In Progress tab contains the Proposed, In Review, and Confirmed statuses . PIR automatically imports Answered or Closed Medidata Rave queries containing specific prefixes such as PD or Potential PD . The system pulls records from designated PD Listings . You map these listing records to PDAP descriptions . You manually add deviation records directly in the PIR dashboard . PIR flags potential duplicate records sharing the patient, site, visit, and PDAP description . 
## What are the Benefits of Protocol Integrity Report?
 PIR consolidates all protocol violations into a streamlined dashboard . The system eliminates complex manual queries . PIR provides dynamic updates to action plans . Automated audit trails deliver a secure record for regulatory reconstruction . The dashboard supports fast identification of critical data quality issues . 
## How Do I Get Started?
- Access RBQM, and select Protocol integrity report . 
- Review the report. 
 You can preform the following actions:
- Add proposed deviation to enter a manual deviation . 
- Review  potential deviations to process Rave queries . 
- Select records in a PD listing to submit listing deviations . 
- Submit protocol deviations to process the selected listing records .

===== PAGE: protocol_integrity_report_deviations_workflow.html | Protocol Deviations and Protocol Integrity Report Workflow =====
## Protocol Deviations and Protocol Integrity Report Workflow
 Protocol Integrity Report (PIR) deviations initially have the Proposed status, regardless of source. You can review or dismiss these deviations.
## PIR Overview
- Proposed PD – The initial creation state for all protocol deviations (PD) (for example, from Medidata Rave or listings). This state requires you to assign a description from the PDAP. The PDAP description prepopulates for listing sources. You can also manually add PDs, To learn more, see  Investigate Protocol Deviations Using the Protocol Integrity Report . 
- In Review – The state when a deviation is ready for evaluation after you assign a PDAP description, reviewer and due date. Assigning these updates the status to In Review. 
- Confirmed – The state when a reviewer verifies accuracy and checks for duplicates. Actionable outcomes include: 
- Marking the deviation as confirmed and assigning an approver (for example, a clinical research associate, or CRA) with a due date 
- Reassigning the deviation for further review to keep the In Review status 
- Marking the deviation as dismissed with a mandatory reason (for example, non-PD or duplicate) 
- Approved – The approver (for example, a CRA) performs a holistic evaluation. Options include: 
- Approve – Select to update the status to Approved 
- Dismiss – Provide a reason (for example, duplicate) to remove the deviation from the protocol deviation list 
 Note : 
 For EDC queries:
- EDC queries with the Closed or Answered statuses appear as potential deviations. The system categorizes other queries as potential deviations if they start with one of the following phrases: "PD," "Protocol Deviation," "Potential PD," “PDSD”, or "Potential Protocol Deviation". 
- You can review the answer text to confirm if a protocol deviation occurred. 
- If confirmed negative, you can dismiss the query to exclude it from the PIR. 
- If confirmed positive, users accept the deviation to move it to 'Proposed' status. 
 For listings:
- You can create listings for submitting protocol deviations. To learn more, see  View, Create, and Edit Draft Listings .
- You must submit a description, visit, and PDAP description. 
- You can only map visits to datasets also used in the expression builder. 
- Records submitted for PD are appear in PIR. 
- Submitted records appear in Listings marked as Reviewed.

 Note : You  can publish audit data sets only if you have the Manage Audit Trail Review permissions added to your role in Cloud Administration. 
 Published audit data listings do not support:

- Submit vendor queries. 
- Cross-dataset listing creation 
- Missing records 
## Publish Audit Data 
- If necessary,  create an audit data set . 
- Optional . From the right top corner of the page, click Saved chats . 
 The Saved chats slide-out panel shows all the saved chats.  
 Note : You must save a chat to publish the data as an audit dataset. The Publish as dataset button in the top right corner of the Data Preview section remains disabled for unsaved chats.
- Select a saved chat. 
- Do one of the following:
- Click Rerun .
 The interactive chat shows a confirmation message " Great, re-running your dataset." The query runs without any change. The Data Preview shows a data snapshot that matches the query criteria.
- Optional. Click Retry. 
- Click , the More icon, and then click  Publish as dataset to publish.
 Note :
- You cannot publish an audit dataset without saving the audit trail chat first . The Publish as dataset button remains disabled for unsaved chats. 
- For any study, you can only publish a maximum of 10 data sets. The Publish as dataset button remains disabled once the study reaches this limit. Contact your Medidata representative if the Publish as dataset button gets disabled after 10 audit data sets are published in your study, if you want to publish further, or to delete an active, published audit data set. 
- Enter a data set name in the Save to Datasets window. 
- Click Confirm .
The data set is available in the study once published.
 Note :  Once published, audit datasets appear for use in Data Sets, Listings, and KRIs within 15 to 30 minutes. Updated data appears in published audit datasets based on a weekly audit workflow that runs at 9:00 am (EST), on Monday. You cannot publish and download a data set if the Data Preview section shows no records.  
## Limitations in Published Audit Datasets
 Audit data sets you publish are available to use throughout your study in Data Sets , Listings , KRI Dashboard . However, some limitation exists for published data sets.
- You cannot use audit data sets for cross-data comparison. This means that while building a data set in the expression builder in listings or KRIs, you cannot use an audit data set along with a Medidata Rave data set. You can use a single audit data set in the expression builder. 
- You cannot view individual patient pages in Rave from published data sets.  
- Similarly, you cannot create listings or KRIs with audit time or audit dates. Published data sets also do not show updated queries if the question includes  dynamic dates. For example, a question like Show audit data for last two days, shows data specific to the date when you first asked the question. If you run the published data set at another time, it may bring in new data, but ATR does not automatically adjust to reflect relative dates. 
## Inactive Patient Records
 Audit trail review (ATR) captures all actions taken within Rave, including in records for inactive patients. You can therefore, preview, download, or publish records for inactive patients if their audit records are available in the audit trail. However, Numeric KRIs and percentage KRIs created for such audit data sets do not account for inactive patients. Listings you create using audit data sets may contain inactive patients. However, for listings tracked in  Clean Patient Tracker (CPT), inactive patients do not appear in CPT.

===== PAGE: qtl_configuration.html | QTL Configuration =====
## QTL Configuration
 Quality tolerance limits (QTLs) are study-level metrics that indicate if a study  parameter's reported data has breached a pre-identified data quality threshold . QTLs target and monitor the greatest risks to  a study's: 
- Safety 
- Conduct 
- Performance 
- Compliance 
- Data quality 
 QTLs that reach or exceed a threshold indicate that the QTL's target study parameter can warrant investigation and mitigation. Tracking QTLs helps: 
- Ensure the study conduct operates as planned. 
- Identify and prevent or mitigate systematic issues early on in the study that may: 
- Threaten patient safety or study efficacy. 
- Invalidate the reliability of the study findings. 
 You can create and activate custom QTLs in QTL Configuration and track QTL performance in the QTL Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory . D ata sets and variables you use to create QTL configurations appear with a Rave, external or derived label next to the name. Similarly,  Data sets and variables with critical data points to the study appear with a blue flag . 
 Each QTL has a value that is computed based on RBQM's statistical analysis of your study data. QTLs are calculated at the study level. The QTL value calculations are reflected as a percentage. 
 QTLs are a foundational aspect to risk-based quality management (RBQM) . 
 You can use QTL Configuration to: 
- View the list of custom QTLs available in your study environment . 
- Define and add custom QTLs that target specific facets of your study data that you want to monitor for risk. 
- View patients that meet or do not meet a QTL configuration's query conditions . 
- Activate QTLs to get consumed, analyzed, and calculated by RBQM, and then rendered in the QTL Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory. 
- View patients that meet QTL configuration query conditions . 
 The QTL Dashboard allows you to: 
- Track the QTLs in your study and their respective values. 
- Determine which QTLs exceed the upper or lower tolerance limit of what is considered acceptable for that study metric. 
 Based on your observations made from the Quality Tolerance Limits page, you can determine: 
- The issues or risks that require investigation or mitigation.  
- The best approach or mitigating actions to take on the issues or risks. For example, writing an issue against the QTL and capturing the QTL on a risk inventory. 
- The effect the mitigating actions have made on the issues or risks over time. 
 You can use QTL Configuration to deactivate QTLs from getting consumed, analyzed, calculated, and shown in the QTL Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory when that QTL no longer requires analysis. 
 Tip: The Difference Between QTLs and KRIs
 Quality tolerance limits (QTLs) only target the greatest study-level risks to quality and safety. Whereas  key risk indicators (KRIs) can target risks at the site, country, or study level and provide more focus on site monitoring. KRIs can target any specific area of interest within the study, no matter the priority or bearing on study conduct. In general, study parameters whose reported QTL values exceed an acceptable threshold pose a greater threat to the study and warrant more immediate mitigating actions than parameters with outlier KRI values.
 To learn more about KRIs, see  KRI Configuration .

===== PAGE: qtl_dashboard.html | QTL Dashboard =====
## QTL Dashboard
 At study startup, your project team should preidentify study-level parameters that are critical to quality and define QTLs that you want to monitor for risk. The QTL Dashboard graphically renders each parameter's QTL percentage value and QTL performance relative to the expectation , threshold , and upper limit based on RBQM's statistical analysis. You can use the QTL Dashboard to evaluate high-level study health and to identify and investigate potential underlying systemic issues affecting study performance. 
## What Are Quality Tolerance Limits (QTLs)?
 QTLs are study-level metrics that indicate if a study parameter's reported data has breached a preidentified data quality threshold or upper limit . To learn more about QTLs, see What You Need to Know About Quality Tolerance Limits (QTLs) from Transcelerate. 
## What Is the Purpose of QTLs?
 QTLs monitor the emergence of systematic errors on critical variables and data that may be prone to patientive bias, ultimately impacting: 
- Patient safety 
- Study conduct and performance 
- Compliance 
- Data quality 
- Study reliability 
 ICH E6 (R2) describes in Section 5.0.4: “The Sponsor should decide which risks to reduce and/or which risks to accept. The approach used to reduce risk to an acceptable level should be proportionate to the significance of the risk…Predefined quality tolerance limits should be established, taking into consideration the medical and statistical characteristics of the variables as well as the statistical design of the study, to identify systematic issues that can impact patient safety or reliability of study results. Detection of deviations from the predefined quality tolerance limits should trigger an evaluation to determine if action is needed.” 
## What Is the QTL Dashboard?
 The QTL Dashboard graphically renders:
- Each predefined study parameter's QTL percentage value. 
- RBQM's statistical analysis and approximation of the QTL threshold and upper limit. 
- RBQM's statistical analysis of whether the parameter's QTL value is within a healthy range of the expected QTL value or whether it exceeds the threshold value or upper limit value. 
 You can observe and track RBQM's analyses on the QTL Dashboard from three different perspectives:
- Live View – Meters that show each study parameter's currently observed QTL value and QTL performance based on RBQM's most recent study data analysis. The Live View depicts the QTL performance relative to the expectation, threshold, and upper limit.  
- Patients View – Funnel plots that show each study parameter's currently observed QTL performance relative to the expectation, threshold, and upper limit based on the number of patients enrolled in the study. However, in particular, the Patient View shows the QTL's projected threshold and upper limit values based number of enrolled patients using RBQM's statistical analysis. 
- Time View – Line graphs that show each study parameter's observed QTL value recorded over time on each date that RBQM performed a study data analysis. The Time View depicts the QTL's historical performance relative to the expectation, threshold, and upper limit. 
## What Is the Purpose of the QTL Dashboard?
 The QTL Dashboard allows you to c learly, quickly, and confidently evaluate the health and performance of study-level parameters that are critical to study quality. 
 The QTL Dashboard's Live View allows you to evaluate a parameter's current health and status and confirms whether or not the parameter is performing as expected. Parameters whose QTL values exceed RBQM's defined threshold and upper limit values indicate potentially underlying systemic issues, which may compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues. 
 The Time View allows you to: 
- Analyze address historical trends in a parameter's QTL percentage values over time. 
- Identify and investigate unusual QTL values or unanticipated changes at specific timepoints. 
- Monitor QTL performance after performing mitigating actions on the study. 
 The Patients View enables you to project a parameter's QTL performance based on number patients enrolled in the study. Therefore, you can position yourself earlier on in study to make sound study criteria adjustments to avoid potential downstream systemic issues. 
## Who Uses the QTL Dashboard?
 Study managers, central monitors, medical monitors, and others can use QTLs. For example, if a QTL indicates that the number of patients experiencing troubled breathing exceeds the upper limit threshold, a study manager can pause the study to investigate the cause.
## What Are the Benefits of Tracking QTLs in the QTL Dashboard?
 Tracking QTLs helps: 
- Ensure the study conduct operates as planned. 
- Identify and prevent or mitigate systematic issues early on in the study that may: 
- Threaten patient safety. 
- Impact study efficacy. 
- Invalidate the reliability of the study findings. 
## What Are the Most Frequently Tracked QTLs?
 The following parameters are the most frequently selected QTL targets in industry: 
- Percentage of patients randomized who discontinued the study treatment prematurely (before protocol-defined time point) or withdrew consent  
- Percentage of patients lost to follow up 
- Percentage of mis-randomized or mis-stratified patients  
- Percentage of patients missing protocol required end point.  
- Percentage of patients missing critical end points (for example, noncompliance with critical assessments) 
- Percentage of patients on prohibited therapy. 
## How Does RBQM Determine and Flag At-risk Parameters?
 See At-risk Parameter Detection Methodology .
## How Do I Use and Interpret the QTL Dashboard?
 See  Investigate Data Using the QTL Dashboard .
## How Do I Generate QTL Reports?
 See  Generate and Download QTL Reports .
## How Do I Refresh the QTL Dashboard to Show the Latest Data?
 See Schedule or Trigger When QTL Dashboard Refreshes and Outputs the Latest Study Data Analysis .

===== PAGE: raise_and_resolve_signal_issues.html | Raise And Resolve Signal Issues =====
## Raise And Resolve Signal Issues
 Issues are confirmed findings that indicate potential problems with your study data,  the result of a signal validated through central monitor review, site discussions, or site visits.  You can raise and resolve issues internally within Signals, or send them to an external issue management system for resolution. Before you send  issues for resolution externally, you must integrate Signals with the chosen issue management system, Medidata CTMS.  
 This results in : 
- Streamlined issue logging. 
- Reduced recurrence of duplicate issues. 
- A clear line of sight of site or country  issues and issue status. 
- Reduced time and cost required to create and manage issues. 
- An enhanced work experience and productivity in a centralized location. 
- An improved ability to identify and mitigate risks to  protocol compliance , patient safety, data integrity, and overall study quality. 
 Important : You  can only view or create issues for sites and countries assigned to you. 
## Raise An Issue For Resolution Internally Within Signals
- Access RBQM , and then click  Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals page appears. 
- In the Signals list table, click , the More icon, for a signal with status O pen or Reopened . 
- From the list of options, click Raise as Issue .
- Select one of the following:
- Protocol Deviation 
- Non-protocol Deviation
