That is, the Submit Query button remains disabled if  the listings contain derived datasets where the source variable does not come from a Rave dataset. 
 Important : You must upgrade all previously created derived datasets in Data Connect to submit queries in Data Surveillance. 
## View and Create Vendor Queries for Patient Records
 You can create vendor queries for approved listing records directly in Data Surveillance. You can group multiple patient records into vendor query sets and assign them to approved vendors within vendor groups for action. For example, the vendor can supply the missing records, or provide further clarification. Vendor Queries:
- Enable you to report and track issues with external data. 
- Act as a bridge  to relay queries and issues between vendors and Data Surveillance users. 
- Manages discrepancies and inconsistencies with vendors. 
- Facilitate faster reconciliation of Rave and external vendor data. 
 You can also build easily downloadable and shareable vendor query sets for vendor consumption and action. Alternatively, you can submit vendor query sets directly to vendors, receive responses and track the progress of submitted vendor queries. Vendor queries s ave time and effort by integrating vendor communication into your data review process and ensure study data integrity. 
 Note : You can create Vendor Queries only if you have the Submit Vendor Issues and Manage Issue Sets building blocks associated with your role in the Cloud Administration study group.

## Mark Individual Records as Reviewed or Unreviewed or In Progress
 You can investigate and review all data records captured by an approved listing's conditional expression. You can then mark records as reviewed; for example, if the record:
- Is acceptable or not considered a finding. 
- Was queried and received a sufficient response. 
 You can also mark records as unreviewed. For example, if during post-analysis, your study team determines that a record previously marked as reviewed is an actual finding that should have been queried. In which case, you can mark that record as unreviewed to ensure your team does, indeed, track and review the finding. Or perhaps a record was marked as reviewed in error and should revert to unreviewed. 
 You can also mark records as in progress; for example if the record: 
- Was queried, and no response received. 
- Is not yet acceptable as insufficient response received. 
 Marking records as in progress indicates that the reconciliation cycle is in progress, and not complete, hence the record cannot be marked as reviewed, but is not either completely unreviewed.
 Note : For records captured by listings that are currently being tracked for Clean Patient Tracker analysis , Clean Patient Tracker marks reviewed records as clean. All unreviewed records get counted in Clean Patient Tracker as unclean records and outstanding tasks.

 A dropped status for records indicates records dropped after a data refresh as they no longer meet the criteria configured in the listing's conditional expression. 
 When a listing is refreshed, records that no longer meet the filter criteria (due to data updates) are automatically removed from the view. This results in the loss of visibility for records that may have already been reviewed or contain comments. To ensure data continuity by retaining "dropped" records in the listing if they possess historical review data or user comments, regardless of whether they still satisfy the primary filter expression.

===== PAGE: review_recist_1_1_dashboard_findings.html | Review RECIST 1.1 Dashboard Findings =====
## Review RECIST 1.1 Dashboard Findings
 Patients in oncology studies have cancerous tumors measured at baseline, and again at various junctures of the study. Study managers target a set of marked tumors and monitor growth, shrinkage, disappearance, or appearance of new tumors closely. Clinical research conductors assess how the patients respond to the treatment in the study based on the tumor change. You can use the RECIST 1.1 Dashboard to view and analyze: 
- The tumor burden change in patients participating in the study by specific scan visit type. 
- Individual patient journeys comprised of various tumor response stages throughout the study. 
- The discrepancies in tumor response measurements:
- Calculated based on information that sites enter, and that
- Calculated by the proprietary RECIST 1.1 algorithm.
- Tumor burden, tumor burden response, and scan visit information obtained at specific sites.
- The total number of patients at various stages of the overall tumor response in the study.
## Find the Tumor Burden Change Data
 To help find the tumor burden change data, you can:
- Filter study data by scan visit type.
- Drill deeper to view individual patient progress. 
- Sort records in the tumor response by patient table 
- Filter through patient records table to identify discrepancies. 
 By default the Scan Visit is set to Last Scan Visit when the RECIST 1.1 Dashboard appears. That is, the RECIST 1.1 waterfall plot shows all scheduled or unscheduled visits at which the patient underwent scans to measure the tumor.

===== PAGE: review_reports.html | Review Reports =====
## Review Reports
 Review Reports is a Data Surveillance and RBQM capability that enables you to create and manage custom reports to capture activity logs and findings across data review and reconciliation cycles conducted within Data Surveillance and RBQM.  
## What is Review Reports?
 Review Reports is a Data Surveillance and RBQM  capability  that allows you to capture activity logs and findings across data review and reconciliation cycles. 
## What Is the Purpose of Review Reports?
 Review Reports   enables   you to create   review reports, which include data findings   from Data Surveillance and RBQM collected during a review period. With   Review Reports, study   managers streamline data collection and reporting. For example, you can:
- Analyze and review KRI outliers identified in the KRI Dashboard. 
- Analyze and review outliers identified in Statistical Monitoring's Data Anomaly Detection Plots. 
- Monitor patients for data consistency in Data Surveillance. 
## Who Uses Review Reports?
 Study managers.
## How Does Review Reports Work?
 Review Reports allows you to create reports based on a specific category of data, for which you want to log and capture findings. For example, you can create a report for a specific study, an indication, or even a site. 
 Once you create reports in Review Reports, you can then add report entries for specific data findings within those reports. For each report entry, you can log:
- A description of the data finding. 
- The Data Surveillance or RBQM capability and data set variable in which you observed the finding. 
- The study, country, site, and patient in which you observed the finding. 
- The priority in which you must address the finding, and the actions required to address the finding. 
 You can share review reports with stakeholders to communicate findings and manage actions taken on findings.
## What Are the Benefits of Review Reports?
 Review Reports improves your ability to conduct trial assurances by allowing you to: 
- Record study findings within the Data Surveillance and RBQM without relying on external tools like Excel.
- Build and access customized, easy-to-read reports for the all Data Surveillance capabilities and the RBQM > Statistical Monitoring and RBQM > KRI Dashboard capabilities.
- Streamline data collection and reporting of review cycles.
## How Do I Create Review Reports?
 See Add, Edit, And Delete Review Reports.

===== PAGE: risk_assessment.html | Risk Assessment =====
## Risk Assessment
 The risk assessment documents areas of risk identified by cross-team study members and enables teams to:
- Identify and address high priority risks that most require attention and mitigation. 
- Evaluate risk performance. 
- Review and approve risk plan reports. 
## What Is the Risk Assessment?
 The risk assessment is a continually iterated document that collects and communicates valuable information about how study teams execute their risk management plan. 
## What Is the Purpose of the Risk Assessment?
 The risk assessment enables study teams to proactively, collaboratively, and centrally: 
- Document and manage the data, processes, and risk categories identified as critical to the study outcome. 
- Document and manage risks associated with each critical data, critical process, and risk category.
- Score risks to measure and determine which risks most require focus and mitigation. 
- Add risk mitigation strategies to decrease or eliminate risks. 
- Associate QTLs and KRIs to risks to measure risk performance. 
 The risk assessment also enables appointed study team members to review and approve risk plan reports.
## Who Uses the Risk Assessment?
 Risk Assessment administrators create and activate critical data, critical processes, and risk categorization templates for study teams to use when creating risk assessments. 
 Risk managers: 
- Create, build, and finalize the study team's risk assessment drafts. 
- Manage risks by: 
- Updating risk status. 
- Documenting actions taken to address or manage risks. 
- Updating risk review frequency. 
- Adjusting risk scores. 
- Marking risks as reviewed. 
- Closing risks. 
- Adding and managing QTLs, KRIs, and risk mitigations associated with risks. 
 Other study team members who help devise the risk assessment can be assigned to acknowledge risk plan reports review and approve risk plan PDFs. 
## How Does the Risk Assessment Work?
 As part of the risk assessment, a cross-functional group of study team members—such as site members, data managers, medical monitors, pharmacists, coordinators, and so on—review the draft study protocol. Each team member identifies based on their expertise the protocol design areas that can prove difficult, burdensome, dangerous, unreliable, and present a risk to the study's success, approval, or validity. 
 Risk Assessment enables risk managers to create and build the risk assessment by: 
- Identifying and documenting the following risk assessment components: critical data , critical processes , risk categories . 
- Identifying and documenting the risks associated with each critical data, critical process, or risk category. 
- Scoring risks based on the following risk factors: Probability, Impact , Detectability . 
- Assigning a risk weight to risk categories to rank the category by importance. 
- Associating risks with QTLs and KRIs to track risk performance. 
- Documenting risk mitigation strategies for specific risks. 
 Study team members who help devise the risk assessment and are assigned to acknowledge risk plan reports can sign their acknowledgement on the active risk assessment's risk plan report PDF. 
 Risk Inventory gathers all study risks documented as part of the ongoing risk assessment version history in one consolidated list. Risk managers and other study team members can collaboratively use the Risk Inventory to:
- Assess the study's identified risks and associated details with each risk . 
- Prioritize the evaluation and review of risks based on risk score, rank, review status, and review due date. 
- Evaluate risk QTL and KRI performance. 
- Determine risk mitigating actions. 
- Update risk details and statuses as necessary. 
 Note : The study's risk assessment is a continually edited, updated, and versioned document. Each time you create a risk assessment, you create a new draft version of the risk assessment for that study. A study only has one active, editable risk assessment draft version at a time. Finalized risk assessment drafts get added to the risk assessment snapshot history as an archived, noneditable draft.
## What Are the Benefits of the Risk Assessment?
 The risk assessment helps you document, monitor, and address study risks ensuring:
- Protocol compliance, patient safety, data quality, and data integrity. 
- Product or treatment efficacy. 
- Faster, more efficient studies with greater chances of study success, approval, and validity. 
## How Do I Create Risk Assessment Drafts?
 See  Create Risk Assessment Drafts .

===== PAGE: risk_score_methodology.html | Risk Score Methodology =====
## Risk Score Methodology
 Risk Assessment calculates the risk score for: 
- The entire study, also known as the Study Total Risk Score. 
- All combined risk categories included the Risk Assessment, also known as the Total Risk Categorization Score. 
- Individual risk categories, also known as the Risk Category Score. 
- Individual risks, as known as Risk Scores. 
 Each type of risk score calculation is independent of the others and uses different calculation methodologies. 
## Study Total Risk Score
 The Study Total Risk Score shows at the top of the Risk Inventory page. 
 Study Total Risk Score = The combined total risk score of all risks in your study designated with the risk status of Open or Watch 
 Risks designated with the risk status of Closed or Transfer do not get tallied toward the study total risk score. The study total risk score can give you a general sense of the study's overall level of risk. 
## Total Risk Categorization Score
 The Total Risk Categorization Score shows at the top of the Risk Assessment > Risk Categorization page. 
 Total Risk Categorization Score = The combined total risk category score of all risk categories included in the Risk Assessment 
 For example: 
- 10 risk categories with the following risk category scores: 10 + 12 + 8 + 10 + 6 + 4 + 15 + 15 +10 + 10. 
- The sum of the risk scores for all categories equals 100. 
 The Total Risk Categorization Score uses a color-coded meter to indicate the study's level of risk. Green indicates minimal risk; yellow indicates moderate risk; red indicates high risk. The color associated with the score is calculated by dividing the Total Risk Categorization Score by the number of risk categories x 27. Risk Assessment then converts the result to a percentage. In the example above, the percentage that determines color calculates as 100/(10 x 27) = 0.37 or 37%.  
 Risk Assessment shows the color of the Total Risk Categorization Score as Yellow based on the percentage: 
- 0-32% (Green)  
- 33%-66% (Yellow) 
- 67%-100% (Red) 
 For example: 
 The Total Risk Categorization Score can give you an overall sense of the study's level of risk. 
 To learn how to view the score, see View the Total Risk Categorization Score . 
## Risk Category Score
 Risk Assessment calculates the risk category score for each risk category based on the following risk factors: Impact, Detectability , Probability.  
 Risk Category Score = (Probability x Impact x Detectability) x Risk Category Weight 
 On a 3-point risk score scale, the maximum risk score is 27. Color coding indicates the severity of the risk where values 0.1-3.0 appear in green (minimal risk), 3.1-9.0 appear in yellow (moderate risk), and 9.1-27.0 appear in red (high risk). On a 5-point risk score scale, the maximum risk score is 125. Color coding indicates the severity of risk where values 0.1-5.0 appear in green (minimal risk), 5.1-25.0 appear in yellow (moderate risk), and 25.1-125.0 appear in red (high risk). 
 Risk category scores enable your team to: 
- Better understand which risk categories pose the biggest threat to the study outcome. 
- Prioritize the risk categories in which you develop risk mitigation strategies for. 
- Track risk categories to monitor whether their risk level is increasing or decreasing. 
- Determine the effectiveness of risk mitigation strategies and whether or not additional or adjusted mitigations are needed. 
 To learn more, see:
- Score a Risk Category's Level of Risk to the Study 
- Assign a Risk Score Weight to a Risk Category 
 Tip : Risk Assessment tallies the collective sum of each risk category's score to determine the Total Risk Categorization Score. To learn more, see Total Risk Categorization Score . 
## Risk Scores
 You can identify and add to the risk assessment the study risks associated with critical data, critical processes, and risk categories.  
 When logging risks, you can s core each risk in your study by assessing the probability, impact, and detectability of the risk on a 3- or 5-point scale (depending on your study's configuration. This score is known as the risk score . Risk Assessment calculates the risk score based on the following risk factors: 
- Impact — Indicates the amount of impact to the clinical trial if the risk becomes an issue.
- On a 3-point risk score scale:  High impact = 3, Medium impact = 2, Low impact = 1. 
- On a 5-point risk score scale:  High impact = 5, Medium impact = 3, Low impact = 1. 
- Probability — Indicates the likelihood that a risk becomes an issue.
- On a 3-point risk score scale:  High probability = 3, Medium probability = 2, Low probability = 1. 
- On a 5-point risk score scale:  High probability = 5, Medium probability = 3, Low probability = 1. 
- Detectability — Indicates how difficult it is to detect a risk before it becomes a systemic issue. A low detectability score usually means lower risk.
- On a 3-point risk score scale:  Difficult to Detect = 3, Medium to Detect = 2, Easy to Detect = 1.
- On a 5-point risk score scale:  Difficult to Detect = 5, Medium to Detect = 3, Easy to Detect = 1.
 Risk Score = (Probability x Impact x Detectability) 
 Risk Assessment automatically multiplies the Probability, Impact, and Detectability risk factor scores to generate the overall risk score. On a 3-point risk score scale, the maximum risk score is 27. Color coding indicates the severity of risk where values 1-3 appear in green (minimal risk), 4-9 appear in yellow (moderate risk), and 10-27 appear in red (high risk). On a 5-point risk score scale, the maximum risk score is 125. Color coding indicates the severity of risk where values 1-5 appear in green (minimal risk), 6-25 appear in yellow (moderate risk), and 26-125 appear in red (high risk). 
 Risk scores enable your team to: 
- Better understand which risks pose the biggest threat to the study outcome. 
- Prioritize the risks in which you develop risk mitigation strategies for. 
- Track risks to monitor whether the risk level is increasing or decreasing. 
- Determine the effectiveness of risk mitigation strategies and whether or not additional or adjusted mitigations are needed.

===== PAGE: rounding_and_propagation.html | Rounding and Propagation =====
## Rounding and Propagation
 The Rounding and Propagation analysis heatmaps show:
- Potentially rounded or propagated vital measurements at each site. 
- The severity in which the rounding or propagation occurs for each vital measurement at each site. 
 You can use the Rounding and Propagation heatmaps to identify potentially unreliable data or noncompliant sites, and then further investigate or report your data findings as necessary. 
## What Is Rounding and Propagation?
 Statistical Monitoring analyzes a study's vital sign measurements recorded at each site for: 
- Rounding – A patient record that is captured as a: 
- Value requiring no decimal precision ending in 0 or 5, or 
- Value requiring decimal precision which has been rounded off to the nearest integer and ending in 0 or 5. 
 A patient must have at  least 3 records rounded—whether consecutive or non-consecutive—for RBQM to consider the patient as a risk. For example: 
- 
- For vital sign measurements requiring no decimal precision such as systolic blood pressure, if the values recorded are  122, 120, and 124, then RBQM assesses that patient as having 1 out of 3 (33%) rounded values. 
- Or for vital sign measurements requiring decimal value precision such as temperature, if the values recorded are 100.24, 100.00, 95, 99 then RBQM assesses the patient as having 2 out of 4 (50%) rounded values. 
- Propagation – A patient record that is recorded from a previous visit due to lack of collection or intention to propagate. Records must be propagated at least three times consecutively to be considered as at risk in RBQM's algorithm. For example, if a patient had a recorded blood pressure of 126/83 in three consecutive site visits. 
 Note : If a patient has a vital sign measurement with less than three records, then that patient's records for that vital sign are not included in RBQM's rounding or propagation analysis.
## What Is the Purpose of Rounding and Propagation Analysis?
 Since sites manually enter and collect vital signs, it is critical that sites follow protocol and record data accurately. Poor data could lead to major systemic issues in study conduct and could even compromise patient safety. 
 Rounding and propagation analysis helps you:
- Distinguish between reliable and potentially unreliable data in the vital signs collection case. 
- Identify and investigate sites that:
- May not be following the study protocol correctly. 
- May be falsifying or fabricating data. 
- May be performing misconduct in aspects of the trial outside of data collection. 
## Who Uses the Rounding and Propagation Analysis Heatmaps?
 Central monitors.
## What Are the Benefits of Using the Rounding and Propagation Analysis Heatmaps?
 Leveraging RBQM's analysis of your study data enables you to more efficiently identify potentially unreliable data or noncompliant sites than manual analysis could otherwise allow. RBQM's clear, easy-to-interpret heatmap analyses and summary tables enable fast and accurate interpretation and confident investigatory or mitigating actions made.

## Schedule or Trigger When KRI Dashboard Refreshes and Outputs the Latest Study Data Analysis
 Users with the proper permissions can: 
- Schedule when and how often the KRI Dashboard renders and reflects a specific study's latest study data analysis.  
- Manually trigger the KRI Dashboard to render and reflect a specific study's latest study data analysis. 
 When a refresh successfully processes:
- All users receive a notification email. 
- The notification is posted in the Medidata Notification Center. 
 Important : KRI Dashboard data refreshes occur independently and separately from data refreshes that occur in other RBQM capabilities such as QTL Dashboard and Statistical Monitoring.
 In Data Surveillance and RBQM, s tudy data automatically refreshes four times daily at approximately 9:00am (EST), 3:00pm (EST), 9:00pm (EST) and 3:00am (EST), and the data presented within the user interface is current as of 11:00 pm (EST) the previous day, 5:00 am (EST) the same day, 11:00 am (EST) the same day, 5:00 pm (EST) the same day, respectively. Each study data refresh produces a data snapshot. Updated data from Medidata Rave and activated datasets from Data Connect are available in 6 to 12 hours within Data Surveillance and RBQM. For more information, see Clinical Data Studio's Data Pipeline. 
## Set Data Refresh Schedule
 Users with the proper permissions can schedule when and how often the KRI Dashboard renders and reflects a specific study's latest study data analysis. Therefore, you can control when the KRI Dashboard renders your latest batch of study data to accommodate  your organization's data review schedule and pace. 
 Important : Only authorized users can view the KRI Scheduler page and set the data refresh schedule. 
- Access RBQM , and then click KRIs in the left-hand menu.
The KRI Dashboard shows . 
- Click KRI Scheduler .
- Select the following:
- Refresh Schedule – Select the frequency in which you want RBQM to trigger the data refresh. 
- Start  – Select the time of the month that you want the data refresh to trigger. The Start menu only appears if you select a Monthly , Bi-Monthly , or  Quarterly frequency. 
- Day  – Select the weekday within the specified weekly, monthly, or quarterly cadence that you want the data refresh to trigger. The Day menu does not appear if you select First Day of the Month or Last Day of the Month from the Start menu.
 Tip: Display This Week's Latest Study Data
 To show the current week's latest data, select the Weekly frequency, and then select the weekday that is two days ahead of the current day. For example, if today is Tuesday and you want to view the latest data for this week, select the Weekly frequency, and then select Thursday .
- Click Save .
 The KRI Dashboard will automatically, periodically refresh to show visual renderings of the latest study data analysis as scheduled.
 Note : The KRI Dashboard only refreshes if new or updated study data is uploaded for use in RBQM since the last successful data refresh. 
 Tip :  The upper- right corner of all KRIs capability pages shows the time stamp of the currently rendered study data's most recent completed run through RBQM's analytics.  For example,  . 
 Depending on study data volume, there may be lag time between when the data refresh triggers and when the updated data renders in the KRI Dashboard. So newly rendered data analyses that you view in the KRI Dashboard can reflect the data snapshot from a day or two prior.

===== PAGE: sd_-_create_and_view_stacked_datasets.html | Create and View Stacked Datasets =====
## Create and View Stacked Datasets
 Study data can sometimes contain datasets that share numerous common variables. For example: 
- Medidata Rave may include variations of the same type of eCRF, or 
- Study data may come from multiple sources such as a Rave vitals dataset and an external vitals dataset, or 
- Screening data and study collection data may have similar data points. 
 You can merge datasets with common variables into one dataset called a stacked dataset. Stacked datasets include all variables from all the source datasets, even variables without any common matches across the source datasets. You can use stacked datasets across the Data Surveillance and RBQM capabilities just like you use any other dataset. For example, to build data listings , visualizations , patient profile design elements , or derived variables . Or you can use stacked datasets to configure data mappings , custom QTLs , or custom KRIs . 
 In instances where multiple datasets have numerous shared variables, merging the datasets into one stacked dataset: 
- Simplifies the organization of your study data. 
- Streamlines your ability to access, review, and work with study data throughout Data Surveillance and RBQM. 
- Optimizes the reports, statistical analysis, and visual outputs that Data Surveillance and RBQM produce on your study data. 
 Note : You require the   View Detect CSM Configuration building block to access the Stacked Datasets page. You require the   Manage Detect CSM Configuration building block to create stacked datasets. 
## Access and View Stacked Datasets
 You can view the list of stacked datasets in your study along with associated details for each dataset. You can also view:
- All variables that comprise a specific stacked dataset. 
- The common variables across all source datasets that comprise a stacked dataset. 
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM , and then click Configuration > Stacked Data Sets in the left-hand menu.
The Stacked Datasets page appears. The table lists all stacked datasets in your study.
 Column Descriptions 
- Name – The unique dataset name. 
- OID – The dataset's unique object identifier. 
- Source Datasets – The original datasets that were merged to form the stacked dataset. 
- Created On – The stacked dataset creation date. 
- Created By – The user who created the stacked dataset. 
- In the Name column, click any stacked dataset name.
The Stacked Dataset window appears and shows the following information:
 Field Descriptions 
- Full Match – The number of variables that exist in and are common across datasets being previewed.
- Partial – The number of variables that exist in and are common across at least two datasets but not all datasets being previewed. 
- No Match – The number of variables that only exist in one dataset and are not common across any other dataset being previewed. 
- Variables – The list of unique variable OIDs existing across all datasets being previewed. 
- Stack – Specifies whether the variable OID is a full match, partial match, or has no common matches across any other data sets being previewed.
- Full – The variable OID exists in and is common across datasets being previewed.
- Partial – The variable OID exists in and is common across at least two datasets but not all datasets being previewed. 
- No Match – The variable OID only exists in one dataset and is not common across any other datasets being previewed. 
- Source Datasets – The list of prospective datasets that would be merged to create the stacked dataset. A black check mark indicates that the variable exists within the dataset. 
## Create Stacked Datasets
 You can merge datasets with common variables into one dataset called a stacked dataset. Stacked datasets include all variables from all the source datasets, even variables without any common matches across the source datasets. 
 You can use stacked datasets across the Data Surveillance and RBQM capabilities just like you use any other dataset. For example, to build data listings , visualizations , patient profile design elements , or derived variables . Or you can use stacked datasets to configure data mappings , custom QTLs , or custom KRIs . 
 Stacked datasets: 
- Simplify the organization of your study data. 
- Streamline your ability to access, review, and work with study data throughout Data Surveillance and RBQM. 
- Optimize the reports, statistical analysis, and visual outputs that Data Surveillance and RBQM produce on your study data. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Configuration > Stacked Data Sets in the left-hand menu.
The Stacked Datasets page appears.
- Click New Dataset . 
- In Dataset Name , enter a unique name for the stacked datasets. 
- In Dataset OID , enter a unique stacked dataset OID. The OID is the dataset object identifier, which helps identify and track the dataset. 
- In the Select Source Dataset section, select the check box for each dataset you want to merge into the stacked dataset.
 Note : You can merge up to 10 source datasets to create a stacked dataset.
- Click Preview .
The Stacked Dataset Preview window appears and shows the following:
 Field Descriptions 
- Full Match – The number of variables that exist in and are common across datasets being previewed.
- Partial – The number of variables that exist in and are common across at least two datasets but not all datasets being previewed. 
- No Match – The number of variables that only exist in one dataset and are not common across any other dataset being previewed. 
- Variables – The list of unique variable OIDs existing across all datasets being previewed. 
- Stack – Specifies whether the variable OID is a full match, partial match, or has no common matches across any other data sets being previewed.
- Full – The variable OID exists in and is common across datasets being previewed.
 Note : There must be at least one variable OID that is a full match across datasets to save and create a stacked dataset.
- Partial – The variable OID exists in and is common across at least two datasets but not all datasets being previewed. 
- No Match – The variable OID only exists in one dataset and is not common across any other datasets being previewed. 
- Source Datasets – The list of prospective datasets that would be merged to create the stacked dataset. A black check mark indicates that the variable exists within the dataset. 
 Tip : Previewing stacked datasets helps you assess the common variables across a set of datasets to determine if merging the datasets into one stacked dataset is an appropriate decision.
- Click Close . 
- Confirm your source dataset selections, and then click Save .
 Note : There must be at least one variable OID that exists in and is common across all selected source datasets to create a stacked dataset.

===== PAGE: set_upper_and_lower_time_limits.html | Set Upper and Lower Time Limits =====
## Set Upper and Lower Time Limits
 The workflow progress bar below depicts where defining date settings occur within the recommended patient profile design workflow. 
 You can set the study's lower time limit and upper time limit (in study days) that Patient Profiles pulls data for timelines or graphs. Typically, the lower limit is the earliest study day a patient can be screened; for example, -28. The upper limit is the latest study day a patient can possibly have based on the visit schedule. The lower and upper time limits set the x-axis for the timeline and graphs within patient profiles. 
- 
 Access the design. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Patient Profiles in the left-hand menu.
 The Patient Profile Designs page shows the Published Designs and Draft Designs   tabs, which contain the list of designs in your study environment. 
- On the Patient Profiles Designs page, do one of the following: 
- Click the Published Designs tab.
 Published Designs Tab Column Descriptions 
- Name  – The patient profile design's name. 
- Type – Indicates whether the patient profile is one of the following types: 
- Detect – The patient profile design is integrated with an accessible directly from other Data Surveillance and RBQM capabilities. 
- View Only – A read-only patient profile design. 
- Last Refresh Date – The time stamp when the last data refresh was performed for the profile design. 
- Published Date  – The time stamp when the profile design was marked as master. This field displays for Published Designs. 
- Updated By  – The user who most recently updated the patient profile design. 
- Click the Draft Designs tab.
 Draft Designs Tab Column Descriptions 
- Name  – The patient profile design's name. 
- Last Updated – The time stamp of when the most recent update was made to the draft patient profile design. 
- Updated By  – The user who most recently updated the patient profile design. 
- Optional . Click any column header to sort the designs list. Clicking once sorts the list in descending order (A to Z, 0 to 9) by the selected column header; twice sorts in ascending order (Z to A, 9 to 0).
 Note : Published Designs and Draft Designs lists appear in the reverse chronological order based on the Published Date and the Last Updated dates, respectively. 
- Click anywhere within the row of the design you want to access. 
 The Design page appears and shows the Profiles tab by default. 
- On the Design page, click the Settings tab. 
- Enter the Lower Time Limit and Upper Time Limit to define the window of time in which you want Patient Profiles to pull data for timelines or graphs. 
- Click Save .

===== PAGE: signal_configuration.html | Signal Configuration =====
## Signal Configuration
 You can configure within RBQM the modules that Data Surveillance and RBQM uses to produce automated Signals for: 
- Patient Profiles 
- KRI Dashboard 
- QTL Dashboard 
- Potential Duplicate Patients 
- Rounding and Propagation 
- Under-Over Reporting Events 
- Weekend and Holiday Visits 
 The signals you see on the Signals page are automated indications of potential issues in the modules you configure. The Signals page also includes user-generated signals.
 While configuring signals for individual modules, you can set up thresholds based on which automated signals get created. You must choose the modules you want the signals to report on. For example, if you do not enable KRIs in Signals Configuration, and add custom configurations, no signals get created for any KRI in your study when signals data refreshes.  
 Study data automatically refreshes daily at approximately 7:30 AM (EST). When you refresh data on the Signals page, automated signals generate for configured modules based on the source module's last successful data update, and the threshold set for each module. Once you configure a signal, observations appear as signals based on custom configurations and the latest data snapshot for individual modules when you next refresh data. This means you can determine the exact version of the signals data in each module based on its snapshot date. Signal configuration changes made after 7:30 AM EST do not show in the automated signals report until the next day.

===== PAGE: signals.html | Signals =====
## Signals
 In central monitoring, a signal is an alert or indication of a potential problem, risk, or deviation in a clinical study.   Signals get  detected remotely by analyzing study data centrally, which monitors to proactively identify potential risks in the study data.  Signals help sponsors  focus resources  on sites or issues needing immediate attention, improving data integrity and patient safety. 
 A signal is an alert or indication of a potential study data issue that is identified through Clinical Data Studio's data analysis. RBQM's Signals capability enables central monitors to auto-generate or manually generate signals reports, which centrally identify, track, and enable actioning on signals that RBQM observes in your study data. Central monitors can use Signals to make clear, efficient, actionable insights on study data, ensuring that critical data quality issues are identified and addressed promptly. 
## What Is Signals?
 Signals is an RBQM capability that supports the creation of automated and manual signals. Each signal is an observation that meets a set threshold and derives data from a module configured for signal generation. 
 What Is the Purpose of Signals? 
 Signals provides central monitors a  threshold-based tool to centrally identify, track, and take action on potential study data issues .  With Signals, you can: 
- Consolidate indicators or observations on study data into a single, centralized report. 
- Track the health of study data using observations. 
- Manage data quality issues. 
- Assign tasks to study team members to investigate further. 
- Perform robust data interrogation, data review, and reconciliation at the individual patient level and at the aggregate level. 
- Identify data quality and patient safety issues sooner. 
## Who Uses Signals?
 Clinical study managers, clinical research associates, site monitors, central monitors, safety monitors, medical monitors, data managers, biostatisticians, programmers, and clinical reviewers use Signals. 
## How Does Signals Work?
 Signals   ingests study data from:  
- Patient Profiles 
- KRIs 
- QTLs 
- Potential Duplicate Patients 
- Rounding and Propagation 
- Under/over Reporting 
 When you refresh data on the Signals page, signals generate for configured modules, based on the source module's last successful data update, and the set threshold for each module. On the Signals page, each configured module shows the last snapshot date and time from its source module.  This means you can determine the exact version of the signals data in each module based on its snapshot date. 
 While configuring signals for individual modules, you can set up thresholds based on which automated signals get created. You must also choose the modules you want the signals to report on. For example, if you do not enable KRIs in the Signals Configuration and add custom configurations, no signals get created for any KRI in your study when the Signals data refreshes.   Once you configure a signal, observations appear as signals based on custom configurations and the latest data snapshot for individual modules when you next refresh data.   
 To get the most updated signals, you must refresh the Signals data daily. Auto-generated signals appear based on the latest data snapshot for each configured module available at 7:30 am (EST). If you make any   custom signal configurations   after 7:30 am (EST), the changes are not visible on the Signals page until the next day.
## What Are the Benefits of Signals?
 Signals enables central monitors to: 
- Streamline the identification, tracking, and management of data quality issues across study data. 
- Continuously monitor and ensure potential risks get mitigated before they escalate as issues. 
- Enhance efficiency, reduce manual effort, and improve decision-making for users involved in central monitoring and central statistical monitoring. 
- Provide clear, actionable insights, ensuring that critical data quality issues are identified and addressed promptly. 
## How Do I Access Signals?
 See View and Access Signals.

===== PAGE: site_risk_alert_methodology.html | Site Risk Alert Methodology =====
## Site Risk Alert Methodology
 The   KRI Dashboard   visually signifies sites that RBQM assesses as being medium or high risk to your study's performance relative to all sites in the study by appending the site name with a Medium , , or High , , icon. The Medium and High signal icons help you quickly identify and determine sites that may warrant investigation. 
 RBQM uses the following methodology to determine a site's risk level: 
- All nine system KRIs that are categorized under the Data Collection risk category.
- AE Entry Delay 
- Manual Query Rate 
- Missing Visit Percentage 
- Modification Rate 
- Non-System Query Delay 
- Percent Out of Window Visit 
- System Query Delay 
- System Query Rate 
- Visit Entry Delay  
- Any custom KRIs that your team has activated for inclusion in its risk level calculation.   To learn more, see Add or Remove KRIs from RBQM's Site Risk Calculation . 
 All KRIs have an assigned risk category. Each risk category has an assigned weight (low, medium, or high) that a particular KRI risk category carries when the site's risk score is calculated.  
 Note : The default weight for the Data Collection risk category is Medium; however, you can change any risk category's weight at any time. To learn more, see Configure KRI Risk Category Weight for Site Risk Calculation . 
  The s ite risk algorithm converts the risk category weights to the following numeric risk category weight values: 
- Low = 0.16 
- Medium = 0.33 
- High = 0.5 
 Meanwhile, the s ite risk algorithm takes the selected KRI value at each site, and then based on the KRI value's color-coded level of risk, converts the KRI output  to a numeric value . 
 Then for each site, each KRI's value is multiplied with the KRI's risk category weight value to produce the KRI value's weighted level of significance . 
- Red** indicates that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site resulting in its KRI value to be an extreme outlier. 
- Yellow* indicates that there is a strong association indicating that there may be an underlying cause at the site resulting in its KRI value to be an outlier. 
- Green indicates that there is nothing about the study data at the site that would raise alarm about the risk being monitored. The site or country is likely operating and reporting data as expected. 
- Gray indicates that there are fewer than two patients at the site, which is not enough data to determine risk level. 
 To learn more, see  KRI Risk Level Alert Methodology .
 The site risk algorithm takes the selected KRI value at each site, and then based on the KRI value's color-coded level of risk, converts the KRI value to a significance value :
- Red** = 3 
- Yellow* = 2 
- Green = 1 
- Gray = 0 
 Then for each site, the site risk algorithm multiplies each KRI's  significance value with the KRI's risk category weight value to produce the KRI value's weighted level of significance .
 For example, let us say Site A is tracking KRI 1. And KRI 1 is color-coded in Red** on the KRI Dashboard, indicating that the KRI value is an extreme outlier. This means that KRI 1 has a significance value of 3 . And then let's say KRI 1 is assigned to the Safety risk category. And the Safety risk category has a weight of Medium, which we convert to a risk category weight value of 0.33 . Then, you calculate: 
 (The KRI's significance value ) x (the KRI's risk category weight value ) = the KRI value's weighted level of significance . 
 So: 3 x .33 = .99. Therefore, KRI 1's weighted level of significance is .99. 
 The site rank is determined through a three-step calculation: 
- Weighted Significance – RBQM calculates the weighted level of significance for every individual KRI at a site and sums them together. 
- Impact Factor –  Simultaneously, it calculates the "Impact Factor" by totaling the risk category weights for all KRIs tracked at that site. 
- Final Ranking –  Finally, the sum of the weighted significance is divided by the Impact Factor to produce the final Site Rank. 
 Sites are categorized into risk levels based on their rank percentile relative to all other sites in the study: 
- High Risk (site rank is at 75th Percentile and Above) – These sites are flagged with a High icon, next to their name. 
- Medium Risk (site rank is between 50th to 74th Percentile) – These sites are flagged with a Medium icon, next to their name. 
- Low Risk (site rank is below 50th Percentile) – These sites carry no icon, indicating performance within the expected range. 
 Note on Statistical Ties: In the rare event that the 50th and 75th percentiles share the same site rank value, the following logic is applied: 
- High Risk: Sites at the 51st percentile and above (marked with a High icon ). 
- Medium Risk: Sites exactly at the 50th percentile (marked with a Medium icon, ). 
- Low Risk: Sites below the 50th percentile (no icon).

===== PAGE: sites_that_under_or_overreport_events_detection_methodology.html | Sites That Under or Overreport Events Detection Methodology =====
## Sites That Under or Overreport Events Detection Methodology
 The Under-Over Reporting Events Plot visualizes event   reporting patterns across adverse events (AE), concomitant medication (CM), and medical history (MH) at the site and country level. 
 To determine sites and countries that are over or underreporting events, RBQM first performs the following event rate calculations at the site and country level: 
- Adverse Events (AE) Rate – The average number of adverse events reported per exposure time. Calculated as: N umber of AEs / Exposure Time in Months
 Note : Exposure time is the number of study days across all patients.
- Concomitant Medication (CM) Rate – The average number of reported concomitant medications per unit of reported adverse events and ongoing medical history events reported. Calculated as:  Number of CMs / (Number of AEs + Number of Ongoing MH) 
- Medical History (MH) Rate – The average number of reported medical history events per enrolled patient at the site or country. Calculated as: N umber of MH / Total Patients
 RBQM then identifies sites and countries with outliers in reported AE, CM, and MH rates. For this,   reported events are assumed to be events in a Poisson distribution. Hence, reported events are compared to the expected events under Poisson Continuous Distributed Functions (CDF) based on which p-value are computed. Then, RBQM calculates the  95% and 99% confidence interval limit  for each rate under the different aggregations. 
 The Under-Over Reporting Events Plot then visualizes event   reporting patterns and identifies sites under or overreport events using three separate funnel plots :
- Adverse Events (AE) – Graphs the reported rate of adverse events over time in months for each site and country in the study. 
- Concomitant Medication (CM) – Graphs the reported rate of concomitant medications compared to the combined number of reported adverse events and ongoing medical history events for each site and country in the study. 
- Medical History (MH) – Graphs the reported rate of medical history events compared to total number of enrolled patients at each site and country in the study. 
 See the following examples:
 Tip : Click images to enlarge.
 Adverse Events 
 Concomitant Medication 
 Medical History 
 | 
 | 
 | 
 Each site and country's reported data is represented as a blue data point on each graph. RBQM normalizes the study-wide reported event data and visually outputs funnel lines representing the data's:
- Upper 99% Limit – An AE rate that is at the 99% confidence interval above the study's average AE rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported AE rate lies above the upper 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers. Extreme outliers may warrant prompt investigation to  understand the type of events that are overreported; for example, signs and symptoms versus diagnosis . The Upper 99% Limit is represented by the uppermost solid, blue line in the funnel plot: 
- Upper 95% Limit – An AE rate that is at the 95% confidence interval  above the study's average AE rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported AE rate lies above the upper 95% limit to be potential outliers. Outliers may warrant investigation to understand the type of events that are overreported; for example, signs and symptoms versus diagnosis . The Upper 95% Limit is r epresented by the uppermost dotted, gray line in the funnel plot: 
- Mean – The average reported AE rate across all sites or countries in the study. The mean is represented by the solid, yellow, middle line in the funnel plot: 
- Lower 95% Limit – An AE rate that is at the 95% confidence interval  below the study's average AE rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported AE rate lies below the lower 95% limit to be potential outliers. Outliers may warrant investigation to understand type of events that are underreported; for example, mild events . The Lower 95% Limit is r epresented by the lowermost dotted, gray line in the funnel plot: 
- Lower 99% Limit – An AE rate that is at the 99% confidence interval below the study's average AE rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported AE rate lies below the lower 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers. Extreme outliers may warrant prompt investigation  to understand the type of events that are underreported; for example, mild events . The Lower 99% Limit is r epresented by the lowermost solid, blue line in the funnel plot:

===== PAGE: stacked_datasets.html | Stacked Datasets =====
## Stacked Datasets
 Stacked datasets are derived datasets that you create by merging datasets with common variables into one dataset. Stacked datasets: 
- Enable for simpler study data organization and review. 
- Optimize Data Surveillance's and RBQM's statistical analysis and visual output of data. 
## What Are Stacked Datasets?
 Stacked datasets are derived datasets that you create by merging datasets with common variables into one dataset. Stacked datasets include all variables from all the source datasets, even variables without any common matches across the source datasets. 
## What Is the Purpose of Stacked Datasets?
 Study data can sometimes contain datasets that share numerous common variables. For example: 
- Medidata Rave may include variations of the same type of eCRF, or 
- Study data may come from multiple sources such as a Rave vitals dataset and an external vitals dataset, or 
- Screening data and study collection data may have similar data points. 
 Stacked datasets enable you to merge datasets with common variables into one dataset.  
## Who Creates and Manages Stacked Datasets?
 Data managers.
## What Are the Benefits of Stacked Datasets?
 In instances where multiple datasets have numerous shared variables, merging the datasets into one stacked dataset: 
- Simplifies the organization of your study data. 
- Enables you to review your study data, create data listings, build patient profiles, and create derived variables faster and easier by streamlining the datasets you must access, review, and work with. 
- Simplifies the configuration process when mapping the data sets and variables that Data Surveillance and RBQM use to consume and produce the reports, statistical analysis, and visual output for:
- Data anomaly detection and trends . 
- Event incidence and under-over reporting events . 
- Potential duplication patients . 
- Rounding and propagating vital sign records . 
- AI Data Reconciliation reports . 
- Data visualizations . 
- RECIST 1.1 analytics . 
- Optimizes the statistical analysis and visual outputs that Data Surveillance and RBQM produce on your study data to be as clean and accurate as possible. 
## How Do Stacked Datasets Work?
 The Stacked Datasets capability in Data Surveillance and RBQM enables you to create stacked datasets . You can then:
- View and investigate the stacked datasets as part of your overall study data review process. 
- Use stacked datasets to : 
- Build data listings . 
- Create visualizations . 
- Add elements to patient profile designs . 
- Configure within Data Mapping the datasets and variables that Data Surveillance and RBQM use to consume and produce the reports, statistical analysis, and visual output for: 
- Data anomaly detection and trends . 
- Event incidence and under-over reporting events . 
- Potential duplication patients . 
- Rounding and propagating vital sign records . 
- AI Data Reconciliation reports . 
- RECIST 1.1 dashboard plots . 
- Define and add custom QTLs and custom KRIs that target specific facets of your study data that you want to monitor for risk. 
- Create derived variables . 
 In addition, you can view the list of stacked datasets in your study along with details for each stacked dataset such as: 
- Creation and modification dates. 
- Source datasets from which the stacked datasets derive. 
 Note : On the Data Sets page, Data Listings page, and Visualizations page, the list of available datasets appends stacked dataset names with the green DERIVED icon. Note that Data Surveillance appends derived variable names with a blue DERIVED icon. 
## How Do I Create Stacked Datasets?
 See  Create and View Stacked Datasets .

===== PAGE: statistical_monitoring.html | Statistical Monitoring =====
## Statistical Monitoring
 In the world of clinical trials, Risk-Based Quality Management (RBQM) is the overarching strategy used to ensure patient safety and data integrity. Statistical Monitoring (SM) is the "analytical engine" of that strategy.
## What Is the Purpose of Statistical Monitoring?
 Instead of sending monitors to every single clinical site to manually check all data sources, SM uses advanced analytics and statistical algorithms to remotely "scan" trial data for anomalies, compliance, inconsistencies and other problems that may impact data quality and trial outcome. This reduces onsite work and cost and enables real time data driven risk identification and proactive monitoring and mitigation.
## Who Uses Statistical Monitoring?
 Typically central monitors and data managers with insights being relevant to safety and clinical teams as well as biostatisticians. 
## How Does Statistical Monitoring Work?
 CDS SM approach is a combination of unsupervised ML checks designed for identification of unexpected risks and as an exploratory tool, and the set of targeted statistical analyses, like Over/Under reporting, Incidence plots, Duplicate patients, Rounding and Propagation, Weekend and Holiday visits. 
 In the context of Risk-Based Quality Management (RBQM), normalized statistical analysis is frequently the superior approach because it relies on domain-specific logic rather than raw mathematical distance. Let’s clarify this statement. 
 Contextual Relevance (Signal vs. Noise) 
 Unsupervised machine learning treats data points as coordinates in space. It flags "outliers" based on statistical variance, but it doesn't understand why a data point is different. 
 The Normalized Solution like CDS Over and underreporting, by normalizing eg Adverse Events (AEs) against Exposure (Patient-Days), you account for the fact that a patient on a drug for 300 days is naturally more likely to have an event than one on for 10 days. Normalization effectively "levels the playing field," ensuring you are measuring performance quality rather than just volume. 
 Reducing "False Positives" through Domain Logic 
 Unsupervised ML is "noisy." It often flags sites for harmless reasons. 
 If you normalize e.g. CM reporting by the number of AEs and Medical History (MH) entries like we have done in CDS, you are looking for proportionality . It makes sense for a patient with a long medical history and multiple AEs to have more CMs. A site is only a "true" outlier if they have high AEs/MH but zero CMs- a classic sign of underreporting that unsupervised ML might miss or bury in other "anomalies." 
 Interpretability and "The Why" 
 CSM findings are sent to busy CRAs and you must be able to explain why a site was flagged and what action has to be taken. 
 An unsupervised model might flag Site 101, but when a monitor asks why, the answer is often: "Because its multi-dimensional vector was 3 standard deviations from the centroid." This is not actionable for a clinical monitor. 
 With normalized stats, the explanation is intuitive: "Site 101 is being flagged because their AE reporting rate per 100 days of exposure is 60% lower than the study average, despite having a similar patient profile." This gives the monitor a clear starting point for a root cause analysis. 
 Stability in Small Data Sets 
 Unsupervised ML generally requires large volumes of data to "learn" what is normal. In the early stages of a Phase II or III trial, data is sparse. 
 With low patient counts, unsupervised models become unstable, flagging almost everything as an anomaly because a "normal" baseline hasn't been established thus delaying proactive risk monitoring to when ‘sufficient’ data is collected 
 Statistical normalization (like using a Poisson distribution for AE rates) works even with smaller cohorts because it is grounded in established probability math and clinical expectations. Similarly rule based, analytical approaches like rounding and propagation are based on industry reality on e.g. how many consecutive assessments of e.g. weight or BP can look the same before the concern is that the site is not evaluating patients at each visit, using appropriate research approved process or tool. 
 Below are the CSM analyses provided in RBQM: 
- Data Anomaly Detection – Determine your study data's outliers, anomalies, unusual data associations, risks, trends, and missing data at the data point-, patient-, site-, and country-level. 
- Weekend and Holiday Visits – Investigate potential falsified or erroneous patient records in your study data. 
- Potential Duplicate Patients – Identify and investigate: 
- Sites with potential duplicate patients across all site locations in your study. 
- Individual patients who may be duplicate patients . 
- Rounding & Propagation – Distinguish between reliable and potentially unreliable data in the vital signs collection case. 
- Event Incidence – View the reported events and the incidence rate in which those events occurred within a  domain at the site and study level. 
- Under-Over Reporting Events – Identify potentially noncompliant sites and countries whose AE, CM, and MH reporting patterns significantly differ from the study norm. 
 In addition, the below list of capabilities is typically used with above to further understand and monitor possible risks - at the site, country or study level, on all data including audit data. 
- KRI Dashboard – View and assess insights into site and country performance and compliance using key risk indicators. 
- QTL Dashboard – Identify systemic- and protocol-level issues that affect trial outcome and patient safety. 
- Audit Trail Review 
- Create audit trail reviews  to extract insights from operational study data. 
- Publish audit data sets and use to build KRIs and listings in a study. 
 The advantage of CDS CSM is the ability to auto-generate signals from all various targeted analyses without the user needing to identify each signal separately. For more information, see Signals .

===== PAGE: strength_of_association_description_and_calculation_methodology.html | Strength of Association Description and Calculation Methodology =====
## Strength of Association Description and Calculation Methodology
 Strength of association is a numeric value that indicates the probability that patients at an individual site will have reported the same or similar numeric or text values for a particular  variable . RBQM calculates strength of association on a range from 0.00 to 1.00. The higher a variable's strength of association with the site variable, the more likely you can predict the value of that variable for a new patient at a given site. RBQM calculates strength of association using an appropriate measure of effect size  depending on the variable types.
 Take gender for example. Suppose a study has two sites: Site A and Site B. If Site A is all male patients and Site B is all female patients, then the strength of association for the gender variable in that study is 1.00. If a variable has a strength of association of 1.00, and if you know at least one data point value for a given site, then you can predict with one hundred percent accuracy that all other data points at that site have the same value.

===== PAGE: the_risk_inventory.html | Risk Inventory =====
## Risk Inventory
 The Risk Inventory is a real-time, comprehensive list of all study risks and associated QTLs and KRIs documented in the Risk Assessment. You can track, monitor, and manage risks from the Risk Inventory to:
- Ensure study teams perform risk reviews on time. 
- Prioritize the risks that your team monitors and addresses based on risk level. 
- Evaluate risk QTL and KRI performance to determine whether the risk level is increasing or decreasing. 
- Determine risk mitigating actions to take or assess the effectiveness of actions taken. 
## What Is the Risk Inventory?
 The Risk Inventory is a consolidated, real-time list of all:
- Risks documented as part of your study's risk assessment and risk review details associated with each risk. 
- QTLs associated with a risk in your study along with QTL details and performance metrics. 
- KRIs associated with a risk in your study along with KRI details and the current KRI values. 
## What Is the Purpose of the Risk Inventory?
 The Risk Inventory enables study teams to collaboratively track, monitor, and manage risks. For example, you can:
- View the real-time, comprehensive list of all documented study risks in one centralized location. 
- View each risk's status; for example, whether the risk is open or closed. 
- Monitor risk review details such as last risk review date, target review date, and review status—for example, Due Soon or Overdue—to ensure study teams completes risk reviews on time per the study protocol. 
- Assess each risk's  risk score to help prioritize the risks that your team monitors and develops risk mitigation strategies for. 
- View the list of QTLs and KRIs associated with a risk in your study. 
- Evaluate risk QTL and KRI performance to determine whether the risk level is increasing or decreasing. 
- Determine risk mitigating actions to take or assess the effectiveness of actions taken. 
- Update risk details and statuses as necessary. 
 To learn more, see:
- View and Monitor the Risk Inventory 
- Manage Risks from the Risk Inventory 
## Who Uses the Risk Inventory?
 Risk managers.
## How Does the Risk Inventory Work?
 When creating and building the study team's Risk Assessment, risk managers can: 
- Identify and document the following risk assessment components: critical data , critical processes , risk categories . 
- Identify and document the risks associated with each critical data, critical process, or risk category. 
- Score risks based on the following risk factors: Probability, Impact , Detectability . 
- Assign a risk weight to risk categories to rank the category by importance. 
- Associate risks with QTLs and KRIs to track risk performance. 
- Document risk mitigation strategies for specific risks. 
 The Risk Inventory gathers all study risks documented as part of the Risk Assessment in one consolidated list. Risk managers and other study team members can view the list of all risks , as well as associated risk and risk review details. For example, you can: 
- View a risk's status; for example, whether the risk is open or closed or incomplete. 
- View risks whose risk reviews are overdue or due soon. 
- Sort the Risk Inventory based on risk score to help prioritize the risks that your team monitors and addresses. 
- Evaluate risk QTL and KRI performance. 
- Determine risk mitigating actions to take or assess the effectiveness of actions taken. 
 From the Risk Inventory, you can also directly access individual risks to:
- View and edit an individual risk's details . 
- Document risk review actions taken . 
- Mark risks as reviewed . 
- Close risks . 
- Add and manage QTLs associated with risks . 
- Add and manage KRIs associated with risks . 
- Add and manage risk mitigations . 
 You can also download the risk inventory to view locally in a PDF or share with others outside of RBQM.
## What Are the Benefits of Using the Risk Inventory?
 The Risk Inventory helps you view, monitor, and address study risks ensuring:
- Protocol compliance, patient safety, data quality, and data integrity. 
- Product or treatment efficacy. 
- Faster, more efficient studies with greater chances of study success, approval, and validity. 
## How Do I Access the Risk Inventory?
 See  View and Monitor the Risk Inventory .

- Action –  Address Missing Pages 
- Click the number in the Missing Pages column for your target patient. 
- Missing pages can be auto-populated from Rave or added manually. Type the updated count. Click Save .
 Notes for Auto-populated Missing Pages Count 
- If your instance of Clean Patient Tracker is configured to auto-populate missing page counts from an external dataset or Rave, you cannot manually edit entries in the Missing Pages column. That is, the field is read-only. 
- The missing pages count autopopulated from Rave is the Expected to Date count, and not the total number of pages expected per patient. 
- The Expected to Date count excludes folders for future visits based on the entry window dates. That is, Missing Pages Count = Expected to Date - Touched. 
- Expected to Date is the count of all forms for the patient, and is based on the end window related to the instance date. 
- If the end window is yesterday's or today's date, the associated forms are counted. 
- If end window is tomorrow, the associated forms are not counted. 
- If no end window is defined, all forms are counted. 
- If the end window is defined on a folder, and if the date is less than or equal to the current date and time, then it is counted. Otherwise, it is not counted. 
- Touched (Entered) is the count of forms for the patient that have submitted data. 
 Calculation Rule  
Missing pages from Rave are calculated based on the forms that exist for a patient. For example, if an edit check adds a form to a patient as a result of a value entered (male patient, hence no pregnancy form), that form is not included in future calculations of the missing pages count. So in this example, the count for missing pages for male patients does not include the form. For more information on Expected to Date and Entered, see Rave Page Status Report. 
- To learn more, see  Configure Manual or Automatic Missing Page Count Entry. 
- Action – Review Open Queries 
- Click the hyperlinked number in the Open Queries column. A new browser window opens, automatically filtered to show only the open queries for the specific patient. For more information, see Open EDC Queries. 
-  Action – Address AI Reconciliation and Listings 
- Click any hyperlinked number in an AI Reconciliation or Listing column. A new browser window opens showing the listing or AI Reconciliation report you selected or configured,  pre-filtered for that patient so you can begin vetting records immediately. 
-  Action – Outstanding vendor queries  
- Click any hyperlinked number in the Vendor Queries column.  A new browser window opens showing the outstanding open vendor queries you selected,  pre-filtered for that patient so you can begin vetting records immediately.

This ensures the dashboard reflects your most recent work and updates the Clean status of the patient.  To learn more, see  Trigger Clean Patient Tracker to Recalculate Outstanding Records Based on the Latest Study Data . 
 Vendor Support
 If your study tracks vendor-specific data, click the hyperlinked number in a Vendor column to view outstanding vendor queries for that site.

===== PAGE: treatments_without_conditions_or_ongoing_mh_algorithm_methodology.html | Treatments Without Conditions and Ongoing MH Algorithm Methodology =====
## Treatments Without Conditions and Ongoing MH Algorithm Methodology
 Patients undergo treatments in response to a condition in a study. The AI Reconciliation algorithm identifies treatments that do not treat a condition, and for which the treatment start date lies outside the time period of the condition. A treatment is considered to treat a condition if the treatment matches the condition in the Knowledge Graph . 
## Descriptions used in the Algorithm
 Term 
 Description 
 | Adverse Event (AE) 
 | Any unfavorable and unintended sign, for example, abnormal laboratory findings, symptoms, or diseases, temporally associated with the use of a medicinal product, whether or not considered related to the medicinal product. 
 | Condition 
 | An adverse event that occurs after the patient enters a study. It is possible for a condition to not appear in an AE form. 
 | Treatment 
 | A tr ea tm e nt i s a m edica t i on or pro ced ur e. 
 | Finding 
 | A finding is a data anomaly. Treatments can be findings if either, or both of the following are true:
- Time frame Match - A treatment is administered outside the condition's time frame. For ongoing MH, no time frame alignment is required. 
- Indication Match - A treatment's indication does not match any condition in the Knowledge Graph or verbatim comparison.  
 The algorithm does not consider treatments if any of the following hold true: 
- The treatment is missing a coded term. 
- The treatment ended before the patient onboarded the study. 
- The treatment's indication suggests it is used for purposes where a condition is not expected, such as diagnostic procedures, prophylates, birth control, or recreational use. 
- The treatment's ATC code classifies it as a vitamin, vaccine, mineral supplement, or general nutrient, indicating no specific condition association is anticipated. 
 | Related 
 | T he c on di t i on i s l i n ked to t he tr ea tm e nt i n t he knowledge graph   w i t h c on di t i on - tr ea tm e nt p ai r. 
 | Unrelated 
 | The condition is linked to the treatment in the knowledge graph with condition-treatment pair. 
 | In-time frame 
 | 
- Conditions in the same time frame of the treatment that are not related to the treatment per the knowledge graph. 
- Conditions in the same time frame of the treatment that are not related to the treatment per the indication-AE raw term / AE-preferred term match. 
 Concomitant Medication (CMs) or Concomitant Procedure (CPs) that ended before the patient on-boarded the study do not qualify as a finding as the anomaly is not relevant to the study.
 | Out-of-time frame 
 | Conditions related to the treatment as per the Knowledge Graph, but where the treatment started before the condition started, or after the condition ended. 
 | Match 
 | The c on di t i on p ai rs w i t h either both, or any   m edica t i on,   or pro ced ur e i n t he Knowledge Graph, and t he m edica t i on a n d / or pro ced ur e o cc urs w i t hi n t he t i m ef r a m e o f t he c on di t i on st a rt i n g a n d e n di n g . 
 | Confidence Level 
 | T he   deg r ee o f ce rt ai nty t ha t a da t a a nom a ly   su ch a s t he ab s e n ce o f a n ece ss a ry tr ea tm e nt f or a gi v e n c on di t i on, exists. 
 | User linked 
 | 
 You can submit l i n k s be tw ee n c on di t i ons a n d tr ea tm e nts   us ed to up da t e t he c on fide n ce 
 l e v e l . 
  C on fide n ce l e v e l   up da t es f or us e r l i n k s i n - t i m ef r a m e , b ut does   up da t e   f or t h os e out - o f -time frame. AI Reconciliation does not distinguish between links submitted by mistake or those submitted intentionally. Once linked, the algorithms consider that the treatment treats the condition. You can confirm the validity of the links submitted in the Knowledge Graph.
 | User feedback 
 | 
 You can provide feedback by clicking the thumbs up or thumbs down icon for the findings. AI Reconciliation uses this feedback for performance tracking. 
## Data Requirements
The algorithm requires the following data points for every treatment record:
- T h e i nt e rpol a t ed (" st a n da r di z ed ") st a rt da t e 
- T he i nt e rpol a t ed (" st a n da r di z ed ") e n d da t e 
- T he v e r ba t i m o f t he t e rm 
- T he c o ded t e rm

- T he   i nt e rpol a t ed   (" st a n da r di z ed ")   st a rt   da t e 
- T he   i nt e rpol a t ed   (" st a n da r di z ed ")   e n d   da t e 
- T he   v e r ba t i m   o f   t he   t e rm 
- T he   c o ded   t e rm

 The algorithm requires the following data for every history record: 
- T he on g o i n g f l ag 
- T he v e r ba t i m o f t he t e rm
