===== PAGE: trends.html | Trends =====
## Trends
 Trend plots graphically show a single variable's data at each site side by side using a box-and-whisker plot or stacked bar chart. You can use trend plots to pinpoint sites with abnormal or incorrect data that may warrant investigation. 
## What Are Trends Plots?
 Trends plots graphically show side by side a single variable's data across all study sites .
 Trend analyses for numeric variables render as box-and-whisker plots .  Trend analyses for text variable render as stacked bar charts. 
## What Is the Purpose of Trends Plots?
 Trends plots allow you to clearly view and compare a variable's patient-reported data across sites to help you pinpoint sites with abnormal or incorrect data.
 Statistical Monitoring also computes a strength of association for each variable. To learn more, see  Strength of Association Description and Calculation Methodology . 
## Who Uses Trends Plots?
 Site monitors, data managers, central monitors, medical monitors, and more use trends plots.
## What Are the Benefits of Trends Plots?
 Trends plots greatly improve your ability to focus on and monitor variables that are important to your study. The ease with which you can visually compare data across sites helps you pinpoint sites with abnormal or incorrect data that may warrant investigation.
 By knowing a variable's strength of association, you gain clearer expectations for how each individual site should report patient data. For example, if at a particular site a variable with a high strength of association contains data points with a high degree of variance, you may want to investigate that site.
## How Do I Access and View Trends Plots?
 See  Access and View Trends Plots .
## How Do I Refresh Trends Plots to Output the Latest Study Data Analysis?
 See  Schedule or Trigger When Statistical Monitoring Refreshes and Outputs the Latest Study Data Analysis .
## How Do I Use and Interpret Trends Plots?
 See  Investigate Data Using Trends Plots .

===== PAGE: trigger_clean_patient_tracker_to_recalculate_outstanding_records_based_on_the_latest_study_data.html | Trigger Clean Patient Tracker to Recalculate Outstanding Records Based on the Latest Study Data =====
## Trigger Clean Patient Tracker to Recalculate Outstanding Records Based on the Latest Study Data
 Data Surveillance users with the proper permissions can m anually trigger Clean Patient Tracker to recount the number of outstanding patient data cleaning tasks that require vetting and review. The counts are based on the latest study data retrieved in Data Surveillance for: 
- Data listing records that require review. 
- AI Data Reconciliation report records that require review. 
- Open queries in your study that require response. 
- Pending or unaddressed vendor queries per patient. 
- Targeted Source Document Verification (TSDV) or Source Document Verification (SDV) counts from Medidata Rave. 
 The upper- right corner   of the Clean Patient Tracker page shows the timestamp of   the last time that Clean Patient Tracker counted the number of outstanding tasks. 
 Tip : For the most up-to-date counts, first refresh individual listings on the Listings page and refresh the AI Reconciliation reports , and then recalculate   in Clean Patient Tracker .
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Clean Patient Tracker in the left-hand menu.
The Clean Patient Tracker page shows. 
- Click Recalculate .
Clean Patient Tracker refreshes to recount and revisualize the outstanding patient data cleaning tasks that require vetting and review.

===== PAGE: under-over_reporting_events.html | Under-Over Reporting Events =====
## Under-Over Reporting Events
 The Under-Over Reporting Events Plot graphically shows event reporting patterns across adverse events (AE), concomitant medication (CM), and medical history (MH) at the site and country level. The Under-Over Reporting Events Plot helps you identify potentially noncompliant sites and countries whose event reporting patterns significantly differ from the study norm. 
## What Are the Under-Over Reporting Events Plots?
 The Under-Over Reporting Events Plot contains three separate funnel plots :
- Adverse Events (AE) – Graphs the reported rate of adverse events over time in months for each site and country in the study. 
- Concomitant Medication (CM) – Graphs the reported rate of concomitant medications compared to the combined number of reported adverse events and ongoing medical history events for each site and country in the study. 
- Medical History (MH) – Graphs the reported rate of medical history events compared to total number of enrolled patients at each site and country in the study. 
 Each site and country's reported data is represented as a blue data point on each graph. RBQM normalizes the study-wide reported event data and visually outputs funnel lines representing the data's:
- Upper 99th Percentile Threshold – An event rate that is at the 99% confidence interval above the study's average event rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported event data lies above the upper 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers, which may warrant prompt investigation. 
- Upper 95th Percentile Threshold – An event rate that is at the 95% confidence interval above the study's average event rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported event data lies above the upper 95% limit to be potential outliers, which may warrant investigation. 
- Mean – The average reported rate across all sites or countries in the study. 
- Lower 95th Percentile Threshold – An event rate that is at the 95% confidence interval below the study's average event rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported event data lies below the lower 95% limit to be potential outliers, which may warrant investigation. 
- Lower 99th Percentile Threshold – An event rate that is at the 99% confidence interval below the study's average event rate at a particular time in the study. RBQM considers sites or countries whose reported event data lies below the lower 99% limit to potentially be extreme outliers, which may warrant prompt investigation. 
## What Is the Purpose of the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot?
 You can use the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot to identify potentially noncompliant sites and countries whose AE, CM, and MH reporting patterns significantly differ from the study norm. Based on your findings, you can further investigate sites and countries that may be under or over reporting event data before generating an issue for an on-site or remote monitor. 
## Who Uses the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot?
 The following types of users, among many others, use the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot:
- Central Monitors 
- Data Managers 
- Medical Monitors 
## How Does RBQM Detect Sites and Countries That Under or Overreport Events?
 See  Sites That Under or Overreport Events Detection Methodology .
## Event Data Interrogation Criteria and Workflow Example
 As part of your under-over reporting event evaluation, you should consider the following data interrogation criteria:

## What Are the Benefits of Using the Under-Over Reporting Events Plot?
 The Under-Over Reporting Events capability's highly contextual vantage point allows earlier insight to signals of risk, and encourages better allocation of monitoring resources. By analyzing event reporting rates, you can i dentify whether sites and countries are under or over reporting adverse events, concomitant medications, and medical history. 
 Based on your findings, you can determine appropriate corresponding actions such as to:
- Investigate data further using the following Clinical Data Studio capabilities:
- Event Incidence – To understand potential types of missing events. 
- Patient Profiles – To understand the study population and impacted patients. 
- KRI Dashboard – To identify potential data entry delays and delays in event reporting. 
- Datasets – To review aggregated, underlying study data reported at a site or country of interest. 
- Create issues for statistically significant event reporting variation signals to flag monitors to investigate root cause. 
- Investigate sites to ensure they follow proper protocols and procedures. 
- Provide training or corrective actions to the site. 
- Ensure sites are equipped to collect accurate and timely safety information. 
## What Are the Benefits of Using Each Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Analysis Type?
 Traditional clinical trial monitoring processes do not provide visibility into reporting patterns, which require cross-site evaluation to identify potential risk signals like event over- or underreporting. Leveraging the RBQM Under-Over Reporting Event capability's advanced analytics, intuitive visualizations, and real-time data from all patient data sources ensures adequate data and risk surveillance, as well as comprehensive and timely safety reporting. 
 Furthermore, each Under-Over Reporting Events Plot Analysis type provides the following benefits:
- Adverse Events (AE)   – You can use the Under-Over Reporting Adverse Events plot to identify sites and countries that have significantly different patterns of adverse event (AE) reporting compared to the study norm. Identifying, monitoring, and appropriately addressing sites and countries that may be under or over reporting adverse event data ensure:
- Patient safety oversight. 
- Drug labels include appropriate safety information, including potential drug-to-drug interactions. 
- Concomitant Medication   (CM)   – You can use the Under-Over Reporting Concomitant Medication plot to identify sites and countries that have significantly different patterns of concomitant medication reporting compared to the study norm. Identifying, monitoring, and appropriately addressing sites and countries that may be under or over reporting concomitant medication data can help address:
- Unreported adverse events and medical history events. 
- Variability in over-the-counter medication reporting. 
- Medical History (MH)   – You can use the Under-Over Reporting Medical History plot to identify sites and countries that have significantly different patterns of medical history reporting compared to the study norm. Identifying, monitoring, and appropriately addressing sites and countries that may be under or over reporting medical history event data ensures:
- Patient eligibility is properly assessed. 
- There are no unreported exclusionary medical history conditions. 
- Adverse events are indeed newly emerged events as opposed to the potential worsening of previously unreported medical history events. 
- View Side by Side – You can simultaneously view and compare the Adverse Events, Concomitant Medication, and Medical History funnel plots. Adverse events, concomitant medication, and medical history funnel plots tend to correlate with each other. Viewing all three side by side helps you identify anomalous event data that may warrant investigation.

===== PAGE: unified_scheduler.html | Unified Scheduler =====
## Unified Scheduler
 In clinical studies, data managers require the latest study data to start data review and reconciliation. Unified Scheduler is a capability that  automates data refreshes across Data Surveillance modules . It complements existing on-demand manual refreshes by ensuring data is ready for governance checkpoints and review windows automatically .  
## What Is Unified Scheduler?
 The Unified Scheduler is a centralized solution that automates data refreshes across Data Surveillance capabilities like Listings, AI Reconciliation, Patient Profiles, and Custom Graphs . Unified Scheduler complements existing on-demand refresh capabilities by supporting scheduled refreshes . 
## What Is the Purpose of Unified Scheduler?  
 Unified Scheduler provides a single location to manage scheduling and refresh activities for Data Surveillance capabilities . Rather than navigating to multiple modules, schedule and automate refreshes from one centralized hub . Scheduled refreshed data becomes available by 8:00 AM (EST) on the scheduled day . 
## On Demand Versus Scheduled Refreshes  
 Unified Scheduler does not replace on-demand refresh capabilities . You can start on-demand refreshes from within Listings , AI Reconciliation , Patient Profiles , and Custom Graphs to manually update data independently of predefined automated scheduled refreshes .  
 In Listings and Custom graphs, you can perform an on-demand or scheduled refresh for up to 15 selected items in a single request . Items already scheduled or queued for data refresh today disable automatically and are unavailable for selection . 
 Total daily refreshes combine both scheduled and on-demand refreshes : 
- Listings and Custom Graphs:   Allow up to four refreshes per day for a listing or custom graph. 
- Patient Profiles and AI Recon: Allow up to two refreshes per day per patient profile design or AI Reconciliation report . 
## Who Uses Unified Scheduler? 
 Data managers and study team members need specific permissions to schedule refreshes.

  For more information, see Data Surveillance Building Blocks and Permissions . 
## What Are the Benefits of Unified Scheduler? 
 Unified Scheduler enables you to: 
- Ensure data is refreshed and available when needed for governance and review activities . 
- Reduce manual effort and operational overhead . 
- Support predictable workflows for data managers . 
- Maintain a scalable and auditable framework for managing data refreshes . 
- Manage data flexibility through scheduled and on-demand refresh options . 
## How Does Unified Scheduler Work?
 Unified Scheduler allows you to create scheduled data refreshes for modules based on permissions. Scheduled refreshes follow logic and rules for each module.  For Listings , you can create multiple batches with a maximum of 15 listings per batch. Each listing belongs to only one schedule, and the total daily refreshes, combining scheduled and on-demand, is limited to 20 listings. For AI Reconciliation, a single global schedule updates all eight reports simultaneously in the study.  Patient Profiles allows for multiple schedule batches, but each individual batch contains only one published design. You can create multiple batches for Custom Graphs , but each custom graph belongs to a single schedule, and each schedule includes a maximum of 15 graphs per batch. 
## How Do I Access Unified Scheduler?
 Create, Edit, and Delete Data Refresh Schedules .

 You can use Data Surveillance's Vendor Configuration to:

 The Vendor Group list provides an easy-to-read view of all active and inactive vendor groups or vendor organizations in Data Surveillance. You can sort and filter the vendor group list to help find the vendors you want to view. 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Configuration > Vendors in the left-hand menu.
The Vendors page appears.
 Column Descriptions 
- Name – The unique label that identifies the vendor group. 
- Updated By – The name of the person who last updated the vendor group record. 
- Updated On – The date the vendor record group was last updated. 
- Activate – indicates that the vendor group is active. Active vendor groups get assigned vendor issue sets in Data Surveillance. Inactive vendor groups cannot get assigned vendor query sets.

 You must activate vendors groups so that you can add vendors, and assign vendor query sets.

- For Vendor users in a vendor group, follow the same process as step 2 to activate. 
 Note: A vendor group must have at least one active vendor.

 Using Vendor Query Sets, you can communicate queries and issues with vendor groups where action is required by the vendor and not a site. 
 Data Managers can assign vendor queries to vendors from an active vendor group. Vendors in a vendor group are users with limited or full access in  Cloud Administration .
 Note : You can only add vendor users already in a specific study to a vendor group. Vendor users need the Submit Vendor Feedback building block to respond to vendor queries. Contact study administrators to add vendors in Cloud Administration.

 You cannot edit or delete existing vendor groups or vendor users. However, you can deactivate vendor groups or vendors so that they are not available to assign vendor query sets in Data Surveillance.

===== PAGE: vendor_queries.html | Vendor Queries =====
## Vendor Queries
 Data with missing or incorrect information can undermine study integrity or even patient safety. Reconciliation between third-party vendors and data in Medidata Rave is common and necessary to ensure accurate data is being reported in both systems.  With the Vendor Queries, you can report external data issues and track communication with vendors. For example, you can create Vendor Queries for: 
- Data Managers to group issues by vendor during data reconciliation. 
- Programmers to enquire the completeness and accuracy of lab data imports. 
- Study team members to manage records with outstanding data issues. 
## What Is Vendor Queries?
 Vendor Queries is a Data Surveillance capability that enables you to manage external data queries and issues with vendors. 
## What Is the Purpose of Vendor Queries?
 While reconciling data, you may identify patient records with incorrect or missing vendor data. You can use Vendor Queries to group data listing records with external data issues into vendor query sets, track communication with vendors, and mark records as reviewed once the vendor responds.   
## Who Uses Vendor Queries?
 Study managers and data managers.
## What are the Benefits of Using Vendor Queries?
 Vendor Queries:
- Allows users to easily track all Vendor Queries in a central location.  
- Provides easy management of discrepancies and inconsistencies with vendors. 
- Facilitates faster reconciliation of Rave and external vendor data. 
 You can also build easily downloadable and shareable vendor query sets for vendor consumption and action. Vendor Queries s aves time and effort by integrating tracking of Vendor Queries into your data review process and ensures study data integrity. 
## How Does Vendor Queries Work?
 When reviewing an approved listing's results, you can report issues on external data by creating Vendor Queries. When creating Vendor Queries, you can group multiple patient records into a single vendor query set. You can then  submit the vendor query sets you raised for patient records to approved vendors. Once the vendor responds to the queries, you can mark the patient records as reviewed.  
 You can also: 
- View Query sets . 
- Download query sets. 
- Submit Vendor Query sets . 
- Delete query sets . 
- View and export Vendor Audit Reports . 
## How Do I Create Vendor Queries?
 See Create Vendor Queries .
## How Do I Access Vendor Queries?
 See Access and View Vendor Queries .

===== PAGE: view__add__and_manage_listing__custom_kri__and_qtl_template_groups.html | View, Add, and Manage Listing, Custom KRI, and QTL Template Groups =====
## View, Add, and Manage Listing, Custom KRI, and QTL Template Groups
 In Templates, you can save listing, custom graph, QTL, or custom KRI configurations, respectively, as templates. When you save templates, you export and store the templates in a template group. Template groups generally comprise a collection of templates that you might logically bundle together and use when building studies. For example, you could have a template group that consists of one or more listings, or a combination of listings, QTLs, and KRIs. Templates in the template group may pertain to studies based on therapeutic area, phase, or therapy. Template groups live at the client division (CD)  level . You can access and reuse templates for any study across multiple client divisions.  Your organization has its own client division-level global template library in Data Surveillance. You can create template groups in the Data Surveillance Library. The template library also stores and lists the collection of your organization's templates groups and associated templates.
 In Templates, you can access your organization's template groups to import and reuse listing, custom graph, QTL, and KRI templates when creating listing, custom graph, QTL, or KRI configurations across studies.
## View the Template Groups and Individual Templates in Your Organization's Template Global Library
 You can view the list and details of the templates groups and their associated templates contained within your organization's template library.
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM . 
- Click the  Platform Library tab. 
- Click Template Groups   in the left-hand menu.
The page containing your organization's global template library appears. 
- If necessary, to view the templates stored in a template group, click the template group name in the  Name column. 
- In the template group page, click the  Listings tab, Custom Graphs  tab, KRIs tab, or QTL tab to view the list of templates for listings templates, custom graphs, custom KRI or QTLs, respectively.
 Tips
- Click any column header to sort the list by column in alphanumeric order. An up or down arrow next to the column name shows the column that the list is currently sorted by. 
- Click and horizontally drag the border of any column header to resize columns.

 You can edit template group names and descriptions. For example, you can fix a typo or misspelling in a name or description or make an update that more clearly identifies or describes the group.
- Access Data Surveillance or RBQM . 
- Click the  Platform Library tab. 
- Click Template Groups   in the left-hand menu.
The page containing your organization's global template library appears. 
- For the template group you want to manage, click edit icon in that row. 
- If necessary, edit the  Name . 
- If necessary, edit the Description .
 Tip : Avoid naming groups or wording descriptions in such a way that might unblind or compromise other studies or study users.
- Click Save .

===== PAGE: view__create__and_edit_draft_listings.html | View, Create, and Edit Draft Listings =====
## View, Create, and Edit Draft Listings
 At study startup, study teams perform a risk assessment and define the high-risk, critical, or complex study data to monitor for data quality and integrity. To aid in data monitoring, you can use Data Surveillance to create data listings , which identify and report patient data records that may indicate a study risk.   Listings are built using manually configured conditional expressions that parse your study data to capture patient records within a specified variable that match the expression's defined conditions . For example, you can configure an expression to capture patient data records for female patients below age 50 who have had a serious adverse event . The records captured by the listing are data points your study team would want to review and investigate. 
 By creating and using listings, you can: 
- Increase the amount of data you can review while saving time and effort. 
- Ensure protocol compliance, patient safety, data quality, and data integrity. 
- Direct more effective study-mitigating actions. 
 Note : You must have the Manage Data Reviewer building block to create or edit listings. All newly created listings initially save as draft listings. However, you can approve listings when ready. 
 You can also:
- View your study's current set of draft listings and associated high-level details. 
- Edit draft listing configurations. 
## Access and View Draft Listings
 You can view your study's current set of draft listings as well high-level details associated with each draft listing . 
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Listings in the left-hand menu.
The Listings page shows. 
- On the Listings page, click the Draft Listings tab.
The Draft Listings table shows the following:
 Column Descriptions 
- Name – The listing's object identifier (OID). 
- Expression – The listing's user-defined conditional expression, which Data Surveillance runs against your study data to capture the patient records within a specified variable that match the expression's defined specifications. In general, expressions are built to identify and report high-risk data points that your study team can review and investigate as necessary. 
- Rave Enabled – A check mark indicates that you can directly within Data Surveillance view and submit Rave queries on the patient records captured by the listing . 
- Created By – The user who created the listing. 
- Last Updated – The listing's creation date or when the last saved edit occurred. 
- Updated By – The user who most recently updated the listing. 
- If necessary, filter or sort the Draft Listings table. 
## Filter the Draft Listings Table
 To help find the draft listings you need, you can filter the Draft Listings table to show:
- Specific draft listings by name. 
- Only Medidata Rave-enabled draft listings or only listings that are not Rave enabled. 
- Only draft listings created by specific users. 
- Only draft listings that were last updated by specific users. 
- If necessary, access the Draft Listings table . 
- Click the Filter button, at the top-right corner of the Draft Listings table. 
- Click one or more of the following filters:
- Name – Filter to show specific draft listings. 
- Rave Enabled – Filter to show only Rave-enabled draft listings or only listings that are not Rave enabled. 
- Created By – Filter to show only draft listings created by specific users. 
- Updated By – Filter to show only draft listings that were last updated by specific users. 
- Select one or more filter items. 
- Click Apply . If filtering by Rave-enabled listings, click Yes or No . 
- If necessary, click Clear Filters to revert to the Draft Listing table's default view. 
## Sort the Draft Listings Table
 To help find the draft listings you need, you can sort the Draft Listing table's columns vertically in ascending or descending alphanumeric order. For example, you can sort to more quickly find a specific listing name. Or you can sort the Last Updated column to find the most recently updated or longest unupdated draft listings.  
- If necessary, access the Draft Listings table . 
- In the Draft Listings table, click any column header to sort the table by column in ascending alphanumeric order.
An up arrow, , appears next to the column name. 
- Click a column header twice to sort the table by column in descending alphanumeric order.
A down arrow, , appears next to the column name. 
## Create Draft Listings
 You can create data listings to identify and report patient data records that may indicate a study risk. Data listings are built using manually configured conditional expressions that run against your study data to capture the patient records within a specified variable that match the expression's defined conditions . For example, you can configure an expression to capture patient data records for female patients below age 50 who have had a serious adverse event . The data records captured by the data listing's expression, in general, are the high-risk data points that your study team would want to review and investigate. 
D ata sets and variables with critical data points to the study appear with a blue flag . 
 Data listings: 
- Increase the amount of data you can review while saving time and effort. 
- Ensure protocol compliance, subject safety, data quality, and data integrity. 
- Promote more effective study-mitigating actions. 
- Do not require technical expertise or specialized personnel to create and build. 
 Note : All new listings initially save as draft listings. However, you can approve listings when ready.
 Tip : Play the video below to learn how to create draft listings.
 &amp;amp;lt;p&amp;amp;gt;&amp;amp;lt;br/&amp;amp;gt;&amp;amp;lt;/p&amp;amp;gt;  
- Access Data Surveillance , and then click Listings in the left-hand menu.
The Data Listings page shows. 
- On the Data Listings page, do one of the following: 
- To create a listing from scratch, click New Listing . 
- To create a listing from an existing listing configuration template: click the Draft Listings tab > click Import Template > select the Template group > select the template from the Templates list > click Import . To learn more about templates, see Data Surveillance Template Library . 
- In Name , enter a unique name for the listing.
The name serves as the listing's Object identifier (OID). For example, "AESER+AESER_TXT". Names cannot include special characters.    
- In the Define Listing section, do the following: 
- Enter or select a data set. 
- Enter or select a variable.
 Note: The left-hand side Datasets pane does not show interpolated values such as _INT or _DTC, as these are presented as the EDC source variable. So   _INT variables you see in Data Connect, do not appear for selection in listing datasets as they are consumed implicitly within the date field. 
- Select a comparator, such as= or !=, and then select or enter a comparator value.
The list of selectable comparators differ whether you select a date, number, text, or time variable. The comparator value serves as the conditional threshold, which measures and flags whether specified conditions are met regarding the selected comparator.
 Comparators and Comparator Value Descriptions 
 Selected Variable Type 
 Comparator 
 Description 
 Comparator Value Entry 
 | Text, Numeric, Date, Time 
 | = 
 | Flags patients whose reported value within the selected variable is equal to the comparator value entry. 
 | 
 For text variables: enter a text value.
 For numeric variables: enter a number value or click and drop a variable from the list of data sets. 
 For date variables: select a date from the calendar picker or click and drop a variable from the list of data sets.
 For time variables: enter the time using the following 12- or 24-hour format: 
- 12-hour Format – HH:nn am/PM 
- 24-hour Format – HH:nn 
 Note : 
Cross dataset comparisons – When using a variable as the comparator value, the originally selected variable and the comparator can be from two different datasets, except for audit datasets. Cross dataset comparisons are not outer joins. The listing includes only records that exist on both sides of the comparison expression, returning patients and values that match. 
For example, on comparing an SRPP and MRPP record like DEM.Age and VS.BPS, the SRPP data repeats for each MRPP record. That is, for every BPS record, the patients' age is shown.

 | != 
 | Flags patients whose reported value within the selected variable is not equal to the comparator value entry.

- Optional : To add multiple conditions to the expression, click the Plus icon, , to the right of the data set, and then select And or OR to the left of the data set name. 
- AND  – Specifies that all individual conditions and conditions within a grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
- OR – Specifies that at least one individual condition or grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
- Repeat step 4 for each individual condition.
 Note : For complex expressions with OR and AND, you must use parentheses (()) to combine and separate the conditions. For example, the expression   AE.AEPT equals COUGH AND DEM.AGEIC greater_than 50 OR AE.AEPT contains RES  returns different results as compared to  ( AE.AEPT equals COUGH AND DEM.AGEIC greater_than 50 ) OR AE.AEPT contains RES . 
 Ensure forms or data sets you use to build a listing for all patients, hold true for the question you are asking. That is, you cannot build a listing to evaluate a data set that only a screen fail patient has, and/or a data set that only an enrolled patient has, because there is no instance where both these data sets exist for a single patient. Therefore, the combined listing configuration statement always results in zero patients.

 Note : You can only map visits to datasets that the Expression Builder uses.
The Protocol Integrity Report (PIR) tracks submitted records. Submitted records automatically receive the Reviewed status in Listings.

- To ensure the data listings do not capture an overly large number of records, we recommend when adding columns that you use:

- You can use published audit data sets in the expression builder, however you cannot data sets for cross data comparison. This means while building a data set in the expression builder in listings or KRIs, you cannot use an audit data set along with a Rave data set. You can use a single audit data set in the expression builder.
- Enter or select a variable.

 Note:

- The data set on the right side of the expression must be the target data set; typically external data from the lab. 
- The source data set and the target data set must be the same data type.

- AND  – Specifies that all individual conditions and conditions within a grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
- OR   – Specifies that at least one individual condition or grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
 Note: When building multiconditional missing records expressions, the list of target data sets that you can select only includes the data set currently used in the original missing records expression.

- OR – Specifies that at least one individual condition or grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true.

 Note: When comparing fields in a listing's expression, query submission is supported only for the variables on left-hand side (LHS) of the equation.   To ensure a variable appears in the   Field   dropdown , it   must   be positioned on the   LHS   of the comparison expression in the   Define Listing   section.   The right-hand side (RHS) of the expression is not restricted to Field selection, as you can enter free text, select values from a dropdown, or drag and drop fields for comparison.

 Table Column Descriptions 
- PatientID – The ID of the patient whose data matched the criteria specified in the listings conditional expression. 
- Site – The site that the patient belongs to. 
- Country – The country in which the site resides. 
- Variable – Each column header to the right of the Country column header represents a variable that the data listing's expression is configured to run against. The variable column header shows the human-readable variable name at the top and the variable Object identifier (OID) at the bottom. And then the column lists the variable's data point entries captured by the data listing's conditional expression. 
 Note : If you leave the expression incomplete or leave the Name field empty, the Preview Listing button remains disabled. If the listing shows more records than the preconfigured threshold, a warning appears. You must edit the listing so that search records are less than the preconfigured threshold.

If the listing shows more records than the preconfigured threshold, a warning appears. You must edit the listing so that search records are less than the preconfigured threshold.
- Click Save Draft .
 Note : The 
 Save Draft button remains disabled until you click
 Preview Listing .
 The listing saves with Draft status and appears in the Draft Listings tab.
## Add Columns to Listings Without Defining the Column in the Listing Expression
 When creating data listings, you configure conditional expressions to capture patient records within a specified variable or variable grouping that match a set of criteria. Listings then produce a list of patients that have data records that meet the criteria set in the listing's conditional expression. The list of patients contains a data column for each variable defined in the expression and the corresponding data recorded for each patient in that variable. 
 Sometimes you may want a data listing's results to include a data column showing patient records for simple variables such as age or demographics. Therefore, you can configure listings to add data columns directly to the listing results without having to build the columns in through the conditional expression. You can add multiple columns and delete columns as well. 
 Adding data columns directly into listings:
- Helps keep data listing conditional expressions simpler and cleaner. 
- Enables you to more easily add simple data columns—for example, age or demographics—to data listing results without building tedious arguments in the listing's conditional expression. 
- Do any of the following: 
- Create a draft listing 
- Edit a draft listing . 
- Edit an approved listing . 
- In the New Listing or Edit Listing window, c lick the Add Column button.
 indicates that the Add Column expression builder is in an active state. 
- In the Add Columns section, enter or select a data set.
 Notes
- To ensure the data listings do not capture an overly large number of records, we recommend when adding columns that you use:
- Data sets that are already defined in the core data listing expression. 
- Single record per patient data sets, such as demographics. 
- You can use a maximum of ten different data sets in the Add Column section. 
- Data Columns do not act as an outer join, and only patients that exist in both data sets appear. 
 Important : Do not give a derived variable the same name as an existing metadata column (for example, "region name"). If you configure a listing using a derived variable that shares a name with a metadata column, the column returns a null value in the listing results. 
- Enter or select a variable. 
- To add multiple columns to the listing, click the Plus icon, , to the right of the data set, and then select another dataset and variable. 
 Note : The data listing results show the added variable columns to the right of the variable columns included as part of data listing's conditional expression. 
## Build Listings to Report Missing Records
 You can build data listings to identify and report patient records that exist in Rave but are missing from external lab data. To do so, you must map a relationship between the source and target datasets so that the listing can recognize what you consider to be a record. The listing then returns items that are present in the source dataset but missing in the target. 
 Buliding listings to report missing records helps you quickly and easily reconcile Rave data and external lab data to accurately identify missing lab data. You can then create vendor issues directly from the data listing results to communicate data issues and queries with vendors. This helps ensure that you account for and acquire the lab data you need for your study. 
- Do any of the following: 
- Create a draft listing 
- Edit a draft listing . 
- Edit an approved listing . 
- In the New Listing or Edit Listing window, click the  Missing Records button.
 indicates that the Missing Records expression builder is in an active state.
- In the Missing Records section, enter or select a data set.
 Notes
- The data set on the left side of the conditional expression must be the source data set; typically the data from Rave. 
- The list of available source datasets that you can select only include data sets currently used in the core data listing expression. 
- Enter or select a variable. 
- Select a comparator, such as= or !=, and then select or enter a comparator value.
 Notes
- You can only select "=" as the comparator. 
- The data set on the right side of the expression must be the target data set; typically external data from the lab. 
- The source data set and the target data set must be the same data type. 
- To add multiple missing records conditions to the expression, click the Plus icon, , to the right of the data set, and then select And   to the left of the data set name. 
- AND  – Specifies that all individual conditions and conditions within a grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true.
 Notes
- You can only select AND when building multiconditional missing records expressions. 
- When building multiconditional missing records expressions, the list of target data sets that you can select only includes the data set currently used in the original missing records expression. 
- Repeat steps 3-6 for each individual missing records condition. 
## Exclude Patient Subsets from Listings
 You can configure listings to exclude certain patient subsets. 
- Do any of the following: 
- Create a draft listing 
- Edit a draft listing . 
- Edit an approved listing . 
- In the New Listing or Edit Listing window, click the Exclude Patients with.... button.
 indicates that the Exclude Patients with ... expression builder is in an active state.
- Enter or select a data set. 
- Enter or select a variable. 
- Select a comparator, such as= or !=, and then select or enter a comparator value.
- To add multiple conditions to the expression, click the Plus icon, , to the right of the data set, and then select And or OR to the left of the data set name. 
- AND  – Specifies that all individual conditions and conditions within a grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
- OR – Specifies that at least one individual condition or grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
- Repeat steps 3-6 for each individual condition. 
## Enable Viewing and Submitting Rave Queries on Listing Records
 You can configure data listings to allow you to view and submit standardized, predefined Rave queries o n records captured in the listing's results. 
 Note : To enable Rave Queries on data listing records, you require the following permissions:
- Submit Queries via Data Surveillance 
- Manage Data Reviewer or View Data Reviewer 
- Do any of the following: 
- Create a draft listing 
- Edit a draft listing . 
- Edit an approved listing . 
- In the New Listing or Edit Listing window, c lick Enabled Rave Query .
 indicates that the Rave Query Details builder is in an active state. 
- In the Rave Query Details section: 
- Select a data set and variable combination.
The Form and Field fields populate by default based on the variable you select. For example, if you select Ethnicity from the Demographics data set, the Form reads: Demographics (DEM) and Field reads: Ethnicity (ETHNIC).
- Select a marking group from the Folder menu. 
- Enter the Rave query text into Default Query Text . 
 Note: When comparing fields in a listing's expression, query submission is supported only for the variables on left-hand side (LHS) of the expression. To ensure a variable appears in the Field dropdown, it must be positioned on the LHS of the comparison expression in the Define Listing section.  The right-hand side (RHS) of the expression is not restricted to Field selection, as you can enter free text, select values from a dropdown, or drag and drop fields for comparison. 
## Build Listings That Compare Dates
 You can create listings that compare two dates. For example, you can create a listing that  shows the dates of all vital signs assessments done before the informed consent date to help identify protocol deviations. 
- Do any of the following: 
- Create a draft listing . 
- Edit a draft listing . 
- Edit an approved listing . 
- In the New Listing or Edit Listing window > Define Listing section, do the following: 
- Enter or select the first date (OID) data set and variable. For example AE.AESTDAT.
- Select a comparator, such as= or !=, and then select or enter a comparator value.
The list of selectable comparators differ whether you select a date, number, text, or time variable. The comparator value serves as the conditional threshold, which measures and flags whether specified conditions are met regarding the selected comparator.

## View, Filter, and Sort the KRI Configurations List
 The KRI Configurations list provides an easy-to-read, comprehensive view of all system KRIs  and custom KRIs available in your current  study environment . You can sort and filter the KRI Configurations list to help find the KRIs you want to view or act on. 
## View the KRI Configurations List
 You can use the KRI Configurations list to view details about specific KRIs or find KRIs you want to act on. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > KRIs in the left-hand menu.
The Key Risk Indicators page appears.
 Field Descriptions 
- Name  – The unique label that identifies the KRI. 
- Risk Category – A broad, categorized area of risk within which individual key risk indicators are identified, tracked, and mitigated.  Risk categories and data sets have a parent-child relationship. 
- Type  – Indicates whether the KRI is a System KRI or Custom KRI. 
- Status  – Indicates whether the KRI is active or inactive. Active KRIs get their data filtered, calculated, and rendered in the KRI Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory. Inactive KRIs do not get calculated or appear in the KRI Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory. System KRIs are active by default. 
- Activate  –  indicates that the KRI is active. Active KRIs get their data filtered, calculated, and rendered in the KRI Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory. indicates that the KRI is inactive. Inactive KRIs do not get calculated or appear in the KRI Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory.
 Note : System KRIs are active by default.
- Items  – The number of KRIs listed in the KRI Configurations list based on the filtered view. 
## Filter the KRI Configurations List 
 To help find the KRIs you need, you can filter the KRI Configurations list to show:
- All KRIs in your study environment , 
- Only platform -wide system KRIs, 
- Only the user-defined custom numeric KRIs in your study environment, or 
- Only the user-defined custom percentage KRIs in your study environment, or 
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > KRIs in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Key Risk Indicators page > KRI Configurations tab, click Filter KRIs . 
- Select one or more of the following:
- System – Shows only system KRIs, which are standard assessments performed by Medidata that stand out as widely applicable to all studies. System KRIs are always in active state. You cannot inactivate system KRIs. To learn more about the available system KRIs and how they are calculated, see KRI Descriptions and Calculation Methodologies . 
- Numeric – Shows only custom numeric KRIs, which are user-created metrics designed to target and support a specific endpoint or area of interest for risk analysis. 
- Percentage – Shows only custom percentage KRIs, which are user-created metrics designed to target and support a specific endpoint or area of interest for risk analysis. 
## Sort the KRI Configurations List 
 To help find the KRIs you need, you can sort the KRI Configurations list by KRI name, Risk Category, Type, or Status in ascending or descending alphanumeric order. The default is ascending order.
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > KRIs in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Key Risk Indicators page > KRI Configurations tab, click a column header to sort the column in alphanumeric order. Click again to reverse the order. 
## View High-level Calculation Details About a Specific KRI
 On the Key Risk Indicators page > KRI Configurations tab, you can quickly view: 
- A brief, detailed description about any KRI. 
- For percentage KRIs: the number of patients that meet a percentage KRI criteria over the number the patients the KRI calculates against. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Configuration > KRIs in the left-hand menu. 
- On the Key Risk Indicators page > KRI Configurations tab, hover your cursor on any KRI name in the Name column.

## View And Access Signals
## Access and View Signals
 You can view your study's current set of signals as well high-level details associated with each signal. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Signals in the left-hand menu.
The Signals table shows the following:
 Column Descriptions 
- Signal ID   – Signal number associated with the auto-generated or user defined signal. 
- Site – The site associated with the signal.
For QTLs, the site reads as "All Sites". 
- Country  – The country where the site is situated. For QTLs, the field reads as "All Study Countries".
- Patient  – One or many patients who meet the signal threshold at the site. The field shows up to 10 patients, with the remaining concatenated with a "+" icon. 
- Analysis – One module from Patient Profiles, KRIs, QTLs, Under and over Reporting, Rounding, Propagation, or Potential Duplicate Patients. 
- Name – The variable for the module on which the signal is generated. Some example are  KRI Name, AE Entry Delay, Missing Visit Percentage, Manual Query Rate,Non-System Query Delay, Percent Out of Window Visit, Number of SAEs per Patient-Month, Number of AEs per Patient-Month etc. 
- Observation – An automated observation based on the text used in signal threshold. Updated observation values appear in the signal report only if the value is at or above the set threshold. Sample description text for a KRI AE Entry Delay of 17 days when you set a threshold as "high" - The AE Entry Delay of 973 exceeds the threshold of 17 .
 Note : If the observation value falls below the module's configured threshold, it does not get updated when you refresh Signals data. The last value at which the threshold was met shows as the observation.
- Description – A description based on a combination of the observation and a system defined or custom description you entered while configuring the signal for a module. Sample Description text - The site is an outlier considering the time it takes to report AEs (considering AE Visit Date and First Entry Date). Please follow up with the site to ensure adequate processes and resources are in place. 
- Due Date – The due date for the signal. 
- Status – A signal has the following statuses: 
- Open – A signal assigned to an assignee. 
- New  – A newly created signal not yet assigned to an assignee. 
- Resolved – A signal marked as resolved. 
- Watched – A signal that may require intervention or action, but currently is being watched. No action is made upon a watched signal, it is not assigned to an assignee. 
- Dismissed – A signal that is dismissed. For example, if the observation may not be a potential issue for the time period in review. 
- Closed – A signal closed as no longer of interest. 
- Reopened – A signal reopened after it was closed. 
- Assignee – The name of the person assigned to the signal for further action. If no assignee exists, click the  Add assignee option to assign the signal to an assignee. 
- Category – Select from a list of existing categories or create a new category. 
- Opened By – The person who opened the signal. 
- Opened Date – The date the signal was opened. 
- Closed By – The person who marked the signal as closed. 
- Closed Date – Date the signal was closed. 
- Issues – A yes or no value that indicates if a signal is an issue. 
- Issue Type – A signal can have a protocol deviation or a non-protocol deviation issue type  
- Issue Target – An issue associated with a signal can be external or internal. 
- If necessary,  filter or sort the Signals table. 
## Filter the Signals table
- If necessary, access the Signals table . 
- Click the Filter button, at the top-right corner of the Signals table. 
- Click one or more of the following filters:
- Signal ID  – Filter to show specific signals. 
- Site – Filter to show signals based on sites.  
- Country – Filter to show signals in the country where the site is situated. 
- Patient – Filter to show one or many patients who meet the signal threshold at the site. 
- Analyses – Filter to show signals based on the modules configured for signal generation. 
- Name – Filter to show signals based on the module's variable on which the signal was generated. 
- Status – Filter to show signals by specific status. 
- Optional . Select one or more filter items. 
- Click Apply .  
- If necessary, click Clear Filters to revert to the Signal table's default view.

- Select a comparison operator. 
- Enter or select a comparator value.
 The comparator value serves as the conditional threshold, which measures and flags whether specified conditions are met regarding the selected comparator. 
- To add multiple conditions to the expression, click the Plus icon, , to the right of the data set, and then select And or OR to the left of the data set name. 
- AND  – Specifies that all individual conditions and conditions within a grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
- OR – Specifies that at least one individual condition or grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
- Repeat step 4 for each individual, added condition.
 Notes
- Listing expressions can use a maximum of six data sets and 10 different variables in the expression for listings. 
- For complex expressions with OR and AND, you must use parenthesis (()) to combine and separate the conditions. For example, the expression   AE.AEPT equals COUGH AND DEM.AGEIC greater_than 50 OR AE.AEPT contains RES  returns different results as compared to  ( AE.AEPT equals COUGH AND DEM.AGEIC greater_than 50 ) OR AE.AEPT contains RES . 
- Optional. T o add data columns directly to the data listing results without having to build the columns in through the conditional expression, do the following: 
- Click the Add Column button.
 indicates that the Add Column expression builder is in an active state. 
- In the Add Columns section, enter or select a data set. 
- Enter or select a variable. 
- To add multiple columns to the listing, click the Plus icon, , to the right of the data set, and then select another dataset and variable. 
- Optional. To configure the expression to  identify and report patient records that exist in Rave but are missing from external lab data, do the following: 
- Click the Missing Records button.
 indicates that the Missing Records expression builder is in an active state.
- In the Missing Records section, enter or select a data set. 
- Enter or select a variable. 
- Select a comparator, such as= or !=, and then select or enter a comparator value.
- To add multiple missing records conditions to the expression, click the Plus icon, , to the right of the data set, and then select And or OR to the left of the data set name. 
- AND  – Specifies that all individual conditions and conditions within a grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
- OR – Specifies that at least one individual condition or grouped conditional set must be met for the expression to be considered true. 
- 
 Notes: 
- When building multiconditional missing records expressions, the list of target data sets that you can select only includes the data set currently used in the original missing records expression. 
- Repeat steps b-f for each individual missing records condition. 
- To configure the expression to exclude certain patient subsets, do the following: 
- Click the  Exclude Patients with.... button. 
- indicates that the Exclude Patients with ... expression builder is in an active state.

===== PAGE: view_and_monitor_the_risk_inventory.html | View and Monitor the Risk Inventory =====
## View and Monitor the Risk Inventory
 You can use the Risk Inventory to view all:
- Risks documented as part of your study's risk assessment, as well as associated risk and risk review details. 
- QTLs associated with a risk in your study, as well as how well the QTLs are performing. 
- KRIs associated with a risk in your study, as well as the KRIs' current KRI values. 
 You can also use the Risk Inventory to monitor and track the risk score of each study risk. Doing so enables your team to:  
- Better understand which risks pose the biggest threat to the study outcome. 
- Prioritize the risks in which you develop risk mitigation strategies for. 
- Track risks to monitor whether the risk level is increasing or decreasing. 
- Determine the effectiveness of risk mitigation strategies and whether or not additional or adjusted mitigations are needed. 
 To learn more, see Risk Scores .
## View and Monitor Study Risks, Risk Details, and Risk Reviews
 You can use the Risk Inventory to view the list of all risks documented as part of your study's risk assessment, as well as associated risk and risk review details. For example, you can: 
- View a risk's status; for example, whether the risk is open or closed. 
- View risks whose risk reviews are overdue or due soon. 
- Sort the Risk Inventory based on risk score to help prioritize the risks that your team monitors and addresses. 
 Data for the highest study environment level appears by default. 
- Access RBQM , and then click Risks   in the left-hand menu.

 | Review Frequency 
 | 
 The frequency of the risk review.
 For new risks:
- 
- Weekly – The Target Review Date is 7 days after the risk is entered. For example, if the risk is entered on February 1, then the Target Review Date is February 8. 
- Every Other Week – The Target Review Date is 14 days after the risk is entered. 
- Monthly – The Target Review Date is 30 days after the risk is entered. 
 Note : 30 days are added to the Entered date. For example, an Entered date of February 1 (nonleap year) shows a Target Review Date of March 2, that is, 30 days after the Entered date.
- Quarterly – The Target Review Date is 90 days after the risk is entered.  
 For existing risks, the Review Frequency is calculated as Weekly, Every Other Week, Monthly, or Quarterly based on the Last Risk Review Date instead of the Entered date.
 | Risk Status
 | 
 Status of the risk:
- Open – The risk is currently included as part of your study's ongoing risk assessment. The risk shows in the Risk Inventory and gets tallied in the study's total risk score. 
- Watch – The risk is open, but considered a lower priority in your risk assessment and likely requiring a lower review frequency. The risk shows in the Risk Inventory and gets tallied in the study's total risk score. 
- Transfer – The risk has been transferred to another party or organization to manage and is no longer a part of your risk assessment. The risk shows in the Risk Inventory, but does not get tallied toward the study's total risk score. 
- Closed – The risk is no longer tracked as part of your study's ongoing risk assessment. For example, the risk is irrelevant to the study to due to protocol changes or the risk is deemed acceptable to your study. Risks marked as closed do not appear in the Risk Inventory and do not get tallied in the study's total risk score.

The risk score is calculated by multiplying each risk factor's score together (Probability x Impact x Detectability). The maximum risk score is 27. 
- A risk score of 1-3 appears with a green color-coded block and indicates a minimal risk. 
- A risk score of 4-9 appears with a yellow color-coded block and indicates a moderate risk. 
- A risk score of 10-27 appears with a red color-coded black and indicates a high risk.

 | Risk Response
 | The appropriate course of action to manage the risk:

- Eliminate  – The risk no longer requires including in the study's risk assessment. You can close or delete the risk for your study. 
- Mitigate  – The risk requires mitigating actions to lower the risk's severity. 
- Monitor  – The risk requires monitoring and review but no mitigating actions. 
- Transfer  – The risk should be transferred to another party or organization to manage and no longer be a part of your risk assessment.

## View QTLs Associated with Risks and Evaluate QTL Performance
 QTLs are study-level metrics that indicate if a study parameter's reported data has breached a preidentified data quality threshold or upper limit . QTLs monitor the emergence of systematic errors on critical variables and data that may be prone to subjective bias, ultimately impacting: 
- Patient safety 
- Study conduct and performance 
- Compliance 
- Data quality 
- Study reliability 
 You can view the list of all QTLs associated with a risk in your study as well as each  QTL's details: 
- For oversight to ensure the study team is following the risk plan 
- As a reference for another study's risk assessment.

The Risk Inventory page shows.

 Tips
- Use the Search field to filter the QTLs table to show specific QTLs. 
- Use the table's horizontal scrollbar to view all columns. 
The QTLs table shows the following QTL information:
 Column Descriptions 
 Column 
 Description 
 | Observed Value 
 | 
 The current observed percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's criteria as of the most recent data analysis. 
 A green value indicates that the percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's specified criteria is considered within a healthy range of the expectation . Generally, in range QTLs require no action. 
 A yellow value indicates that the percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's specified criteria have exceeded the tolerance threshold . RBQM considers parameters whose QTL values exceed the threshold as at risk. This indicates potential underlying systemic issues, which can compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine the root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues. 
 A red value indicates that the percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's specified criteria has exceeded the tolerance upper limit . RBQM considers parameters whose QTL values exceed the upper limit as high risk. This indicates potential underlying systemic issues, which can compromise study safety and integrity. You should investigate such parameters to determine the root cause and to prevent or mitigate study issues. 
 A red value and a fully red bar indicate a QTL excursion. RBQM  flags and identifies QTL excursions when : 
- The percentage of patients that do not meet the study parameter's specified criteria has exceeded the tolerance upper limit, and 
- It is impossible to move the QTL value back within a healthy range of the QTL's expected value no matter the actions taken by the project team. 
 QTL excursions indicate that the study quality is compromised to the point that the study may need to be shut down or restarted. 
 | Parameter/QTL Name 
 | The QTL name of the parameter.  A parameter is a study variable that is assessed at the study level.  When used in the context of a QTL, parameters are measures that detect potential issues that can  be mitigated. 
 | Expectation 
 | The expected percentage of the patient population that will not meet the study parameter's criteria. QTL percentages that RBQM assesses as in range of the expectation are considered healthy and do not require any action. 
 | Tolerance Limit 
 | 
 The QTL's tolerance limit, which includes the:
- Threshold 
- Upper Limit 
 | Attached to Risk ID 
 | The ID of the risk associated with this QTL. Click the link to open the risk details page where you can edit risk details, QTLs, KRIs, or Risk Mitigations.
 | Risk Name 
 | The name of the risk associated with this QTL. 
 | Risk Origin 
 | The name of the critical data, critical process, or risk category that the risk is associated with.  
 | Risk Score 
 | A   calculated number (score) that reflects the risk's severity. When adding a risk or updating a risk's review details, you can score each of the following risk factors, Probability, Impact, and Detectability, on a scale of 1 to 3. The risk score is calculated by multiplying each risk factor's score together (Probability x Impact x Detectability). The maximum risk score is 27. 
- A risk score of 1-3 appears with a green color-coded block and indicates a minimal risk. 
- A risk score of 4-9 appears with a yellow color-coded block and indicates a moderate risk. 
- A risk score of 10-27 appears with a red color-coded black and indicates a high risk. 
 | No. of Risk Mitigations 
 | The number of risk mitigations associated with the risk. 
## View KRIs Associated with Risks and Evaluate KRI Performance
 Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) are predefined study metrics that enable you for the duration of the study to systematically:  
- Identify and track known or anticipated risks to data quality. 
- Evaluate country and site performance in a study. 
- Ensure study conduct operates as planned. 
 Examples of KRIs include patient accrual rates and data query rates.
 You can track KRI performance using KRI values . KRI value calculations reflect as a percentage, count, mean, rate, or standard deviation. 
 You can view all key risk indicators (KRIs) associated with a risk in your study as well as each KRI's details: 
- For oversight to ensure the study team is following the risk plan. 
- As a reference for another study's risk assessment. 
- To view the KRIs' latest recorded KRI values. 
- To view the current risk score of the risk that each KRI is associated with. 
 Tip: You can also edit a KRI's detail. For example, you can: 
- Update the KRI name or description in care of entry error, typo, or for additional clarity. 
- Update the KRI's value. 
 To learn more, see  View and Edit the Details of KRIs Associated with Risks . 
 To learn more about KRIs, see About Key Risk Indicators .

 The Quality Tolerance Limits page, which contains the Quality Tolerance Limits list, appears.
 Field Descriptions 
- Parameter  – A study variable that is assessed at the study level. 
- Status  – Indicates whether the QTL is currently active or inactive. Active QTLs are set so that their data gets filtered, calculated, and shown in the QTL Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory. Inactive QTLs do not get calculated or appear in the QTL Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory. 
- Date Added – The QTL's original creation date. 
- Date Updated – The most recent date in which the QTL update occurred. Date Updated is blank for unmodified QTL configurations. 
- Updated By – The user who most recently updated the QTL. Updated By is blank for unmodified QTL configurations. 
- Activate  –  indicates that the QTL is active. Active QTLs are set so that their data gets filtered, calculated, and shown in the QTL Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory. indicates that the QTL is inactive. Inactive QTLs do not get calculated or appear in the QTL Dashboard, Risk Assessment, and Risk Inventory.
 Tip : In the Parameter column, if you hover your cursor on a QTL name, a popup shows t he number of patients that reached or exceeded the QTL threshold out of the total number of patients that the QTL has calculated against. For example, 265 out of 2899 patients.

===== PAGE: view_historical_data_snapshots.html | View Historical Data Snapshots =====
## View Historical Data Snapshots
 Statistical Monitoring provides a list of historical data snapshots . You can select a data snapshot to enter History View mode to see how the data looked throughout Statistical Monitoring when the snapshot occurred. By viewing historical data snapshots, you can efficiently audit studies and reconcile the data and actions made between snapshots.
- Access RBQM , and then click Statistical Monitoring > History in the left-hand menu.
 The History page lists all prior data snapshots from most recent at the top to oldest at the bottom. 
- Click the row of the snapshot you want to view.
Statistical Monitoring automatically navigates you to the Overview page in History View. While in History View, a blue banner appears at the top of all Statistical Monitoring pages. The banner indicates the date when the historical snapshot's data refresh occurred. For example:
 In addition, the upper- right corner of all Statistical Monitoring pages shows the time stamp of when the historical snapshot in view occurred.  For example:  
- Click Exit History View in the blue banner to revert to the latest data snapshot. 
 Notes About History View
- History View mode shows the actions that occurred in the immediate data snapshot following the snapshot date you selected to view. For example, say you selected to view a data snapshot with a date of 17 Oct 2020 and the following data snapshot took place on 22 Oct 2020. In such case, History View mode shows the data in Statistical Monitoring as of 17 Oct 2020, but shows the actions made in Statistical Monitoring up until 22 Oct 2020. 
- While in History View mode:
- Data is read-only. 
- The Data Anomaly Detection page > Summary section > Actions column does not appear. 
- The Event Incidence page > Summary section > Actions column does not appear. 
- You cannot deep link into Issue Management. 
- You cannot update track review data. 
- Track reviews and issues created are those that occurred against the selected historical snapshot or previous snapshots. That is, the created dates may be after the snapshot date, but before the following snapshot. 
- On the Issues slide-out panel, the Assignee column and Status column do not appear. 
- On the Issues slide-out panel, the Is Closed column appears.
 Note : If the issue was resolved after the date of the snapshot in view, then Is Closed has a value of No . If the resolved date occurred before the date of the snapshot in view, then Is Closed has a value of Yes .

===== PAGE: view_module_data_snapshot_status.html | View Module Data Snapshot Status =====
## View Module Data Snapshot Status
 The signals you see on the Signals page are automated indications of potential issues in the modules you configure in Signal Configuration . The Signals page also includes user-generated signals.
 While configuring signals for individual modules, you can set up thresholds based on which automated signals get created. You must choose the modules you want the signals to report on. For example, if you do not enable KRIs in Signals Configuration, and add custom configurations, no signals get created for any KRI in your study when signals data refreshes.  
 Once you configure a signal, observations appear as signals based on custom configurations and the latest data snapshot for individual modules when you refresh Signals data.  This means you can determine the exact version of the signals data in each module based on its snapshot date. Custom configuration changes made after 6:00 AM EST do not show in the automated signals report until the next day.

The Signals page appears. 
- From the top right corner above the Signals table, click .

- Name – Name of the modules configured for automated signal generation in Signal Configuration .
 Note : For Patient Profiles, the name indicates the profile design for which a flag is set as the threshold for signal generation.
- Snapshot Date –The last snapshot date and time from data refreshed in the source module.
 Note : For Patient Profiles, the snapshot date indicates the date when the profile design was refreshed.
